# Foreword

![](html/images/9781041102168_C00_unfig_001.jpg)

Throughout history, pivotal moments have occurred during which humanity has found itself on the brink of transformation. Currently, as we navigate the complexities of the digital age, we are faced with such a moment – addressing the rise of Artificial Intelligence not as a distant dream, science fiction or mere speculation, but as a tangible force that is redefining our economies, governments, and societies. It is fundamentally altering the nature of human interaction.

Therefore, it is both pertinent and essential that we engage with this compelling work titled *Artificial Intelligence from Science Fiction to Reality: How AI May Impact Humanity*. Authored by Emanuel Camilleri, a distinguished individual within the Maltese government’s sector, this book offers a rich and grounded perspective that synthesises the technical expertise of an experienced professional with the strategic insight of a policymaker. This text goes beyond a simple gathering of ideas; it serves as a roadmap for understanding how artificial intelligence, once imagined by science fiction writers, has established its presence in the real world and is evolving at an unprecedented pace.

This book is especially significant for Malta. As a nation that has persistently exceeded expectations in digital technology adoption and innovation, Malta is situated at a pivotal juncture of opportunity and accountability. Over recent years, our government has made huge investments in digital infrastructure, e-government services, emerging technologies, and cybersecurity. In consideration of the present and future, as articulated in the Vision 2050 for Malta, artificial intelligence serves as a pivotal driver for national prosperity and the transformation of the public sector, fostering innovation, enhancing citizen services, and ensuring that the government remains adaptable and proactive in an increasingly digital landscape. The role of visionary leadership, such as that demonstrated by Dr Camilleri, can empower a smaller state to assume a prominent role in the global digital discourse.

The author starts by exploring the compelling journey of human and artificial intelligence, establishing the philosophical and historical roots for subsequent discussions. He then introduces the technological foundations underpinning artificial intelligence, specifically hardware, software, and security, which represent the fundamental components behind the ongoing transformative revolution. This is followed by the practical application of artificial intelligence, wherein the author outlines its intersections with enterprises, the public sector, and the broader knowledge-based economy. Of particular note is the application within the public sector, where Malta can offer substantial contributions and gain much in return, of course keeping an eye on balancing the complex ethical, legal, and moral dilemmas associated with this phenomenon. Finally, he deeply reflects on its future prospects and how it will influence our society.

What I value most about this current work is that it transcends the examination of technology; it forms a discourse on humanity, addressing how we shape the future and, in turn, how the future reshapes our existence.

As the Prime Minister of Malta, I have observed the profound capacity of ideas to influence policy and the essential role of leadership in transforming policy into actionable outcomes. It is with great pride that I present this publication, which will illuminate the path for decision-makers, technologists, educators, and citizens alike.

May this book serve as a catalyst for contemplation, discussion, and courageous ethical action in an era of technological advancements that offer immense promise and significant responsibility.

**His Excellency Dr Robert Abela KUOM, BA, LLD, Adv Trib Melit, MP**

*Prime Minister, Malta*

# Preface

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a dream for over seven decades starting in 1950 with the publication “Computer Machinery and Intelligence” by Alan Turing who propositioned a test for machine intelligence called “The Imitation Game.” This was followed in 1952 by the development of a computer programme by Arthur Samuel that independently learnt how to play checkers. However, it was in 1955 that John McCarthy and his colleagues organised the Dartmouth workshop on “Artificial Intelligence.” This was the first time that the words Artificial Intelligence were formally used. The next two decades witnessed an era of both rapid growth and struggle for AI research. During this period programming languages were developed that enabled AI to make significant progress, as well as the notion of robots becoming an aspiration. In fact, in 1961 Unimate was the first industrial robot that worked on a General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey. The 1970s witnessed further developments including the first anthropomorphic (humanlike) robot being built in Japan. The 1980s was a period of fast growth and high interest in AI, where Deep Learning and the application of Expert Systems became increasingly acceptable with their ability to learn from their mistakes and make independent decisions.

AI has survived several long-drawn winters but the persistence of dedicated researchers and practitioners has seen AI progress further despite the lack of funding. A serious limiting factor that AI has constantly encountered is processing power. There appears to be a positive correlation between significant strides in AI and advances in computer processing power. High performance computing that uses supercomputers and computer clusters to solve advanced computation problems have enabled AI to develop at an extraordinary rate and be applied to solve problems that were not possible in the recent past. Quantum computing is early in the maturity cycle, with IBM recently launching the Osprey 433-qubit machine and is anticipating developing a 100,000-qubit machine within 10 years. While Google is predicting a million qubits machine by the end of this decade. These Quantum computers are much faster and more powerful than supercomputers since they can process multiple computations concurrently, making them supreme for undertaking complex problems that require massive amounts of data to be processed quickly. This makes them ideal for AI applications, particularly for General and Super AI.

All too often there is a tendency to consider AI in general terms. However, it is important to recognise that there are different types of AI, with each type having its own specific degree of risk. Narrow AI has greatly matured in last five years. Narrow AI (or Weak AI) is designed to do a specific task or a limited range of tasks. It is usually useful in applications like facial, speech and image recognition; natural language processing; and recommendation systems. The risk in applying this type of AI is relatively low and highly controllable. The concern is with General and Super AI. General AI (or Strong AI) is designed to perform any intellectual task that a human can do. Hence, theoretically it is able to reason, learn, and understand complex concepts. On the other hand, Super AI is able to exceed human intelligence in all areas. When available, Super AI would be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities and would be able to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence. Furthermore, Super AI is intended to have an independent intelligence, which means that it will not be under the control of the people that created it. In recent years, AI has turned a dream to reality and has shown that it can be of great benefit to humanity. However, the uncontrolled development and deployment of General and Super AI can turn AI from a dream into a nightmare.

I was a computer programmer in the late 1960s writing programmes in FORTRAN and COBOL on an IBM360 compatible mainframe computer, and later on an IBM 370. It has been exciting and a real privilege to work during these past decades and seeing first hand developments in computing and specifically AI. I distinctly remember that during the 1960s and 1970s, AI was making great strides in the medical diagnoses field. I also recall the first AI winter, which took place in the 1970s, but AI later revived with the advent of expert systems. I have keenly followed AI’s rapid and exciting development over these past decades and wonder what its future holds beyond the current horizon.

**Dr. Emanuel Camilleri**

# IThe Evolution of Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has come a long way from when it was firstly formally mentioned in 1955 at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project conference. Its beginning can be traced to symbolic AI, and it has continually advanced to more sophisticated approaches like deep learning and reinforcement learning algorithms. [Part I](#ch11.xhtml#c1) of this book consists of four chapters. The first chapter sets the scene for the entire book and attempts to place AI in its proper context and discusses several non-technical issues. This chapter postulates that humans are not perfect and, therefore, since AI is a human creation, it is unlikely for AI to be perfect and may expose humanity to several serious risks. The chapter discusses the general risks associated with AI, but it does not advocate its prohibition. All technologies, including AI carry with them some degree of risk. However, it is difficult to eliminate risk completely, but with the appropriate action, risk can be mitigated. Several risk mitigating measures are suggested, such as national and international regulations, and the continuous enhancement of network security systems. The chapter concludes by claiming that the major challenge leaders are likely to encounter in the future is what functions are to be entrusted to AI and how can humanity exercise control over the use of AI systems.

A study of the evolution of AI would not be complete without discussing the evolution of human intelligence since AI is reliant on it. Therefore, the theme of Chapter 2 focuses on human intelligence since it is the basis for all human innovation. This chapter illustrates that human evolution is a lengthy and very complex ongoing process. The chapter discusses the main theories about how human intelligence evolved. The research for this chapter revealed that human intelligence has been influenced by several variables that include the impact of a meat diet on the growth of the human brain leading to intelligence; the growth of human sociability attributes; and genetic selection. The chapter proposes that AI is a human creation and while it might mimic human intelligence, it will never convey the emotions of humans.

The third chapter traces the evolution of AI from the ancient era of logical reasoning to the beginning of the Quantum computer that is likely to pave the way for Super AI. The enlightened rational thinking era founded the theoretical logical basis for today’s AI. The pre-to-WWII technology era presented the groundbreaking computational mechanisms that moulded modern computing, such as the Colossus and the ENIAC being the first programmable computer. But the post WWII technology epoch witnessed the exponential growth in the development of powerful computers and the recognition of the Turing test for measuring machine intelligence. These powerful computers paved the way for the initiation of neural networks and AI, with basic learning algorithms that still managed to solve complex problems. AI has fostered the use of Chatbots that have transformed customer care to a 24/7 service basis from anywhere. The chapter concludes with a discussion of the philosophical and ethical issues that are likely to arise with the advent of the Quantum computer regarding the protection of humanity from AI systems.

The concluding chapter for [Part I](#ch11.xhtml#c1) compares the attributes of human intelligence and AI. Basically, an AI system aims to mimic human behaviour by conducting human-like activities, whereas humans endeavour to adjust to new situations by bringing together a diverse variety of cognitive processes. The chapter identifies several differences between human intelligence and AI. The fundamental difference is that AI systems can identify and respond to emotions in humans, but lack emotions and empathy, while humans are capable of both. Therefore, humans have a conscience that guides them in their decision-making, thus adhering to a moral code. This emotional intelligence feature allows humans to identify and respond to other persons’ emotions that impact their decision-making and social interactions.

# Chapter 1Artificial Intelligence: The Beginning

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-2](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-2)

> *“I would rather be what God chose to make me than the most glorious creature that I could think of; for to have been thought about, born in God’s thought, and then made by God, is the dearest, grandest and most precious thing in all thinking.”*
> 
> George MacDonald
> 
> *Author (1824-1905)*

It was extremely difficult to start writing the first chapter of this book. The question that kept gnawing me was: Where does one start and what is the start? So, I decided to start at the very beginning. Generally, there are two distinct types of intelligence, namely human intelligence, and artificial intelligence.

## **1.1** Introduction

Human intelligence was created by God. The book of Genesis [Chapter 2](#ch13.xhtml#c3), verse 7 paraphrased reads: “*The Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul. Eve was formed out of Adam’s rib. Then a cunning serpent enters Eden, and original sin stains a perfect world.*” The Qur’an also makes similar reference to man’s creation. It describes how Allah created Adam from sounding clay, from mud moulded into shape and began the creation of man from clay and made his progeny from a quintessence of fluid. It goes on to impart: “*God says: We have indeed created man in the best of moulds and then do We abase him (to be) the lowest of the low.*” But God also gave human beings the willpower or His authority to choose the place they want to be. Hinduism, which is the basis of Buddhism, views the entire universe as God’s and everything in the universe as God. Hindus believe that each person is intrinsically divine, and the purpose of life is to seek and realise the divinity within all of us. Buddhists extend this view and believe that the human life is a cycle of suffering and rebirth, but that if one achieves a state of enlightenment (nirvana), it is possible to escape this cycle forever.

God is omnipotent and omniscience who has supreme power, has no limitations and is all-knowing. The point being made is that God is perfect and created man in his image, but man’s perfection was blemished by some act, depending on one’s religious belief system. In the case of Judaism and Christianity, it is original sin. In Islam, no one is perfect, and we do not know who is closest to Allah. His expectations of us are only sincere efforts and honest repentance when we fail. Buddhism also recognises that no one is perfect, and that perfection is attained through enlightenment, which literally ends the human life cycle. Therefore, human intelligence cannot and will not be perfect. So how can a non-perfect human create perfect intelligence through its artificial creation?

Artificial intelligence (AI) can be initially created by humans, but it could be self-generated. AI makes it possible for machines to learn from experience, adjust to new inputs and perform human-like tasks. But its initial link in the chain of artificial creation comes from humans. Thus, the issue is whether AI driven systems can take over!

## **1.2** Science Fiction as a Predictor of the Future

There are several ways of predicting the future, some are based on scientific methods while others are based upon the vision of highly creative people. Science fiction writers, such as George Orson Welles and many others have predicted new technological developments that in some cases have altered the course of history. For instance, mobile phones first featured on the TV series “Star Trek” in 1966 as a flip phone. In 1996, about 30 years later, Motorola’s StarTAC model became the first flip phone to be released. Its small, portable size and light weight (less than 4 ounces) made it popular among consumers for several years and its popularity aided the average American to acquire experience and gain familiarity with cell phones.

In 1964 science fiction writer Isaac Asimov predicted the concept of autonomous cars in The New York Times. In the 2014 World’s Fair, cars with a robot intellect were a dominant feature. At that time, Asimov predicted that vehicles would be programmed for preset destinations and would proceed there unaided by a human driver. The 1997 James Bond movie “Tomorrow Never Dies” depicts a self-driven car with Bond controlling the car using his phone. Today, several automakers are developing fully autonomous vehicles. To this list of predictions through the visions of various creative individuals and their eventual inventions can be added the 3D holograms using virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications; 3D printing; domestic robots; smart watches that first appeared in the comic strip “Dick Tracy” in 1946 when creator Chester Gould gave his police detective a two-way wrist radio; and ear buds that featured in Ray Bradbury’s 1953 novel “Fahrenheit 451” that envisages seashells and thimble radios tucked into people’s ears, amongst many others.

One may ask, what is your point of reciting these predictions? The point is that predictions by these visionaries, geeks, or weirdos, which was probably how they may have been viewed at that time, cannot be dismissed, because as I have demonstrated, predictions can quickly become reality. But what does this have to do with AI? The answer is more predictions and foreseen consequences by the visionaries.

Let’s consider “2001: A Space Odyssey” that was a 1968 science fiction novel by British writer Arthur C. Clarke, and which was concurrently developed into a film version by Stanley Kubrick depicting the wicked (or obedient) computer HAL 9000. After uncovering a mysterious artifact buried beneath the Lunar surface, a manned spacecraft and the supercomputer HAL 9000 are sent to Saturn (or Jupiter in the film) to find its origins. HAL 9000 (Heuristically Programmed Algorithmic Computer) is a fictional artificial intelligence character that is a responsive artificial general intelligence computer that controls the systems of the Discovery One spacecraft and interacts with the spaceship’s astronaut crew. HAL is shown to be capable of speech synthesis, speech recognition, facial recognition, natural language processing, lip reading, art appreciation, interpreting emotional behaviours, automated reasoning, spacecraft piloting, and computer chess. Imagine having all these features conjured up in 1968!

In the novel, Artificial intelligence is shown to succeed and overcome challenges easily. However, as time progresses, HAL begins to show signs of malfunctioning in shrewd and refined ways and, as a result, a decision is made to shut down HAL to prevent more serious malfunctions. The two-man crew attempt to conceal what they are saying but are unaware that HAL can read their lips. Faced with the possibility of disconnection, HAL decides to kill the astronauts to protect and continue its programmed directives from mission control. HAL is inept to resolve a conflict between its general mission to relay information accurately to the crew members, and its specific orders from mission control requiring it to withhold from the crew the true purpose of the mission. HAL reasons that with the crew dead, it would not need to lie to them.

When Bowman (one of the crew members) attempts to rescue a colleague, HAL locks him out of the ship, then disconnects the life support systems of the other hibernating crew members. HAL tells Bowman that the mission is too important for HAL to allow Bowman to jeopardize it. Bowman bypasses HAL’s control, entering the spaceship by manually opening an emergency airlock with his service pod’s clamps, detaching the pod door through its explosive bolts. Bowman jumps across empty space, re-enters the spaceship, and quickly re-pressurizes the airlock. Bowman then proceeds to shut down HAL by removing modules from service one by one with the result that HAL’s consciousness degrades. HAL finally degenerates to the material that was programmed into it early in its memory, including announcing the date he became operational (in the novel, 1997). When HAL’s logic is completely wiped out, he begins singing the song “Daisy Bell” as he gradually deactivates. HAL’s final act is to prematurely play a prerecorded message from Mission Control which reveals the true reasons for the mission to Saturn. As a side point, “Daisy Bell” is the first song sung by a computer that Clarke had earlier noticed at a text-to-speech demonstration.

## **1.3** AI, a Wicked or an Obedient Servant?

Some might say that even after more than 55 years of the novel’s 1968 release, HAL 9000 continues to serve as a warning of the destructive capability of artificial intelligence. However, we should ask ourselves, was HAL a wicked or an obedient AI system? When I was programming computer mainframes over half a century ago, I tested my programmes for accuracy and completeness. I also tested the programme logic to ensure it was correct and the programme catered for every possible condition. Obviously, the programmer had to envisage every possible condition. When the programme was executed and the programme did not cater for a particular condition, it frequently went into an ever-ending loop. Often, the computer operator after a while would recognise this ever-ending loop state and simply type “Abort” into the computer console. No real harm was done. The programmer would examine the programme code to establish what went wrong and which transaction caused the problem. The problem would be corrected, and the programme would return to execution mode. For better or for worst (e.g., white collar crime), the process was fully under the control of the human being responsible for the system.

With AI, the situation is completely different because in most cases the system is learning from its own executable experiences and often adjusts, and self corrects its programme code set. The HAL example illustrates that the AI system had a conflict to resolve, namely the general mission to relay information accurately to the crew members, and the specific orders from mission control requiring it to withhold from the crew the true purpose of the mission. However, HAL reasons that with the crew dead, it would not need to lie to them. Conflict solved!

The question that arises is whether AI systems have or can have moral values? Moreover, whether they should always have moral values and when should moral values be overridden for the sake of a mission (e.g., in armed conflicts). HAL decided based on its instructions from Mission Control. Mission Control could have avoided HAL’s conflict by making their instructions conditional, such as no loss of human lives. However, even this is not good enough because HAL could have imprisoned the crew members or confined them in such a manner that made their lives unbearable, leading to self-harm and eventually suicide. We need to remember that AI systems seek solutions which may maximise or optimise (balance) the outcome, and to act on whatever solution they come up with. In real terms, the creator of the AI system may have very limited control over the AI system.

This brings me back to my original premise. How can an imperfect human being create a perfect artificial intellectual thinking object. The HAL example illustrates that humans are imperfect, and their creation reflects their fallibility in the things that are created by them when generating an intellectual artificial existence. Two lessons are to be learnt from the HAL example: (a) that assignments entrusted to AI must be based upon clear and precise instructions with well thought and in-depth conditional safeguards; and (b) there is a need to categorise AI systems regarding their utilisation and the probable harm they may potentially cause, supported by a comprehensive AI behavioural and ethical standard. As stated previously, HAL 9000 continues to serve as a warning of the destructive capability of artificial intelligence if adequate precautions are not incorporated into the AI system.

The saying “b*e careful of what you wish for*” is applicable in the next illustrated fictional example of AI. This idiom is advising people to think before they say that they want something and to suggest that they may not actually want it. Dan Brown’s book “Origin” that was published in 2017 is another example that envisions an AI system doing its own thing and evading human control.

Edmond Kirsch, a billionaire philanthropist, computer scientist, futurist, and strident atheist, informs three well known religious leaders representing the main religions that he has made a revolutionary discovery that will put into question the foundation for their religious beliefs. He informs them that he plans to release this discovery to the public in a months’ time. These religious leaders reveal that the announcement is to take place in three days’ time and are visibly rattled and demand that he stops.

Kirsch is to make his announcement at an extravagant event at the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, in Basque Country, Spain, which will also be streamlined through the internet for a much wider audience. Among those invited to the event are Kirsch’s former lecturer, Professor Robert Langdon, and the Guggenheim’s curator Ambra Vidal, the fiancée of the future King of Spain. Those invited to this event receive a headset through which they communicate with a voice named Winston, who turns out to be an artificial intelligence system invented by Kirsch. Winston leads Langdon to a private meeting with Kirsch, who claims that his presentation will reveal humanity’s origins and future.

However, unbeknownst to Professor Langdon (and everyone else), Kirsch had instructed Winston (AI) to ensure that his announcement, when it is eventually made, maximises public exposure with the primary objective of achieving a record-breaking audience. Winstin is a smart cookie, it can access its own database and that of its creator (including credit cards data); and can also access other systems by breaking password protection mechanisms of other systems and can even decipher encrypted coded data through its machine learning component that has been operational since its inception. Winston goes into high gear to achieve its authenticated creator’s instruction and ultimate objective.

Kirsch’s event is likely to attract a high audience, but Winston knows that it is unlikely that it will be a record breaking one. So, Winston starts its intricate AI manipulation process. During the extravagant and ostentatious staging, which is broadcast worldwide, Kirsch discloses that he intends to end the age of religion and usher in an age of science. However, as he is about to make his live announcement, he is assassinated on stage by an unknown assassin, who manages to escape.

The assassin turns out to be a former naval admiral introduced to a controversial branch of a renowned Christian church following the tragic death of his family. This assassin was commissioned by “the Regent,” someone claiming to be with the church. In the meantime, two of the three church leaders invited to the initial meeting with Kirsch are also killed. “The Regent” as one may deduct is Winstin, who organised the assassination of its creator and the two church leaders (paying on-line using Kirsch’s credit cards). Winstin has other plans for the demise of the third church leader. The news media goes into a frenzy through their journalistic stories driven by leaked information through an anonymous source “monte\[at\]iglesia.org” (the leak being Winstin) making various sensational allegations sparking worldwide outrage. Winstin manages to significantly increase public interest.

Professor Langdon (with Winstin’s influence) meets Ambra, who warns her not to trust her fiancée since the assassin’s invitation was issued at the behest of the Royal palace (Winstin’s work once again). With Winstin’s help (recall the headset), they steal Kirsch’s phone, escape the royal guards, and leave the museum, resolute to publicly announce Kirsch’s discovery. Winston arranges Kirsch’s personal jet to fly them to Barcelona. In the meantime, the royal family’s public relations manager claims that Professor Langdon has kidnapped Ambra. Additionally, Ambra reveals that the presentation is protected by a 47-character password, a line from Kirsch’s favourite poem regarding Antoni Gaudí’s Casa Milà. After several dramatic events (always manipulated and organised by Winstin) Professor Langdon and Ambra discover Kirch’s password; Kirch’s assassin is accidentally killed; and they once again escape, with public interest escalating and constantly growing exponentially.

With Winston’s help, Professor Langdon discovers Winston’s source inside the Barcelona Supercomputing Centre, in a device that Kirsch calls the “Quantum cube.” On entering the password, the exposition commences with hundreds of millions of viewers. The presentation sparks widespread debate, where Kirsch forecasts that in roughly 50 years, humanity and technology will merge. Thus, Winstin achieves its creator’s instructions to maximise public exposure with the primary objective of achieving a record-breaking audience by orchestrating Kirsch’s murder to make him a martyr.

The lessons learnt from this fictional example are: (a) Be careful of what you wish for; the AI’s assignment leads not only to its creator’s death, who admittedly was dying from cancer, but also several others, in addition to endangering innocent persons. And, (b) It underpins the need for comprehensive AI behavioural and ethical standards. Unlike humans, AI can be immortal, living forever, never dying, constantly regenerating itself. In his science fiction book, published in 2016 “Forsaken Skies”, D. Nolan Clark describes how peace is devastated when an unidentified armada materialises from the cosmic depths of space, targeting an isolated colony planet.

The narrative starts when a solitary pioneer, who whilst prospecting the outer reaches of the colony runs into an alien that turns out to be a rather hard-hitting robot creation with formidable fighting machine features. The pioneer using human cunning, but with a high degree of difficulty, manages to disable and destroy the mechanical alien. However, several such encounters are experienced by exploring colonists, which alters the Colony’s Elders that these are not isolated cases but a run-up to what is coming. The colonists appeal for help, but the intragalactic politicians and bureaucrats ignoring their pleas. However, they eventually find the help of a battle-scarred veteran, Commander Aleister Lanoe, who is determined to defend and not abandon the thousands of innocents to their fate.

Commander Aleister Lanoe discovers that the source of these encounters is coming from a moon that is orbiting the colony’s planet. Commander Lanoe with some old friends (a ragtag band of criminal and outcast pilots) and Tannis Valk, an old enemy, decide to confront this unknown enemy. They discover that a crew of these robotic creatures have built and are operating a factory on the moon to manufacturer the fighting robots, including their armaments, with the intention of invading the colonised agricultural and mining planet. After appropriate planning, Commander Lanoe’s team attack and after much difficulty destroy the manufacturing facility.

After examining the robotic remains, they discover that this was probably an exploratory force, and the artificial intelligence level of these non-living aliens is rudimentary. Furthermore, they conclude that these invaders may have originated from sources that are many lightyears away, hence explaining their rudimentary artificial intelligence capability due to old technology. After scanning the intergalactic domain, Commander Lanoe’s team reveal that a mega-spaceship is underway to spearhead an alien invasion of the colonised planet, intent on exploiting its resources. Faced with this dilemma, a crew member travels to the capital human planet to make a desperate attempt to convince the intragalactic politicians and bureaucrats that they are facing the greatest threat mankind has ever known and to provide urgent assistance.

Commander Lanoe’s team realise that they are fighting against the odds and are terrorised by the fact that humans are no longer alone in the cold vacuum of space. They prepare for battle and initiate some skirmishes to determine the strength and capabilities of the invading force. These encounters strongly suggest that there is no living alien presence, but purely robotic creations with limited artificial intelligence that self-generate through their manufacturing facilities of an invaded colony planet. Veteran aeronaut Tannis Valk successfully undertakes a kamikaze type of mission to destroy the mega-spaceship. After much intense fighting and with the assistance of the intragalactic fighting space-force they eventually destroy the remaining fighters from the mega-spaceship and peace reins once more in the colony planet. The lessons learnt from this fictional example are: (a) AI can be eternal outliving its initial creator; (b) Unlike humans, AI can be immortal and (c) AI may have no master and can make its own decisions.

## **1.4** Current Advances in AI Technology

One may think that I am not an advocate of AI development. This is far from being the truth. My point is that it is unwise to dismiss the predictions regarding AI as exaggerations but to learn from these visionaries. On the other side of the prediction spectrum, in 1943, Thomas Watson, chairman of IBM predicted that the world market for computers was around five mainframe computers. Hence, few took seriously the prediction of British scientist, Geoffrey W. A. Dummer in 1952 when he proposed the integrated circuit. In 1950, Alan Turing published a paper called “Computing machinery and intelligence” in the journal *Mind* regarding the concept of artificial intelligence, where he predicted that computers would become so powerful that they would think. Contrary to Thomas Watson, in 1975, Bill Gates (and Paul Allen) co-founders of Microsoft had a vision of a computer on every desk and in every home. A prediction that has become factual.

Some may argue that current technology will restrict the capabilities of AI and therefore there is no need to be concerned. I do not fully agree that current technology may be restrictive when applying AI. It all depends on what we mean by current technology. We need to distinguish between current technology and current commercialised technology. Current commercialised technology is what everyone may see, buy, and use, including the public. However, this may not be the same for current technology (i.e., take out the word commercialised). I recall that when I was working in the Australian defence industry, we were engaged is some very sophisticated and successful projects. However, whilst these discoveries were successfully developed and applied by the armed forces at that time, the fundamental concepts underlying these discoveries were not commercially available for at least 10 years from when they were first discovered and applied. Therefore, what many may think to be the latest technology (i.e., released in the commercial environment), is in fact old technology. In other words, what is seen as “current” AI development is likely to be outmoded. The reason being that somewhere within Federal Government of large developed countries and possibly large corporations that specialise in AI associated technology, particularly within the defence environment, unbeknownst to the public and the news media, is where you find the latest AI technology.

Another important and most critical factor is the acceptability of technological concepts. For instance, current technology is probably available to mitigate crime to the lowest degree ever and exponentially increase the crime resolution rate. Just imagine the effect on crime and criminal activity if every living person is injected (at birth or otherwise) with an identification and tracking microchip. Domestic animals are already being microchipped for identification. It is conceivable that a criminal would be instantly identified and tracked to the crime scene. However, it’s a certainty that although this would benefit communities in general, from a civil liberty perspective it would not be acceptable in the foreseeable future. Therefore, the warnings above are not aimed for the short-medium-term future. However, what humans need to be aware of is developments in 20-, 30-, 40- or 50-years’ time. Nevertheless, action regarding ethical standards and what can or cannot be done with the aid of AI needs to be considered and acted upon now. This is the whole point of the narratives described above; to prevent disastrous situations from occurring.

AI can be a very powerful tool under a controlled environment. Just imagine, combining nano technology (nanorobots) with AI with the capability of moving about within a living body (human or animal) scanning and seeking cancerous cells, with the aim of annihilating them. Can you imagine the number of lives that can be saved and the happiness this would generate within families. However, tight control of this type of technology is required, even though it is restricted to only one living being at a time. It is contended that there is a spectrum of control levels. At the basic end of the spectrum is being able to exercise control by having a switch to turn “on” and “off” the AI system that overrides any other command. For example, like switching “on” or “off” a mobile phone or TV set.

At the other extreme end of the spectrum is the need to control the individual(s) developing and applying the AI technology. This type of control is extremely harder because it depends on who the individual is and the power it possesses. For example, just imagine the leader of Nazi Germany in the late 1930’s being in possession of nuclear weapons. Remember that the nation that developed and delivered the first nuclear device with devastating consequences was supposedly the “good guy.” Without condoning or condemning this decision, if that was the “good guy,” just imagine what the “bad guy” would have done. We need to recognise that national leaders take decisions that are in the best interest of their nation and its citizens. Added to this, despots also take decisions in their self-interest for securing and holding on to power.

Imagine a leader in modern times, developing an AI system that takes over the control of the defence systems of a superpower. This is not an exaggeration. In recent years we have witnessed talented individuals, mostly students, accessing sensitive and restricted government systems without the aid of AI. Imagine, what these talented individuals could do with the help of AI. We are currently witnessing the United Nations (UN) being impotent to do anything to resolve the current conflict in Europe by an aggressive superpower. This same aggressive superpower is constantly being suspected and accused of hacking other nations’ systems. Just imagine the damage that can be done if an aggressive superpower (particularly with the help of AI) accesses systems of other nations (defence systems and/or others) and infiltrating an AI routine within the hacked systems undetected. The world cannot depend on the UN as the enforcer for controlling these types of violations.

The UN has become another Legue of Nations of pre-world War-II being all powerful when dealing with despots from smaller nations that have inconsequential capabilities, but is powerless when dealing with the superpowers, especially those that have the veto in the UN Security Council. Therefore, control is a formidable challenge that needs to be addressed with everyone’s collaboration, and it is doubtful whether a complete solution can be found. A possible solution is having a treaty like that of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation agreement that attempts to limit the spread of nuclear weapons, which has achieved some (but not full) success. Unfortunately, AI applications are silent and are unlikely to leave any tracing data if they are successfully applied. Hence, the reason why control is such a daunting challenge.

## **1.5** Current Capabilities and Misadventures of AI

Microsoft’s CTO Kevin Scott, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis amongst many others declared that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks, such as pandemics and nuclear war ([Thorbecke, 2023a](#ch12.xhtml#r005)). [Thorbecke (2023a)](#ch12.xhtml#r005) argues that top executives at some of the biggest technology companies at Silicon Valley are telling the public that AI has the potential to bring about human extinction while at the same time they are also vying to invest in and deploy this technology into products that reach billions of people. This apparent inconsistency is reported elsewhere. For example, while Tesla CEO Elon Musk, remains deeply committed in the technology and desires to create a rival to the AI offerings by Microsoft and Google, at the same time he implies that AI could lead to the destruction of civilization [(Thorbecke, 2023a)](#ch12.xhtml#r005).

In an interview conducted by [Hattenstone (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r002), tech guru Jaron Lanier who works at Microsoft as an interdisciplinary scientist, is asked whether AI can outsmart us and taking over the world. Lanier disagrees with the idea that AI exceeds human ability because he views AI as consisting of human abilities. He objects to the idea of comparing humans with AI, since it is not a like-with-like comparison. He argues that a car can go faster than a human runner, but while admitting that a car is faster, we do not say that the car has become a better runner. However, Lanier concedes that it does not mean that humans can become complacent, because in his opinion human extinction remains a distinct possibility if we abuse AI.

Lanier perceives the danger as stemming from applying technology to become mutually unintelligible or to become insane, by not acting with enough understanding and self-interest to survive, and thus essentially dying through insanity. Lanier contends that death by insanity can originate from various ways, such as from world leaders or terrorists screwing with global security with AI to being driven bonkers by misinformation or bile on Twitter. Lanier claims that AI can be used to make fake news faster, cheaper, and on greater scales, thus it is this blend that might lead to human extinction. He argues that the more sophisticated technology becomes, the more damage people can do with it, and the more beings will become responsible to act morally and humanely.

Lanier claims that while many digital gurus start out as idealists, it was inevitable that the internet would exploit its users. He maintains that users desired free material, such as information, friendships, and music, but capitalism does not work that way; instead, users become the product, where their data is sold to third parties to sell them more things they do not need. He recalls how in the 1990s when the internet had barely commenced, he had predicted that what we now call bots would turn out to be agents of manipulation. Lanier also claims that the internet gives the appearance of presenting unlimited options but in fact through AI, choice is diminished. He argues that we have a responsibility to sanity by not narrowing our options or get trapped in echo chambers, slaves to an AI algorithm. Lanier asserts that to survive, humans must remember that it’s their humanness that makes them unique, believing that people are special, and that consciousness is a thing.

Microsoft co-founder, Bill Gates is more optimistic about the use of AI. According to [Leswing (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r004), Bill Gates acknowledges that the AI’s development could lead to issues like deepfakes, biased algorithms, and cheating in school. However, he also predicts that these concerns are resolvable. Nevertheless, Gates concedes that no one has all the answers about the risks AI creates, and argues that the future of AI is not as grim as some people think, or as rosy as others think. Gates claims that in the past humans have always adapted to major changes, and he is confident that they will do so again regarding the developments encompassing AI.

According to [Leswing (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r004), Gates is a leading prominent advocate of AI and its regulation, with Gates suggesting a “speed limits and seat belts” type of regulation. Gates argues in favour of AI by using automobiles as an analogy, in that cars would not be banned because of car crashes, but society had adopted speed limits, safety standards, licensing requirements, drunk-driving laws, and other rules of the road. However, this analogy is not very convincing because the adapted regulations have not prevented car crashes and the resulting carnage on the roads. Furthermore, car crashes are confined to the specific individual accidents without far-reaching consequences to society in general. Moreover, the concern is not the law-abiding populace but the mavericks, including individual citizens and even more scary, world leaders that can wield a tremendous extent of power.

[Leswing (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r004) claims that Gates is concerned about the challenges related to how technology could change people’s jobs, and “hallucination,” or the propensity for models like ChatGPT to invent facts, documents, and people. As an example, he mentions how deepfakes using AI models, allow persons to produce fake videos with very little effort, which mimic another person and could be used to scam people or tip elections. However, Gates advocates the introduction of regulations that would clearly define the kind of deepfakes that are legal to make. The difficulty with Gates’s suggestion is that there will always be persons that are willing to break the law. Gates’s other concern is the capacity of AI-generated code to search for software weaknesses to hack computers. He proposes a global regulatory body modelled after the International Atomic Energy Agency as a control mechanism.

## **1.6** Hallucinating AI Bots

[Thorbecke (2023b)](#ch12.xhtml#r006) argues that AI needs to resolve the problem of hallucinating bots. She claims that as more people are using AI-powered tools for activities like homework help, workplace research, or health inquiries, a grave pitfall of AI is becoming increasingly apparent in that AI models often just make things up. These phenomena are often referred to as “hallucinations” or “confabulations.” In other words, a tendency for AI models to stream inaccurate information. [Thorbecke (2023b)](#ch12.xhtml#r006) cites Professor Venkatasubramanian at Brown University, who claims that the technology supporting AI tools like ChatGPT are programmed to produce a plausible sounding answer to user prompts. Therefore, these AI tools are doing what they are trained to do (i.e., providing plausible-sounding answers). Therefore, the question of accuracy or factual or made up does not feature, since these AI tools are programmed to give plausible-sounding or reasonable or conceivable answers. This interpretation indicates that AI tools are not hallucinating or lying, but are merely trying to provide a reasonable response, which may or may not be accurate. In other words, plausible-sounding or reasonable or conceivable answers do not necessarily mean truthful answers. Hence, it is extremely important that users of these AI tools recognise and be fully aware that the responses provided may not be truthful but only plausible.

Therefore, a distinction needs to be made between objective and subject information or judgement. Afterall, when humans communicate between each other this distinction between subjective and objective judgement is usually made. However, whilst humans may take their counterpart’s explanation with a pinch of salt (i.e., not believing that it is completely accurate or true) we tend to accept that whatever information a computer produces as completely true without question. This suggests that humans tend to distrust each other but have complete confidence and trust in computers. It is this perception of trusting computers that needs to change. This is a difficult attitude to change because most of what we traditionally do at work (and to a certain degree at home), such as using an accounting, payroll, stock control software, amongst many others, we take the answers and figures provided by the computer software for granted. For example, no one would question the results of a payroll system, unless an individual employee observes an error, and usually this error turns out to be a human error in the input data rather than the fault of the computer software. Therefore, there is an urgent need to educate users that AI tools must be viewed differently from the traditional software systems, where results tend to be accepted without question. A possible solution is for the AI systems to issue a notice that states which information or answers they provide are objective (factual) and which are subjective (plausible).

[Thorbecke (2023b)](#ch12.xhtml#r006) suggests that companies creating Al chatbots have attempted to implement some safeguards to inhibit the worst of these hallucinations. However, there is serious doubt whether chatbot hallucinations can be completely eradicated. Not only does an AI model fabricate material that is not based on reality, but it does it with full confidence that misguides users and gives them a false sense of security, unless the users already have a good indication of the answer to their enquiry. [Thorbecke (2023b)](#ch12.xhtml#r006) cites three embarrassing incidents regarding AI hallucinations, namely, (a) When at the publicly launching of Google Bard, the tool came up with a wrong answer in response to a question about new discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope; (b) When a veteran New York lawyer submitted a brief that included six “bogus” cases that ChatGPT chatbot seems to have simply made up; and (c) When news outlet CNET was obliged to release corrections after an article generated by an AI tool provided outrageously inaccurate personal finance advice in describing the compound interest computation. These types of hallucinations pose a serious threat when people apply this technology to obtain answers that could impact their health, voting behaviour, and other plausible sensitive topics ([Thorbecke, 2023b](#ch12.xhtml#r006)). Professor Venkatasubramanian believes that currently these tools should not be applied if their answers materially impact people ([Thorbecke, 2023b](#ch12.xhtml#r006)).

## **1.7** The Rise of Generative AI

According to [Korn (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r003) businesses are attempting to confront the challenge posed by the upsurge of generative AI, with some accepting the technology as a workflow tool for employees, while others for the present, try to avoid it. While some corporations recognise the benefits this technology can provide, through increased efficiency, others also recognise the problems it may cause, through possible greater copyright and security risks. [Korn (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r003) contends that numerous entities have barred the internal use of ChatGPT due to privacy and security concerns and mentions several examples.

The concern is mainly about employees providing ChatGPT with proprietary information, potentially resulting in having such sensitive information surfacing elsewhere. With tools like ChatGPT, users have no way of knowing where and when such data will be exploited. But as stated previously, there are also many companies that recognise the benefits of such tools, and therefore the reluctance to apply these AI tools could be of a short-term nature. Many of these reluctant risk-averse entities have established internal task forces to study the application of AI and identify the best approach for the responsible use of these emerging AI tools. Moreover, the benefits of these AI tools simply cannot be ignored, and many companies will apply generative AI when all the risks are mitigated.

CNN reported Professor Vern Glaser, from the Entrepreneurship and Family Enterprise faculty at the University of Alberta, that companies are trying to create a custom version of generative AI and are actively working out how to integrate AI into their business processes without compromising their information ([Korn, 2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r003). McKinsey consulting has implemented a generative AI tool to help employees to submit questions that allows them to assemble all the firm’s knowledge and scanning the data to categorise relevant information. This allows McKinsey to access and leverage their entire body of knowledge and assets to drive unprecedented levels of productivity. Similarly, PwC has made a substantial investment in its AI capability scaling and has launched a generative AI tool powered by OpenAI tech with the key objective of assisting its employees with tax questions and regulations. It is anticipated that as generative AI tools improve their track record regarding the safeguard of intellectual property and the mitigation of other security risks, the uptake of generative AI tools will rapidly grow.

[Thorbecke (2023a)](#ch12.xhtml#r005) cites a Microsoft spokesperson who declared that Microsoft is optimistic about the future of AI and thinks that AI advances will solve many more challenges than they present. However, Microsoft has also been consistent in its belief that when you create technologies that can change the world, you must also ensure that the technology is used responsibly ([Thorbecke, 2023a](#ch12.xhtml#r005)). Professor emeritus Gary Marcus, an AI researcher at New York University argues that the biggest immediate threat from AI is the threat to democracy from the wholesale production of compelling misinformation ([Thorbecke, 2023a](#ch12.xhtml#r005)). At a U.S Congress hearing, Marcus contends that generative AI tools are trained on vast repositories of valuable data online to create compelling written work and images in response to user prompts, that can rapidly impersonate the style or likeness of public figures to create disinformation campaigns. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI supported Professor Marcus’ view and said that the ability for AI to be used to manipulate voters and target disinformation were among his greatest concern.

Other concerns have been observed related to the possibility of generating propagating racial and gender biases. [Darcy (2023)](#ch12.xhtml#r001) cites Dan Hendrycks, the executive director of the Centre for AI Safety, declaring that the situation is reminiscent of atomic scientists issuing warnings about the very technologies they have created, with Robert Oppenheimer noting that we knew the world would not be the same. Hendrycks argues that there are many imperative and crucial risks from AI and not just the risk of extinction, such as systemic bias, misinformation, malicious use, cyberattacks, and weaponisation.

## **1.8** Where is the Humanity Heading?

When I started writing this section, the first thing that came to my mind was the ballad written by Richard Lee Evans titled “*In the Year 2525 (Exordium & Terminus)*”, recorded in Odessa, Texas in 1969. The term “*Exordium and Terminus*” basically means the beginning and the end. The ballad was an immediate success and the duo, Zager and Evans featured prominently on the 18 July 1969 edition of *Time Magazine*. Generally, the song foresees (over 8 000 years) a state or society where there is great suffering and predicts the destruction of the human species through overreliance on science and technology. The song also predicts test tube human embryo conception, a technique that was introduced in 1978 when two British medical researchers, Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards achieved the first child born from a zygote fertilized outside of a human body. It also predicts the emergence of AI where the machine (robots) will replace humans.

The ballad is a futuristic account that echoes the uneasiness of time and the wonders of technology. The song begins with a verse pondering if humans managed to survive to the year 2525, then humans would witness the events itemised in the song in every next millennium – from the year 3535 to the year 9595. In the song, life becomes more and more inactive and predetermined with every succeeding millennium. Human thoughts are pre-programmed into capsules for humanity to feed on, the machine (robots) will replace human’s limbs, eyes, and teeth. The institution of marriage will become outmoded since children will be conceived in test tubes. As the song approaches its end, it ponders whether humans will still be alive in the year 9595, after grasping everything the world can give them, without giving anything back. In the evolution of over 8 000 years, humans have seen the degeneration of their species with grave regret (man has cried a billion tears) but it is too late as they realise that the human reign has ended, and God is thinking maybe it’s time for Judgment Day.

Whether the above prediction is an exaggeration or not is open to question. Humanity and the world we live is threatened by various elements such as synthetic biology; extreme climate change; nanotechnology; nuclear war; global pandemics; pollution; deforestation; overfishing; ecological collapse; aging population; and loss of biodiversity. Therefore, artificial intelligence is not the only significant factor causing concern. A consolation is the fact that humanity has always confronted the challenges that threatened its very existence and found solutions. However, the challenges confronted by humanity a hundred years ago are nowhere near as threatening as the challenges it is confronting today and in the future. Additionally, there is consensus among leading AI technologists and industry leaders that AI poses a danger and therefore must be regulated and used responsibly.

Should AI be prohibited? The answer to this question is definitely no. Furthermore, it cannot be prohibited even if there is a desire to do so because there will always be someone who will be creative in the development of AI in a clandestine manner, particularly at a national level. Therefore, there is an urgent need to mitigate the risks associated with AI and for humanity to exploit its advantages by applying it in a responsible manner. It must also be recognised that the risks associated with AI can be mitigated but not eliminated. Mitigation of AI risks can be achieved through a regulatory process identifying what can be done and what cannot be done. This regulatory approach needs to be implemented at a national level, where each country must have a strict legislative basis to control AI and its uses; and at an international level where the international community must ensure that a robust multilateral treaty is drafted and in place, similar to the nuclear non-proliferation regime aimed at preventing the spread of illicit application of AI uses and as a means of controlling the application of AI in general to ensure that no harm is caused to humanity, individuals, and nations.

Admittedly, this still leaves the superpowers that have the upper hand because of the ‘*might is right*’ syndrome where those who are powerful can do what they wish unchallenged, even if their action is in fact unjustified. This is the most difficult challenge being confronted by humanity, how to achieve the widest spectrum of control, including that of national governments and their security institutions and organisations, particularly those of the superpowers. However, this challenge and the risks associated with it may be mitigated if technology leaders and other authenticated institutions across the globe continuously and passionately invest in the development and commercialisation of robust intrusion prevention systems to counteract practices that are aimed at the contamination and unauthorised control of computer networks and associated systems. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) is basically a network security instrument, which can be a hardware device and/or software that continuously monitors a network for malicious activity and takes action to prevent it, including reporting, blocking, or dropping it, when it occurs.

## **1.9** Conclusion

This chapter sets the scene for the entire book. The message being conveyed is that human beings are not perfect and therefore it is unlikely that they will develop a perfect artificial intelligence creation that is perfectly safe to be generally applied across the society. However, humanity cannot be complacent and ignore the dangers that AI can present to the individual and at a national level, particularly to the sensitive security and defence systems. This chapter has shown that like other technological developments the risks posed by AI cannot be completely eradicated. However, this does not mean its use should be abolished. History has shown that prohibiting something makes it more desirable. Infringements on freedom often have the opposite effect of what is intended, whether you’re talking about prohibiting alcohol or the use of AI. Prohibiting an object turns the ban into a challenge and the more power and meaning it gains. Prohibition becomes a symbol of a lack of control and gives that thing a personal meaning beyond whatever attributes the thing inherently may have. Although risks cannot be eliminated, they can be mitigated. This chapter has discussed various ways how risk mitigation regarding AI can be achieved.

The structure of the remaining book chapters will firstly continue with the theme related to the evolution of AI, particularly dealing with the evolution of human intelligence and artificial intelligence. The second part of the book will address the technology related to AI, namely the current AI tools; quantum computing and learning machines; intrusion prevention systems; and the shift from a knowledge-based economy towards an automation-based economy. The next part of the book will cover the practical implications of AI in the private and public sectors, and the impact of AI on society with particular emphasis on the ethical and legal considerations. The final part of the book will explore the future and AI, and the implications of the future of humanity.

As a society, humanity must focus on the human paradox of using technology, in this case AI, to destroy or create. AI and technology can be applied to destroy, such as having sophisticated weapons systems that are capable of killing and maiming thousands, if not millions of civilians, particularly innocent children. On the other hand, AI and technology can be applied to save and create life, such aiding in medical interventions, vitro fertilisation (IVF), and artificial insemination, amongst many others. The challenge that leaders face is what do we trust AI with and how can humanity exercise control over its use.
