# Chapter 2Evolution of Human Intelligence

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-3](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-3)

> *“Young people love what is interesting and odd, no matter how true or false it is. More mature minds love what is interesting and odd about truth. Fully mature intellects, finally, love truth, even when it appears plain and simple, boring to the ordinary person; for they have noticed that truth tends to reveal its highest wisdom in the guise of simplicity.”*
> 
> Friedrich Nietzsche

> German philosopher (1844-1900)

It is appropriate at the outset to discuss the evolution of human intelligence before addressing the various aspects of AI. [Marmelada (2003)](#ch13.xhtml#r018) poses several pertinent questions, namely, when did humans become intelligent, how did our intelligence materialise, what made it emerge, did it occur gradually from the possibilities of the subject (a probability basis), as Darwin suggested, or was it an act of divine creation, as Wallace claimed? Marmelada contends that this longstanding discussion is still relevant today and the discussion regarding how human intelligence originated is far from being resolved and continues to be a controversial topic.

The late 1980s and particularly the 1990s saw the advent of the naturalistic emergentist explanation to the development of human intelligence. This suggested that a transformation in the hominid per diem expenses, which altered eating habits by introducing a comparatively abundant consumption of meat in the diet may have provided a spontaneous growth in brain size, in which intelligence could have begun to develop. [Aiello and Wheeler (1995)](#ch13.xhtml#r008) proposed the Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis. Their theory suggested that individuals with reasonably large brains would have the minimum intelligence to invent tools with which to rupture bones to extract the energetic and nutritious bone marrow. Consequently, this rich diet in animal fats and protein permitted a gradual increase in brain volume, which in time lead to an ongoing increase in intelligence development.

The Aiello and Wheeler Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis proposes that there has been a coevolution of brain size and gut size in humans and non-human primates. Hence, as the brain became larger in human evolution, the gastro-intestinal tract became smaller. According to Marmelada, the brain is a very costly organ to sustain since in a modern adult male the brain requires 20% of the total body energy outflow, and at birth is capable of consuming 60% of the body’s energy. Moreover, he argues that the digestive system, including the intestinal tracts is also a high energy consumption element, consequently the reason why a very large brain and a very bulky digestive system do not usually occur simultaneously in the same living creature. To support the Aiello and Wheeler theory, Marmelada argues that the substitution of an almost exclusively vegetable diet that is very rich in cellulose, by one in which meat, rich in protein, played an essential role, allowed the volume of the brain to increase and the length of the intestines to decrease. Therefore, he suggests that this change permitted greater brain development in which the brain was able to grow and systematically expand over time.

However, there are opponents to the Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis. It is argued that if this hypothesis is correct, then why are large carnivore animals, which have been eating meat for millions of years have had their brains shrink by a third over the last couple of million years. One possible reason is that these species are not hominids, which are omnivores, and therefore, meat consumption is only a part of their per diem expenses. However, research has found that the brains of the Homo sapiens were once larger than they are today, and have seen a steady reduction in human brain size without an associated decrease in body size over the last 20,000 years ([Martin, 2000](#ch13.xhtml#r019)). Evidence presented by [Martin (2000)](#ch13.xhtml#r019) regarding Mesolithic humans, suggests that the size of the human brain has undergone an ongoing decline concurrently with substantial advances in human culture, and that the most significant changes in human society have been accompanied by a continuing decline in brain size. The above illustrates that the controversy related to how human intelligence developed is far from over.

This chapter will consider further the questions posed by Marmelada. This will provide a logical basis for examining and discussing the evolution of AI. AI is the creation of humans, and its creation is limited by human intelligence. However, we need to be aware that once created, AI can continue learning and has the potential (if not adequately controlled) to replicate and generate other AI creations on its own accord.

## **2.1** Introduction

According to the Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis the consumption of large quantities of meat is probable because having voluminous brains provided the potential to have the minimum amount of intelligence to be able to create the tools that offered the likelihood to slaughter and tear apart the remains of large animals. However, the foundation of the Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis is that big brains are gained after consuming meat.

The above arguments present a vicious circle in which a dilemma is created due to mutually conflicting or dependent conditions. In other words, the arguments create a “Catch-22” situation because something cannot happen until another thing occurs, but the other thing cannot occur until the first thing happens. According to [Arsuaga and Martinez (1998)](#ch13.xhtml#r011) the brain enlargement of Homo sapiens could only have been possible in exchange for a variation in the per diem expenses, which in turn transform into a decrease in the size of the digestive tract and, correlatively, of the chewing method. Moreover, they argue that Aiello and Wheeler did not contend that the change in per diem expenses automatically resulted in the growth of the size of the brain but claimed that it was crucial for Homo sapiens to convert to meat-eating to be intelligent. However, there is no precise scientific evidence to explain how human intelligence arose.

If human intelligence has developed through an ongoing but steady development, the question that arises is whether it is possible for animals to have intelligence but at a lower magnitude. This view tends to agree with Darwin’s view that animals have intelligence. On the other hand, the general view is that animals do not have intelligence since they are not able to elaborate concepts. However, animals have highly developed sensory knowledge and are capable of elaborating “perceptions.” It is these perceptions, in concert with the genetic inheritance they possess that is related to how they adapt to the environment, which permit them to have an ample vision of their environment that empower them to survive. Hence, it is argued that intellectual knowledge, and the amplification of theoretical and general ideas, is unique to humans.

Johns Hopkins University define the brain as a complex organ that controls thought, memory, emotion, touch, motor skills, vision, breathing, temperature, hunger, and every process that regulates the human body, and together with the spinal cord embrace the central nervous system. One may argue that in terms of this definition, an animal’s brain has the same function as the human brain. However, the primary distinguishing factors between a human and animal brain is that a human brain has remarkable cognitive capacity, which is the greatest achievement of evolution, whereas an animal’s brain has comparatively less cognitive capacity. Additionally, the human brain allows humans to think about certain things and be motivated by their instincts, intellect, and logic, whereas animals are incapable of reasoning and are simply motivated by their instincts. Therefore, from a scientific point of view, the human brain can be simply viewed as an organ of understanding or intelligence.

The question that arises from this view is whether the human soul exists? Without the presence of a human soul, the existence of religion would become meaningless since there would be no path of providing a lasting and continuing relationship with God. On the other hand, if “understanding” is viewed as a capability of the soul that did not require the subject as an organ, but as an object to particularise concepts, then the human soul becomes spiritual and immortal, and sanctions humans through their sincerity to become a transcendent being that strives to reach beyond the experience of objects to understand being itself. Here, the soul is viewed as the spirit or immaterial part of human beings, the seat of human personality, intellect, will, and emotions, regarded as an entity that survives the body after physical death.

However, the above does not provide the answer to what is the origin of human intelligence? Evolutionary scientists have a dichotomous view, that of Charles Darwin (1809-1882) or of Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913). Both are responsible for the theory that species evolve over time due to natural selection. However, Darwin argued that human evolution could be explained by natural selection, with sexual selection as a significant supplementary principle. On the other hand, Wallace had doubts about sexual selection and eventually concluded that natural selection alone was insufficient to account for a set of uniquely human characteristics. Basically, they both came up with the notion of survival of the fittest. However, they could not establish how variation occurred in a species. Wallace and Darwin differed in the theory of evolution in that Wallace believed plants and animals evolved to their environment and Darwin believed adaptations were driven by competition and that those organisms with traits that favoured survival would pass those traits to their offspring.

Darwin argued that the evolution of the human intellect did not differ significantly from the evolution of the body, in that it was a slow ongoing progression based on small steps over a long-term period along the evolutionary path that differentiates apes from humans. However, Wallace rejected the idea that the human intellect was a result of gradual evolution. He contended that it was an outcome of a supernatural cause, where human intelligence may have resulted from unprecedented variation of the elements within the brain, causing an entirely transformational and profoundly different property called intelligence as an emergent property.

Therefore, the origin of human intelligence can be narrowed down to two options, namely Supernatural as proposed by Wallace or natural as proposed by Darwin (i.e., a Divine creation versus emergence from the subject). In other words, the choice between the notions that human intellect developed all at once with Homo sapiens, or that it was the outcome of gradual evolution. It should be noted that scientific knowledge is not the sole objective valid form of knowledge. The epistemological view which hypothesises that views scientific knowledge as the supreme form of objectively valid knowledge can only be valid if it is complemented with the supposition of another thesis regarding the ontological character, which claims that the only existing reality is of subject material. Hence, they both pose two related questions, ontology asks what exists, and epistemology asks how we can know about the existence of such a thing. Additionally, epistemology and ontology are two branches of philosophy, and their exposition of the authenticity of their claims can only be determined by philosophical and not by scientific reasoning, which inevitable instigate ideological debates regarding the origin of human intelligence.

## **2.2** Evolution of Human Beings

Before the evolution of human beings is discussed, one needs to have an idea of what is meant by evolution. In simple terms, evolution is a biological term that incorporates the process of change in all earthly living species. It refers to a progressive process of change in the living organism and how these living organisms advanced from their descendants. Evolution also embraces several processes such as, mutation, gene flow, genetic drift, and natural selection that enable the various species to initiate, improve, and adjust according to their physical and social environment.

Whether one supports Darwin’s or Wallace’s hypothesis of evolution, there is consensus that the evolution of human beings is a prolonged process that implicated a change from the very early humans to present modern humans over millions of years. Evidence suggests that the chronologically human evolution ranges roughly seven million years, with the occurrence of behavioural modernity around 50,000 years ago. Furthermore, several qualities of human behaviour, such as understanding, sadness, ritual, and the use of symbols and tools, were to some extent evident in Hominidae or great apes but in much less advanced forms than what is found in humans.

For instance, chimpanzees can make tools and use them to obtain food and for social displays. They also have somewhat intricate hunting approaches that entail collaboration, authority, and rank. These creatures appear to be status conscious, are scheming, and capable of deception. Chimpanzees can also gain knowledge to use symbols and recognise some simple facets of human language. A feature that is common in species that display aptitude, such as dolphins, great apes, and humans is an enlarged brain size. Complementing the enlarged brain size there is also a more advanced neocortex, which is concerned with sight and hearing in mammals, a folding of the cerebral cortex, and von Economo neurons that are large bipolar neurons located in fronto-insular cortex and anterior limbic area in Hominidae and humans. These neurons are often viewed as being associated with the social trait and capacity to gauge what another is thinking or feeling. However, whether this behaviour can be classified as intelligence as one would associate with human intelligence is open to question.

It is thought that from roughly 5 million years ago, the hominin brain started to progress swiftly in both magnitude and an associated diversity of functions. Scientific studies suggest that the human being evolved from apelike creatures that lived similar to animals and could not even walk upright. However, it is believed that with the passage of time the size of their brain grew, they learnt how to make tools, it allowed them to retain and recall information, and gradually their social behaviour developed, leading to the advent of the modern human being through the process of evolution (refer to [Figure 2.1](#ch13.xhtml#f1)).

![Figure 2.1 Evolution of Human Beings.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C002_001.jpg)

**Figure 2.1** Evolution of Human Beings.[⏎](#ch13.xhtml#f1b)

The era for the commencement of the Neolithic period, which had witnessed the transformation in the life of early humans, is unknown since it was developing at different places in different dates. The Neolithic age (new stone age) was preceded by the Palaeolithic period (old stone age) and Mesolithic age (middle stone age). In the Palaeolithic period early humans lived in caves or simple huts and were hunter-gathers, using basic stone and bone tools, as well as crude stone axes, for hunting birds and wild animals. This was followed by the Mesolithic age where humans used smaller (microliths) chipped stone tools and had a more hunter-gatherer culture with settlements being temporary and seasonal.

This period ended with the introduction of the growing of crops and animal husbandry, the Neolithic age. The outcome of great consequence of the Neolithic age was the innovative activity of agriculture that permitted humans to cultivate food, where they became food producers rather than purely hunter-gathers. Hence, there was a momentous transition for humans from being nomadic, mainly living by hunting and fishing, and harvesting wild food to practicing cultivation where they established settlements without the need to travel from one place to another in the search of food. This also led to the taming of animals, and eventually to the discovery of the wheel. Through this evolutionary process humans learned to use their available resources more effectively and became skilled tool makers, thus gradually improving their living standards.

## **2.3** Human Intelligence

Generally, intelligence is viewed as the capacity to learn, comprehend and apply knowledge and skills. However, human intelligence is the intellectual capacity of an individual, which is demonstrated by multifaceted cognitive achievements and fluctuating levels of motivation depending on circumstances being encountered and self-awareness. Typically, the magnitude of an individual’s intelligence determines their work effectiveness. It is also important to recognise that human intelligence is a multidimensional concept that incorporates many forms. There is no consensus for the definition of human intelligence. However, there are some mutual features amongst academics regarding human intelligence that include the following:

*    The mental capacity of a person at a particular time and in a particular situation.
*   A mental skill for enabling a person to manipulate things, objects, or events existing in one’s environment, and adapting to new obstacles and issues being encountered.
*   An ability to judge one’s capacity in terms of behavioural or performance quality.
*   An aptitude for abstraction management.
*   A capacity to adjust or adapt to new circumstances.
*   An ability to adapt and address unexpected circumstances as successfully as possible.
*   The skill to respond appropriately to certain stimuli in a given situation.

The nature of human intelligence is a very complex issue; however, research studies have found several typical characteristics, namely:

*   Genetics and environment. Both genetics and environment are key ingredients for an individual’s intellectual development and are both equally important.
*   Dissemination of intelligence: The level of intelligence fluctuates amid the population and adheres to the mathematical Normal distribution. Many within the population are average, with the others being either exceptionally or poorly gifted individuals.
*   Variation of intelligence. People are different and have a diverse level of intelligence. The diverse level of intelligence fluctuates from individual to individual, age to age, and circumstance to circumstance.
*   Impact of age. Intelligence develops according to a person’s life cycle. However, the life-cycle distribution and one’s mental growth varies from person to person. Typically, intelligence peaks between the age of 16 to 20 in an individual, when vertical progression ceases. However, the horizontal amassing of knowledge and attainment of skills continues throughout a person’s life cycle.
*   Gender differences. Gender has no influence on the level of intelligence.
*   Ethnic or cultural differences: Studies have shown that there is no significant difference in the intelligence level of people based on race or cultural groups. The Normal distribution applies, and any variations found are mainly due environmental impact.

Human intelligence is linked with the attributes of creativity, emotion, flexibility, and the capacity to learn from a broad range of experiences. As a comparison, artificial intelligence may mimic human intelligence, but it cannot experience emotions or understand ethical and moral issues. Undeniably, machine and human learning have some common parallels such as reinforcement learning, where the learning process is grounded on rewarding desired behaviours and punishing undesired ones, and can recognise and decode its environment, take actions, and learn through trial and error. In both instances, machine and human learning is based on past experiences. Human intelligence as implied previously incorporates many different intelligence types. These include:

*    Linguistic Intelligence. This is the aptitude for using language effectively, irrespective of whether it is written or spoken. A person with high linguistic intelligence displays reliable skills of reading, writing, speaking, and listening.
*   Logical-Mathematical Intelligence. This is ability to rationalise, evaluate, and resolve problems using logic and mathematical concepts. A person with high logical-mathematical intelligence can apply deductive and critical reasoning, and problem-solving.
*   Spatial intelligence. This is the capacity to visualise and manipulate objects in the mind. Individuals with this type of intelligence can imagine what objects appear like from different views and have good spatial knowledge that enable them to solve difficulties that entail visual logic, such as puzzles, mazes, and maps.
*   Musical Intelligence. This is the talent to understand and create music. An individual with musical intelligence has a good grasp of rhythm, melody, and harmony, and is able recognise musical patterns, valuing different types of music.
*   Bodily-Kinaesthetic Intelligence. This is skill for resolving problems and expressing ideas using the body. Persons with this type of intelligence are normally good at sports, dance, and other physical activities, and can use tools and manipulating objects.
*   Interpersonal Intelligence. This is the ability to understand and relate to others. An individual with high interpersonal intelligence has sound social skills such as communicating, negotiating, and resolving conflicts, and can recognise the emotions and intentions of others.
*   Intrapersonal Intelligence. This is the aptitude to understand oneself. This type of intelligence permits persons to comprehend their own emotions, thoughts, and motivations.
*   Naturalistic intelligence. This is the faculty of appreciating and linking to the natural world. Persons with high naturalistic intelligence are familiar with the environment, animals, and plants, and can classify and identify natural objects.
*   Existential Intelligence. This is the aptitude to examine and contemplate profound philosophical and existential questions, such as the nature of life, death, and the human condition, including spirituality, religion, and the purpose of life. Persons with existentially intelligence are normally profoundly engrossed in philosophy, theology, and the arts.

Understanding the different types of human intelligence assists institutions to acknowledge the strengths and competences of individuals with a variety of backgrounds to help in having an all-inclusive civil society. There are basically two approaches to examining the intelligence theories, namely the psychometric approach and information processing approach. The former approach is based on the concept that depicts intelligence as a combination of abilities measured by mental tests. The latter approach describes how individuals encode information into memory, namely by recording, storing, and retrieving information in their brains, which affects the person’s general behaviour and motivation. The information processing approach explains people’s intellectual reasoning and problem-solving process and is based on the belief that people process the information they are presented with rather than just reacting to inducements. There are several key theories that describe intelligence by these two approaches as itemised below:

*   Uni-factor Theory. French psychologist Alfred Binet proposed that intelligence consists of one factor that is usual for all individual activities. He is recognised for developing the first intelligence test and the concept of mental age.
*   Two-factor Theory. Charles Spearman, an English psychologist, posited that intelligence consists of two components, namely general intelligence (“g”) and specific ability (“s”). General intelligence is viewed as mental energy measured by different tasks, and specific abilities permit a person to tackle a specific kind of problem.
*   Theory of Primary Mental Abilities. Louis Leon Thurstone, an American psychologist, developed the Primary Mental Abilities Test and proposed that a person’s performance on intelligence tests depends on many different abilities, namely verbal knowledge, word fluency, number facility, spatial visualisation, associative memory, perceptual speed, and reasoning.
*   Theory of Cognitive Development. Jean Piaget, a Swiss psychologist, was the pioneer for the information processing approach. His theory of cognitive development focused on the education of children and was related to the mechanisms by which intellectual development advances, and the stages through which children develop. Piaget posited that children explore and observe consistencies and make generalities from these observations. He argued that intellectual development grows from two cognitive processes that work to some extent in a shared fashion, namely assimilation and accommodation. Assimilation includes new information into an already existing cognitive structure, and accommodation, which shapes a new cognitive structure into which new information can be integrated. According to Piaget, cognitive development denotes a dynamic equilibrium between assimilation and accommodation processes.
*   Hierarchical Model of Intelligence. Arthur Robert Jensen an American psychologist found two different types of intellectual ability that he identified as Level 1 and Level 2. Level 1 were considered the skills related to memory and associative functions such as retention of input and rote memorisation of basic skills and knowledge. On the other hand, Level 2 skills were related to abstract and conceptual thinking, including the capacity to change and manipulate inputs, or the capacity to resolve issues.
*   Structure of Intellect Model. Joy Paul Guilford, an American psychologist, proposed that intelligence is a combination of numerous abilities independent in nature. He categorised the components of intellect into three broad categories, namely operations, contents, and products. Applying factor analysis, he further divided these and constructed a three-dimensional grid that combined a factor from each of the three categories to make up a whole.
*    Theory of Multiple Intelligence. Howard Gardner, an American developmental psychologist, posited that the learning process should be tailored to an individual’s strengths in their multiple intelligences. By recognising and developing these intelligences, individuals can enhance their ability to learn and understand information. He has proposed eight multiple intelligences, namely spatial, bodily-kinaesthetic, musical, linguistic, logical-mathematical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic.
*   Triarchic Theory of Intelligence. Robert Sternberg an American psychology professor at Cornell University proposed three distinct types of intelligence that a person can possess, namely practical intelligence, creative intelligence, and analytical intelligence. This theory is based on information processing.
*   PASS Model of Intelligence. This theory of intelligence is rooted in Alexander Romanovich Luria, a Soviet neuropsychologist. He studied work on cognition and proposed that human cognition consists of three separate but interrelated brain systems that support four cognitive processes, namely planning, attention, simultaneous, and successive processing. It was later further developed in 1975 by Das, Kirby, and Jarman and later refined by Das, Naglieri, and Kirby in 1994. Its full form is the Planning, Attention-Arousal, Simultaneous, and Successive (PASS) theory of intelligence.

The above illustrate that there are various definitions of intelligence. Intelligence is mostly recognised as a complex cognitive capability that permits humans to learn and solve problems. These various definitions are supported by numerous theories of intelligence. However, there appears to be a consensus that intelligence is a mixture of cognitive aptitudes that include problem-solving, learning, reasoning, and memory. There is also consensus amongst researchers that human intelligence has evolved progressively over a process of thousands of generations without an extreme change in the environment. [Skottke (2005)](#ch13.xhtml#r024) argues that the challenges humans encounter in modern society have forced the independent domain of intelligence to assume the roles, which other domains would have played in the primitive environment and in which humans have evolved. He argues that there are clear genetic associations that influence people to have a larger cerebral cortex, permitting them to address the challenges that an expanded workload modern life places on the human’s intelligence domain.

Moreover, he contends that evolution has not yet had an opportunity to catch up to the rapid progress humans have made as a society, and this might not be due to humans bypassing the natural selection process. General intelligence is sometimes defined as the ability of a person to attain and apply knowledge. According to [DiLalla (2000)](#ch13.xhtml#r012), various studies have found that general intelligence is at least fifty percent heritable and therefore, can be passed down from generation to generation. It is also held that evolution is a concept where the gene representation of organisms transforms over time. Additionally, it is believed that what drives this change in gene expression is either natural or sexual selection. Furthermore, it is evident that human intelligence has been continually transforming since the advent of the very first hominids. Skottke maintains that environmental and migration factors have influenced human intelligence, apart from the genetic changes. He argues that the migration of people to all the corners of the earth, along with the industrialisation of modern society, has disconnected modern human from its ancestors.

### **2.3.1** General Intelligence as an Independent Domain

According to Skottke, the theories concerning general intelligence are the dependent domain and the independent domain models. He maintains that the dependent domain model considers general intelligence as a broad category that is segmented into smaller specific intelligences, such as mate selection, cheater detection, and face recognition. Hence, with this model, it can be implied that if an individual’s general intelligence is high, then their ability to choose and attain a mate, detect deceits, and recognise people’s faces would also be high, with the reverse also applying. On the other hand, the independent domain theory views general intelligence as just one of several psychological processes, together with mate selection, cheater detection, and face recognition. Under this model, general intelligence is described as the capacity to apply deductive logic and abstract thought.

Skottke argues that the independent domain model is more realistic because it is supported by various empirical studies indicating that the psychological processes of the brain are not connected. He cites a study ([Kanazawa, 2004](#ch13.xhtml#r017)) where very intelligent individuals with IQs above 125 are the least likely to marry of all the cognitive classes, suggesting that mate selection and general intelligence are unrelated. Hence, he claims that all the psychological processes are dedicated to its own area of capability that have been forged over thousands of generations of human evolution. Therefore, he suggests that someone might have increased intelligence but not be able to secure a mate similar to how someone who has the ability to find a mate would not increase their capacity to use logic and abstract thought. Other studies related to genetic influences also support the independent domain model. In his dissertation, Skottke’s concludes that human intelligence may have ceased its growth.

Alexandria Cherry from Rochester Institute of Technology in reviewing Skottke’s arguments notes that the need to work for survival has greatly lessened but this does not mean that the evolution of human intelligence will cease. He argues that human expansion into places of unknown terrain is possible because humanity has enough intelligence to move into outer space and explore other worlds. He claims that maybe this is not the end of the growth of intelligence but just the beginning. He maintains that several studies have shown that intelligence is still rising and poses the question that if intelligence is still on the rise, then what evidence is there that it will slow and eventually stop? Therefore, he asserts that so far, there has been no evidence that human intelligence has ceased its growth.

## **2.4** Evolution of Human Intelligence

Scientists and academics have been interested in the emergence of the human intellect for many decades, with French psychologist Alfred Binet (1857-1911) being a pioneer when he proposed the Uni-factor Theory. While various theories have been proposed that provided significant ideas and insights into how the human cognitive skills have changed through time, the specific origins that have caused the evolution of human reasoning are still being debated. The numerous theories that have been proposed over these past many decades are testimony of the complexities of the extraordinary human intellect. The evolution of the remarkable human intellect is the development of progressively multifaceted mental capabilities and knowledge of our world over a long journey through time. The first humans were predisposed to depend on their physical strength and survival compulsions, but as the human brain evolved, so did their capacity to think, reason, and solve difficult problems.

Currently, our human intellectual development and the associated transformation of extensive knowledge to wisdom is demonstrated by numerous means through the creation of complex high technology machines, such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) that create detailed images of nearly every structure and organ inside the body to detect abnormalities; the ability to send humans into outer space; and the ability to think critically, and to cooperate with others for resolving numerous diverse problems. Theories vary, but a popular theory amongst researchers is that the human intellect developed through natural selection where organisms that are more able to adapt to their environment are more likely to survive and pass on the genes that supported their achievement. This is the evolutionary process that causes species to change and diverge progressively over time. Researchers have found evidence to suggest that in the human ancestry, brain size, and complexity have grown through the passage of time, specifically in the prefrontal cortex. The prefrontal cortex has been found to be linked with higher-order cognitive processes such as decision-making, problem-solving, and planning.

However, there are some researchers that do not entirely agree with a purely natural selection theory and believe that social and cultural factors have significantly impacted the development of the human intellect. For example, language and communication enabled people to share and disseminate information and to learn from each other, thus possibly influencing the growth of higher cognitive abilities. Nevertheless, research has suggested that even cognitive abilities may be influenced by genetic factors, and these have contributed to the progression of human creativity.

### **2.4.1** Factors Contributing to the Evolution of Human Intelligence

There is consensus amongst researchers that the human intellect evolutionary process is a complicated phenomenon shaped by various influences over millions of years. Some of the critical factors that are viewed to have contributed to the evolution of human intellect include the following:

*   Environment. Ecological factors such as availability of food, social interaction, and education are factors that positively affect the development of logical thinking. For instance, contact with contaminants during early development may cause cognitive deficits, whereas education has been shown to strengthen cognitive abilities.
*    Usage of Tools. The ability to make and use tools is the most fundamental quality that distinguishes humans from other animals. It is contended that enhanced cognitive skills, such as planning tasks, solving difficulties, and spatial judgement, were all essential for the evolution of tool usage.
*   Culture. Culture, which embodies social learning and behaviour; values found in human societies; and the knowledge, beliefs, arts, laws, customs, capabilities, and habits within groups of individuals are all essential in the development of the human intellect. For instance, language development was essential for people to communicate knowledge and information, which facilitated the development of superior cognitive abilities.
*   Social Interaction. Humans’ cognitive abilities have been influenced by our extraordinary sociable nature in which social contact becomes an essential component in forming our cognitive aptitudes. Studies have shown that people learn from each other, share knowledge, and create complex social systems through their social contact. This has helped the evolution of our cognitive powers.
*   Genetic Factors. The cognitive competencies of humans have also been significantly influenced by the evolution of genetic factors. Studies have revealed that adult individuals have a heritability of IQ between 57% and 73%, with some recent studies showing heritability for IQ as high as 80%.

Intelligence in human groups adheres to a normal distribution, which has a bell-shaped mathematical function. The peak (middle) of the Normal distribution is the average, with the central measure of dispersion being the standard deviation. The range of the dispersion from the mean (average) for the Normal distribution is ±3 standard deviation. Hence, most individuals in the normal distribution are found in the middle range of reasoning, with fewer people at either extreme of high or low intelligence. The intelligence quotient (IQ) is commonly used to measure intelligence with a mean score of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Therefore, human intelligence ranges from a low of 55 to a high of 145 (i.e., 100 ±3 standard deviation, which is 100 ± 45). In other words, applying this standardised scale, roughly 68% of the population falls within one standard deviation of the mean (between an IQ value of 85 and 115), whereas as around 95% falls within two standard deviations of the mean. (between an IQ score of 70 and 130).

There is consensus amongst researchers that reasoning is a very complex attribute, which is affected by several genetic and environmental factors. The normal distribution implies that the distribution of reasoning in one community is likely. However, there may also be significant differences in the distribution of intelligence between communities due to various variables such as genetics, nutrition, education, and culture. Intelligence is a multifaceted characteristic which is impacted by genetic and environmental factors but should be viewed as only one component of human worth and potential.

## **2.5** Theories on the Evolution of Human Intelligence

The evolution of human intelligence is closely linked to the growth of the human brain and to the origin of language and has been a topic of controversy with the proposition of various theories. There are various leading theories that have been proposed, which include social brain; cultural intelligence; transformative cultural intelligence; self-domestication; social exchange; sexual selection; ecological dominance-social competition; and group selection.

### **2.5.1** Social Brain Theory

The social brain theory was proposed by Robin Dunbar, a British biological anthropologist, and specialist in primate behaviour, who argued that human intelligence did not evolve chiefly to resolve ecological difficulties, but significantly as a process of surviving and reproducing in large and complex social groups. Dunbar concluded that the size of the neocortex, which is the part of the brain linked with cognition and language, relative to the body, is related to the size of a cohesive social group. He maintains that this ratio (neocortex size to the body) limits how much complexity a social system can handle.

Although having a social group does not itself cause intelligence to evolve, he maintains that several behaviours linked with living in large groups, such as reciprocal altruism, deception and coalition formation facilitate the ability to understand the thoughts and emotions of others (the dynamics of the Theory of Mind). He further argues that when the size of a social group increases, the number of different relationships in the group may increase exponentially. Dunbar introduced the 150-rule where humans in general have a social circle of about 150 people, which is also the usual range of social communities in small societies and personal social networks. The success of a social group is viewed as being dependent on its size when initially established, with groups of around 150 being mostly successful, since they are likely to achieve a balance between the minimum size of effective functionality and the maximum size for generating a social environment of commitment to the community. Therefore, Dunbar concludes that when hominids commenced living in sizeable groups, selection facilitated higher intelligence. This is supported by considering the relationship between neocortex size and group size of various mammals.

However, this theory has attracted lot of criticism. Phylogenetic studies (i.e., evolutionary relationships among biological entities) regarding brain sizes in primates suggest that while diet is a predictor of brain size, from a sociality viewpoint (i.e., tendency of groups and persons to develop social links and live in communities) it does not predict brain size when adjustments are made for instances where the diet impacts both brain size and sociality. Researchers have found that animals thriving mostly on raw fruits or succulent fruit-like produce of plants such as roots, shoots, nuts, and seeds (frugivores) tend to exhibit larger brain size than animals that focusses on eating leaves (folivores). A likely explanation for this phenomenon is that frugivory entails extractive foraging, which necessitates higher cognitive processing, since one needs to locate and prepare hard-shelled food, such as nuts and fruit before consuming it. However, some researchers argue that it is not just the act of extractive foraging that stimulates brain size, but the fact that a high energy frugivore diet aids foetal brain growth and requires spatial mapping to locate the embedded foods.

Additionally, the correlation between brain size and sociality becomes a problem for the Dunbar’s social brain theory since insects exhibit an incomparable assortment of social forms to permanent colonies containing many individuals collaborating as a collective organism, with a remarkable span of cognitive skills despite their small nervous systems. Nevertheless, human societies typically remain united by the ability of individuals to comprehend qualities signifying group membership. It is argued that social insects do the same and often recognize members of their colony allowing them to defend against competitors. However, studies suggest that with insects this recognition is attained because of elementary cognitive operations that do not involve long-term memory but because of sensory orientation. This supports the general view that animals do not have intelligence since they are not able to elaborate concepts but have highly developed sensory knowledge that are capable of elaborating “perceptions.”

### **2.5.2** Cultural Intelligence (CQ) Theory

[Earley and Ang (2003)](#ch13.xhtml#r013) introduced the concept of cultural intelligence, which basically refers to the skill to relate and work effectively in culturally diverse situations. This concept was formulated when the world was experiencing unprecedented globalisation and interconnectedness, and at a time when ideological clashes and cultural conflict culminated in the tragic events of 11 September 2001. Nobel Prize laureate Elie Wiesel had identified hatred directed toward culturally different individuals (i.e., “cultural hatred”), as the major source of problems between people, across all times. This theory is akin but distinct from the social brain hypothesis. Cultural intelligence or cultural brain hypothesis claims that human brain size, cognitive ability, and intelligence have increased over generations due to cultural information from a mechanism known as social learning. Furthermore, it postulates a positive relationship between species with a higher dependency and more frequent opportunities for social learning and overall cognitive ability. Earley and Ang argue that social learning permits species to develop cultural skills and strategies for survival, thus overwhelmingly, cultural species should in theory be more intelligent.

This theory acknowledges that humans are the most intelligent species on the planet, with big brains that evolved over millions of years, with ample cognitive abilities and processing power which outcompete all other species. They view humans as an “evolved cultural species” that has an unparalleled dependence on culturally diffused knowledge because of the surrounding social environment. They maintain that social transmission of information disseminates significantly faster in human populations relative to changes in genetics. The rational supporting the cultural intelligence theory is that human beings are the most cultural species in the world and this cultural information has been steadily disseminated through generations to create extensive capacities of cultural skills and knowledge throughout humans, and therefore human beings are the most intelligent species there is. In contrast, Dunbar’s social brain hypothesis maintains that the human brain developed because of complex social interactions in groups. Therefore, the cultural intelligence theory puts more emphasis on the growth in intelligence from socially transmitted information.

Therefore, there is a distinct shift in emphasis from social collaboration to learning strategies. This conflicts with the human general intelligence notion since it focuses on the model that cultural skills and information are learned from others. [Muthukrishna et al. (2018)](#ch13.xhtml#r022) argue that brains expand in response to the availability of information and calories, and thus store and manage more information. They further contend that information availability is affected by learning strategies. These researchers designed a simulation model that captures this co-evolution under different conditions and describes the specific and narrow conditions that can lead to a take-off in brain size, which is a possible pathway that led to the extraordinary expansion in the human species. Their model was based on three primary assumptions, namely that brain size, complexity, and organisation are grouped into one variable; a larger brain results in larger capacity for adaptive knowledge; and more adaptive knowledge increases fitness of organisms. Their model predicted relationships between brain size, group size, adaptive knowledge, asocial/social learning, mating structure, and the juvenile period. These findings had been confirmed by empirical literature by other researchers.

### **2.5.3** Transformative Cultural Intelligence Theory

[Moll (2018)](#ch13.xhtml#r021) proposed a variation to the cultural intelligence hypothesis. The transformative cultural intelligence hypothesis maintains that the human physical cognition is developed and influenced by the social environment around us. This proposition is contrary to the cultural intelligence hypothesis suggested by [Earley and Ang (2003)](#ch13.xhtml#r013), which maintains that it is the human social cognition and not physical cognition which is superior to our nearest primate relatives. However, Moll’s hypothesis views physical cognition in humans as being affected by external social factors, which is unique to humans and not observed in other species.

Molli conducted a study by examining problem-solving under different social conditions of 4-year-old children. Children had to use water to extract a buoyant object from a narrow tube. In the first experiment, the children were confronted with the problem “cold” without clues resulting in that nearly all of them were unsuccessful. In a second experiment, the children were shown a solution-suggesting video, which was pedagogically delivered prior to the task, resulting in that most children (69% in Experiment 1, 75% in Experiment 2) succeeded. Furthermore, showing children the same video in a non-pedagogical manner did not boost their performance above baseline (Experiment 1) and was less effective than outlining it pedagogically (Experiments 1 and 2). The findings suggest that the children’s physical cognition and problem-solving ability was affected by how the task was socially presented to them. The Cultural Intelligence hypothesis was also questioned as to whether only humans’ social, but not their physical, cognition differs qualitatively from that of great apes.

### **2.5.4** Self-domestication Theory (or Reduced Aggression Theory)

The human self-domestication hypothesis maintains that compared to existing primates and extinct hominins, humans exhibit many of the distinctive morphological, behavioural, and cognitive features also observed in domesticated animals. Hence, the self-domestication hypothesis suggests that, like mammalian domesticates, humans have gone through a process of selection against aggression, a process that in the case of humans was self-induced, which has led to the evolution of advanced intelligence in Homo sapiens.

[Shilton et al. (2020)](#ch13.xhtml#r023) argue that the self-induced selection against aggression differentiates humans from other species of monkeys and primates, where aggressivity is still manifested, and has eventually led to the development of quintessential human characteristics such as empathy, social cognition, and culture. They maintain that there are unique aspects of human evolution and suggest that emotional control and social motivation in humans evolved during two major but partially overlapping stages. The first stage came after the emergence of mimetic communication, and saw the beginnings of musical engagement, and mimesis-related cognition, which required socially mediated emotional plasticity and was accompanied by new social emotions. The second stage succeeded the emergence of language, when individuals began to instruct the imagination of their interlocutors, and to rely even more extensively on emotional plasticity, and culturally-learned emotional control.

[Shilton et al. (2020)](#ch13.xhtml#r023) argue that although selection for reduced emotional reactivity was involved in both socially impoverished domesticates and socially sophisticated humans, the differences between the two types of pro-social evolution mean that their inclusion under the same umbrella term of “domestication” is misleading. The above contentions reveal the significant differences between humans and domesticates, thus challenging the notion of human self-domestication.

### **2.5.5** Social Exchange Theory

[Homans (1961)](#ch13.xhtml#r016) initially defined a framework built on a combination of behaviourism and basic economics. Social exchange theory is a concept based on the idea that social behaviour is the result of an exchange process in which people weigh the potential benefits and risks of their social relationships. Hence, when the risks outweigh the rewards, they will terminate or abandon the relationship. Thus, the purpose of this exchange is to maximize benefits and minimise costs. Several studies suggest that social exchange between individuals is a critical modification to the human brain, implying that the human brain could be equipped with a neurocognitive system dedicated for reasoning around social exchange. Hence, this would develop when two parties improve their position by mutually exchanging things, they value less for things they value more. However, selection will only support social exchange when both parties benefit. Therefore, if a party fails to deliver fair benefits (cheaters) this would impend the fulfilment of exchange.

According to [Wischniewski et al. (2009)](#ch13.xhtml#r025) abundant research using various game theoretical approaches has examined apparently irrational human behaviours. They explored the cognitive mechanisms required to compute possible scenarios of cooperation, defection, and the detection of cheating. Evolutionary game theory has revealed that variations for social exchange can be favoured and firmly maintained by natural selection, but only if they include design qualities that enable them to detect cheaters and cause them to channel future exchanges to reciprocators and away from cheaters. They argue that humans use social contracts to present the benefits and losses each party will be receiving. Therefore, humans have developed an advanced cheater detection method, which has an inbuilt proprietary problem-solving scheme that progressed to match the recurring features of their matching problem domains.

Humans do not only need to establish that the agreement is infringed, but also if this infringement was intentionally made. Therefore, humans have developed practices that are focused on revealing intentional cheating through contract infringements. However, a difficulty with the theory that a specific punishment for intentional deception and intelligence to evolve together, is the fact that selective punishment of individuals with certain attributes selects against the attributes in question. For instance, if only individuals that have the skill to remember what they agree to are penalised for breaching agreements, then evolution would have selected against the capacity to remember what one had agreed to. The social exchange theory makes several assumptions about human nature, namely that humans are rational beings; and that they seek rewards and avoid punishments. However, the criteria that humans use to assess costs and benefits differ over time and from person to person.

### **2.5.6** Sexual Selection

[Miller (1998)](#ch13.xhtml#r020) argues that the human mind evolved not as survival machine, but as courtship mechanism. He notes that evolution is driven not just by natural selection for survival, but by an equally important process that Darwin called sexual selection through mate choice. Miller suggests that human intelligence for the essentials of hunter-gatherers to survive is unnecessarily advanced. Miller maintains that language, music, and art, which are viewed as indicators for intelligence, evolved as fitness indicators and not because of their practical value for the survival of ancient hominids.

This model maintains that Hominids’ greater intelligence was impacted by healthy genes, and that the relative speedy evolution of human intelligence was due to a Fisherian runaway positive feedback loop of sexual selection. [Fisher (1930)](#ch13.xhtml#r014) proposed that the exaggerated secondary sexual characteristics of animals could evolve by means of a runaway evolutionary process in which an initial small adaptive dimorphism (the existence of two different forms) was then developed further into a much more heightened trait by an ongoing interactive combination of female selective choice and increased male advantage. For example, in many species, only males have imposing secondary sexual properties such as ornaments and an exhibitionist conduct. However, sexual selection may also be a female characteristic, particularly in somewhat monogamous species. For instance, some researchers believe that sexual selection may explain certain female-specific human qualities, like breasts and buttocks, which are significantly bigger in proportion to total body size, than those found in related species of ape. Particularly when one considers that the human female breasts are found sexually attractive by many men.

It is argued that if breasts of the size found in humans were essential for the purpose of breastfeeding, they would be found in similar size proportions in other species. This rational supports the proposition that sexual selection acts on human females as secondary sexual characteristics. It is also argued that the enlargement of the human brain necessitated more nutrition than the brain of a related species of ape. Additionally, for females to effectively evaluate male intelligence, they needed to be intelligent themselves, explaining that although on average there appears to be no difference in the intelligence level between males and females, there may be a disparity in how they display their intelligence in showy appearances.

### **2.5.7** Ecological Dominance-Social Competition Theory

According to the Ecological Dominance-Social Competition model, human intelligence developed to a substantial level through a mixture of increasing dominance over the environment and the growing importance of social interactions. Consequently, the foremost selective pressure for increasing human intelligence changed from learning to mastering the natural world to competition for dominance among members or groups of its own species.

[Alexander (1989)](#ch13.xhtml#r010) views the evolution of human cognition as implicating the brain as a “social tool” suggesting that many human psychological changes serve primarily to contend with social relationships, with ecological constraints, such as hunting or extractive foraging, being a secondary cause of recent evolutionary change. According to [Geary and Huffman (2002)](#ch13.xhtml#r015) some human cognitive aptitudes, such as theory of mind (TOM) and language, are most easily understood in terms of social selection pressures, even if cognitive skills for interacting with the physical and biological worlds are evident as well. For example, language learning helps improve people’s thinking skills and memory abilities. Research has revealed that bilingual students tend to focus better, disregarding disruptions more effectively than those who are monolingual.

Alexander ([1971](#ch13.xhtml#r009)) and others argue that human social relationships are flexible and complex. They maintain that social success is challenging because it is very difficult to contemplate future moves of a social competitor–cooperator, and to execute suitable countermoves, with further complications owing to networks of several relationships, everchanging coalitions, and deceptiveness. Survival and reproduction within an ever-increasing intricate social structure gradually facilitated advanced social skills, communication of concepts that increasingly resulted in complex language patterns. Thus, competition gradually shifted from controlling the natural elements to influencing other humans. The consequence of this shift was the emergence of leadership or popular acceptance by having more advanced social skills to out manoeuvre other members of the group. Therefore, an individual with better social and communicative skills would be more easily selected.

However, while humans have changed over time and social relationships became more important, it is also evident that concurrently the human brain evolution included cellular, genetic, and circuitry transformation. For example, on a genetic level, humans have a modified gene that is linked to speech and language development and another gene that enables greater dendritic spine density which promotes greater neural connections. Moreover, on a cellular level, research has suggested that von Economo neurons (VENs) are more dominant in humans than other primates, which are associated with empathy, social awareness, and self-control. Moreover, on a circuitry level, studies have suggested that humans display a more complex mirror neuron system, a better link between the two major brain language processing regions, and a vocal control circuit that links the motor cortex and brain stem. The mirror neuron system has been shown to be related with social cognition, theory of mind, and empathy.

### **2.5.8** Group Selection Theory

Group selection theory involves the evolution of group-level modifications through a process of natural selection acting on groups as the focal units. This theory is a segment of a wider theory of multilevel selection, which acknowledges that natural selection can act across multiple levels of the biological hierarchy simultaneously. Group selection may also be viewed as a selection process in which behaviours evolve according to the fitness (survival and reproductive success) of groups or, mathematically, as selection in which overall group fitness is higher or lower than the mean of the individual members’ fitness values. Group selection theory maintains that organism features that impart benefits to a group (clan, tribe, or larger population) can develop regardless of the individual disadvantages that may be present. Thus, the benefits of intelligence bestowed to the group, including the capacity to communicate between individuals, language, the capability to teach others, and other cooperative aspects, have evident value in increasing the survival potential of a group.

This theory also supports Darwin’s theory of natural selection, namely that group-related adaptations must be attributed to the natural selection of alternative groups of individuals, and that the natural selection of alternative alleles (i.e., each of two or more alternative forms of a gene that arise by mutation and are found at the same place on a chromosome) within populations will be opposed to this development. Group-related adaptations and changes are viewed as a consequence of between-group selection as qualities, which transpire to be beneficial in relation to another group and will become increasingly popular and disseminated within a group, intensifying its overall likelihood of surviving a competing group. This theory is also linked to the social brain hypothesis that was discussed previously, which argues that human cognitive complexity arises as an outcome of a higher level of social complexity necessitated by living in enlarged groups. Additionally, these enlarged groups require a higher degree of social relations and interactions, that ultimately bring about an expanded quantity of intelligence in humans.

However, studies have shown that the size of a species’ brain can be better predicted by diet instead of measures of sociality. One needs to note that correlation between variables does not imply a causative measure. Therefore, many other factors associated with nutrition and diet could have been the cause for the appearance of modern human traits such as a larger brain and higher intelligence. Scientifically, it has been shown that diets deficient in iron, protein, iodine, zinc, B vitamins, omega 3 fatty acids, magnesium, and other nutrients either in the mother during pregnancy or in the child during development can result in lower intelligence. However, these may not necessarily influence the evolution of intelligence.

## **2.6** Conclusion

The purpose of this chapter was to illustrate that the evolution of the human being and associated intelligence is a very complex process that has been occurring for millions of years. Furthermore, it is a believed that this evolutionary process is continuing. Moreover, the evolutionary process of human intelligence is still a mystery. It is doubtful whether this mystery will be resolved. Many theories have been proposed but none have been proven with a very high degree of certainty. It appears that the evolution of human intelligence has been influenced by many variables, some of which are known, while others are still to be revealed.

This book is primarily focused on artificial intelligence, which is initially a human creation. However, it is argued that a profound appreciation of artificial intelligence cannot be experienced unless we also truly understand how the human being developed and how its intellect evolved. Hence, the objective of this chapter.

I tend to compare artificial intelligence and human intelligence through analogy, by comparing for instance, synthetic leather with natural leather. They both look and feel the same, but the real proof of the difference is the test of fire. Synthetic leather has its advantages and is less likely to crack, peel, stain, or fade from UV light but it is likely to be highly inflammable. Natural leather is highly resistant to ignition.

The human body and its brain can generate various chemicals and hormones that allow the human being to feel fear, anger, pain, sadness, joy, contentment, happiness, and love. The human brain experiences consciousness, passion, and allows a person to appreciate art, music, poetry, literature, drama, and acting. Artificial intelligence through robots may mimic various human senses, but they do not and can never feel the emotions that humans experience. Whilst reading Boris Pasternak’s book, *Doctor Zhivago*, which won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958, I was impressed by a particular paragraph (page 252) that describes what deep feelings a human may experience and that no artificial intelligence will feel: “What happiness it is to work from dawn to dusk for your family and yourself, to build a roof over their heads, to till the soil to feed them, to create your own world, like Robinson Crusoe, in imitation of the Creator of the universe, and to bring forth your life, as if you were your own mother, again and again.”

Another book which made a lasting impression regarding the experiences of human life is Robert Pirsig book published in 1974, *Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance: An Inquiry into Values*. This book is a narration of a summer motorcycle trip undertaken by a father and his son Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance becomes a personal and philosophical pilgrimage into essential questions on how to live. The book probes into the meaning of quality and the account of modern crisis caused by the absence of quality and how to reconcile the conflict between human’s value and technological needs, to achieve the eventual goal that enhances people’s happiness by awakening one’s inner nature, compassion, and wisdom.

Having said the above, the rest of this book will focus on artificial intelligence. It shall examine how AI evolved over the years, the tools and security systems that it utilises, its impact on the knowledge-based economy, the practical implication of AI, the ethical and legal considerations of AI, and the outlook for society in general in an AI dominated environment.
