# Chapter 3Evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-4](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-4)

> *“Someday, in the distant future, our grand-children’ s grand-children will develop a new equivalent of our classrooms. They will spend many hours in front of boxes with fires glowing within. May they have the wisdom to know the difference between light and knowledge.”*
> 
> Plato (Aristocles, son of Ariston)
> 
> *Greek philosopher (427–347 BC)*

AI is not new concept. In fact, the modern era of AI commenced at an academic conference held at Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire USA in 1956, when the term artificial intelligence was first used. However, the notion that the human brain can be automated is deeply rooted in civilization. [Roy (2023)](#ch14.xhtml#r031) argues that to accurately appreciate the history and evolution of artificial intelligence, one must go back to AI’s ancient roots, where AI begins not with computers and algorithms, but with the philosophical reflections of great thinkers. These great thinkers, include Aristotle who introduced syllogistic logic. Moreover, many ancient civilisations created human-like mechanisms that were thought to have reason and emotion. [Tucci (2021)](#ch14.xhtml#r032), maintains that by the first millennium B.C., philosophers throughout the ancient world were creating new approaches for formal reasoning. She argues that this effort extended over 2,000 years by various intellectuals that included not only philosophers but also theologians, mathematicians, engineers, economists, psychologists, computational scientists, and neurobiologists.

Roy contends that since the birth of the digital age, AI has experienced a remarkable evolution, starting with the first rudimentary programs of the 1950s to the sophisticated algorithms of today. In its embryonic stage, AI was just a series of simple rules and patterns but has now become a very complex and at times frightening development. Over time, AI has ventured into areas that were considered impractical or unattainable, but its capabilities have continuously grown, and its potential appears to be unlimited. The purpose of this chapter is to trace the history and evolution of AI and how it has developed into an awesome powerful instrument that cannot be ignored.

## **3.1** Introduction

A primary objective of AI (or Machine Learning) that is commonly stated, is to reduce the human workload. The objective related to reducing human workload was cited many decades ago when computerisation first commenced. Therefore, AI appears to be following the theme of the initial objective of computerisation. However, as the usage of AI has increased since 1956 when it was first mentioned, it has developed to such a degree that some view it as potentially reigning over human intelligence, and therefore a threat.

As one may appreciate, AI can be viewed as a substantial and complex topic. However, there are many aspects of AI that are straightforward, and AI’s implications become crystal clear. AI can be viewed as a systematic approach towards achieving an assigned task using a computer and associated application software. For instance, character recognition software can transcribe a text image into a text document, which can then be manipulated through additions, deletions, or amendments. Expert systems are another example of AI, where software can specifically focus on a particular subject or aspect, such as presenting a person with a set of specific health related questions and making a diagnosis of person’s physical condition. Furthermore, AI can accomplish an assigned task very quickly since it is integrated with specific hardware and application software that executes an algorithm that has a precise task. The speed at which AI functions depend on the efficiency of the algorithm and the power of the computer technology being used.

Whilst accuracy with the swiftest speed is a key feature of AI, it must be recognised that there have been cases where the AI application hallucinates and provides distorted responses, because it tries to provide the most probable reply and not necessarily the correct reply. [Table 3.1](#ch14.xhtml#t1) illustrates that an AI can be classified by its capability and functionality, with each classification being further subdivided. In terms of capability, only Narrow AI is currently available. General AI that is designed to reason, learn and understand complex concepts and Super AI, which is capable to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence are currently hypothetical and are not available in a practical environment. On a functionality level, Theory of Mind that allows an AI to interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans (e.g., self-drive cars) are currently at an experimental stage. Whereas self-awareness that permits an AI to have an independent intelligence and will not be under the control of the people that created it, is still at the conceptual stage.

**Table 3.1** Classification of AI by Capability and Functionality[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#t1b)

 
| **Capability** || **Definition** |
| --- | --- |
| General AI || General AI or Strong AI is designed to perform any intellectual task that a human can do. General AI is theoretically able to reason, learn, and understand complex concepts. However, this is not yet possible. |
| --- | --- |
| Narrow AI || Narrow AI or Weak AI is designed to do a specific task or a limited range of tasks. It is usually useful in applications like facial, speech, and image recognition; natural language processing; and recommendation systems. |
| Super AI || Super AI is able of exceeding human intelligence in all areas. However, it is a hypothetical AI that is not yet available. When available, it would be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities and would be able to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence. |
| **Functionality** || **Definition** |
| Reactive Machines || This is the simplest AI and does basic operations by reacting to some input with some output, without any learning occurring. This is the 1^(st) stage to any A.I. system. This type of AI does not store inputs nor performs learning. |
| Theory of Mind || Theory of Mind AI types are not available and are at an embryonic stage e.g., self-driving cars. This type of A.I is supposed to interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans. |
| Limited Theory || These types of A.I.’s are able to store historical data and/or predictions for making better predictions. Machine learning architecture for this type of AI is more complex. Every machine learning model needs limited memory to be created, but the model can get deployed as a reactive machine type. |
| Self-awareness || This is a long-term objective of AI in that it achieves enlightenment and becomes self-aware. A self-aware AI has an independent intelligence and will not be under the control of the people that created it. |

The AI types that are currently available have been applied in various industrial sectors to assist public and private enterprises to run successfully and achieve their defined targets. Currently the industry sectors that have adopted AI as a key performance component, include healthcare; banking; education; eCommerce; retail; transportation; entertainment; and fashion. These industries have implemented AI based on state-of-art technology where the capability of technology regulates a substantial portion of their workforce. The outcome of AI and its associated technology significantly decreases energy usage and makes it possible for humans to complete their work in the swiftest way possible. Hence, AI at this level complements human power and aids them to perform their functions in a safe environment. AI becomes potentially dangerous when it acts independently from those that created it. In other words, if an AI application remains under human control, its benefits would be enormous and safe. [Table 3.2](#ch14.xhtml#t2) provides some typical examples where AI is currently being applied.

**Table 3.2** Typical Examples Where AI is Currently Being Applied[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#t2b)

 
| **Type** || **Example** |
| --- | --- |
| Automation || This type of AI is mainly linked with applications that mitigate human inputs, such as process mechanisation, IT and business processes, and private usages. The key work at this level is to operate and control multiple systems and machinery in manufacturing industries. |
| --- | --- |
| Machine Learning || This is based on data usage applying an algorithm that follows a specific pattern to finish the task correctly. Data mining plays an essential role in Machine Learning and organises data for all types and size of entities. Data interpretation is through three variants: Supervised learning, Unsupervised learning, and Reinforcement learning. |
| Natural Language Processing or NLP || This assists in separating human and machine languages, such as in spam detection in a mailbox. It can distinguish the disparity as a result of text translation, analysis, and speech recognition. |
| Robotics || The usage of this technology has widened its application base to nearly all sectors (e.g., in restaurants for delivering food to customers at their tables). |

AI has some definite benefits for all types of entities, such as lessening the human workload and performing it at a faster rate. If used for suitable purposes it provides accurate results with zero error tolerance (however it needs to resolve the problem of hallucinating bots); and can perform multiple tasks effectively on a 24/7 basis. As discussed in [Chapter 1](#ch12.xhtml#c2), AI can provide many benefits as long as it remains under human control. The danger becomes evident if General AI and Super AI using Theory of Mind and Self-awareness functionality become common without adequate control. Furthermore, rogue users of AI, particularly at powerful private or public organisations can cause havoc, unless adequate safeguards are implemented at an international level. AI may imitate humans, but it can never have cognitive functions and natural skills. The previous chapter has illustrated that humans are exceedingly intelligent with natural and cognitive skills driven by ethical values founded by an emotional and social intellect. However, whilst most humans are honest and have a high level of civic duty, there is a very small minority that are not. It is these small minority that are a concern when applying AI.

One needs to remember that machines with sophisticated AI can be devious but with the current technology do not have the ability to think out of the box and create something new. However, humans have the supremacy to think ahead of their ingenuity and invent things to improve society. With current technology, an AI system only executes what the programmer has coded in the computer program. However, humans cannot be complacent because the danger looms as soon as General AI and Super AI using Theory of Mind and Self-awareness functionality become a reality. Therefore, regulatory measures at both national and international levels need to be defined and implemented now as a preventative strategy. Humans are the greatest intellectual creatures on this earth that are sociable, have feelings, and emotions. Recent history has shown that humans can control technology and generate outcomes for improved growth.

## **3.2** The History of Artificial Intelligence

As stated previously, the notion that the human brain can be automated is deeply rooted in civilisation, having its roots dating back to ancient times, where AI is initiated not with sophisticated algorithms, but with the great philosophical thinkers. To appreciate the history and evolution of AI it is appropriate to segment the historical timeline into three main categories, namely: the era of enlightened rational thinking; pre-to-World War II technology era; and post-World War II technology era. This broad classification of the developments that have taken place over the long and difficult journey of AI to its current position, features personages in the ancient history, underlining the evolution from early philosophical ideas to practical innovations in computation and automation.

### **3.2.1** Era of Enlightened Rational Thinking

The era of enlightened rational thinking is veiled by myths and legends dating back to many ancient cultures that built anthropomorphic androids that were believed to possess reason and emotion. [Table 3.3](#ch14.xhtml#t3) provides a summary of events that have influenced the era of enlightened rational thinking that form the foundation for the conceptual development of AI.

**Table 3.3** Summary of Events During the Era of Enlightened Rational Thinking[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#t3b)

 
| **Timeline** || **Example** |
| --- | --- |
| 4th Century – 3rd Century BC || Aristotle initiated syllogistic logic: One of the earliest deductive reasoning methods, setting the basis for logical thinking, a fundamental feature of AI. |
| --- | --- |
| 8-9th Century || Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī, Persian mathematician who initiated Arabic numerals and algebra, and created the words algorithm and algebra. |
| 13th Century || Spanish theologian Ramon Llull inventor of an “art of finding truth.” |
| 13th Century || Roger Bacon and Albert the Great built tools that looked like heads, known as “Talking Heads,” conversational interfaces. These devices likely aided in early tests to imitate human speech and interaction. |
| 14th Century || The “movable type” printing press boosted information dissemination. This invention helped to disperse knowledge that is crucial for AI development. |
| 15th Century || Invention of clocks: First modern measuring tool that gauged time exactly. This was vital for scientific and technological evolution, including AI. |
| 16th – 17th Century || René Descartes viewed animals as merely machines, thus promoting the philosophical notion of mechanizing living beings (“I think, therefore I am”). |
| 17th Century || Blaise Pascal invented the first computational digital calculating device. |
| 17th Century || Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz upgraded Pascal’s calculator with multiplication and division functions. |
| 17th Century || Sir Samuel Morland improved computational technology by through the invention of an arithmetical machine. |
| 17th Century || Thomas Hobbes’s book “The Leviathan” had mechanical and combinatorial theories of thinking. This laid the basis for studying the automatous aspects of thought processes. |
| 18th Century || Thomas Bayes’ Rule is a key law in data science because it explains the act of learning, which is a key concept in AI, particularly for machine learning. |
| 19th Century || Joseph-Marie Jacquard invented the first programmable device using thousands of punch cards laced together. Each row of punched holes corresponded to a row of a textile pattern. This device was a notable advancement in automation and control. |
| 19th Century || Mary Shelley in 1818 published the novel “Frankenstein” that deal with themes of artificial life and the consequences of creating sentient beings. |
| 19th Century || George Boole an English mathematician helped establish modern symbolic logic and whose algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, which is basic to the design of digital computer circuits. |

The first millennium B.C saw the emergence of the great thinkers in various regions of the world, such as Plato and his student Aristotle. They both contemplated the nature of human cognition and reasoning and contributed to the development of formal reasoning approaches. These philosophers studied the notion that the human thought process could be sub-divided into a series of logical steps, like a mathematical process. These early thinkers were over many centuries joined by other important contributors that included theologians, mathematicians, engineers, economists, psychologists, computational scientists, and neurobiologists. Plato and Aristotle initiated syllogistic logic, which is a form of deductive argument where the conclusion follows from the truth of two (or more) premises. Syllogistic logic is the formal analysis of rational terms and operators, and the structures that make it probable to infer true conclusions from given premises. This mode of reasoning set the foundation for what is known as symbolic AI. The concept of symbolic AI is based on the notion that human thought and reasoning can be represented using symbols and rules, which can be manipulated to simulate human intelligence. This idea is analogous to teaching a machine how to think like a person by using symbols to represent concepts and rules to manipulate them.

The Persian mathematician Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī who introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals, and algebra to European mathematicians has to this day made an impact on how computations are conducted. Mathematics using Roman numerals would be impossible because the highest number that can be expressed in Roman numerals is 3,999. The number 4,000 would have to be written as MMMM, which goes against the principle of not having four consecutive letters of the same type together. Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī wrote a treatise on Hindu-Arabic numerals with the Latin translation title of “Algoritmi de numero Indorum” that gave rise to the word algorithm in the English language. Another important contributor to rational thinking was the 13th-century Spanish theologian, Ramon Llull who is best known in the history of ideas as the inventor of an “art of finding truth” (ars inveniendi veritatis). His work was mainly aimed to support the Roman Catholic faith in missionary work but was also created to unify all branches of knowledge. The 13th century also witnessed the creation of “Talking Heads” that were devised by several persons. But Albert the Great and Roger Bacon are two of the most mentioned inventors regarding this invention. Saint Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1282 CE) is claimed to have worked for 30 years on making not just a head, but a man of brass. It was said that he cast together the qualities of his materials under certain constellations. Saint Thomas Aquinas, who was the disciple of Albert the Great and was claimed to have destroyed the mechanical brass head of Albert the Great and mocked the idea that a head or statue could be alive. Roger Bacon also a famous theologian who is claimed to have created a talking brazen head that could answer any question. The narrative appears in the anonymous 16th-century account of “The Famous History of Fryer Bacon” in which Bacon speaks with a demon. These devices are viewed as conversational interfaces that possibly aided in early tests to imitate human speech and interaction. Whether the accounts of the creation of brazen heads are accurate makes no difference. What is important is the fact that the notion of artificial creation that imitate human speech and interaction were envisaged during this period.

There is no doubt that one of the most important inventions, which had the greatest impact for the dissemination of knowledge and making it a highly accessible commodity, was the movable type printing press. The world’s first movable type printing technology for paper books is reported to have been made of porcelain materials and was invented around AD 1040 in China, and a book in 1193 during the Song dynasty documented the use of the copper movable type. The spread of these movable-type systems was mainly limited to East Asia. However, the greatest impact was that of around 1450 when a German goldsmith, Johannes Gutenberg introduced the metal movable-type printing press in Europe, together with advances in casting the type based on a matrix and hand mould. The smaller number of alphabetic characters needed for European languages was an advantage and Gutenberg was the first to create the type pieces from an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony, which remained the standard for about 550 years. The metal type pieces were more durable and produced uniform lettering contributing to high quality and relatively low price of printing. The printing press is viewed as a primary factor that promoted the Renaissance.

The 15th century witnessed a monumental breakthrough regarding the mechanical clock. This was a leap forward, particularly the one built by Henry de Vick at around 1360. However, a significant innovation regarding the mechanical clock was the introduction of the mainspring in the early 15th century, which allowed small clocks to be built for the first time. These clocks measured time accurately, which was of vital importance for technology and scientific experiments. Another important event was the notion that animals were merely machines that was posited by the French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes, who lived during the 16th and 17th century. Descartes believed that all material bodies, including the human body, are machines that operate by mechanical principles. His ideas promoted the philosophical notion of mechanising living beings. Descartes’ notion was not about computational power but about the idea of creating artificial beings with a body autonomous from the soul. Hence, his idea conceptually supports artificial intelligence with the possibility of creating machines that learn from experience, adjust to new inputs, and perform human-like tasks.

The 17th century brought with it a mixture of ideas and inventions. Blaise Pascal was a French philosopher, mathematician, physicist, and inventor. He laid the foundation for the modern theory of probabilities and invented the first digital calculator to assist his father, who was a tax collector. Working for three years, he created a device called the Pascaline, which resembled the mechanical calculator of the 1940s. In recognition of his early computing machine, the computer language Pascal was named after him. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, a German philosopher, mathematician, and logician, invented differential, and integral calculus independently from Sir Isaac Newton and the principles of binary computers based on bits. He improved Pascal’s calculator with the multiplication and division functions.

Another influential figure regarding technology during the 17th century was Sir Samuel Morland who was an English academic, inventor, and mathematician (apart from being a diplomat and spy). He improved Pascal’s calculator and computational technology through his mechanical calculating device. Morland designed three types of a compact calculating machine: one for addition; one for the addition of money; and one for trigonometry. London craftsmen and instrument maker Humphrey Adamson is most likely to have physically constructed these machines. The device was made from brass, and the calculations were displayed on its face, using small, thin, mechanical wheels that turned on the application. Despite the lightweight, and precise nature of these arithmetic machines, they did not market well, being generally described as pretty but not very useful. A different but imaginative philosophical idea was that of Thomas Hobbes in his book *The Leviathan*. A great deal of Leviathan examines how human beings might exist outside of civil society, without government. Hobbes refers to the imagined condition of human life external to civil condition as “the state of nature.” The Leviathan had mechanical and combinatorial theories of thinking that provides the systematic steps in solving a problem based on cognitive styles. This book may be viewed as setting the basis for studying the automatous aspects of thought processes.

The 18th century also revealed some remarkable inventive individuals. Thomas Bayes, a clergyman, and mathematician set out his theory of probability in 1764. His theorem, in probability theory is a means for revising predictions considering relevant evidence, also known as conditional probability or inverse probability. However, Bayes’ Rule is a key and critical rule in data science because it describes how to update a belief, given some evidence. In other words, it explains the act of learning, which is a key concept in AI, particularly for machine learning. Joseph-Marie Jacquard who was a French weaver and merchant in 1801 invented a simplified method by which complex textiles such as damask were woven using thousands of punch cards laced together, with each row of punched holes corresponded to a row of a textile pattern. His invention is viewed as being the first programmable device, which was a notable advancement in automation and process control. Using the same principle, Herman Hollerith a German American statistician, invented the tabulating machine that was an electromechanical machine designed to aid in summarising information stored on punched cards, which was created to assist the processing of data for the 1890 U.S. Census. This was the precursor to the first generation of computers that used punched cards as an input and output device (for storing and printing data). Another important development during the 19th century was when George Boole an English mathematician helped to create modern symbolic logic, whose algebra of logic is now called Boolean algebra. It should be noted that Boolean algebra is a basic concept for designing of digital computer circuits.

However, the description of this era cannot be finalised without mentioning the creative and imaginative work of Mary Shelly in 1818 in her book “Frankenstein.” This book deals with themes of artificial life and the consequences of creating sentient beings. While AI holds the potential to revolutionise the lives of human beings either positively or negatively, the dark reverberations of Victor Frankenstein’s oversights provide a bleak reminder for the need of having ethical frameworks and interdisciplinary collaboration, which would ensure that AI remains a dominant influence for good. [Patowary (2023)](#ch14.xhtml#r029) argues that in the ever-evolving landscape of technology, AI has emerged as a revolutionary force that continues to shape various aspects of people’s lives. He contends that Mary Shelley’s magnum opus, Frankenstein, published nearly two centuries ago, remains an enduring cautionary tale about the perils of unchecked ambition and the consequences of playing God. The book *Frankenstein* reveals that Victor Frankenstein’s relentless pursuit of creating life, serves only to be haunted by the unforeseen horrors of his creation, and has resonated across generations ([Patowary, 2023)](#ch14.xhtml#r029). He argues that this tale of an individual’s excessive pride or self-confidence, raises moral dilemmas, and the intricate relationships between creator and creation continues to transcend time, finding a striking resonance in contemporary discussions on AI and its potential implications.

### **3.2.2** 20th Century: Pre-to-World WarII Technology Era

Whilst the era of enlightened rational thinking established the foundation for logical reasoning and other significant mathematical discoveries, the early to mid-20th century was the birth of the electro-mechanical computer. Although, it was in the 20th century that the concept of AI really began, the initiation of electro-mechanical computers and later the advancement of electronic computers, marked a fundamental turning point. [Table 3.4](#ch14.xhtml#t4) illustrates the important innovations that affected the development of AI during this period.

**Table 3.4** Summary of Events During the 20th Century Pre-to-World War II Technology Era[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#t4b)

 
| **Timeline** || **Example** |
| --- | --- |
| 1921 || Karel Čapek used the word robot in his play “RUR” (Rossum’s Universal Robots). This play contributed to promoting the concept of artificial beings. |
| --- | --- |
| 1936 || Z1 was a motor-driven mechanical computer designed by German Civil Engineer Konrad Zuse. It was a binary electrically driven calculator with limited programmability, reading instructions from punched celluloid film. Its programmable ability was later improved by the Z2 and Z3 models. |
| 1937 || The Atanasoff Berry Computer, later named the ABC, was conceived in 1937 by physics professor Dr. John Vincent Atanasoff and his graduate student, Clifford Berry at Iowa State University. It was designed specifically to solve systems of linear equations and was successfully tested in 1942. |
| 1943 || Colossus the code-breaking computer. It was created during the Second World War to decipher critical strategic messages between the most senior German Generals in occupied Europe. Its existence was only revealed in the mid-1970s. |
| 1943 || Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts are often credited with the invention of the artificial neural network and were a vital influence on the invention of the modern digital computer. |
| 1945 || ENIAC was the world’s first general-purpose programmable electronic digital computer but was not designed with parallel processing capabilities. |

Human beings have always been fascinated by artificial beings. In 1920, Czech writer Karel Čapek wrote the science-fiction play “R.U.R.” which is an abbreviation for Rossumovi Univerzální Roboti. The world premiere of the play was held on 2 January 1921 in Hradec Králové, where the word “robot” was introduced to the English language and generally linked to the science fiction domain. The word “robot” is derived from the Czech language meaning forced labour. In the play, Čapek visualises a future world where robots become the world’s workers that serve and replace humans. He portrays a revolt by the robots that eventual annihilate humans. The play deliberates on what it means to be a human being and the purpose of human life. The play conveys a cautionary message and implicates a scientist named Rossum, who discovers the secret of creating humanlike machines. Rossum’s universal robots are mass produced by other Robots on assembly lines. The idealistic Helena Glory, President of The Humanity League, thinks that Robots have (or are developing) souls, and feels that they should be freed. However, she burns Rossum’s manuscript that describes how to make robots due to her views about the infertility of human women. Čapek portrays robots as having two characteristics, namely that they had outer appearance of men and that they had the ability to think and were devoid of human weaknesses.

The work of Karel Čapek was science-fiction. However, the Z1, a motor-driven mechanical computer designed by German Civil Engineer Konrad Zuse in 1936, was far from being an imaginary object. The Z1 was a binary electrically driven mechanical device with limited programmability, reading instructions from punched celluloid films. It was later improved as a Z2 model by 1940. The Z2 was an electromechanical digital computer with an improved arithmetic and control logic with 600 electrical relay circuits, weighing over 600 pounds. The Z2 could read 64 words from punch cards and in contrast to the Z1, used 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic instead of 22-bit floating point. The Z2 was demonstrated to members of the German Aviation Research Institute (Deutsche Versuchsanstalt für Luftfahrt known as DVL), today known as DLR (The German Aerospace Centre), which is the national centre for aerospace, energy, and transportation research of Germany. The Z2 was upgraded by Konrad Zuse 1941 to the Z3 model. The Z3 was the world’s first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer built with 2,600 relays, implementing a 22-bit word length that operated at a clock frequency of about 5–10 Hz.

In 1998, a replica of the Z3 was tested and found to be in principle a Turing-complete devise, which is an important concept in computer science. A system is Turing complete if it can simulate the activities of a Turing machine, which signifies that the system can perform any computation that is theoretically possible. The Z3 lacked direct conditional branching, but it sustained this definition by speculatively computing all possible outcomes of a calculation. Konrad Zuse has often been viewed as the inventor of the computer, without which AI (and many other concepts) could not become possible.

Another contender for the title as the father of the computer is physics professor Dr. John Vincent Atanasoff from Iowa State University. In 1937, he and his graduate student, Clifford Berry conceived and built the Atanasoff Berry Computer, later named the ABC. The ABC was specifically created to solve linear equations systems and was successfully tested in 1942. It was conceived as a parallel computer with the ability of solving 30 simultaneous operations. The ABC is viewed as the first automatic electronic digital computer. This is contrary to what was commonly understood that the first electronic digital computers were the Colossus, built in England in 1943, and the ENIAC, built in the United States in 1945. However, the ABC’s technology is rather obscure because it was not programmable, nor Turing-complete. Many consider the ABC as the first electronic arithmetic logic unit (ALU), which is an essential integrated unit into every modern processor’s design. Work on the device, particularly the intermediate result storage mechanism and the paper card writer/reader, was terminated due to other Atanasoff’s World War II assignments. The ABC is viewed as pioneering vital principles of modern computing, including binary arithmetic and electronic switching elements. However, its specialised single purpose quality and lack of programmability in terms of a changeable stored program, differentiate it from modern computers. The ABC was designated as an electrical and electronic engineering (IEEE) milestone in 1990 because it contributed to the advancement of the modern computer.

The Colossus is viewed as being the world’s first programmable electronic digital computer. However, it was not a general-purpose computer but was specifically designed to break the German Lorenz cipher. This computer was proposed by General Post Office (GPO) research telephone engineer Tommy Flowers to solve a problem posed by mathematician Max Newman at the Government Code and Cypher School (GC&CS) at Bletchley Park (headquarters for Allied codebreaking). A working prototype Colossus Mark 1 was demonstrated in December 1943 and was commissioned at Bletchley Park by early 1944. The Colossus Mark 2 model was commissioned on 1 June 1944 just in time for the Normandy landings on D-Day and applied shift registers to quintuple the processing speed. This enhancement meant that its operating speed of 5,000 characters per second, which analysed over 100 messages a week was boosted to an astonishing processing speed 25,000 characters per second. It used around 2,500 thermionic valves and was more than two metres tall, to perform Boolean and counting operations. The Colossi computers permitted the Allies to process an enormous volume of high-level military intelligence by intercepting radiotelegraphy messages between the German High Command and their army commands throughout occupied Europe. Alan Turing’s application of probability in cryptanalysis is likely to have influenced its design but he did not design Colossus. It is often viewed by many as being the birth of modern-day computing and its presence was kept secret until the mid-1970s. The Colossus was a vital intelligence gathering machine, which is the basis for AI systems.

An important milestone that influenced the design of the modern digital computer was the work of American neurophysiologist and cybernetician Warren McCulloch and logician and cognitive psychologist Walter Pitts. In 1943, they published a paper “A Logical Calculus of the ideas Imminent in Nervous Activity.” This was the first mathematical model of a neural network. Their paper described how neurons might work by modelling a simple neural network using electrical circuits. They extended the concepts of Alan Turing’s thoughts in his paper “On Computable Numbers.” Furthermore, they specified an approach describing how the brain functions in abstract terms and illustrated how simple elements connected in a neural network can have immense computational power. The McCulloch–Pitt neuron illustrated the binary activation of “1” ON or “0” OFF, which meant that it either discharges with an activation “1” or does not discharge with an activation of “0”. If the activation value is greater than “0”, then the connected path is said to be in an excitatory state else it is known as being in an inhibitory state. The concern with the McCulloch-Pitts neuron concept was its simplicity, since it only permitted for binary inputs and outputs. Their paper did not attract appropriate attention until their ideas were applied by John von Neumann (mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics and Game theory) and Norbert Wiener (the initiator of cybernetics, and the science of communication as it relates to living things and machines), amongst others. The work of Von Neumann and Wiener are fundamental to some key concepts of AI.

However, the world’s first general-purpose programmable electronic digital computer was the ENIAC, which was completed in 1945 but a little too late for World War II usage. The ENIAC was not designed with parallel processing capabilities but is considered important historically, because it established the foundations for the modern electronic computing industry. At its time, the ENIAC showed that high-speed digital computing was possible using the available vacuum tube technology of the 1940s. One must note that programming the ENIAC computer was a complex, manual process that could take days. It was Turing-complete and capable of solving a broad range of numerical problems through reprogramming. Although there were other computers that had various combinations of computational features, the ENIAC had them all in one device.

The ENIAC machine was programmed by rewiring the connections between functional units in the machine, which was a long and tedious process. This was its weakness because it took days to rewire it for every new problem. However, the ENIAC was the most powerful calculating device built at that period. ENIAC had no central memory, it had a series of 20 accumulators that operated as computational and storage devices, with each accumulator storing one signed 10-digit decimal number. By the time the ENIAC was completed, the war was over. It cost almost eight times its original budget of $61,000 and was declared no longer fit for purpose. In November 1946, the ENIAC was shut down but was refurbished with a memory upgrade in July 1947. The upgraded model was extensively used during the Cold War on projects that required calculations for the design of a hydrogen bomb. The ENIAC was replaced by EDVAC (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer), which was built by the Moore School of Electrical Engineering, Pennsylvania. The EDVAC was commissioned at the Ballistic Research Laboratory in 1949, which became a part of the US Army Research Laboratory in 1952. The ENIAC and its successors provided the processing power and paved the way to truly programmable computers making use of computer languages. Thus, making it possible for the development of systems that AI is much dependent on.

### **3.2.3** 20th Century: Post-World War II Technology Era

The post-World War II technology era witnessed an exponential growth in computer technology development and associated operating and application software. According to [Wagner (2019)](#ch14.xhtml#r033) the ever-evolving goal of creating artificial intelligence has fascinated computer scientists for decades. She argues that whether it’s a machine capable of human thought or simply an algorithm capable of solving the game of chess, theories, possible solutions and predictions continue to attract widespread attention. She contends that while it is no longer questionable that computers have much higher capabilities when it comes to processing logic, the question as to whether computers will one day be able to feel like humans remains unanswered.

[Table 3.5](#ch14.xhtml#t5) shows some of the key advances that have influenced the development of AI during this period. In 1950, Alan Turing published his paper, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” that presented the Turing test for measuring machine intelligence. The Turing Test focused on the computer’s capacity to deceive interviewers into believing that its responses to their questions were made by a human being. The Turing Test was a technique used to verify whether a computer can display human intelligence. Thus, if a computer could participate in a conversation with a human being without being detected as a computer, it has demonstrated human intelligence. To pass any of the Turing tests, a device had to have a broad experience of the world, a vivid imaginary capability, and an emotional routine. The test assumed that no sequence of pre-programmed responses was likely to be convincing over an extended period. The significance of this development is the concept of the attempting to equate a computer with a human being through mimicking human intelligence.

**Table 3.5** Summary of Events During the 20th Century Post World War II Technology Era[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#t5b)

 
| **Timeline** || **Example** |
| --- | --- |
| 1950 || Alan Turing releases his paper, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” that presents the Turing test for measuring machine intelligence. |
| --- | --- |
| 1950 || Claude Shannon wrote the book “Programming a computer to play chess” that had a detailed analysis of how to play chess leading the way for using computers in game-playing and AI. |
| 1950 || Isaac Asimov published the ethical guidelines “Three Laws of Robotics” for the behaviour of robots and artificial beings that is influential in AI ethics. |
| 1955 || The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence is viewed as the birth of AI a separate field of scientific research. |
| 1956 || John McCarthy formally uses the term “artificial intelligence” at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project conference. |
| 1957 || The perceptron a basic building block of the neural network, was invented by Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, Buffalo, New York. |
| 1966 || Cessation of the machine translation project due to poor outcomes is first “AI winter,” denoting a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research. |
| 1969 || Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert criticise the perceptron model of Frank Rosenblatt in their book, “Perceptrons.” They provided a mathematical analysis showing the limits of a class of computing machines that could be considered as models of the brain leading to a decline in research on neural networks. |
| 1974 || Paul Werbos initiates the backpropagation algorithm for training neural networks. This supervised learning algorithm is essential for the most powerful machine learning models today. |
| 1980s || Acceptance of expert systems that are knowledge-based AI systems, with Lisp programming being also commonly used for AI research. |
| 1982 || Japan launches the 5^(th) Generation Computer Project that aims to develop a new generation of computers to understand and use human language. |
| 1986 || David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams present a new era of neural computation research through their book, “Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition.” |
| Early 1990s || AI marginalised because expert systems failed to meet expectations. |
| Late 1990s || Acceptance of support vector machines with supervised learning grows and neural networks decline. |
| 2000s || New machine learning algorithms begin to solve a wide range of problems. |

In 1950, continued the theme of applying the computer to mimic human intelligence. As early as 1949 Claude Shannon, an American mathematician and Nobel prize winner, published a paper “Programming a computer to play Chess,” which established the theoretical groundwork for generations of researchers to come. However, it was not until 1950 that he provided a detailed analysis of how to play chess against a human. Shannon liked playing a game of chess in his free time and was capable of lasting for 42 moves against one of the most highly regarded chess players in the world. It was likely that his proficiency and interest stimulated his passion for constructing a superhuman algorithm. However, it was Alan Turing, a year later, that created the first computer chess playing algorithm that was limited because the hardware at the time lacked the necessary processing power. The work by these two scientists paved the way for using computers in game-playing and AI.

Also in 1950, Isaac Asimov published the ethical guidelines “Three Laws of Robotics” for the behaviour of robots and artificial beings. These rules basically were meant to initiate a debate on ethical issues concerning artificial creations. Isaac Asimov was an American writer and professor of biochemistry at Boston University, who is deemed to be one of the big three science fiction writers, along with Robert A. Heinlein and Arthur C. Clarke. He is credited with writing or editing more than 500 books. Isaac Asimov’s “Three Laws of Robotics” are namely, that a robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm; a robot must obey orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law; and a robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. Although science fiction, Asimov’s robot stories explore moral values and sociological habits and have implications for our present epoch. For instance, a robot or in a wider sense an automatic device would do well to abide by these rules. However, such generic rules are continually being violated. Smart bombs and cruise missiles are automatic devices that violate the first and third laws. Computers and technologies operated by computers function according to what they are programmed to do and, will hurt humans if programmed to do so, or if humans get in their way as they are executing their programs. Hence, the Isaac Asimov’s robotics laws probe philosophical-moral issues that are applicable today more than ever when one considers the potential power of AI and its ability to control many systems and devices.

However, it was 1955 that the word artificial intelligence was used to promote a conference to specifically discuss AI. In August 1955, John McCarthy, Dartmouth College; Marvin Minsky, Harvard University; Nathaniel Rochester, I.B.M. Corporation; and Claude Shannon, Bell Telephone Laboratories proposed a two-month, ten-man study of artificial intelligence to be conducted during the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. Their proposal stated that the study is to proceed based on the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it. They contended that an attempt will be made to and how to make machines use language, form abstractions and concepts, solve all kinds of problems now reserved for humans, and improve themselves. They expressed their opinion that a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer ([McCarthy et al., 1955](#ch14.xhtml#r028)).

The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence is viewed as the birth of AI as a separate field of scientific research. Their proposal was accepted and in the summer of 1956 the Dartmouth Summer Research Project conference was held, where John McCarthy formally applies the term “artificial intelligence.” The conference was sponsored by the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). Also in attendance, were Oliver Selfridge an innovator in early computer science and artificial intelligence; Allen Newell, a computer scientist; and Herbert A. Simon, an economist, political scientist, and cognitive psychologist. At the Dartmouth conference Newell and Simon presented their groundbreaking Logic Theorist, which was a computer program capable of proving certain mathematical theorems and was referred to, as the first AI program.

Because of the Dartmouth conference, technology frontrunners anticipated that the development of a thinking machine that could learn and understand to mimic human intelligence was imminent, which resulted in drawing major government and industry support. The direct effect of the 1955 Dartmouth conference was the sponsorship of well-funded basic research for almost 20 years that generated significant advances in AI. Examples of this research include the General Problem Solver (GPS) algorithm released in the late 1950s, which established the basis for developing more complex cognitive architectures; the Lisp computer language for AI programming that is still in use today; and ELIZA, an early natural language processing (NLP) program that paved the way for today’s chatbots.

A key development occurred in 1957 when Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, Buffalo, New York introduced the “perceptron”, which is viewed as a basic building block of the neural network. A demonstration of the “perceptron” was given by the U.S. Office of Naval Research in 1958, where an IBM 704, which was a five-ton computer the size of a room, was inputted with a sequence of punch cards, and after 50 test cycles, the computer taught itself to distinguish cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. Rosenblatt claimed that the “perceptron” was the first machine that could create an original idea. In 1958, Rosenblatt contended that society was about to witness the birth of a machine capable of perceiving, recognising, and identifying its surroundings without any human training or control ([Lefkowitz, 2019](#ch14.xhtml#r026)). Rosenblatt was inspired by the way neurons work together in the brain, giving him the idea for the “perceptron.” The “perceptron” is a single-layer neural network algorithm that arranges input into two possible categories. The neural network makes a guess, for instance, right or left; or dog or cat, and if its guess is wrong, it corrects itself to make a more informed guess the next time around. The neural network algorithm becomes progressively more accurate over thousands or millions of iterations. The perceptron was the first neural network and established the principles for the concept of machine learning.

However, Rosenblatt’s concept attracted sceptics who maintained that the perceptron was not able to remodel the relationship between human and machine. The general outcome was that enthusiasm regarding AI and its potential diminished along with the required funding. One of the first casualties was the cessation of the machine translation project in 1966 due to poor outcomes. This project was driven by visions of high-speed high-quality translation of arbitrary texts, particularly those that interested the military and intelligence communities, who financially supported the machine translation projects quite heavily. However, disappointment regarding this project resulted because of the linguistic problems complexity being encountered that required time and more finance to resolve. In 1966 the National Academy of Sciences ALPAC report criticised the field and, indirectly, those who were working on the project. The ALPAC report was itself condemned as being narrow-minded, biased, and short-sighted. However, the report’s recommendations were accepted, except for increased expenditures for long-term research in computational linguistics. This resulted in the machine translation projects being cancelled everywhere.

Marvin Minsky who was MIT professor regarding neural networks research was very cynical of Rosenblatt’s claims about perceptron’s viability. Minsky doubted whether computers could be programmed to visualise and understand language because the functions depicted by Rosenblatt’s perceptron were just too simple. The concern was that Rosenblatt’s perceptron had only one layer, while modern neural networks have millions. Rosenblatt was working on a unique project with no history, and therefore, did not have adequate knowledge to train networks with multiple layers. However, researchers today, in hindsight, view his algorithm as still being fundamental for training today’s deep networks. In 1969, Minsky and Seymour Papert published the book *Perceptrons* that literally thrashed Rosenblatt’s work and, effectively discredited it. They provided a mathematical analysis showing the limits of a class of computing machines that could be considered as models of the brain leading to a decline in research on neural networks. To make matters worse for Rosenblatt, the following year, Minsky won the A.M. Turing Award, which was computing’s highest honour. The perceptron’s rise and its fall due to the criticism by Minsky and Papert, amongst other concerns, helped to bring about an era known as the first “AI winter,” lasting from 1974 to 1980. During this time, government and corporations backed away from their support of AI research and financing for AI research withered.

On a humanistic note, Rosenblatt referred to Minsky as the loyal opposition and never seemed bitter, even after losing hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in government funds; he was particularly sorry for his colleagues and for his students ([Lefkowitz, 2019](#ch14.xhtml#r026)). Rosenblatt’s “Mark I perceptron” now resides at the Smithsonian Institution, and in 2004, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers established the IEEE Frank Rosenblatt Award ([Lefkowitz, 2019](#ch14.xhtml#r026)). Many academics believe that Rosenblatt’s principles underlying the perceptron assisted to trigger the modern AI revolution, particularly regarding deep learning and neural networks, which can classify online images and enable language translation that are currently transforming society. Rosenblatt died in a sailing accident in 1971 on his 43rd birthday without seeing the thawing of the first AI winter.

Despite the AI winter, in 1974, Paul Werbos an American social scientist and machine learning pioneer, submitted his dissertation regarding the Back-propagation algorithm for training neural networks, which solved the XOR problem and in general made neural networks learning more efficient. The XOR, or “exclusive or,” problem is a classic problem of using a neural network to predict the outputs of XOR logic gates given two binary inputs. An XOR function should return a true value if the two inputs are not equal and a false value if they are equal. Initially, the term “back-propagating error correction” was pioneered by Frank Rosenblatt in 1962. However, he did not know how to apply it even though a continuous precursor of backpropagation was already being used in the context of control theory. Backpropagation normally refers to the entire learning algorithm. It aims to prevent redundant calculations of intermediate terms in the chain rule, which is normally derived through dynamic programming and is important for multilayer perceptrons. One should recall that multilayer perceptrons was a major weakness with Rosenblatt’s model. Werbos’ development is significant because a supervised learning algorithm is essential for the most powerful machine learning models today.

The 1970s and 1980s witnessed several key developments in expert systems and natural language processing. Of particular significance was the research of the 1980s regarding deep learning techniques and the general acceptance by the industry of Edward Feigenbaum’s expert systems, which mimicked the decision-making process of a human expert. Edward Feigenbaum, a computer science professor at Stanford University and founder of Stanford’s Knowledge Systems Laboratory, jointly with Raj Reddy, pioneered the design and construction of large-scale AI systems, exhibiting the practical importance and potential commercial impact of AI technology. Their program would request an expert in a field how to respond in an assumed circumstance, and once this was learned for practically every situation, non-experts could receive advice from that program. These expert systems were commonly used in various industries. During this time, the Lisp programming continued to improve and was also commonly used for AI research. The first version of Lisp was created by John McCarthy in 1959 at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and was written for the IBM 704 mainframe using punched cards.

Along its journey, AI encountered many challenges, a major one being the “frame problem.” Simply put, the “frame problem” is about how AI systems can understand and process the world around them. For instance, one may describe the characteristics of an object to an AI system. However, a problem is encountered when not all the characteristics are described or are known at that time. Hence, a difficulty develops in that the AI system would not specifically know these missing characteristics, and it also does not know that it has a limited knowledge about them. Therefore, the challenge for AI systems is to understand that they might be missing additional information. The human learning process is not just to learn facts but also to recognise and learn trends, patterns, relationships, and context. This is why the human thought process is so complex. This human learning process permits us to bridge the gaps when we come across new information. However, the early AI systems did not have this ability; so even as they improved their ability to process information, they still had a difficulty with this frame problem. Hence, the early AI systems could not recognise that their knowledge was incomplete, which therefore, limited their capacity to learn and adjust, thus posing a key barrier for AI advancement.

To resolve this dilemma, AI developers introduced “slots” (or windows) for knowledge that permitted an AI system to realise that it did not have all the information about an object or, a certain topic and introduced “scripts” or “frames” to stand for the standard sequence of events in a particular situation. This enabled the AI system to bridge the information gaps and anticipate what might transpire. This method allowed an AI system to make advances in resolving the frame problem. However, AI systems are still not sophisticated enough to compare with the flexibility and adaptability of the human intellect. The success of Edward Feigenbaum’s expert systems and others inspired a new period of AI interest that attracted significant financing during the 1980s. Hence, in the early 1980s, Japan and the United States boosted funding for AI research, which assisted in reviving it. AI systems through vastly improved expert systems, ultimately exhibited the true value of AI research by producing real-world business-applicable and value-generating systems. The first expert system, known as XCON was commissioned and used by Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC). XCON was a sizeable system, containing about 750 rules. While it could construct and execute the numerous orders submitted to it, it still necessitated expansion and sophistication by DEC before it, could become the reliable system that it is today. At that time the system was estimated to generate over $40 million in profit for DEC each year.

Technological progress, that facilitated AI development continued and in 1982 Japan launched the 5th Generation Computer Project that aimed to develop a new generation of computers to understand and use human language. This project was a ten-year programme with an investment of about $400 million that was initiated by Japan’s Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) to produce computers making extensive use of parallel processing and logic programming. The project was to deliver a computer with supercomputer-like performance and to provide a platform for future developments in artificial intelligence. This 1980s project is viewed as being ahead of its time, but its extreme ambitious goals led to commercial failure. However, it was the origin of concurrent logic programming that inspired a talented generation of engineers and scientists. The initial failure of the 5th generation computer project and the failure of expert systems to meet expectation are likely to have led to the second AI winter that lasted until the mid-1900s, until innovative progress on neural networks, and the advent of big data boosted the current resurgence of AI.

As Ashleigh Brilliant an English-born American author and cartoonist said, “You can’t stop progress, but you can help decide what is progress and what isn’t.” During the so called second AI winter, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams in 1986 introduced a new era of neural computation research through their book, “Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition.” Basically, their publication promoted backpropagation and illustrated how it could be used to train multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). The Backpropagation, or backward propagation algorithm is intended to test for errors working back from output nodes to input nodes, and is a vital mathematical tool for improving the accuracy of predictions in data mining and machine learning using experience. Their paper is viewed as groundbreaking in the development of neural networks and helped to renew interest during the AI winter. These researchers also focused on the specific shortcomings of neural networks that were highlighted by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert in their 1969 book “Perceptrons” that discredited Rosenblatt’s neural network model. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams showed that backpropagation could be used to train perceptrons to solve these problems, thus largely justifying Rosenblatt’s original neural network model. Currently, backpropagation is the most widely used method for training neural networks because it is a robust and flexible technique that can be exploited to resolve a wide variety of problems.

Despite the absence of government funding the momentum for AI development continued to grow. In the 1990s, AI was maturing and evolving rapidly with the introduction of new approaches such as improved neural networks and machine learning. This secured acceptance, particularly with the robust resolution of the frame problem. Support vector machines (SVM) gained popularity due to their machine learning algorithm that utilised supervised learning models to solve complex classification, regression, and outlier detection problems by performing optimal data transformations that determine boundaries between data points based on predefined classes, labels, or outputs.

One must distinguish between machine learning and neural networks. Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence and refers to computers that learn from data without being explicitly programmed. Neural networks are a specific type of machine learning model, with many interconnected nodes that process information and make decisions being modelled to mimic the human brain. The fundamental concept regarding neural networks is that their learning capabilities are acquired from data to improve their performance over time. They have advanced to be exceptionally good at pattern recognition, that enable them to be used for image recognition, natural language processing, and similar tasks. Therefore, an AI system with machine learning capability neural network contains algorithms that learn and continually improve their performance. As one may imagine, having neural networks with these machine learning capabilities results in having a very powerful and awesome capacity. As neural networks and machine learning algorithms became more advanced, they began to outperform humans at certain tasks. For instance, in 1997, a chess playing computer program called Deep Blue was able to defeat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. This was a key milestone for AI, because it demonstrated in a practical sense that computers could outperform humans at a task that required complex reasoning and strategic thinking.

One needs to recognise that machine learning algorithms absorb enormous amounts of data and can identify patterns in that data to make predictions or classifications. Hence, machine learning became a key feature in the evolution of AI because it permitted AI systems to learn and adjust without needing to be explicitly programmed for every possible situation. It is this machine learning capability that has permitted AI to become an all-purpose flexible utility. It is this capability that allowed Dragon Systems in 1997 to develop speech recognition software that was implemented on Windows, and which was viewed as a huge leap forward in the challenge towards spoken language interpretation. This development means that all the knowledge about the world does not need to be hard coded into the system, since neural networks and machine learning algorithms are able learn from data and continually improve their performance. The outcome is that these AI systems can handle new situations and make inferences that were not explicitly programmed into them.

In the 2000s, AI has continued to advance in many different fields, with new machine algorithms beginning to solve a wide range of problems. In the early 2000s, AI systems significantly improved at language translation, and image captioning that generated textual description of an image. They even became better at answering questions that later advanced to Chatbots. Moreover, the 2010s witnessed the rise of deep learning, a more advanced form of machine learning that allowed AI to tackle even more complex tasks. These deep neural networks attain advanced results, including image recognition, natural language processing, and machine translation. Deep learning allowed AI to start making advances in fields like speech recognition, image classification, and self-driving cars.

The 2010s and 2020s saw further progressive developments in the AI language models. However, it was in the late 2010s that AI language models advanced to the sophistication level that is currently being experienced. Initially, the 2010s AI systems were focused on features such as image recognition, natural language processing, and machine translation. However, by the late 2010s and early 2020s, language models like GPT-3 started to make headways in the AI world by generating text that closely imitated human writing. Chat Bots and GPT models made enormous headways in the industry. These language models could even write in different styles, from formal, casual, and humorous, providing new opportunities for the application of AI. AI has moved away from just high-speed computations and pattern recognition. It could now generate creative content that is comparable with human writers. However, AI developers still have several challenges to be resolved, such as overcoming Chatbot hallucinations and other similar weaknesses.

Whilst the future of AI will be discussed in a separate chapter, it is appropriate to provide a brief outlook of the potential future developments. Research indicates that the next stage in the development of AI is what is referred to as “Artificial General Intelligence” or AGI. The AGI systems are viewed as being capable of performing any intellectual task that can be performed by a human being. This the opposite to “narrow AI” of the 2010s, which could execute only specific tasks. Hence, the objective of AGI is to generate AI systems that can learn, adapt, and act like humans, to conduct a wide scope of tasks. The development of AGI appears to be taking two main approaches, namely symbolic AI, and neural network-based AI. Symbolic AI systems apply logic and reasoning to resolve problems, while neural network-based AI systems mimic the human brain and apply huge networks of interconnected “neurons” to process information and make decisions.

There is little consensus among technologists about the best approach to take for the development of AGI, since both methods have their strengths and weaknesses. Symbolic AI systems that followed the original approach and are still currently being used in many applications that apply rules and logic to represent and solve problems. Their strength includes their accuracy and reliability, and their ability of conducting tasks that require reasoning and planning. However, they are not very efficient for carrying out tasks that are unstructured or ambiguous since they lack flexibility. Therefore, they find it difficult to adapt to new situations. On the other hand, neural network-based AI systems are viewed as being more flexible and adaptive, but they can be less accurate and reliable, and are more difficult to interpret.

Basically, the objective in the future AI development is to upgrade to Super AI, which is capable of exceeding human intelligence in all areas. When available, it would be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities and would be able to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence. Super AI will also bring about two other AI functionalities, namely Theory of Mind and Self-Awareness. Theory of Mind AI types are supposed to interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans, while Self-awareness AI aims to achieve enlightenment and becomes self-aware, with an independent intelligence, and will not be under the control of the people that created it. These types of developments will turn the AI debate from a technological issue to a very difficult philosophical topic, where ethical issues became of immense importance for the protection of the human being’s future existence. However, these types of AI are likely to require more processing power than is currently available.

This is where the development of the quantum computer comes into play. In 2023, IBM announced that the world’s first quantum computer, with more than 1,000 qubits, will be ready for use in 2023. However, to date no further announcements have been made. Some technologists think that currently, quantum computing is still in the very earliest stages of its development. Nevertheless, it has been reported that in the fiscal year starting April 2023, Japan’s Fujitsu company with the collaboration of the Riken research institute was to provide various industries access to the country’s first home-grown quantum computer that has 64 superconducting qubits. There appears to be consensus amongst technology observers that it will be at least 2030 before quantum computers are ready for general use. There are also rumours that NASA’s quantum computer project is currently on hold since the US government is concerned about merging AI and quantum computers. A quantum computer is viewed as transforming the way humans think about computing, increasing processing speeds exponentially, and granting access to previously inaccessible data.

The acute concern with the quantum computer is the well-known risk that criminals or states could use it to crack public key infrastructure (PKI) that is used to secure a multitude of common web interactions. For instance, credit card transactions and stock exchanges could be attacked by fraudsters; air traffic systems and GPS signals could be manipulated; and the security of critical infrastructure, like nuclear plants and the power grid, could be vulnerable to unauthorised access with criminal or terrorist intent. Hence, many believe that AI Quantum computers will have the possibility of breaking available encryption systems, which are based on complex mathematical enigmas that are difficult for traditional or current computers to solve. The general concern is that Quantum computers could be used by unauthorised users to access sensitive information such as financial records, medical data, and government secrets, including nuclear weapons systems.

## **3.3** Conclusion

The purpose of this chapter was to provide a brief history of the evolution of AI up to the current period. The journey to date has been a long, difficult, and at times, turbulent one, and there is little doubt that it will continue to be challenging. [Figure 3.1](#ch14.xhtml#f2) depicts the major events that have impacted the evolution of AI for the identified development periods, namely the Era of Enlightened Rational Thinking; the 20th Century: Pre-to-World War II Technology Era; and the 20th Century: Post World War II Technology Era.

![Figure 3.1 Summary of the Events Impacting the Evolution of Artificial Intelligence.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C003_001.jpg)

**Figure 3.1** Summary of the Events Impacting the Evolution of Artificial Intelligence.[⏎](#ch14.xhtml#f2b)

There is no doubt that the ancient thinkers, be they philosophers, mathematicians, theologians, scientists or play writers have had a direct influence on the development of AI through the art of logical thinking and linguistic expression. The years leading to the WWII, and the war years, witnessed a giant leap in the technological development. This development was based on the mathematical discoveries of the ancient thinkers and expanded through the invention of other tools of a mechanical and electrical nature that utilised previously documented mathematical and scientific knowledge. This resulted in the first programmable computers and the pioneering work related to the artificial neural network. The launching of the first computers inspired writers, who were not necessarily scientifically orientated to kindle their creative imagination and conjure up artificial existence, such as the term robot. Admittedly, the idea of mechanised living beings was partly due to the vivid imagination of science fiction writers dating back to the 17th century and the frightening vision in 19th century with the creation of Frankenstein’s artificial life.

However, the post-world war era witnessed an exponential leap in technological developments, particularly in electronics. Electronics formed the basis of all major inventions related to machines, aeroplanes, weaponry, and many others, all requiring design computations and production control systems, once they were ready for manufacturing. The improvement and the general demand for computers became a critical factor to enhancing development in every sphere. More powerful computers were continually being sought, driven by new concepts in robotics, neural networks, and general-purpose AI. Today, machine learning, deep neural networks, chatbots, amongst others are common knowledge to students, managers and other professions. They are not long viewed as mysterious. This is not to say that their underlying concepts are not complex, but that they appear to be accepted as the way to future economic development.

It is often said that history repeats itself. The timeline at [Figure 3.1](#ch14.xhtml#f2) illustrates that the development of AI has at times been restrained or held back by the computing power available at a particular period. Moreover, whenever a new and powerful computing power has been developed, AI appears to make a forward leap. Hence, it is envisaged that the Quantum computer will likely provide an opportunity for AI to make an evolutionary leap into the realm of the Super AI. This will mean that it will be likely possible to develop and implement General AI or Strong AI, which is designed to perform any intellectual task that a human can do and is able to reason, learn, and understand complex concepts. Furthermore, it will also mean that Narrow AI or Weak AI that is designed to do a specific task or a limited range of tasks like facial, speech and image recognition; natural language processing; and recommendation systems will be improved and strengthened. However, the big leap will be the Super AI, which will likely exceed human intelligence in all areas and be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities by learning and adapting at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence. This will also likely bring about new AI functionalities, such as Theory of Mind AI that will interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans, and Self-awareness AI, where AI will achieve enlightenment and becomes self-aware with independent intelligence that will not necessarily be under the control of the people that created it.

Whether this development is good or bad for humanity in general is debatable, and only time will tell. As previously explained, the critical concern with this type of development is the high well-known risk that criminals or states could use it to crack public key infrastructure that is used to secure a multitude of common web interactions. It could leave us open to intentional manipulation of critical facilities, such as credit card transactions; stock exchanges; air traffic systems and GPS signals; and the security of critical infrastructure, like nuclear power plants and their associated distribution grids; and weapons systems. Hence, many believe that AI Quantum computers will have the possibility of breaking available encryption systems, which are based on complex mathematical enigmas that are difficult for current computers to solve. The general concern is that Quantum computers could be used by unauthorised users to access sensitive information such as financial records, medical data, and government secrets, including nuclear weapons systems. AI will no longer be a technical issue; it will basically become a philosophical debate. There will come a time and not into the distant future, that it will not be a question of what a computer system (supported by AI) can do, but what we human beings will trust these computer systems to do.

There is an urgent need today to consider and formulate a robust and safe legal mechanism on a national and international level to address the security risks that the future highly sophisticated AI systems supported by 5^(th), or even 6^(th), generation computers will pose to world security in general and the existence of humanity in particular. This legal mechanism needs to be explored and defined now before Super AI and Self-awareness AI are extensively developed and become readily available. As a further mitigation measure, it is also essential that research funding is forthcoming for the continuous development of security encryption systems or intrusion prevention system (IPS) to address the evolving threat landscape. These measures are doable but should be undertaken now before we are overtaken by future events.
