# Chapter 4Contrasting Human and Artificial Intelligence

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-5](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-5)

> *“Could one make a machine which would have feelings like you, and I do?”*
> 
> Alan Mathison Turing OBE, FRS
> 
> *English mathematician, computer scientist, logician, cryptanalyst, philosopher and theoretical biologist (1912-1954)*

There is little consensus on the definition of AI but there is common agreement that AI has some of the abilities of human intelligence. Although AI is a human creation, the terms AI and human intelligence are sometimes confused and used interchangeably. It must be recognised that they are two distinct processes with their own distinctive features. While AI must be supported by powerful computing technologies that allow them to imitate cognitive processes such as learning and problem-solving, human intelligence is based on a living being with an assortment of mental attributes such as emotions, creativity, awareness, and memory, amongst others. With the technology that is currently available on the commercial marketplace (excluding possible covert state establishments), developing an AI with human intelligence it is not yet doable. However, with the advent of more advance super computers, such as Quantum technology and sophisticated intelligent learning algorithms, there is the potential to create approaches significantly like those used by human beings.

Despite the differences between AI and human intelligence, most AI applications can perform effectively the specific tasks allocated to them with precise accuracy, however, with limited ability. Humans are restrained by their physique; for example, they must sleep, eat and rest. However, unlike humans an AI does not succumb to fatigue or stress and can operate on 24/7 basis with consistent performance. Human intelligence utilises brain power, memory, and cognitive abilities while AI is reliant on the data provided by humans. Having said this, it must also be recognised that once the seed (data from humans) is provided, an effective AI system is able to learn and expand its knowledge far beyond the data that was originally provided by humans. Stephen Hawking is reported to have said that the development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of humans as it would take off on its own, and re-design itself at an ever-increasing rate. He argued that humans, who are limited by slow biological evolution, could not compete, and would be superseded ([Medeiros, 2017](#ch15.xhtml#r040)).

AI makes extensive use of cognitive computing, which has made it possible to have expert systems, theoretically replacing the human expert. This type of technology has been found to be effective in such fields such as medicine and education. AI is viewed as an amalgamation of various disciplines, including computer science, electronic engineering, mathematics, biology, physiology, and philosophy. These disciplines have been founded by human knowledge built over many centuries. It must be emphasised that AI is the creation of humans. It is humans that have designed and programmed the algorithms which permit AI systems to execute very complex problems and continue to self-learn; thus, making AI more resourceful. However, currently there is no doubt that the human intellect is more developed than AI in terms of self-awareness, social interactions, and multitasking.

## **4.1** Introduction

It has been said that there is no comparison between human and AI for the simple reason that human intelligence is far more superior. However, one also needs to consider the fact that humans themselves differ in terms of their level of intelligence, which follows a normal mathematical distribution. The normal distribution illustrates that there is an average level of human intelligence, with a percentage of individuals being below average and others above average. One also must remember that it is humans that have created AI. However, I would suggest that the humans that have contributed to the creation of AI are likely to be on the above average intelligence level. Therefore, when comparing human and artificial intelligence, there is a need to establish that the comparison is between the average human and the average AI system. A point at issue is whether AI follows the normal distribution and whether the average level (and respective spread from the average) is higher or lower than that of human intelligence. Hence, whether it is possible to compare like with like is an issue.

Another important factor is the fact that there are different types of intelligence. For instance, if the level of memory (in terms of information on all types of topics) is a type of intelligence, then I would suggest that computers and their associated AI systems would be far more superior than that of an individual human being no matter what level of intelligence that individual may have. However, this is assuming that the comparison being made is between an individual human being and an AI system. However, this is not a fair comparison because the initial data that is inputted into an AI system is an assortment of human knowledge and not just from one specific individual. Therefore, if a collective approach is taken, where the collective knowledge (past and present) of humans is taken into consideration then it is doubtful whether an AI system is currently superior. The basic reason being that current AI systems are founded upon the past and present knowledge of humans, so at minimum AI would be equal but not superior to human intelligence.

However, when an AI system has extensive learning capabilities, this human advantage is likely to diminish gradually over time because an AI system will probably learn more swiftly. For example, in 1997, a chess playing computer program called Deep Blue was able to defeat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. It is likely that to reach world chess champion status, Garry Kasparov would have had many years of intensive practice playing chess. In fact, this was a key milestone for AI, because it demonstrated in a practical sense that computers could outperform humans at a task that required complex reasoning and strategic thinking.

Potentially an AI system will learn at a much faster rate than that of humans, particularly if humans take a back seat and allow the AI to do its thinking for them. For example, taking myself as a case in point. Before the simple calculator became cheaply available, I was able to do arithmetical calculations mentally very quickly without the aid of artificial tools, such as the calculator. Today, I would find it difficult to add a column of five or six numbers quickly, simply because of being reliant on the calculator or some other electronic tool, such as EXCEL. I also remember, that when I was completing my master’s degree exam, I had to practice for hours in the task of plain handwriting because I became so dependent on using a word processor and keyboard that my handwriting abilities became very rusty indeed. The point that is being made is that humans need to be extremely cautious about being too dependent on a machine to do the things that they normally do, particularly thinking and attaining knowledge and eventually wisdom.

In the first chapter of this book reference was made to the lyrics of the song “In the Year 2525 (Exordium & Terminus)” by Zager and Evans. When I came to writing this chapter, I reread closely the lyrics of this song, which may seem an exaggeration to many, but the words above referring to being too dependent on computers and their associated AI systems reflect exactly the sentiment being expressed by this song. In fact, this song is conveying a message that if humans allow machines to do the normal things they do, both physically and mentally, even their biological qualities will diminish as the human being evolves in the future. Obviously, whether humans will remain intellectually superior or not, only time will tell. Furthermore, before comparing human and AI it is appropriate that the meaning of intelligence and learning are explored and understood. When we refer to intelligence and learning, what exactly do we mean?

## **4.2** Intelligence and Learning

[Lee (2020)](#ch15.xhtml#r038) argues that while it may be unlikely that humans will have superintelligent computers or robots like the ones in films such as Terminator anytime soon, investigating the differences between human intelligence and AI can help us better understand the future of technology and our relationship with it. Lee contends that only when humans have created artificial life that can physically replicate by itself, that they have created truly AI. Until then, machines will always only be surrogates of human intelligence, which unfortunately still leaves open the possibility of abuse by people controlling the AI.

It is not the intention of this chapter to examine the many theories that are in existence regarding human intelligence. The objective of this chapter is to ascertain the general meaning of intelligence so that one can understand its underlying characteristics. According to [Sternberg (2023)](#ch15.xhtml#r042), human intelligence is a mental quality that consists of the abilities to learn from experience, adapt to new situations, understand, and handle abstract concepts, and use knowledge to manipulate one’s environment. He argues that the question of what exactly defines human intelligence is contested, particularly among researchers of AI, though there is broader agreement that intelligence consists of multiple processes, rather than being a single ability.

Sternberg contends that the main emphasis in a definition of intelligence, is that it is not a cognitive or mental process as such but somewhat a discerning combination of these processes that is purposively directed toward effective adaptation. He cites the example of a physician who learns about a new disease, adapts by perceiving material on the disease in medical literature, learning what the material contains, remembering the crucial aspects that are needed to treat the patient, and then utilising reason to solve the problem of applying the information to the needs of the patient. Therefore, intelligence, in general is not a single ability but an effective combination of many abilities. Furthermore, measuring intelligence has attracted a lot of attention over many decades and standardised intelligence tests became popular during the 20th century. However, the limitations of intelligence tests have been extensively recognised.

The above definitions of intelligence refer to learning, yet intelligence and learning tend to have separate definitions and are often discussed individually. However, the difference between these two concepts is not well defined when it comes to the actual task of learning. Research has shown that there is a strong correlation between intelligence and learning, the likelihood being that the relationship is a causal one. It is important to understand that by applying their intelligence, humans are able to learn, articulate concepts, comprehend, and employ logic and reason. Moreover, research has shown that human intelligence incorporates the capability to recognise patterns, plan activities, be creative, solve complex problems, make rational decisions, retain and recall information, and use language to communicate. Intelligence can also be viewed as the human ability to solve complex problems or make rational decisions with the outcomes aiding the performer, and has evolved to adjust to different environments for their survival and reproduction ([Weder, 2020](#ch15.xhtml#r043)).

Currently, intelligence is often viewed in terms of analytical and reasoning skills, which are vital and critical components to successful learning. However, there are other types of intelligences, such as language communication abilities or emotional awareness that influence an individual’s learning process. Learning is the process of gaining new understanding, knowledge, skills, attitudes, values, behaviours, and preferences. It could be viewed as a mental exploratory expedition, where the individual gains from this experience, contributing to its intellectual and behavioural development. According to [Ambrose et al. (2010)](#ch15.xhtml#r034), learning is a process that leads to change, which occurs because of experience and increases the potential for improved performance and future learning, with the change in the learner to possibly occurring at the level of knowledge, attitude, or behaviour. As a result of learning, individuals come to see concepts, ideas, and/or the world differently. Learning is the direct outcome of how an individual understands, interprets, and reacts to their experiences. The learning process provides an individual with an opportunity to develop and apply intellectual skills and thinking processes, such as problem-solving; motor skills, values and attitudes; and develop interpersonal and social skills that are important for personal development. Intelligence and learning are two concepts linked with brainpower and cognitive functioning. Hence, the better the brain works, the greater the likelihood that an individual will learn and develop its intelligence.

[Mehta (2021)](#ch15.xhtml#r041) argues that humans are not all naturally skilled at the same things. Some are more athletic and have better coordination, some are more linguistic, while others are good with numbers and visualizing patterns. Furthermore, he contends that most people do not fully understand their range of abilities, and as a result make the wrong career choice, or they might enjoy their jobs, but struggle to identify effective learning techniques that will help them excel further. Therefore, it may be concluded that individuals are not intellectually the same but have different talents and capabilities. Mehta argues that humans possess multiple intelligences and cites Harvard University Professor Howard Gardner’s book *Frames of Mind* that was first published in 1983, which proposes that there are eight types of human intelligence, with each representing different ways of how a person best processes information (refer to [Figure 4.1](#ch15.xhtml#f3)). Furthermore, Mehta maintains that a high level in one intelligence category does not necessarily influence the level one has in another. The eight types of intelligence identified by Gardner are as follows:

![Figure 4.1 Howard Gardner’s Eight Types of Human Intelligence.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C004_001.jpg)

**Figure 4.1** Howard Gardner’s Eight Types of Human Intelligence.[⏎](#ch15.xhtml#f3b)

1.  Spatial intelligence: The ability to think abstractly and in multiple dimensions.
2.  Bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence: The ability to use one’s body in a way that demonstrates physical and athletic prowess.
3.  Musical intelligence: The capacity of being sensitive to rhythm, pitch, meter, tone, melody and timbre, entailing the ability to sing and/or play musical instruments.
4.  Linguistic intelligence: The capability of being sensitive to the meaning of words, the order among words, and the sound, rhythms, inflections and meter of words, including memorising information and reading.
5.  Logical-mathematical intelligence: The ability to analyse problems logically, carry out mathematical operations and investigate issues scientifically, including solving abstract problems.
6.  Interpersonal intelligence: The ability to interact effectively with others; being sensitive to other people’s moods, feelings, temperaments and motivations, including able to understand and relate to those around you.
7.  Intrapersonal intelligence: The capacity of being sensitive to one’s own feelings, goals and anxieties, including the capability to plan and act in the light of one’s own traits.
8.  Naturalistic intelligence: The ability to understand the distinctions in nature, including the differences between plants, animals, and other elements of nature and life.

[Figure 4.1](#ch15.xhtml#f3) indicates that intelligence has many aspects which provide human beings with the various attributes that help the individual to undertake an assortment of tasks. Additionally, understanding these various aspects allows humans to have a comprehensive model of what intelligence really is and provides a baseline for comparing it with AI to ascertain the differences between the two. An important issue that needs to be addressed is the process of transforming data to information to knowledge and finally to wisdom. It is essential to evaluate this transformation process to see how intelligence through learning develops in humans and whether this differs in the case of AI.

## **4.3** The Journey of Transforming Data to Wisdom

The general opinion is that humans tend to be superior to AI in varying environments, particularly at tasks that require empathy. Human intelligence incorporates the capability to understand and interact with the emotions and sensitivities of other human beings, which an AI is not capable of doing. This last statement needs a little more clarification. People can have empathy for others and this feeling can be genuine or made-up. For instance, an actor in a movie or play can mimic the emotions of the character that he/she is role playing. The more acting talent a human has, the better the individual’s acting performance. For example, winning an Oscar award for best actor or actress is one of the highest measures of one’s talent to act. Therefore, a human can have genuine feelings or can play act, but an AI can only possibly have the latter, play acting. It is argued that unlike humans, which is a living being, AI can only play-act the part of emotions. Additionally, a person can play act and still put feeling into the role. A robot can be programmed to make a sad or happy facial expressions but there is no true feeling and is likely to be amateurish even at role playing.

Before going into the specific differences between human intelligence and AI, it is appropriate at this stage to examine how data is transformed to wisdom. For example, consider an aubergine. It starts its life as a seed and evolves from the seed into a seedling and then a plant; and from a plant as the fruit itself, with each evolutionary phase adding to the development of the final product. The transformation process from raw data to wisdoms evolves in a similar fashion. Data is raw factual material, which is used as the basis for reasoning, discussion, or calculation. On the other hand, wisdom is the ability to think and act, applying the information, knowledge and experience, understanding, common sense, and insight that is accumulated over time. Therefore, data is at starting point of the data-wisdom transformation spectrum with wisdom being at the other end of the spectrum. It is argued that the process of transforming data to wisdom is different for humans and AI. Additionally, this transformation process brings into the open the human superiority over AI.

[Figure 4.2](#ch15.xhtml#f4) demonstrates the evolutionary process that takes places as data is transformed to information; information is transformed to knowledge; and knowledge is transformed to wisdom. In fact, this transformation process may be viewed as the basis for both human and AI learning systems, with the transformation process reaching the summit in terms of wisdom, the accumulation of which generates intelligence.

![Figure 4.2 Data Transformation Process.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C004_002.jpg)

**Figure 4.2** Data Transformation Process.[⏎](#ch15.xhtml#f4b)

### **4.3.1** Data: Raw Material for the Data Transformation Process

Data are the basic raw facts that an individual and an organisation collect in their day-to-day activities. Both the individual and the organisation are continually being inundated with raw facts, which may or may not be relevant to their needs. At this level, the raw facts are classified into some kind of order to facilitate the determination of their relevance. Hence, the collected data is filtered for relevancy and is prearranged in a manner that allows it to be absorbed in memory in the case of an individual or inputted into a computer system in the case of an organisation to be accessed and utilised at any time by the individual and the organisation’s AI systems.

Humans and AI systems alike are amassing an immense and escalating quantity of data in dissimilar formats and from diverse sources. Obviously, AI systems are able to handle much more data than an individual human being. What is absorbed into human memory is limited to what a particular individual deems important. What is stored in AI systems may include: (a) operational or transactional data, related to such things as revenue, expenditure, human resources, and accounting, amongst many others; (b) non-operational data, such as macro-economic data, industry sales and forecasts; and (c) meta-data that consists of descriptive data about the data itself, such as logical database design or data dictionary definitions. Moreover, at an AI level, data is typically prearranged into a repository that is referred to as a database and may take the form of numbers; words; observations or descriptions of things; pictures; and video and audio recordings. An individual’s repository is its memory.

There are two primary sources of data for humans and AI systems, namely internal and external sources. The internal data source for humans is how they feel in terms of emotions and signals that their bodies may provide regarding their health. The AI systems obtain internal data about their organisation that reflects the internal environment of that organisation, such as its financial health. External data is generated from sources outside the human being and the organisation and reflects the external environment. However, this where we start to see the major difference between humans and AI. Humans receive external data through the various senses, namely, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. AI systems initially receive data that humans feed it and then continues to learn from other data encounters. AI systems are smart enough to process different categories of data. For instance, they can analyse audio and video data that may include pattern recognition and image analysis and are applied for detecting abnormalities in terrorist exposure scenarios. However, AI systems do not have the extensive sensory facilities that humans possess, that carry nerve impulses from the sense organs toward or to the brain. AI system can be programmed to have some sensory facilities but nowhere as extensive as found in humans.

### **4.3.2** Information: The Transformation of Data into Information

Information is the transformation of raw data into something that is meaningful, significant and may have implications for the entity using it. For example, an individual may have several ingredients, but by themselves these ingredients are meaningless. However, by applying a recipe, the ingredients can be converted to a product that is cooked and eaten. On an organisational AI level, consider a digital file of taxpayers registered with the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) for a particular geographic region that contains their personal and financial details. This digital file may contain millions of entries. By itself this data has no value. However, data may be transformed into information by analysing or summarising it by a specific locality, income group, gender, marital status, employment position, age groups, education level, and so forth. This analysis (or transformation) may be needed to establish the average age of the taxpayers in a particular locality, and the minimum-maximum age per category (gender, position, marital status).

Hence, an entity may obtain a finer appreciation of the information that is generated in terms of better decision making. It should be noted that the actual decision-making function is entering into realm that is beyond the information level and is boarding on the knowledge-wisdom domains. However, at the transformation of data into information level, humans and an AI system are both capable, but humans have the added advantage of their sensory abilities such intuition, whilst the AI systems have the advantage of speed.

### **4.3.3** Knowledge: The Transformation of Information into Knowledge

Data and information can be transformed into knowledge by examining historical patterns and future trends. Knowledge can be visualised as consisting of two corresponding and related components, namely the explicit details and the comprehension of these explicit details. Hence, the explicit details are acquired from the application of the data and information to address “how” questions to provide an insight about the magnitude and characteristics of some object. On the other hand, the comprehension of the explicit details is the objective of the analysis (i.e., why are we analysing these explicit details).

On a human level, a doctor may conduct research to examine whether there is a causal relationship between alcohol and various health problems. Through his research the doctor collects various pieces of evidence (data and information) and gains knowledge about specific situations. On an organisational level, through an AI system, a manager of a public health facility may want to know which services are to be encouraged and supported by this facility. Hence, data and information regarding the utilisation of the services offered at the health facility are analysed to provide the knowledge regarding the beneficiaries of the services being provided; in other words, the service recipient behaviour (how). This in turn will allow the manager to decide which health services should be supported and enhanced. This will aid the health facilities manager to select those services that are most responsive to any promotional effort that may be undertaken (objective or why).

The above example illustrates that knowledge is the extensive exploitation of data and information, in combination with the ability, competencies, ideas, intuitions, commitments and motivations of the manager involved. Hence, the transformation of data and information into knowledge is the outcome of the synergy that combines human aptitudes and the application of the available data and information in an AI system. Admittedly, an AI could be capable of deciding itself, but once again the emotional feeling of a human is an essential feature for certain decisions, particularly where life and death is an issue.

### **4.3.4** Wisdom: The Transformation of Knowledge into Wisdom

Wisdom is the amalgamation of knowledge and experiences into insights that intensify an entity’s (individual or organisation through its AI system) comprehension of relationships and the meaning of these relationships to enable one to make a correct judgement. Therefore, wisdom is the ability to make the right judgments and decisions, and hence transforms data, information, and knowledge into intelligence. In other words, knowledge is viewed as a tool, with wisdom being the skill needed to apply it. Wisdom is a subtle quality that is gained through extensive experience and when documented forms the basis for AI. Thus, as more experience is gained and documented, the higher level of intelligence that is generated. However, as one may appreciate, this is not easy to accomplish or sustain because to be wise implies a great deal of knowledge and experience that must continually be updated, maintained and sustained.

The objective of the data-information-knowledge transformation process is the attainment of wisdom. In other words, to have an evaluated understanding of what is going to take place. Hence, wisdom is concerned with the future and incorporates vision and design. With wisdom it is not a matter of grasping the past and present but to be able to forge the future. However, it must be recognised that wisdom is the pinnacle, thus it is not easy to achieve since one needs to move successively through the other transformation phases before it may be finally gained. In addition, once wisdom is gained it must be sustained with further knowledge; hence it takes an on-going demanding effort.

To place things into context, the previous sections have explained that an entity (individual or organisation) starts with raw data that must be gathered and organised; processed and transformed to information through summarisation and analysis. This information is transformed to knowledge by integrating the data and information in a form that is suitable for decision making. Over time, the accumulation of knowledge becomes wisdom. Wisdom deals with the future because it incorporates foresight and creativity; therefore, it is not a matter of coming to terms with the past and the present. This process takes place at an individual level through brain power or at an organisational level through its AI system. However, in the absence of an AI system, the organisation attains wisdom through the brain power of its management team.

Those organisations, which do not have an AI system in place, are viewed as being at the information transformation stage, where decisions are made by those that possess individual knowledge. Hence, a key aim of an AI system is knowledge management with the objective of breaking the mind barrier, where decisions are made by individuals based on organisational knowledge. Organisations must strive to manage the knowledge gained over the years and transform it into wisdom, so that correct and effective decisions are made, preferably by the individual, supported by an AI system.

Hence, the central issue that must be addressed is related to what wisdom involves in a practical sense. [Lacewing (2009)](#ch15.xhtml#r037) in his examination of practical wisdom (from the Greek word ‘phronesis’; sometimes translated ‘prudence’) argues that Aristotle defines wisdom as a true and reasoned state of capacity to act regarding the things that are good or bad for man. He argues that while practical wisdom involves knowledge of what is good or bad, it is not merely theoretical knowledge, but a capacity to act on such knowledge as well. [Lacewing (2009)](#ch15.xhtml#r037) contends that this capacity requires:

1.  Seeing things clearly. The ability to perceive, considering the general conception, and what is required in terms of feeling, choice, and action in a particular situation.
2.  Acting in prudent and effective ways. Having a general conception of what is good or bad, which Aristotle relates to the conditions for human flourishing.
3.   Acting with the well-being of the whole in mind (holistically). Practical wisdom involves understanding what is required in a particular situation in the light of a general understanding of what is good.
4.  Deeply understanding the situation. Hence, having the ability to deliberate well.
5.  Knowing when to act and when not to act. That is, the ability to act on that deliberation.

Furthermore, [Malone (2003)](#ch15.xhtml#r039) contends that wisdom also involves being able to react to crisis calmly with an effective holistic response; and being able to anticipate potential problems and avoid them. Wise people generally share optimism that life’s problems can be solved and experience a certain amount of calm in facing difficult decisions. It is posited that an organisation which has a management team that possess the above attributes and can repeatedly and consistently apply these attributes will have a tremendous competitive advantage.

One must recognise that an AI system has the advantage of speed and memory capacity when compared to an individual person but lacks emotions (feeling). An individual can come up with a balanced decision, considering factual tangible matters and intangible elements. The intangible elements might be the consequences for other beings. For instance, a decision regarding the downsizing of an organisation needs to consider the consequences of the decision on the motivation and commitment of the individuals working for the organisation, particularly those who will likely be retained. Hence, many organisational decisions in a practical sense do not just consider the numbers but also the consequences on those that will be directly affected by the decision. Furthermore, an organisation is normally managed by a management team that can express their feelings about a particular challenge being encountered. This is a weakness of the current AI systems, the ability to feel (emotional perceptions). To overcome this weakness, it would be preferrable if decisions are taken by humans with the aid of an AI system, where human emotions can play an important role in the final decisions.

## **4.4** The Growing Challenge between Human Intelligence and AI

The questions that are often raised are whether AI will ever outstrip human intelligence and whether there is something so exceptional about human intelligence that it may never be replicated. There is wide consensus that human intelligence experiences constraints that are not applicable to computers. However, computers also have their constraints as well, which are not applicable to humans.

Computers are exceptional when it comes to seed in number crunching. For example, AI has often exceeded human intelligence when confronted by an individual in circumstances such as playing chess and other games. Deep Blue the chess playing computer developed by IBM defeated in 1997 the chess world champion, Garry Kasparov. This triumph was viewed as a symbolic demonstration of the intellectual escalation of AI leading some researchers to believe that AI will surpasses human intelligence in every sphere. Such an event is what is known as “technological singularity.” The technological singularity is a hypothetical future point in time at which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, resulting in unforeseeable consequences for the human civilization. The term was first used by John von Neumann in 1958, where the term “Singularity” described a hypothesis that developments in science, especially in the fields of informatics, nanotechnology, and biology will ultimately lead to the invention of an artificial general intelligence (AGI). [Kurzweil (2005)](#ch15.xhtml#r036) predicts the singularity will coincide with the next epoch, “The Merger of Human Technology with Human Intelligence,” but after the singularity, the final epoch will occur, “The Universe Wakes Up.”

No one knows precisely when humans will create AGI (or superintelligence), but Kurzweil believes that the singularity will occur by approximately 2045. [Weder (2020)](#ch15.xhtml#r043) argues that true intelligence requires life, which can be defined as a process of self-replication and sustains that superintelligence is either impossible or something in a very distant future. Weder maintains that true intelligence should promote but not interfere with the replication of the genes responsible for its creation, including the necessary hardware like the brain. She argues that without this constraint, there is no objective criteria for determining whether a particular solution is intelligent. Weder claims that machines will always only be surrogates of human intelligence, which unfortunately still leaves open the possibility of abuse by people controlling the AI.

Self-replication is not the only difficulty that will be encountered when creating an AI which will be more intelligent than humans. The intelligence of living beings, including animals is extraordinary because this type of intelligence can discern complex items and generate swift actions in different methods in various countless circumstances. Knowledge about how the brain works is not complete and will require perfect information about how the brain functions before AI systems can be developed to replicate human intelligence. [Weder (2020)](#ch15.xhtml#r043) claims that the first signs of the emergence of superintelligence will occur when machines like Terminators come on the scene and surpass humans in acquiring energy and other resources that they need for their repairs and replications.

One needs to recognise that human intelligence is connected directly to the human brain, while an AI system uses algorithms to imitate and may even exceed human performance in some tasks, such as computations. Generally, human intelligence has natural cognitive abilities such as feeling, imagination, creativity, intuition, empathy, and reflexes, amongst others. These attributes are extremely problematic for computers to mimic fully or replicate accurately. However, today’s AI systems do not need these natural abilities because the functions they perform are reliant on data processing power to store and retrieve information and execute rule-based software at a rapid and accurate rate that is much higher than humans can achieve. Because of this processing power, AI systems learn new tasks swiftly by trial and error, and do not require instruction guides or advice from humans.

AI systems are better at recognising complex patterns or shapes through structural models like multi-dimensional entities. AI algorithms iteratively improve their comprehension of patterns by altering their internal constraints based on feedback. Hence, by comparing their extrapolations with known results, the algorithms improve their ability to identify subtle patterns. These techniques are very useful to improve overall quality of medical images in MRI and CT scans, improving diagnostic accuracy and contributing to better patient care. A shortcoming of an AI system is that it lacks the flexibility of human intelligence when it needs to think outside the box or improvising when caught unawares, which are very useful in emergency situations. While AI systems are improving at recognising emotions in photographs and videos, they still do not have any emotions themselves. This may raise ethical issues in the future, particularly given the fact that an AI system may at times be inaccurate or susceptible to simple deceptions. Moreover, since an AI system depends on human inputted data for training and feedback loops during its learning progression, it may be liable to unintended human influence, with the system not functioning as anticipated due to human biases and errors. However, this type of risk is also present in non-AI systems. There are many other differences between human intelligence and AI, which will be discussed in the next section.

## **4.5** Specific Differences Between AI and Human Intelligence

Although there are some similarities between AI and human intelligence, [Table 4.1](#ch15.xhtml#t6) illustrates, that there are also many specific differences between them. As has been shown previously, AI is an innovation created by human intelligence, while humans are biologically gifted with cognitive abilities, such as thinking and reasoning. Norbert Wiener who theorised on feedback mechanisms in the 1950s was a pioneer in the field of cybernetics, which is recognised as the emergent scientific field of AI. Wiener is reported to have argued that modern “thinking” machines are much faster at working out certain problems than their human designers and are being constructed to think like humans. However, it was John McCarthy who used the term “artificial intelligence” for the first time at the Dartmouth Conference that specifically dealt with the theme of AI as the main topic.

**Table 4.1** Specific Differences between AI and Human Intelligence[⏎](#ch15.xhtml#t6b)

 
| **Features** || **AI** || **Human Intelligence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergence || Norbert Weiner who theorized on criticism mechanisms. || Humans are naturally gifted with cognitive abilities, such as thinking and reasoning. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State || Machines are digital that use binary code. || Brain is analogous, processing data in a continuous and non-linear fashion. |
| Essence || The aim of AI is to mimic humans and do the work that humans would normally do. || To combine a range of cognitive actions to adapt to new situations. |
| Physical Limitations || No physical limitations and can operate on a 24/7 basis. || Limited by physical capabilities and requires rest and maintenance |
| Energy use || Generally, only use 2 watts. || The human brain uses about 25 watts. |
| Processing || Based on algorithms and mathematical models. || Based on cognitive processes and biological structures. |
| Function || Rely on input of data and instructions. || Use of memory, processing capabilities, and cognitive talents. |
| Accuracy || Produces accurate results as it is programmed to optimise a given task or system based on rules or algorithms. || Room for “human error” but it has the capacity for creativity and innovation beyond the limitations of programming. |
| Adaptability || Can adapt to new data and situations but it takes time to adapt to new changes. || Can adapt to new states, learning from experience (decisions based on context). |
| Flexibility || Can perform fewer tasks at the same time and can learn duties one at a time. || Has multitasking ability and perform differing and concurrent roles. |
| Emotions || AI lacks emotions and empathy || Capable of feeling emotions & empathy. |
| Learning ability || Based on data and feedback loops and acquires knowledge by machine learning. || Human intelligence is based on experience, intuition, and creativity. |
| Speed || Able to process vast amounts of data and perform complex calculations rapidly. || Humans are much slower at processing large quantity of data. |
| Creativity || AI has limited ability to be creative or think outside of the box || Humans are capable of creativity, imagination, and innovation. |
| Decision making || Extremely objective because its analysis is based on factual accumulated data. || Decisions may be affected by subjective elements that are not figures alone. |
| Social Networking || AI has difficulty understanding the nuances of social and emotional cues, which are essential for effective human interaction. || Ability to process complex social and emotional information, interpret nonverbal communication, and respond appropriately to social situations. |
| Ethics || AI does not have a moral code or conscience || Human Intelligence has a moral code and conscience that guides decision-making |

The human brain processes data in a continuous and non-linear fashion, whilst computers, which are the basis for AI are digital that use binary code. The primary aim of AI is to mimic humans, where they attempt to perform the work that is normally done by humans. In contrast humans combine a range of cognitive activities to adjust to new situations. This is a significant difference between AI and human intelligence. AI systems are designed to execute specific tasks and are optimised for them. While these systems can learn to perform new tasks, they still require a considerable amount of training and data to do this. In contrast, human intelligence is much more adaptable, with humans being able to learn quickly and adjust to new circumstances.

A strong advantage of AI is that it does not have physical limitations in terms of fatigue and can operate on a 24/7 basis. AI is no match for humans in terms of physical activity that uses bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure. However, the human is limited in that it requires rest and maintenance. There is also a difference in energy consumption. While a computer uses about 2 watts of energy, the human brain uses about 25 watts. AI and human intelligence also differ in the way they process data. AI’s processing is based on the use of human created algorithms and mathematical models. Whereas human intelligence is based on cognitive processes and biological structures. This difference means that AI relies on input data and programming instructions, whereas human intelligence applies memory, processing capabilities, and cognitive talents.

This also means that AI and human intelligence are different in their creativity and intuitive capabilities. AI systems can furnish new ideas and solutions based on their specific training data and algorithms, but unlike humans their capacity to be creative and intuitive is lacking. Humans are creative and can discover innovative ideas and solutions that are not based on any existing processes or experiences. Humans can apply their sensitivity and experience to make associations and solve problems that AI systems would have difficulty with. This also has an impact on how AI and humans react. AI can adapt to new data and circumstances, but it takes time to adjust to new fluctuating situations. Whereas humans can adjust to new completely new states, learning from experience, and making decisions based on context.

An AI system can provide accurate results according to how it is programmed to optimise a given function based on rules. However, humans have the capacity for creativity and innovation beyond the limitations of programming but are prone to “human error.” This feature also means that humans tend to be more flexible and are able to perform in multitasking mode by executing differing and concurrent roles. On the other hand, AI can perform fewer tasks simultaneously and tend to learn tasks one at a time. One of the key differences between AI and human intelligence is their learning method. An AI’s learning approach is based on data and feedback loops and assimilates knowledge by machine learning. However, human intelligence is based on experience, intuition, and creativity. Therefore, AI systems apply pre-programmed algorithms and input data to learn from their circumstances and improve their performance over time. This is known as machine learning and involves training the system with large amounts of data to identify patterns and make extrapolations. On the other hand, human intelligence is a result of a complex interchange of genes, surroundings, and experience. Humans have an innate cognitive ability that may vary from one individual to another. Thus, humans develop and refine their intelligence through exposure to different situations, experiences, education, and social interactions.

An important difference between AI and human intelligence is their capacity to comprehend language and context. Humans can understand the meaning behind words, double meanings, and phrases, as well as the social and cultural context in which they are applied. On the other hand, AI systems are not very proficient in natural language processing, since they still have difficulty comprehending the nuances of the human language and the context in which it is applied. However, once this difficulty is overcome, an AI system will have unlimited ability in this field in all languages concurrently. A sole individual may master several languages, but an AI system will have no such restriction. Furthermore, in terms of social networking, an AI system has difficulty comprehending the nuances of social and emotional cues, which are important for effective human interaction. On the other hand, humans have the capacity to process complex social and emotional information, interpret nonverbal communication, and respond fittingly to social situations. This also means that humans are able to make decisions that may be influenced by subjective factors and not just by facts and figures. However, an AI system is extremely objective because its analysis is founded on factual accumulated data.

It must be noted that currently, an AI system has very limited capacity to be creative or to think outside of the box, contrary to humans, who are very capable of imagination, creativity, and innovation. This is offset to some extent by the AI system’s ability to process vast amounts of data and perform complex calculations rapidly, whereas humans are much slower at processing a large quantity of data. However, the greatest difference between AI and humans is the emotional factor. AI systems can identify and respond to emotions in humans, but they lack emotions and empathy, while humans are capable of both. This also means that an AI system does not have ethical behaviour through a moral code or conscience, whilst most humans do. Emotional intelligence is a vital feature of human intelligence since it permits humans to identify with others, recognise their emotions, and encourage social relationships. Hence, humans are capable of a complex range of emotions that impact their decision-making and social interactions.

## **4.6** Harmonisation between Human Intelligence and AI

The human brain is the only source of intelligence that humans possess, which also controls their feelings, thoughts, memories, and actions throughout the human life span. On the other hand, an AI system depends on a computer (that can be replaced and upgraded) in the effort to think and learn to resemble a human. The human brain has the capacity for rational deliberation and decision-making, while an AI system can think and learn like humans according to a suite of executable programmed algorithms. However, an AI system can be viewed as a tool to be exploited by humans to help them increase their living standards. For example, AI systems are being used in healthcare to produce images of internal organs and diagnose diseases and/or suggest treatments; it is being applied in finance to forecast share prices on the stock market and execute econometric models for defining better economic policies, and a multitude of other important applications.

While the human brain is a very powerful organ, it is not capable of doing the computations at the speed that AI systems can do. However, one must recognise that it is the power of the human brain that invented these applications and many others. These are typical examples where humans and other living beings benefit from the collaboration between the human brain and AI systems, including their underlying equipment controlled by sophisticated computers, and operated by humans. An important issue regarding AI is how far should humans engage in its development. For instance, there is work currently being conducted regarding the integration of human AI. This refers to the integration of AI into the human brain and systems with the primary aim of making them smarter. This integration allows humans and an AI system to learn from each other much more quickly to ensure that humans and the AI system constantly move forward as fast as possible. However, human AI will likely have its limitations, particularly in areas such as reasoning, social interaction, emotions, and common sense.

There are potential issues with human intelligence and AI but only if the AI application is abused by human operatives. Furthermore, ethical concerns are likely to arise regarding how an AI application will impact society in the future. For example, AI surveillance systems gather immense volumes of data, including personal information, without an individual’s explicit consent. Additionally, data violations involving facial recognition data amplify the possibility for identity theft, stalking, and harassment because, unlike passwords and credit card information, faces cannot easily be changed. However, human centred AI, which focuses on the interactions between humans and AI systems attempts to interface with its users (humans) in a way that is natural for them, permitting individuals to use an AI that is more spontaneous, supportive, and satisfying. Nevertheless, several ethical concerns need to be considered when developing and using AI, including the possible risks presented by AI that negatively impact society, and have implications for human rights. These ethical considerations will be treated in detail in a separate chapter.

## **4.7** Conclusion

Currently there is little consensus on the precise definition of AI but there is common agreement that AI has some ability to think and mimic humans in certain aspects. It must be recognised that even though AI is a human creation, the terms AI and human intelligence are two distinct processes with their own distinctive features. Furthermore, while an AI system and human intelligence have some similarities, there are significant differences between the two that have been summarised in [Table 4.1](#ch15.xhtml#t6). AI systems can perform many tasks quickly and efficiently that normally require human intelligence, but their biggest weakness is the lack of adaptability, imagination, creativity, intuition, and emotional intelligence that most humans possess. Research has revealed that human intelligence is a complex interaction of genes, experience, and environment. This permits humans to comprehend, define and recognise concepts, and interact with the world around them in approaches that AI systems are not able to imitate. It is important to recognise that as AI continues to develop and grow in acceptance, one needs to appreciate the differences and comprehend the unique strengths and shortcomings of both AI and human intelligence.

As highlighted in the previous chapter, the word “robot,” which was first used in a 1920 in a play” R.U.R.” by Karel Čapek to describe an artificial automaton, derives from the Slavic word robata, which means “forced labour.” Often humans still think of (ro)bots and androids as monotonous, obedient slaves. It is important to recognise that as technology improves in processing capacity and AI continues to improve, humans must be able to maintain control over the AI systems and not simply think that an AI is mindless.

Often, humans feel themselves as being at a far superior evolutionary level in the biological creation order and view other species at a much lower level of realisation to be in complete control and to subject other living forms a lower status and few rights. Humans need to be conscious that all living things have feelings and sense pain and suffering. Furthermore, humans must not be complacent about artificial creations. This complacency stems from the fact that humans do not recognise the potency of AI. Humans often feel very frustrated whenever they have an experience of interacting with a dull online customer service bot or an automated phone service, reaching the general conclusion that AI is not particularly smart. Contact with a human is often more successful in getting a better customer service, where one can explain the situation without feeling that they are communicating with a non-existent entity.

In conclusion, AI and human intelligence are both extraordinary achievements of engineering and biological development, respectively. However, there are many critical differences between them that makes them very distinctive. Human intelligence is centred on the chemical and electrical activity of the brain, while AI is dependent on computer systems. Furthermore, human intelligence is very well suited for tasks such as pattern recognition and natural language processing, while AI is more suited for tasks such as data mining and machine learning. It is unlikely that devises capable of thinking like humans will be created in the very short-term because technologists still do not fully understand how the human brain fully functions. Therefore, currently human intelligence has full control of how AI develops but this does not mean that this situation will not change. It is too early to know whether AI will eventually pose a serious risk to existence of humanity. Some experts believe this is a possibility due to the anticipate considerable growth of AI in the next decade or so. However, if legislative action is undertaken on a national and international level, and continuous and considerable investment in security systems are embarked on, then it is not likely that AI will pose a serious threat to humanity and any threatening risk is mitigated.
