# IIThe Technology Supporting Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) like many other software-based applications requires robust technological support in terms of effective hardware and software tools that operate in a secure environment. [Part II](#ch16.xhtml#c6) of this book consists of three chapters, with each chapter focusing on a distinct topic, namely AI associated hardware, software and security.

There is no doubt that most of the current AI applications execute on the traditional Von Neumann architecture. Unfortunately, this architecture executes instruction in a sequential manner that limits the capabilities of AI applications. It must be recognised that hardware is the fundamental pillar of all computer-driven functionalities and acts as a bottleneck to development. Hence, technological advancement is very much dependent on the capacity, capabilities, and sophistication of the hardware. [Chapter 5](#ch17.xhtml#c7) is devoted to computer hardware focusing on fourth and fifth generation computers and tracing their development over the past six decades. The chapter discusses Quantum computing that aims to resolve the Von Neumann bottleneck by applying quantum states of subatomic particles to store information and execute multidimensional quantum algorithms.

Additionally, [Chapter 5](#ch17.xhtml#c7) examines a completely different approach to computing, namely neuromorphic hardware that aims to emulate the human nervous system allowing parallel processing for specific tasks. Neuromorphic chips have extraordinary potential that are being exploited in robotics; visual object recognition; gesture and smell recognition; medical monitoring; self-driving vehicles to identify and interpret their environments; and identification of diseases, amongst other applications. Neuromorphic chips have futuristic innovation features that when fully developed will revolutionise the way we view the capabilities of robotics. This chapter also examines current developments related to hardware chips that focus on specific dedicated tasks, which can be integrated as part of application systems that may include neuromorphic computing, such as Edge Computing Chips, Application Specific Integrated Circuits, Field Programmable Gate Arrays, and Complex Programmable Logic Devices.

It is an axiom that hardware on its own has no value unless it is supplemented by suitable software. Hence, [Chapter 6](#ch18.xhtml#c8) is dedicated to software as an essential component of effective hardware and explores several AI programming languages that are crucial for developing AI applications. Moreover, this chapter examines IBM’s Qiskit SDK, which is designed for the IBM Quantum Platform to execute specialised AI applications. However, the discussion on software would not be complete unless hardware description languages are also considered. Hence, Verilog and VHDL are examined since these are particularly useful for specific hardware related to AI, such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays. Furthermore, AI algorithms are discussed because of their importance in relation to executing AI tasks that would otherwise require human intelligence, such as speech and voice recognition; text recognition; image recognition; video analytics; generative Al; and natural language processing. Finally, the chapter focuses on neuromorphic computing and spiked neural networks. These are explicitly designed for parallel processing and have tremendous potential for AI applications since they are expected to be able to adjust to their environment, accessing external sources through the cloud if necessary to seek more information when required.

AI has great potential for humanity, but it has also a devastating ability to be destructive unless it is developed and executed in a safe environment. Hence, the closing chapter for [Part II](#ch16.xhtml#c6) is dedicated to security. It is a fact that the advancement of AI is attracting the attention of very clever threat actors that are continuously seeking ways to exploit weaknesses in cybersecurity. This chapter evaluates the evolving threat landscape and how the risk of cybersecurity penetration may be mitigated by implementing powerful intrusion prevention systems (IPS) that are located directly behind the firewall. An IPS offers an extra layer of protection by having powerful algorithms that continuously check network traffic to detect threats and take action to neutralise them.

This is not to say that a firewall is not essential. In fact, Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) act as the vanguard for cybersecurity by employing application-specific rules, protect against malware, block anomalous behaviour and prevent actors from entering the network through a nonstandard port. The aim is to keep ahead of threat actors. While IPS and NGFW protect the network, a public key infrastructure (PKI) defends data that is being transmitted by creating digital certificates that cryptographically connect ownership of a public key with the entity that owns it, with the specific aim of sharing these keys for data encryption and authentication. Finally, this chapter examines centres for AI safety that are nonprofit research organisations, which focus on the mitigation of AI risks and are continuously promoting innovative ways to continually come up with solutions because the war against threat actors will not cease.

# Chapter 5Artificial Intelligence Hardware

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-7](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-7)

> *“There will always be rocks in the road ahead of us. They will be stumbling blocks or stepping stones; it all depends on how you use them.”*
> 
> Friedrich Nietzsche
> 
> *German philosopher (1844-1900)*

AI systems are very much dependent on the processing power of the computers that are used to execute the various AI programmes. In the past, traditional computer hardware has been the greatest limitation to the development of AI. AI hardware refers to specialised computer hardware that is designed to facilitate and assist in the execution of AI related tasks effectively. Hence, AI hardware specifically supports the required infrastructure to execute algorithms and other essential models efficiently to optimise the hardware’s processing power. AI hardware includes a variety of items, such as specifically designed computer microprocessor chips. This type of hardware has the primary goal of executing AI programme suites faster and use less energy in the process. The AI hardware may support Lisp machines that are general-purpose computers designed to efficiently execute Lisp as their main software and programming language. They also support neuromorphic computing, physical neural networks, and event cameras that apply imaging sensors that responds to local changes in brightness.

Neuromorphic computing (or neuromorphic engineering) refers to the design of both hardware and software computing elements that have the objective of modelling bio-inspired computer systems that imitate the human brain and nervous system. An example of neuromorphic engineering is the self-driving car. A self-driving car needs to make prompt decisions to correctly navigate and avoid collisions. This type of technology requires considerable computing processing power. Therefore, by using neuromorphic hardware and software, self-driving cars can execute tasks quicker and consume lower energy in contrast to traditional computing.

On the other hand, a physical neural network entails the representation in a tangible form of artificial neural networks into physical systems, enabling real-time computation and interaction. In contrast to virtual neural networks, physical neural networks provide the possibility to link the gap between the digital and physical worlds. Whereas, traditional neural networks occur only in the digital domain, functioning via mathematical models and algorithms, physical neural networks integrate AI with tangible objects and environments, allowing real-time computation, interaction, and sensory feedback between the digital and physical domains. This chapter will discuss these hardware developments and others in detail to provide an insight into the potential that AI may provide through its applicability for the benefit of humanity.

## **5.1** Introduction

History has shown that AI applications have made considerable advances when more powerful computers have been developed and released in the commercial marketplace. As observed in a previous chapter, the term “Artificial Intelligence” was first formally applied at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence in 1956. However, the conceptual models for AI were established in 1943 when American neurophysiologist and cybernetician Warren McCulloch and logician and cognitive psychologist Walter Pitts, published a paper “A Logical Calculus of the ideas Imminent in Nervous Activity.” This was the first mathematical model of a neural network. Their ideas were applied by John von Neumann (mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics and Game theory) and Norbert Wiener (the initiator of cybernetics, and the science of communication as it relates to living things and machines), which are viewed as being fundamental to some key concepts of AI.

McCulloch and Pitts are viewed as the pioneers of the artificial neural network and were a fundamental inspiration for the invention of the modern digital computer. It was also the era for the first-generation computers (1940-1956), at a time when in 1943 the Colossus computer became famous for its code-breaking capabilities, during the Second World War. John McCarthy and his colleagues instigated the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on AI in 1956. This came at the early beginning of the second generation of computers (1956-1963), which at that time were viewed as the most powerful computers, unparalleled with what had been discovered at that juncture. These so-called powerful computers provided the inspiration for McCarthy and his colleagues to push through their AI initiatives.

Nevertheless, despite the increase in the computing power that the second generation of computers provided, the computing processing unit and the external storage memory were very limited, and therefore, the processing power was restrained. This computing limitation and the substantial criticism of the Rosenblatt’s perceptron model are likely to have resulted to the termination of the machine translation project in 1966 due to poor AI outcomes, leading to the first “AI winter,” which denoted a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research. The second-generation computers moved away from the use of bulky vacuum tubes and applied transistor technology instead, and enhanced core storage. Transistors provided the computer with more computing power, including computational speed. This development generally resulted in the reduction of the size and cost of computers, including less heat generation when compared with vacuum tubes. Additionally, the second-generation computer brought with it the concept of the Central Processing Unit (CPU), enhanced internal and external data storage memory, programming languages, and input and output devises. Programming languages, such as FORTRAN, ALGOL, and COBOL simplified programming when compared with machine and assembler programme coding.

The third-generation computers (1964-1971) predicted (and realised) a shift from sizable transistors to integrated circuits (IC), made from silicon. An integrated circuit, also referred to as a chip, microchip, or microelectronic circuit, is a semiconductor wafer on which thousands or even millions of tiny resistors, capacitors, diodes and transistors are engineered and manufactured. In other words, an IC is an integrated system of multiple miniaturized and interconnected components embedded into a thin substrate of semiconductor material (typically a silicon crystal). It has proven to be a fundamental element of all contemporary electronic devices. Hence, its development provided the third-generation computer with enhanced speed and reliability. This era also saw the birth of the minicomputer as distinct from the mainframe computer.

The introduction of the minicomputer meant that small-to-medium firms could afford their own computer facilities due to lower hardware costs. The difficulty during this period was a scarcity of applications software that permitted organisations to use a computer to execute their administrative functions, such as accounting, payroll, stock control, amongst many others. These types of computers had an operating system that was designed to handle completely the inner operation of the computer itself. Additionally, it also had applications computer programmes (written in computer languages, such as COBOL and FORTRAN, amongst others) that were designed to perform a specific organisational function, such as executing a suite of programmes related to the accounting, stock control, and payroll. The operating system permitted the third-generation computer to execute multiple jobs simultaneously by allocating each application system fractions of a second of processing time sequentially. The high speed of these computers gave the impression that because of this time-allocation process, these multiple application systems were being executed in parallel. In fact, these computers were not designed with a parallel processing feature.

The release of the third-generation computer coincided to some extent with the first AI winter, with most research being directed towards traditional application software development. In the late 1960s, the development of perceptrons and connectionism was contemporary and stimulating. Unfortunately, most of the research development funding for AI came from the United States Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). However, the Mansfield Amendment approved by the United State Congress obliged DARPA to fund research directed by a specific mission. This triggered DARPA to terminate funding of new AI research. Moreover, in 1973, the British Parliament commissioned James Lighthill to review the state of AI in the United Kingdom. The Lighthill report was very critical of the achievement attained by AI and declared that the breakthroughs did not fulfil the desired expectations and that the study of AI could be conducted in other sciences. AI was comparatively new in the 1960s and 1970s with high expectations that it would be epoch-making development. However, the termination of funding from DARPA, the damaging Lighthill report, together with unfulfilled high expectations, resulted in the unsustainable development of AI.

## **5.2** Fourth-Generation Computers (1971-Present): New Processing Capabilities

Fourth-generation computers were based on the development of the first microprocessors that exploited the IC. However, during this era, the large-scale of integration circuits (LSI) were also introduced. Genuine LSI circuits had about 10,000 transistors and came on the computing scene around 1974 and utilised for computer main memories and other microprocessors. The advantage of this technology enabled hardware manufacturers to group thousands of transistors and other related components on a single silicon chip about the size of a baby’s fingernail to perform arithmetic, logic, and control functions. The computers using microchips were called microcomputers that provided ever smaller size computers, with larger capacities. In the late 1970s, the very large-scale integration (VLSI) was introduced that integrated hundreds of thousands of transistors on a single silicon semiconductor microchip. Technologies such as multiprocessing, multiprogramming, time-sharing, operating speed, and virtual memory made it a speedier and a more user-friendly device. The fourth-generation computers allowed the development of personal computers that gave birth to computer networks. This era ended the 1943 prediction of Thomas Watson, chairman of IBM that the world market for computers was around five. On the other hand, in 1975, Bill Gates and Paul Allen co-founders of Microsoft had a vision of a computer on every desk and in every home. A prediction that has come true over the past few decades.

The fourth-generation computers brought mixed fortunes for AI. The early years of its development overlapped with the AI winter of 1974-1980, which encountered a period that lacked AI research funding. However, even though AI research funding was virtually non-existent, private research through academic and industrial sources continued at a slower pace. Hence, significant results were still achieved due to these more powerful and faster computers that overcame some of the difficulties encountered by AI, which had up to that time gave disappointing outcomes. By 1974, these more powerful computers enabled Paul Werbos to initiate the backpropagation supervised learning algorithm for training neural networks. Additionally, by the 1980s the Lisp programming language was commonly used for AI research, paving the way for the acceptance of expert knowledge-based AI systems. However, in the 1990s AI was sidelined once again because these expert systems failed to meet (once again) the high expectations.

Nonetheless, despite this downturn, AI research witnessed the growth and acceptance of support vector machines (SVM) with supervised learning and the decline of neural networks. An SVM is mostly used in classification problems, such as text classification, image classification, spam detection, handwriting identification, gene expression analysis, face detection, and anomaly detection. By the 2000s these more powerful computers enabled new machine learning algorithms begin to solve a wide range of problems. However, one must recognise that even though fourth-generation computers are very fast and powerful, they are not specifically designed for AI systems.

Commonly, these computers can be viewed as general purpose computers that enable the execution of the current AI systems, such as deep neural networks that have since attained advanced results, including image recognition, natural language processing, and machine translation. More recently, Chat Bots and GPT models have made enormous headways in the industry. In other words, AI is an ancillary objective of fourth-generation computers. As such, these computers are a major limiting factor to the development of AI. This means that General AI, which is designed to perform any intellectual task that a human can do, such as being able to reason, learn, and understand complex concepts; and Super AI that exceeds human intelligence in all areas and would be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities and would be able to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence, are not currently possible using this type of technology. Furthermore, far more advanced computers are required for Theory of Mind AI types that interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans and for having self-awareness AI that has an independent intelligence and will not be under the control of the people that created it.

## **5.3** Fifth-Generation Computers (Present and Beyond): New Era for AI Processing

The fourth-generation computer has relegated AI as an ancillary application. This has restricted AI’s development to Narrow AI (or Weak AI), which is designed to do a specific task or a limited range of tasks, such as facial, speech, and image recognition; natural language processing; and recommendation systems. On the other hand, fifth-generation computers and other related technology are specifically designed with AI as their primary objective. The fifth-generation computers provide new opportunities for AI to edge towards General AI and Super AI that will enable these systems to possibly exceed human intelligence and interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans and thus achieve self-awareness.

In 1982, Japan’s Ministry of International Trade and Industry launched the Fifth-Generation Computer Project with the objective to develop a new generation of computers to understand and use human language. This generation is based on parallel processing hardware and AI software, which exploit super large scale integrated (SLSI) chips that contains millions of components on an individual chip. Parallel processing is much faster than the multiprogramming serial processing operating systems used by fourth-generation computers. Apart from using VLSI and later SLSI architecture, the key technologies applied for the Fifth-Generation Computer System include, better data flow control, logic programming, knowledge basis based on relational database and applied artificial intelligence and pattern processing ([Moto-oka, 1983)](#ch17.xhtml#r048). The Japanese initiative was meant for a new generation of computers that were envisaged for the 1990s.

According to [Moto-oka (1983)](#ch17.xhtml#r048), the research and development period set for this project was ten years, divided into three phases as shown in [Figure 5.1](#ch17.xhtml#f5). The first phase was related to the initial development of basic computer technology, which comprised of three basic modules, namely modules of individual functional mechanisms for the inference subsystem using parallel mechanism; modules of individual functional mechanisms for knowledge base subsystem based on knowledge-based technology; and basic software system with problem-solving, knowledge base, and intelligent interface capabilities utilising VLSI technology.

![Figure 5.1 Fifth-Generation Computer Project Development Phases.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C005_001.jpg)

**Figure 5.1** Fifth-Generation Computer Project Development Phases.[⏎](#ch17.xhtml#f5b)

Moto-oka also explained the conceptual details of the project as shown in [Figure 5.2](#ch17.xhtml#f6). He clarified that database machines and present mainframe computers will be networked to organise worldwide information systems. [Figure 5.2](#ch17.xhtml#f6) illustrates that the fifth-generation computer was based on three aspects, namely the human applications subsystems, modelling software subsystems, and the machine hardware subsystem, with each aspect having a two-way communication interface. The access to the system is through the human applications subsystem utilising user language (speech, natural language, pictures, and images), which acts as the external intelligent interface of basic software system, communicating with the modelling software subsystems via the intelligent programming system and the knowledge-based system.

![Figure 5.2 Fifth-Generation Computer Project Conceptual Details.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C005_002.jpg)

**Figure 5.2** Fifth-Generation Computer Project Conceptual Details.[⏎](#ch17.xhtml#f6b)

The modelling software system comprises of two key elements, namely, knowledge-based management system and the problem-solving and inference system, with the former communicating with the latter. The modelling software system communicates with the hardware system through three levels, namely the knowledge base machine, problem-solving, and inference machine, and the intelligent interface machine. According to Moto-oka the emphasis in computer systems is envisaged to shift towards the human system by significant enhancement of the logic level of the hardware system and by the positioning of the modelling system between the hardware and man. He explains that the interface between the software and hardware systems would be the kernel language. The entire software system would be realised in the kernel language, and the hardware system would directly execute the kernel language.

However, [Swinbanks and Anderson (1992)](#ch17.xhtml#r051) reported in March 1992 that the Japanese project was in difficulties. They report that after ten years and an investment of more than $400 million, all Japan had produced was a handful of parallel computers, the largest three of which have only a quarter of the target number of processors. By the end of that year, [Reid (1992)](#ch17.xhtml#r050) reported that the Japanese government formally terminated the “Fifth Generation” computer project, after a decade-long research effort that was supposed to create a new world of computing power but turned out to have little impact on the global computer market. However, the Japanese Fifth-Generation Computer project provided an important and forceful impetus for computer engineers and scientists in Silicon Valley to enter a competitive race to produce their own version of the Fifth-Generation Computer. Therefore, despite its failure, the Japanese fifth-generation project had flung the gauntlet to the rest of the computer world to come up with a functional fifth-generation computer that has at its basis the AI objective. The key features of the fifth-generation computer include:

*   Exploiting ULSI (Ultra Large-Scale Integration) technology in computer design.
*   Expansion in superconductor technology and parallel processing.
*   Multi-processor-based systems, with parallel computing.
*   Having magnetic-enabled chips that stores information, encrypts transactions, and facilitates transaction processing.
*   Use of optical fibre in circuits.
*   User-friendly interfaces with multimedia features.
*   Development of natural language processing (NLP).
*    Massive development in storage capacity, with faster and larger storage capabilities.
*   Interfacing powerful computers with AI.
*   Use of AI, such as navigating, browsing, video analysing, and image processing, amongst others.

### **5.3.1** The Quantum Computer

According to [Nasrin (2023)](#ch17.xhtml#r049), current fifth generation of computers are being created with an emphasis on quantum computing and artificial intelligence (AI). She contends that the move from computations to communication will be among the primary changes brought about by these fifth generation of computers. Nasrin believes that these computers will be able to link to one another and share information in ways that earlier generations were unable to do, making it possible to solve problems more effectively and collaboratively, resulting in the creation of fresh and original solutions.

Furthermore, [IDQ (2024)](#ch17.xhtml#r046) assert that in October 2023, the Californian quantum start-up Atom Computing announced it had created the world’s first quantum computer with over 1,000 qubits (1,180). They announced that this signified a substantial advancement on the previous record holder, IBM’s Osprey with 433 qubits. However, this declaration conflicted with the IBM announcement of its own 1,121 qubit Condor computer model. IBM claims that Condor pushes the limits of scale and yield in chip design with a 50% increase in qubit density, advances in qubit fabrication and laminate size, and includes over a mile of high-density cryogenic flex IO wiring within a single dilution refrigerator. They maintain that Condor’s performance is comparable to the 433-qubit Osprey but solves scale and paves the way for future hardware design.

A qubit is like a binary bit, which is the basic unit of information in traditional computing. A qubit (or quantum bit) is the basic unit of information in quantum computing. IBM currently uses a blend of aluminium and niobium, the two most used materials for a qubit. A superconducting qubit is typically a tiny loop or line of metal that behaves like an atom, which is an inherently quantum object.

In the meantime, in an issue of The Telegraph on 25 November 2023, Joe Pinkstone, Science Correspondent reports that the British government was to invest £2.5 billion in quantum technologies over the next ten years. UK Science Minister, Andrew Griffith, outlined a ten-year goal that would put quantum technology at the forefront of a plan to commercialise science. The UK Government’s strategy aims to have quantum computers and networks running by 2035, and it is also anticipated that the technology will provide the NHS with new-era tests by 2030. The Minister claims that the Quantum can break current encryption and create incorruptible communication networks for defence purposes, while quantum clocks and sensors can revolutionise everyday applications like Sat Navs, mobile phones, and healthcare screening.

### **5.3.2** What is Quantum Computing?

Quantum computing is a multidisciplinary topic encompassing features of computer science, physics, and mathematics that applies quantum mechanics to solve complex problems faster than on classical computers. The discipline of quantum computing includes hardware research and application development. One must also make a distinction between AI and quantum computing. AI is a software routine or process, whereas a Quantum Computer is the hardware that executes the AI software. AI is like having an app (software application) on a mobile phone and the mobile phone (hardware) being the physical device that executes the app (process or application software).

Essentially, quantum computing is based on the principles of quantum theory and makes use of the quantum states of subatomic particles to store information. Quantum theory is the theoretical core of modern physics that explains the nature and behaviour of matter and energy at the atomic and subatomic level, which is commonly referred to as quantum physics and quantum mechanics. The notion at the root of quantum computing is to demolish the barriers that have limited the speed of computers by exploiting the counterintuitive physics of subatomic scales.

Researchers have found that certain features of quantum mechanics are counterintuitive and can seem paradoxical because they describe behaviour that is quite different from what one would expect. For example, hot water can freeze faster than cold water, which may seem contrary to the normal intuition. This event is known as the Mpemba effect, which challenges the normal understanding of the physical properties of water. Scientists think that the increased evaporation rate of hot water and the formation of a thin insulating layer of ice may contribute to this counterintuitive behaviour. One of the most interesting examples of quantum mechanics predictions is that a pair of particles can be entangled. Hence, when two particles are entangled, it is impossible to describe the properties of one of them without referring to the other, since they behave as a single entity. It is not the intention of this text to prove the complex properties of quantum physics since this requires a much more detailed discussion on the topic. The author’s intention is to highlight in general terms that quantum computing is revolutionary and is very different from traditional computing.

Traditional computers operate on binary bits however quantum computers operate on quantum bits called qubits. A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data that traditional computers can process and store. A bit is always in one of two physical states, either on or off as in a light switch. The state of a bit is often represented by a single binary value, normally a 0 or 1. On the other hand, qubits are physically attained from minute quantum objects such as electrons and protons. Additionally, quantum computing is based on two quantum mechanical laws, namely superposition and entanglement. Furthermore, superposition does not restrict qubits to one of two possible values (1 or 0), but it can exist as a composite of both.

This feature facilitates quantum computers to function much faster than traditional computers. Entanglement is unique to quantum physics and unifies several separate particles, which ensures that what occurs to one particle will affect the other particles. When this principle is applied to quantum computers, this allows all particles to handle all their qubits together. This means that calculations are not executed in sequence but in parallel (i.e., simultaneously). These two important features (superposition and entanglement) combined with quantum computing provide the potential for an exponential speed enhancement to computing using quantum technology when compared with traditional processing.

### **5.3.3** How Quantum Computers Work

As stated previously, a traditional processor uses binary bits to perform its operations, whereas a quantum computer uses qubits (CUE-bits) to run multidimensional quantum algorithms. According to [IBM (2024)](#ch17.xhtml#r045), Quantum algorithms take a novel and unique approach to solve complex problems, such as simulating molecular behaviour or chemical simulations, by creating multidimensional computational spaces. A Quantum computer is based on several innovative principles:

*   *Superconductors*: While a desktop computer uses an air flowing device, such as a fan to keep it from overheating, the quantum processors necessitate a very cold temperature, about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, to retain their quantum states and avoid “decoherence” ([IBM, 2024](#ch17.xhtml#r045)). Decoherence is the process by which the information of a quantum system is modified by the system’s interaction with its environment that form a closed system, hence creating an entanglement between the system and heat bath (environment). On the other hand, quantum coherence is realised when an individual particle has wave functions that can be divided into two separate waves, thus the waves operate together in a coherent way to achieve quantum coherence. Decoherence is avoided by using super-cooled super-fluids to achieve ultra-low temperatures where certain materials exhibit an important quantum mechanical effect: electrons move through them without resistance, making them “superconductors.” According to [IBM (2024)](#ch17.xhtml#r045), when electrons pass through superconductors they correspond, forming “Cooper pairs.” These pairs can conduct a charge across barriers, or insulators, through a process known as quantum tunnelling. Two superconductors placed on either side of an insulator form a Josephson junction.
*   *Control*: IBM’s quantum computers use the Josephson junctions as superconducting qubits ([IBM, 2024](#ch17.xhtml#r045)). The behaviour of the qubits is controlled by firing microwave photons at them, which enable them to hold, change and read out individual units of quantum information.
*   *Superposition*: On its own, a qubit is not very useful. However, by placing the quantum information a qubit holds into a state of superposition, which represents a combination of all possible configurations of the qubit, a group of qubits in superposition can create complex, multidimensional computational spaces ([IBM, 2024](#ch17.xhtml#r045)). This enables complex problems to be presented in new ways in these spaces.
*   *Entanglement*: According to [IBM (2024)](#ch17.xhtml#r045), quantum entanglement is an effect that correlates the behaviour of two separate things, hence when two qubits are entangled, changes to one qubit directly impact the other.
*    *Interference*: An environment of entangled qubits placed into a state of superposition causes waves of probabilities that act as the outcomes of a measurement of the system. These waves can build on each other when many of them peak at a particular outcome or cancel each other out when peaks and troughs interact; these are both forms of interference ([IBM, 2024](#ch17.xhtml#r045)).

[IBM (2024)](#ch17.xhtml#r045) explains that a computation on a quantum computer uses the following process:

*   Preparing a superposition of all possible computational states.
*   A quantum circuit, prepared by the user, uses interference selectively on the components of the superposition according to an algorithm.
*   Many possible outcomes are cancelled out through interference, while others are amplified.
*   The amplified outcomes are the solutions to the computation.

A concern with quantum computers appears to be related to error correction or error mitigation, which has currently not been fully resolved. IBM have adopted Qiskit, an open-source, Python-based quantum software development kit (SDK). The quantum SDK is a complete quantum computing stack in simulation that includes an intuitive user interface; a compiler; and a quantum runtime environment optimised for running hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. Qiskit has modules that cover applications in finance, chemistry, optimisation, and machine learning. Python currently is at the vanguard of AI programming due to simplicity, versatility, and powerful libraries. Python is a high-level interpreted language, which allows rapid development and testing, which is a key feature in the iterative process of AI projects.

### **5.3.4** Neuromorphic Hardware

Neuromorphic hardware has the primary aim of emulating the human nervous system by applying dedicated computing architectures that imitate the structure (morphology) of neural networks. The idea is inspired by the way the human brain functions, where biological neurons and synapses work together. In the nervous system, a synapse permits a neuron to pass an electrical or chemical signal to another neuron or to the target effector cell. Hence, in a similar fashion, the network consisting of interconnected processors, known as neurons, allow it to have a parallel processing capability that permits the network to execute multiple tasks concurrently. The concept is based on a bottom-up approach where dedicated processing units imitate the behaviour of neurons directly in hardware, and a network of physical interconnections (bus-systems) allow a faster exchange of information.

These neuromorphic devices are not as flexible as the traditional central processing units (CPUs), however, due to their parallel processing ability they provide outstanding performance and improved energy efficiency, particularly when training and inferencing (predicting) of deep neural networks. The parallel processing ability is very important because the traditional computers that are based on the Von Neumann architecture, execute instructions sequentially, and process the data held in centralised memory. The outcome of such a process is that computing performance is restricted by the data transfer rate between the CPU and the external memory unit. This is known as the Von Neumann bottleneck.

Modern application systems are more demanding and require faster processing that non-parallel architectures cannot provide. Furthermore, the ability to parallelise computations is also limited by the access to shared memory resources. Additionally, the highly parallel structure of deep neural networks requires specific distributed memory access patterns, which are hard to map efficiently onto conventional computing technology. Hence, neuromorphic hardware addresses this problem by having AI integrated into these devices and systems. This allows neuromorphic hardware to be trained with wide-ranging datasets, making it suitable for far-reaching applications, such as speech recognition, natural language processing, and image detection. Moreover, the neuromorphic hardware’s level of accuracy is extraordinary, since it rapidly learns from substantial volumes of data.

Neuromorphic architectures and associated neuromorphic hardware designs vary from networks with binarized weights in digital hardware that are similar to regular feedforward neural networks (NN) to analogue in-memory accelerators of convolutional neural networks and event-based spiking neural network accelerators. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is an artificial neural network that is utilised mainly for image recognition and processing because of its ability to recognize patterns in images. However, the optimal design choice depends on the specific application and its explicit requirements, such as energy efficiency, latency, flexibility, or peak performance.

The first attempt at designing neuromorphic hardware was in the 1950s with analogue circuits having been used to implement neural networks in hardware. With the analogue methodology, the real-valued quantities of the neural network model are epitomised by real-valued physical quantities like analogue voltages, currents, or charges. Operations such as multiplication and addition are realised directly by the application of the laws of physics that pertain to Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws. Ohm’s law states that the current in a circuit is equal to the potential difference divided by the resistance of the circuit. While Kirchhoff’s voltage law states that the sum of the voltages around a circuit loop must equal zero, when following a consistent measurement direction of voltages for each element around the loop. Therefore, Kirchhoff’s Laws quantifies how current flows through a circuit and how voltage varies around a loop in a circuit. This means that the aggregate of the voltage steps as it goes around a circuit loop must end up back where it started. Moreover, Kirchhoff’s current law maintains that the sum of all currents into a circuit node (or a junction) must equal zero, meaning that the total current flowing into a node must equal the current flowing out of that node. This is a consequence of charge conservation.

Hence, circuit equations can be ascertained using Ohm’s Law, which presents the relationship between voltage and current in a resistor (V=IR), and Kirchhoff’s Current and Voltage Laws, which regulate the currents entering and exiting a circuit node and the sum of voltages around a circuit loop, respectively. This application of physical laws means that the numerous coefficients of the neural networks are either hardwired by suitable chosen resistive elements or can be programmed into novel memory cells distributed throughout the circuit, which radically diminishes the bottleneck of memory-transfer.

The development of neuromorphic chips is an important breakthrough, particularly the advances made in the 2010s in spiking neural networks (SNNs) and event-driven computing. The focus at that time was to improve efficiency and power-aware neuromorphic hardware designs. The Human Brain Project and the development of specialised neuromorphic chips have paved the way to demonstrate the potential of neuromorphic technology. In 2014, IBM developed the TrueNorth neuromorphic chip that is utilised in visual object recognition and has lower power consumption than traditional Von Neumann hardware, and in 2018, Intel developed the Loihi neuromorphic chip that has had applications in robotics as well as gesture and smell recognition. [Table 5.1](#ch17.xhtml#t7) provides a chronological itemised details of various neuromorphic chips that have been developed in the past several years, showing the software and application areas. Neuromorphic hardware is currently rapidly evolving, with academic and commercial research projects focusing on improving the effectiveness and applicability of neuromorphic systems that are so vital for resolving complex tasks in AI. Neuromorphic hardware based on analogue circuits are not flexible but are dedicated to a particular network architecture thus they are highly optimised for a specific purpose. This feature allows analogue accelerators to be exceptionally power-efficient and highspeed due to their asynchronous in-memory computing. This makes them ideal for specialised computing and signal processing that require ultra-low-power and real-time applications such as processing of low-dimensional senor signals in audio, medical and condition monitoring applications. Other significant neuromorphic computing applications include self-driving vehicles that can apply neuromorphic computing hardware to augment their capability to identify and interpret their environments; in medical diagnosis, where neuromorphic hardware can help in image detection features for the identification of diseases; and may be utilised in Internet of Things (IoT) devices to compile and analyse data, supporting effective data processing and decision-making.

## **5.4** Specific Hardware Associated with Artificial Intelligence

Earlier in this chapter it was shown that Al hardware was viewed as specialised computer hardware designed to execute Al-related tasks efficiently. This specialised computer hardware also includes specific chips and integrated circuits. These provide much faster processing and consume less energy, providing the needed infrastructure to execute Al algorithms and models effectively. It is also observed that the function of Al hardware in machine learning is critical for supporting the execution of complex programmes for deep learning models.

In comparison with traditional computer hardware such as the central processing unit (CPU), Al hardware can execute numerous processes faster, thus significantly decreasing the time and cost needed for algorithm training and execution. Due to the growing demand and popularity of AI and machine learning models, the global AI hardware market size was valued at USD 53.71 billion in 2023, and it is projected to surpass around USD 473.53 billion by 2033 and is likely to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 24.3% from 2024 to 2033 (Source: Precedence Research, [www.precedenceresearch.com/](http://www.precedenceresearch.com/)). Some of this specialised computer hardware is described in the following paragraphs.

### **5.4.1** Edge Computing Chips

Edge AI concerns the deployment of AI technologies directly on devices at the network edge, such as Internet of Things devices (IoT), smartphones, and edge servers. This allows real-time data analysis and decision-making to take place without relying on cloud infrastructure or other centralised systems. Therefore, Edge AI chips play an essential part in this concept by providing the necessary computational power to process AI algorithms efficiently and effectively. Additionally, these specialised processors are designed specifically to run Al models at the network’s edge. They also function as dedicated hardware accelerators specifically designed to execute AI workloads at the edge, and are optimised for real-time processing, low-latency operations, and power efficiency. They greatly lessen latency because they process data near its source, improving the overall performance of AI ecosystems. By offloading AI computations from the central systems or the cloud to local devices, these chips enable faster response times, reduce network bandwidth requirements, and enhance data security. Data security is improved by minimizing the amount of data that needs to be transmitted to the central systems. Since, these chips mitigate data transmission to remote servers they reduce energy consumption and optimise power efficiency.

A key advantage of Edge AI chips is that chip architectures and designs, such as the neural processing unit (NPU) and specialised accelerators, are specifically customised to optimise AI workloads. Edge AI chips are used in various applications, such as in smart homes and IoT devices by supporting voice assistants, video analytics, and smart cameras that permit local processing and reducing dependence on central systems. Edge AI chips are also used in healthcare and telemedicine by monitoring patients remotely helping to provide real-time diagnostics, and personalised healthcare recommendations. On the industrial front, Edge AI chips accelerate intelligent control systems, predictive maintenance, and quality control for automation and robotics on the shop floor. Edge AI chips also support autonomous vehicles and drones with real-time object detection, collision avoidance, and navigation.

However, Edge AI chips have limitations. For example, Edge AI chips have constrained computing power of edge devices, because unlike cloud servers, they have limited access to resources, including processing power, memory, and storage. This limits their processing capabilities when executing complex AI algorithms that require significant computational capabilities. Although Edge AI chips mitigate the transmission of private data to central systems, they often process sensitive data locally, such as personal health information or video surveillance material that still require protection from potential unauthorised infringements.

Compatibility issues may occur when integrating edge AI chips with existing systems and devices to ensure seamless integration with different hardware and software components. However, chip manufacturers and developers are aiming for standardisation and are providing appropriate frameworks and software development kits (SDKs) to assist seamless integration and ensure compatibility across different platforms. These limitations are being mitigated by the emergence of the NPUs. These are specifically designed for AI computations to handle more complex AI workloads and are optimised for executing deep learning models that deliver accelerated AI performance with improved power efficiency. ### **5.4.2** Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASIC)

Generally, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) are a diverse category of integrated circuits (ICs) that assist designers to optimise sophisticated electronic devices. There is no consensus amongst electronics professionals regarding the definition of an ASIC. In fact, there is disagreement on what an ASIC is or whether a particular component should be classified as an ASIC. However, a working definition that portrays common acceptable features is that an ASIC is an integrated circuit designed for a specific customer, application, or market using cell-based techniques, where the necessary functional blocks are taken from a cell library, interconnected, and simulated to provide the desired system functions and level of performance ([Analog Dialogue, 1990](#ch17.xhtml#r044), p.12). Furthermore, this definition excludes ICs designed with traditional “custom” design techniques.

According to [Keim (2023)](#ch17.xhtml#r047), the full definition identifies an ASIC as an IC that offers customised functionality but does not require a fully customised design process; instead, the customised functionality is achieved through a process that is analogous to PCB design. Keim argues that for an ASIC, designers take functional blocks from a library, interconnect them, and verify functionality and performance via simulation. Keim also maintains that the term “application specific” in an ASIC is somewhat misleading because he argues that in electrical engineering, “application” normally refers to the practical purpose of electrical equipment (i.e., the type of useful work the device is intended to perform).

[Wasay (2023)](#ch17.xhtml#r052), views ASICs as being designed for targeted tasks like image processing, speech recognition, and cryptocurrency mining. He argues that their objective is to accelerate AI procedures to meet the specific needs of an enterprise, thus delivering an effective infrastructure that boosts overall speed within the ecosystem. For example, distinct from traditional central processing units (CPUs) or graphics processing units (GPUs), ASIC miners are designed for a single goal, basically to execute the specific hashing algorithm that garbles data to make it unreadable, which are critically required for mining a particular cryptocurrency. These hashing algorithms are one-way programs, which means that the text cannot be unscrambled and decoded by anyone else. Hence, this singular focus permits these ASIC miners to deliver unparalleled performance and energy efficiency in comparison to general-purpose hardware. Apart from the fact that these integrated circuits simplify the deployment of complex machine-learning mechanisms, they are also capable of managing significant volumes of data, which makes them instrumental in training artificial intelligence models. These ASICs may be used in diverse areas that include natural language processing of texts and speech data.

[Keim (2023)](#ch17.xhtml#r047) argues that ASICs are not application specific as they might seem and are not limited to a particular application. To support his argument, he cites that a highly integrated data converter ASIC, which may be designed primarily for medical imaging applications, can also be utilised for industrial video processing or a multichannel automotive sensor network. He also claims that a more generic ASIC, such as a system-on-chip (SoC) ASIC, which is initially designed for smartphones, incorporates enough functionality to be successful in a wide variety of applications. Therefore, Keim maintains that task-specific integrated circuit (TSIC) or functionality-specific integrated circuit (FSIC) is a more accurate term. Moreover, he argues that generally, an ASIC is designed so that one chip can efficiently perform a specific combination of tasks. However, he insists that even if this combination of tasks is initially needed for a specific application, there may be various other applications where this ASIC would be an effective and desirable alternative to off-the-shelf ICs.

ASIC development, particularly if it involves non-recurring engineering (NRE) can take a substantial amount of time and cost before a single chip can be manufactured. Essentially, NRE covers the research, design, development, testing, and other tasks required to create a new product or custom design. It also includes the up-front costs sustained during the new product development. However, the NRE is a once only cost that is normally encountered when designing, developing or manufacturing of a new design, product or customised devises. This essentially means that a customer requiring a new product or product modification would need to pay for the NRE costs or any other costs incurred for the design modification. [Figure 5.3](#ch17.xhtml#f7) illustrates an example of a device that has gone through the ASIC design process applied by Intel and Google, which is a “programmable networking device” for “cloud and communication service providers.” According to [Keim (2023)](#ch17.xhtml#r047), ASICs are a crucial addition to high-performance and high-volume electronic devices that cannot be optimally designed using off-the-shelf components.

![Figure 5.3 ASIC Design Process Applied by Intel and Google.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C005_003.jpg)

**Figure 5.3** ASIC Design Process Applied by Intel and Google.[⏎](#ch17.xhtml#f7b)

The decision to outsource the NRE depends on whether the component is considered to be a strategic product and whether the capacity, skills and experience required to design the product exist internally. Normally, companies do not tend to outsource strategic products. Keim argues that management can only justify NRE’s high development costs for high-volume projects with demanding performance requirements. It is only in such circumstances that an ASIC can realistically become economically advantageous. An alternative option if a customised ASIC is not available is to seek a programmable logic device, such as a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) or complex programmable logic device (CPLD).

### **5.4.3** Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)

A Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) is an advanced integrated circuit that belong to a category of devices known as programmable logic. An FPGA is a very flexible device because it can be configured to be any digital circuit that is required by the user without any physical modifications, such as soldering or jumper wires. Therefore, the user can customise its function since all that needs to be done is to merely insert a configuration into the FPGA and it will behave like the circuit the user requires. Hence, an FPGA is bases on random access memory (RAM) through programmable logic and therefore can behave like any feasible circuit as needed and be reconfigured any number of times.

FPGA’s flexibility makes it ideal for implementing Al software because it can be customised and programmed to meet the explicit requirements of the Al ecosystem thus being “field programmable.” This is possible because an FPGA consists of configurable logic blocks (CLBs) that are interconnected and programmable thus providing it with the ability for running a wide range of AI applications. A CLB is the fundamental repeating logic resource on an FPGA, which when linked together by routing resources, the components in the CLBs perform complex logic functions, implement memory functions, and synchronise code on the FPGA. Moreover, a FPGA chip can be programmed to process operations of differing complexity levels, adjusting to the system’s specific requirements. Although FPGAs operate like other read-only memory chips but a higher gate capacity, its key feature is its re-programmability capability, which means that it can be programmed various times. Another beneficial feature is that FPGAs provide better security because their all-inclusive architecture guarantees robust protection, making them trustworthy for secure Al applications.

A schematic diagram to create designs for FPGAs digital circuits is not advisable due to the magnitude and complexity the digital circuits within it. Typically, the user would define the function of the circuit that is required, and the device will automatically apply this to generate a circuit corresponding to the defined function. Therefore, FPGAs is like programming by inputting text, but the outcome is not software but hardware. An FPGA is ideal for rapid prototyping and final system design and are very suitable for applications, like AI, edge computing, system security, 5G, factory automation, and robotics.

A key advantage of FPGAs is their programmable characteristic that permits the designer to rapidly program and re-program the device to perform any function that is required. The re-programmability feature is doable at any time by using downloadable software updates during and after the FPGA has been integrated into an application. This feature allows a rapid time-to-market design that can be developed and modified concurrently with the overall system design. Furthermore, FPGAs have a parallel processing capability unlike non-sequential traditional processing through a “sea of gate” architecture. Parallel processing is highly suitable for high performance computing applications, such as AI that permit the FPGA to produce significantly higher performance exercising lower clock speeds that consume lower power.

However, FPGAs tend to be costly because of the design resources it consumes to cater for the diversity and complexity of its functional features. The cost of an FPGA depends on the amount of silicon needed to manufacture it; the extent of research and development required to design it, including the tooling; and the somewhat low volume demand when compared to other commonly used processors for everyday devices, apart from their high-power usage to operate it. On the other hand, to design a customised digital circuit out of discrete logic takes time and is costly, and with very little flexibility if a modification is required.

Although a circuit created directly in silicon has superior speed and efficiency in performance, its flexibility index is non-existent. Furthermore, custom silicon is very much dependent on economies of scale because it has extensive upfront costs for tooling and setup; and unless tens of thousands of these chips are made, it becomes a more expensive approach when compared with a FPGA chip. As stated previously, an FPGA has flexibility and may be modified without penalty. An FPGA is a tool and like every other tool it has its uses depending on whether the solution to use an FPGA makes sense, when other cheaper and more efficient chips are available. For instance, you do not use a sledgehammer to crack a nut.

FPGAs are very useful for AI associated applications because they can be configured (and re-configured) depending on the role that they are to play. FPGAs use dedicated software that is usually provided by the FPGA supplier. Developers would design the logic to be executed in the FPGA by using either graphical design capture or a hardware description language (HDL). Graphical design capture language (e.g., C and C++) is generally utilised for smaller FPGAs. On the other hand, HDL is used to describe the behaviour or structure of digital circuits (ICs) and might be applied to stimulate the circuit and check its response. Examples of HDL are VHDL (very high-speed integrated-circuit hardware description language) and Verilog. Other HDLs include JHDL (Java HDL) and Active-HDL (proprietary HDL by Cypress Semiconductor Corporation).

The HDL software compiles the design by integrating the logic that best fits the target FPGA, after which the software creates a bitstream that is downloaded to configure (program) the FPGA, making it ready to perform its defined role. Designers may opt for a rapid development strategy by using a suite of software design tools and IP (Intellectual Property), or pre-configured design blocks, such as those offered by Lattice Semiconductor (FPGA Design Software). Such a strategy would lessen the time, effort and complexity required in the design process to fast-track the creation of bitstreams that execute on Lattice FPGAs. Lattice FPGAs include AI and machine learning (ML) inferencing, data co-processing, embedded vision, and secure system control amongst many others.

### **5.4.4** Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD)

CPLD is another type of programmable logic device. It is similar to a SPLD (simple programmable logic device). However, a SPLD is the simplest, smallest, and least-expensive forms of programmable logic devices, with a complexity that is far below of a CPLD. A SPLD normally consists of a few hundred gates, whereas a CPLD contains of a few thousand logic gates. Hence, a CPLD is more likely to have implications for AI specific applications. However, CPLDs are less complex than FPGAs, which also makes them useful in AI applications.

CPLD comprises of multiple programmable array logic (PAL) structures known as function blocks (also known as macrocells). Hence, a CPLD is a logic device with completely programmable AND/OR arrays and macrocells. Macrocells can also be defined as functional blocks responsible for performing sequential or combinatorial logic. These function blocks are linked by a programmable interconnect, which is known as GIM (global interconnection matrix) that contains complex logic operations and logic for implementing disjunctive normal form expressions. Hence, by reconfiguring the GIM, different logic circuits can be achieved, which allow the CPLDs to interact with the outer world using digital inputs/outputs.

There are several similarities between CPLD and FPGA that include being a programmable logic device consisting of logic gate arrays, which may be programmed using HDLs such as Verilog HDL or VHDL. However, there are several critical differences. A CPLD normally has a few thousand logic gates, whereas an FPGA can have millions of logic gates. Therefore, an FPGA can accommodate complex circuits and systems, but this complexity comes at a higher cost, which make CPLDs more suitable for less complex applications. Additionally, CPLDs feature a built-in non-volatile EEPROM (electrically erasable programmable random-access memory), whereas FPGAs feature a volatile memory. Therefore, a CPLD can preserve its memory contents when powered off, while an FPGA does not retain its memory content. This means that because of this feature, a CPLD can resume operating straightaway after power-up, but most FPGAs require a bit-stream from an external non-volatile memory for start-up.

Furthermore, FPGAs have an irregular signal processing delay because of its highly complex architecture combined with the user’s custom programming that affect its performance. However, the pin-to-pin delay of CPLDs is significantly lower due to the simpler architecture that makes it faster. Note that a signal processing delay is a crucial issue in the design of safety-critical and embedded real-time applications. FPGAs operate at higher frequencies and have more complex logic processes and therefore are likely to have higher power consumption than CPLDs. This means that a FPGA based system requires better thermal management. Note that the objective of thermal management is to maintain a system within its operating temperature tolerance. This is a critical issue with electronic devices because effective thermal management dissipates excess heat to prevent overheating. Therefore, thermal management is an extremely key concern in FPGA-based systems since they frequently use heat sinks and cooling fans that require bigger, more complicated power supplies and distribution networks. Additionally, CPLDs have a better information security feature because the memory is integrated into the chip itself. On the other hand, many FPGAs have external non-volatile memory that increases the potential data security risk even though they have data encryption algorithms included.

CPLD manufacturers include Lattice Semiconductor, Atmel, Xilinx, and Altera (owned by Microchip, AMD, and Intel, respectively. CPLDs are commonly used in many low-to-medium complexity digital control and signal processing circuits, such as bootloaders for FPGAs and other programmable systems. CPLDs are small in size and have low power consumption, which make them ideally suited for portable and handheld digital devices. They are also regularly used as address decoders and custom state machines in digital systems, and in safety-critical control applications. [Figure 5.4](#ch17.xhtml#f8) depicts the stages for CPLD programming and development. It illustrates that the programming and development stages of an CPLD consists of three phases, namely system definition and CPLD model selection; setting up the programming and testing environment; and finalisation for housing the CPLD and adjoining electronic components for prototype production. The CPLD goes through a meticulous testing process before it is sent for the production process.

![Figure 5.4 Stages for CPLD Programming and Development.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C005_004.jpg)

**Figure 5.4** Stages for CPLD Programming and Development.[⏎](#ch17.xhtml#f8b)

## **5.5** Conclusion

This chapter has traced the development of computer hardware in relation to the advancement of AI. The chapter examines the pioneering applications of AI using earlier generation of computers and then focuses on the fourth and fifth generation computers. Starting with largescale integrated circuits (LSI) in the early 1970s, moving to the very largescale integrated circuits (VLSI) of the late 1970s, and progressing to the super largescale integrated circuits (SLSI) in the early 1980s.

However, history has shown that the capability of AI applications is limited by the processing power of the computing architecture that is being utilised. Traditional computers that are based on the Von Neumann architecture, which execute instructions sequentially and process the data held in centralised memory have proven to be a serious limitation. This limitation is due to the restricted data transfer rate between the CPU and the external memory unit, known as the Von Neumann bottleneck. The Quantum computer is aimed at addressing this weakness and is making big strides in processing speed where the use of the quantum states of subatomic particles to store information is being applied to run multidimensional quantum algorithms. IBM has announced the development of the Condor quantum computer model with 1,121 qubits. Other manufacturers such as the Californian quantum start-up Atom Computing are also making significant progress in this area.

Another important development is in Neuromorphic hardware that has the primary aim of emulating the human nervous system by applying dedicated computing architectures that imitate the structure (morphology) of neural networks. The Neuromorphic hardware uses the laws of physics, namely Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws to permit parallel processing for specific tasks. For example, the spiking neural networks (SNNs) and event-driven computing of the 2010s that focused to improve efficiency and power-aware neuromorphic hardware designs. Of particular importance is the development in 2014, when IBM developed the TrueNorth neuromorphic chip that is utilised in visual object recognition and in 2018, Intel developed the Loihi neuromorphic chip that has had applications in robotics as well as gesture and smell recognition.

Neuromorphic hardware is ideal for specialised applications such as medical and condition monitoring applications; self-driving vehicles to boost their capability for identifying and interpret their environments; in medical diagnosis for the identification of diseases amongst many other applications. The chapter also discusses other dedicated hardware, such as Edge Computing Chips, Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASIC), Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), and Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD). This dedicated hardware allows the programmability of the chips for specific tasks and are integrated as part of applicable systems. This dedicated hardware may also be integrated with the neuromorphic computing. Developing computers that mimic the human brain is a futuristic objective that will transform the current limited AI applications to what is known as Super AI. However, developing chips that mimic the human brain is currently a reality but limited to specific tasks.

# Chapter 6Artificial Intelligence Software

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-8](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-8)

> *“Continuous improvement is better than delayed perfection.”*
> 
> Mark Twain
> 
> *Author (1835-1910)*

Typically, hardware on its own is of no value but supported by the appropriate software it could become a very powerful tool. The previous chapter focused on different types of AI hardware. However, it also illustrated that for the AI hardware to be of any use it must have the software to make it functional. For instance, for its Quantum Computer, IBM have adopted Qiskit, which is an open-source, Python-based quantum software development kit (SDK). The quantum SDK is a comprehensive development tool that includes an intuitive user interface; a compiler; and a quantum runtime environment optimised for running hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. Additionally, Qiskit has application routines written in the Python software language regarding finance, chemistry, optimisation, and machine learning. Python is a high-level interpreted language, which allows rapid development and testing, which is a key feature in the iterative process of AI projects. Furthermore, Python is currently at the forefront of AI programming due to its simplicity, versatility, and powerful libraries.

This is also applicable to the specific AI hardware related to Edge Computing Chips; Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA); and Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD). These all require some type of applications software for them to provide the benefits that they have been designed for. For example, Edge Computing Chips that concern the deployment of AI technologies directly on devices at the network edge, such as Internet of Things devices (IoT), smartphones, and edge servers have standard software development kits (SDKs) to assist seamless integration and ensure compatibility across different platforms. Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) are programmed using either graphical design capture or a hardware description language (HDL). Graphical design capture language, such as C and C++ is normally used for the smaller FPGAs, while HDL is used for the larger FPGAs and utilise VHDL (very high-speed integrated-circuit hardware description language) and Verilog. Other HDLs include JHDL (Java HDL) and Active-HDL (proprietary HDL by Cypress Semiconductor Corporation). Complex Programmable Logic Devices (CPLD) apply similar programmable languages as a FPGA, namely Verilog HDL or VHDL. For further details regarding HDL refer to Keim (2020).

Neuromorphic computing to be of applicable use must also be supported by software. For example, the Spiking Neural Processor T1 chip produced by Innatera uses the Talamo programming language applicable to smart-sensing, wearables, and IoT. SynSense, which manufacture the Speck, Xylo, and DynapCNN chips use diverse programming languages, such as Sinabs, Samna, and Rockpool for smart sensing and smart vision processing. Charlotte Frenkel that manufacture the ReckOn and Odin chips use the standard Verilog programming language mainly for task-agnostic learning over second-long timescales at the extreme edge and general-purpose experimentation platform for bio-inspired edge computing applications.

This chapter will examine several significant aspects, namely AI programming languages; AI algorithms; and neuromorphic computing. When examining AI software, there may be serval instances that overlap with the AI hardware aspects to ensure that a clear understanding is conveyed.

## **6.1** Introduction

Basically, software is a collection of instructions, data or programs that are utilised to operate computer hardware and execute specific functions. Software can be viewed as complementary to hardware. In fact, it may be envisaged as being the opposite of hardware or the other side of a coin, where hardware is the head, and the software is the tail side. Hardware describes the physical features of a computer, whereas software is a broad term used to indicate the applications, scripts, and programmes that execute on a hardware device. A software application can vary depending on the programme that is uploaded on the hardware, whereas the hardware has a fixed, non-flexible function.

There are two main types of software, namely system (operating) and application software. System software is designed to run the computer’s hardware and provides a platform for applications to execute conjointly with the hardware. On the other hand, application software achieves a specific need and performs stipulated tasks. The other types of software consist of programming software, which provides the programming tools that software developers use to generate and create applications; middleware that lies between the system and applications software; and driver software that operates the computer devices and peripherals.

### **6.1.1** Software History

In the early days, software, whether operating or applications, was created for specific computers on a proprietary basis that was packaged as part of the hardware it executed on. In the 1960s and 1970s most hardware and associated software was for mainframe computers and minicomputers. However, the mid to late 1970s witnessed a variety of microcomputers in the form of desktop or portable computers coming on the commercial market for business applications. During this period, software was sold and distributed on floppy disks, sometime later, around 1982, CDs were used and later still, around 1997, DVDs became a common software distribution medium. The main difference between a CD and DVD is basically the data storage capacity. DVDs use a different (shorter) wavelength laser that provide a much higher resolution of optical data allowing a DVD to store as much as 7 to 14 times as much data as a CD. Currently, most software is acquired and directly downloaded over the internet at either a once only cost or at a flexible usage licence cost, normally on a yearly basis. Moreover, software can be purchased directly from the software owner’s website or application service provider websites.

It was not until the late 1950s that the term software was used. During this era, software was not commercially available even though varying types of programming software were being generated. Early software development was restricted to scientists and other technicians who working for the bigger organisations developed their own software. It should be noted that during this era, hardware was very costly and only large organisations like governmental entities or large corporations could afford to purchase the hardware and employ the scarce technical human resources.

[Figure 6.1](#ch18.xhtml#f9) provides a general timeline regarding the history of software. Like hardware, computer software has developed through various generations. Early software, which is often referred to as first- and second-generation software languages were low-level machine languages. First-generation languages were machine language statements written in binary code (0 or 1), which basically reflected the computer hardware circuitry state of on (1) or off (0). These languages were difficult to write and understand, and very problematic for tracing programming errors. In June 1948, Tom Kilburn, who was a computer scientist wrote the world’s first piece of software for the “Manchester Baby” computer at the University of Manchester United Kingdom in binary code as part of his thesis “A storage system for use with binary digital computing machines.”

![Figure 6.1 General Timeline Regarding the History of Software.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_001.jpg)

**Figure 6.1** General Timeline Regarding the History of Software.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f9b)

The second-generation languages were still machine based but were an improvement on the first-generation languages, called assembler languages. Assembly language contained human-readable statements that were converted to machine language using an assembler. Hence, an assembler converted written coded instructions to machine-level instructions. As early as 1947, Kathleen and Andrew Donald Booth working for the Institute for Advanced Study, at Princeton University developed the first assembly code in which a language is used to represent machine code instructions, namely coding for A.R.C (automatic relay computer). However, the word “assembler” is commonly accredited to Wilkes, Wheeler, and Gill in their 1951 book “The Preparation of Programs for an Electronic Digital Computer.” They used the word to represent “a program that assembles another program consisting of several sections into a single program.”

An important milestone was when in the early 1950s General Motors’ Research division created the first operating system, GMOS for its IBM 701 and in 1956 for its IBM 704 computer. Third-generation computer languages came on the scene in the late 1950s. However, it was not until 1958 that John Tukey, a statistician used the word “software” when writing an article about computer programming. This era also coincides with the release of the FORTRAN and COMTRAN (precursor to COBOL) programme compilers in 1957, followed by the LISP compiler in 1958. The BASIC interpretive programming language came on the scene in 1964, followed by PASCAL in 1970, and later in 1974, by COBOL, ADA, and the first SQL language. During the 1960s and 1970s applications software were mainly developed in-house by organisations that could afford a structure to support its electronic data processing activities. However, several important commercial software packages such as PERT (program evaluation and review technique: ICL 1900 PERT) and SPSS (statistical package for social science) were released in 1966 and 1968, respectively.

In 1971, AT&T released the first edition of the Unix operating system and IBM introduced the first 8-inch (20 cm) floppy disk. However, a significant breakthrough for consumer software was the release by Apple of the Apple II personal computer (PC) in 1977, followed by the first spreadsheet software by VisiCorp that released VisiCalc for the Apple II.
