The 1980s witnessed an exponential growth in both hardware and software that saw Microsoft releasing its MS-DOS operating system, which became the standard for all IBM compatible PCs, paving the way for making commercial software being available to the average consumer. Furthermore, hard disc drives became the standard for PCs with manufacturers bundling software in their PCs. 1983 also saw the birth of the free software movement with Richard Stallman’s GNU (GNU is not Unix) Linux project for creating a Unix-like operating system with the source code being made freely available. Apple released its Macintosh line in 1984, which was followed by Microsoft Windows 1.0 for the IBM compatible PCs. Additionally, the mid-1980s witnessed the release of important software applications, including AutoDesk’s AutoCAD, and Microsoft Word and Excel. Moreover, floppy disks that were introduced in the 1960s became a major software distribution media in the 1980s, with the CD-ROM being a major player in 1989.

The reader needs to recall that the 1980s witnessed the birth and acceptance of expert systems with the Lisp programming language and the launching of the 5th Generation Computer Project. Furthermore, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams in 1986 introduced a new era of neural computation research through their book, “Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition.” Additionally, the Salk Institute and the University of California launched an academic journal “Neural Computation” with the first issue being the Spring of 1989, with Terrence Sejnowski being the Editor-in-Chief. By 1990, the Python computer language was launched, which has become a popular programming language for AI applications. During the 1990s the internet became very popular and by 1999 Salesforce.com utilised cloud computing to pioneer software delivery over the internet, with the term software as a service (SaaS) coming into vogue by 2000. The iPhone was launched in 2007, and mobile applications begin to take hold. By 2010, DVDs became obsolete as users purchased and downloaded software from the internet and the cloud.

Concurrently with this development, fourth-generation languages were being developed as early as 1984, with MatLab from Matrix Laboratory; and Python in 1990, apart from Perl, Ruby, SQL. These fourth-generation languages consisted of commands that are similar to statements in the human language and are mainly used in database programming and scripting. There has also been a growth in the fifth-generation programming languages that are chiefly applied for AI. These programming languages have visual tools to develop a computer program. Examples of fifth-generation programming languages include OPS5, Mercury, ICAD, and KL-ONE. OPS5 is a rule-based computer programming language that has been used in successful expert systems, while Mercury is a functional logic programming language made for real-world applications. Additionally, ICAD (Intelligent Computer-Aided Design) has an open architecture that can use all the power and flexibility of the underlying language. The original implementation of ICAD was on a Lisp machine (Symbolics). While KL-ONE is a language based on frame language that reflects a related idea. This computer language is what is referred to as a knowledge representation system applying semantic networks and frames. These fifth-generation languages will be discussed in more detail later.

The above software developments facilitated the creation and growth of supervised learning in the 1990s, and machine learning algorithms for solving problems in the 2000s, which are vital for AI applications. Furthermore, these programming languages allowed deep neural networks to achieve advanced results around 2010, and the current enhancement of Chat Bots and GPT models. Without the above software developments, todays AI software would not be possible. AI software is specifically aimed at processing voluminous amount of data to execute tasks that require human intelligence, including image recognition, video analytics, generative AI, voice recognition, text recognition, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) that enable a computer to understand, interpret, and generate human-like text.

## **6.2** AI Computer Programming Languages

This section will describe in some detail the key AI computer programming languages, including programming languages related to specific AI hardware that were discussed in the previous chapter. It should be noted that software programmes written in most of these computer languages execute on the traditional Von Neumann computers.

### **6.2.1** Lisp

Lisp (list processing) is a programming language that was specifically intended for manipulating data strings in a simple and effortless manner. It has been in use since 1958 and is considered as one of the oldest programming languages still in use. Lisp commenced as an interpretive programming language, without the need of a compiler, similar to the original BASIC programming language. With interpretive programming languages, the source code is interpreted directly on the system. However, interpretive programming languages are slower to run than the compiled versions. Currently, most computer programming languages, including Lisp, have a compiler that generates an executable version that achieves faster programme execution velocity.

Lisp has influenced the development of other computer programming languages due to its different dialects. The current Lisp-based computer programming languages (Lisp dialects) include: Clojure; Emacs Lisp; Common Lisp; Julia; Racket; and Scheme. Lisp is very popular in higher education, where students may learn the relevant programming tactics in preparation for practical applications. Lisp is expressed as a function of at least one object. It processes symbolic information rather than numbers, thus making it very suitable for AI programmes. An object can be another function, data items either as constants or variables, or data structures. Lisp is easy to learn and use, making it very popular in the academic arena for teaching computer programming. Lisp can be applied for a variety of uses such as a basic programming tool, AI applications, machine learning, and quantum computing.

Currently, Lisp dialects are applied to generate code in a range of use-case scenarios. Use-case scenarios specify a meticulous description of how a certain use-case evolves. These scenarios are described by charting a sequence of interactions between the external actor and the system, showing the different steps and conditions that may arise during execution. Use-case scenarios provide a deeper or more detailed view to help developers and stakeholders visualise the specific user interactions. Use-case scenarios are defined by applying two basic elements, namely the flow of events; and use-case templates. The flow of events defines the step-by-step progression of actions within a use-case, with each step in the flow of events linking to a specific action or decision point. This provides an all-embracing view of the user-system interaction, identifying alternate flows and exceptions that are important for foreseeing different paths a use-case may take. On the other hand, use-case templates present a standardised structure for documenting use-cases, by having areas for placing the use-case name, description, actors, preconditions, postconditions, and the leading and alternative flows. These, templates provide a systematic way to collect and manage information to ensure consistency across various use-cases within a project.

The application of a use-case scenario is best illustrated through an example. [Figure 6.2](#ch18.xhtml#f10) shows an example for an online shopping system. The use-case scenario in this case is a situation where a customer is placing an order through an online shopping system. Hence, the use-case is the customer’s order placement, and shows the customer instigating the process of purchasing the required objects online.

![Figure 6.2 Use-Case Scenario: Example of the Common Online Shopping System.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_002.jpg)

**Figure 6.2** Use-Case Scenario: Example of the Common Online Shopping System.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f10b)

[Figure 6.2](#ch18.xhtml#f10) illustrates that the use-case is the high-level description of the functionality, which is the placing an order. As can be seen, the use-case scenario breaks the task of placing an order into smaller, manageable steps, by detailing these steps from logging-in to confirmation. Additionally, the flow of events specifies a step-by-step sequence for the scenario, identifying the actions and decision points. The Online Shopping System use-case diagram is a clear visual representation of the main functions and interfaces within an online shopping platform. The diagram describes the various tasks and processes included in the system that allows users to understand the overall system structure and behaviour. The use-case diagram includes the important tasks of the system such as searching and viewing product details; adding goods to the shopping cart; and updating the shopping cart and viewing its contents. The diagram also illustrates the checkout and payment process such as placing an order; choosing the payment method; and providing the shipping address; apart from showing tasks related to managing user accounts, including updating profile information and displaying the order history. Applying the use-case diagram provides a homogenous structure for documenting the use-case, which ensures a consistent method across the different use cases in the system.

Common Lisp has several advantages such as the unmatched read–eval–print loop (REPL) also termed an interactive top-level or language shell that aids to interact with running a web app; the exception handling mechanism; performance; ability to build a self-contained executable process; stability; good threads story; strong typing, amongst others. REPL is a simple interactive computer programming environment that takes single user inputs, executes them, and returns the result to the user. Hence, a program written in an REPL environment is executed piecewise.

Lisp has been successfully used in several major applications for many years. For example, in 1984 Richard Stallman developed the text editor GNU Emacs that was written in a Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp, which is also utilised to write Emacs configs and extensions. At around 2009, Common Lisp was used for Grammarly, which is an online service to process English texts. Grammarly applies AI to analyse the text and makes recommendations on how it may be improved. Apart from being a grammar and spell checker, it also checks the text for text brevity, vocabulary, and tone.

Another application written in Common Lisp is the Allegro Network File System (NFS) Server that is used by Boeing 747 and 777. An NFS is a means of storing files on a network, which is a distributed file system that allows users to access files and directories located on remote computers and handle these files and directories as if they were local. In the aviation field, both Boeing and Airbus use Piano, which is a software package written in Common Lisp for aircraft design development and analysis. Generally, Piano is a powerful tool for major airframe and aero-engine manufacturers, research and governmental institutions, and environmental organisations worldwide. ITA Software which is normally associated with the system for air tickets search and pricing is currently part of Google’s travel industry department that develops most of its software using Common Lisp. Common Lisp is also the main programming language used by the Portuguese Siscog software provider, which develops decision support systems designed for resource planning, allocation, and management in the transportation sector. Their software is used for the London Tube.

CircleCI is a CI/CD tool that supports rapid software development and publishing, uses a Lisp dialect Clojure. They also use ClosureScript for frontend development. CircleCI permits automation across the user’s pipeline, from code building, testing to deployment. Additionally, CircleCI integrates with GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, and Bitbucket to create builds when new code lines are committed. Furthermore, computer-aided design systems AutoCAD applies the AutoLISP dialect as the internal application development language. Riemann, which is a tool for distributed system monitoring, is also mostly written in Clojure that offers greater flexibility and fault-tolerance. This system aggregates events from user servers and applications and combines them into a stream and then transmits them for further processing or storage. The above illustrates that the Lisp computer programming language is a very versatile software development tool for a variety of practical applications.

### **6.2.2** Python

Python is a general-purpose computer programming language, which can be used across technology and domains. It has been around for over three decades and has become a very popular programming language, particularly for AI based applications. Additionally, Python is a high-level programming language that can process data arrays, variables, objects, complex arithmetic, and Boolean expressions, as well as other abstract concepts. Hence, it is a very versatile computer programming language.

Python is an interpretive computer programming language, which means that it does not have a compiler to convert the programming code to machine language before it can be executed. Although, complied languages tend to be faster to execute, Python is used as an emulator or a virtual machine, which is based on an existing machine’s native code, therefore it can be directly understood by the hardware. Python is a powerful language because it has a dynamic-type system and automatic memory management to support various programming methods, such as object-oriented, functional, imperative, and procedural, amongst many others.

Python has been utilised for a range of functions, including machine learning; creating websites; software testing; and controlling self-driving cars. A big advantage of Python is that it is accessible for every operating system and is open source, therefore, it is free to use and distribute. Furthermore, Python can be exploited by developers and non-developers. Python can be applied to carry out complex statistical computations, manipulate and analyse data, and achieve other data-related tasks. It can also be used to generate data visualisations and create machine learning algorithms. The data visualisation feature can facilitate the creation of graphs, histograms, pie charts, and 3D diagrams. Python is also supported by library routines that help developers to write their programs rapidly and efficiently involving data analysis and machine learning.

Python is very useful for developing the back end of a website or application that is unseen by the user and is normally responsible for storing and organising data, making certain that routines on the client-side work. Hence, its role is to communicate with the frontend, sending and receiving information to/from servers, processing data, and linking with databases, URL routing, and safeguarding security. Python has a replication feature for those tasks that are performed on a repetitive basis, using automated processes called scripting. This automation feature is exploited to execute simple math, convert files, test for errors across multiple files, and remove duplicates in data. Python is the friendliest language when compared with other object-oriented programming (OOP) languages.

OOP is based on the concept of objects that may contain data and code, where data is in the form of fields, and code in the form of procedures. [Figure 6.3](#ch18.xhtml#f11) illustrates some of the key advantages of using Python for AI development that include access to an extensive library of routines, a high level of support from the developer’s community, high flexibility, and is platform independent with an open-source classification. Python is considered as one of the best computer programming languages for AI because it is about 80% less complex as other OOP languages. Additionally, its key AI features include the availability of prebuilt libraries routines such as NumPy for performing scientific calculations, SciPy for doing high-end computations, and PyBrain for machine learning.

![Figure 6.3 Advantages of Using Python to Create AI.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_003.jpg)

**Figure 6.3** Advantages of Using Python to Create AI.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f11b)

The NumPy (Numerical Python) routine is used to store generalized data that consists of a one N-dimensional array and has tools for integrating C/C++ codes, Fourier transformation, random number capabilities, amongst many other functions. SciPy supplements Nympy allowing extremely fast and efficient processing since the high-level commands and classes permit for easy data manipulation and visualisation. The SciPy library is written in an assortment of languages such as C, C++, Fortran, and Python. Moreover, PyBrain is an easy to use open-source library of python for implementing Machine learning algorithms to solve problems quickly. Pandas is another open-source library built on top of Python for dealing with data structures and operations that are very powerful, flexible, and easy to use as analytical instruments, particularly for data analysis and manipulation. The Matplotlib library is used for producing high-quality 2D graphic representations and can access up to six graphical user interface tools, web application servers as well as Python scripts.

[Figure 6.4](#ch18.xhtml#f12) shows the main Python libraries for general AI. There are four main Python libraries for General AI, namely AIMA (AI: A Modern Approach), pyDatalog, SimpleAI, and EasyAI. AIMA is not a software library but a university textbook on AI regarding the Python algorithm implementation. This textbook was written by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig in 1995, with the fourth edition published in 2020. pyDatalog is Python’s logic programming engine that provides logic programmers with an extensive standard Python library that can express complex algorithms rapidly. This logic engine is a meticulous declarative language with strong academic foundations that has excellent features for managing complexity. The pyDatalog code is concise and used for simulating intelligent behaviour for games or expert systems; probing complex sets of related information such as data integration or natural language processing; and executing recursive algorithms, for instance on hierarchical data structures.

![Figure 6.4 Python Libraries for General Artificial Intelligence.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_004.jpg)

**Figure 6.4** Python Libraries for General Artificial Intelligence.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f12b)

The other two libraries that are regularly used are SimpleAI and EasyAI. SimpleAI is Python’s application of various AI algorithms that are explained in AIMA and provide intuitive, well-documented, and tested libraries. Whilst EasyAI is a minimal Python engine that permits two players to play games using AI, namely Negamax and transposition tables for Game-solving. Negamax is the search variant form of minimax search that depends on the zero-sum property of a two-player game. Basically, Negamax is minimax but with less code.

Python is an important component of AI programming languages because it has well established frameworks like its scikit-learn machine learning library. This library meets most of all the requirements of current AI development due to its user-friendly visualisation features. The scikit-learn library consists of highly efficient tools for machine learning and statistical modelling including classification, regression, clustering, and dimensionality reduction. It integrates a broad range of machine learning algorithms for medium scale supervised and unsupervised problems, particularly applicable to non-specialist users by having a general-purpose high-level language. Scikit-learn has the following important features:

*   Supervised learning algorithms. The scikit-learn toolbox has generalized linear models, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, and Bayesian methods, amongst many others.
*   Cross-validation. This feature implements several approaches for checking the accuracy of supervised models on unseen data.
*   Unsupervised learning algorithms. This is supported by several algorithms such as clustering, factor analysis, principal component analysis, unsupervised neural networks, and many others.
*   Assorted toy datasets. These are fictional dataset for exploratory data analysis (EDA) and to test simple prediction models. These datasets can be used to train fine-tuned models for toy detection by exploring datasets and export the dataset into a required valid format.
*   Feature extraction. The module can be used to extract features in a format supported by machine learning algorithms from datasets consisting of formats such as text and image (e.g. Bag of words). A bag-of-words model (BoW) is a method of extracting features from text in documents for use in modelling in machine learning algorithms.

In Python, it is an extremely popular language because nearly every concept is easily validated with 20 to 30 lines of code making it a very powerful and rich language to facilitate the programmers’ effort in the development of AI applications.

### **6.2.3** Intelligent Computer-Aided Design (ICAD)

ICAD is a knowledge-based system (KBE) that could capture the intention underlying the product design. Basically, KBE is the integration of object-oriented programming, AI, and computer-aided design (CAD). Hence, KBE systems have the objective of gathering product and process information to enable engineers and other professionals to reproduce or model engineering processes. Therefore, KBE systems allow engineers to generate a geometric design and other essential design information from a model of a product or process. This means that when a particular product or process specifications are modified or new design versions are required, the rules in their current model evaluate the new specifications and a new geometric design is created automatically.

The outcome of a KBE is to automate parts of the process or its entirety from a specified product model. As a result, the product model functions as a computer representation of the design process, which describes the how, why, and what of a design. This also means that a KBE product or process model can contain legacy programs, physics-based analysis, spreadsheets, databases, cost models, and other information from its external environment. Generally, KBE becomes a powerful way of integrating the knowledge from many entities, divisions, departments, and people that together contribute towards the creation of an organisation’s products. [Figure 6.5](#ch18.xhtml#f13) illustrates the ICAD process in which the engineers would specify the input requirements, and the information is extracted from the organisation’s internal and external environment and existing CAD. All this information is exploited by the ICAD system as its primary input data for processing, which generates the CAD models, process design, material requirements planning data, bill of materials, and the associated cost analysis, and ancillary reports

![Figure 6.5 ICAD Knowledge-Based System.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_005.jpg)

**Figure 6.5** ICAD Knowledge-Based System.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f13b)

An example of an ICAD system is the Fujitsu Manufacturing Industry Solution COLMINA Design and Manufacturing Support iCAD SX(1) for machinery design, which is claimed to be powered by the world’s fastest 3D CAD engine. The system reduces design work for large-scale industrial machinery. Fujitsu’s ICAD package is an integrated system that processes everything from conceptual design studies to shop drawings using 3D models of machinery, steel parts, and conduits. Their latest model released in 2020 implements significant enhancements to memory access processing and processing speed of ultra-largescale data expanding the number of parts that can be handled to as many as 3 million parts in the design examination and verification of machine equipment.

Fujitsu has also developed and implemented new design functions that allow mechanical, electrical, and control designers to retain and use operation and manufacturing information, as well as functions that enable the use of 3D data in manufacturing and maintenance services. This feature facilitates the efficient data sharing between departments in a digital environment by linking common 3D data from design upstream to manufacturing and maintenance services, thus aiding in the decrease of lead time. From the initial design stage, the system can directly add to the 3D data, the motion information including the amount of movement, sequence of movements, and timing of a 3D device model. This enables the examination of movements, processes, and cycle times while confirming the positional relationship with peripheral parts. Additionally, the 3D equipment models, and machining information make it possible for the system to calculate the cost of parts and check the consistency of surface roughness and fitting tolerance between parts in the early phase of design.

Fujitsu’s ICAD system helps to shorten the development period and reducing the number of manufacturing processes in the manufacturing industry. It enables design departments to hasten product development and enhance quality, concurrently with improving the efficiency of processing and assembly operations. Intelligent Computer-Aided Design (ICAD) techniques have been used as a basis to facilitate the development of Integrated Product Design (IPD) systems by providing a more ‘‘complete’’ design tool to assist the designer in all phases of the product design. One should note that the main goal for implementing an IPD system is to achieve an integrated approach, where all the primary constituents, such as the CAD tools, numerical analysis tools, data bases, knowledge bases, and expert systems, work cooperatively to perform various tasks associated with that design task.

### **6.2.4** KL-One

KL-One is a knowledge representation system used in AI, which was developed in the early 1980s by John McCarthy and Patrick Hayes. KL-One is a frame language based on the formalism of description logics, in the tradition of semantic networks and frames. KL-One has an automatic reasoning engine that can authenticate a concept (referred to as a frame) ontology and generate new information through logical reasoning about the ontology based on the initial information provided by an expert in a particular field of knowledge. Ontology is a means of how to determine if things exist or not, as well as the classification of existence. It attempts to take things that are abstract and establish that they are, in fact, real.

The principal unit of information in KL-One is called a Concept, which denotes a set of objects often referred to as Frames. These form hierarchies using subsume-relations. The terminology of KL-One views a super class as subsuming its subclasses, with multiple inheritance being permitted. A concept (frame) is said to be well-formed if it inherits from more than one other concept; and all the concepts, except the top concept (usually THING), must have at least one super class. In KL-One, descriptions are separated into two fundamental types of concepts, namely primitive and defined. The primitive type belongs to the domain concepts, which are not fully defined. In other words, the given and known properties of a concept are not adequate to classify it. Primitive type concepts are also viewed as incomplete definitions. On the other hand, defined concepts have complete definitions where their properties are fully known. Hence, these properties (attributes) provide all the required (or adequate) knowledge and conditions to classify the concept. Moreover, a slot-concept is called roles, and the values of the roles are role-fillers. There are several types of roles that may be applied in different situations. However, the most common and important role type is the generic RoleSet, which describes the fact that the role may be filled with more than one filler. For example, one can construct a Concept representing the set of all people where each person has a birthdate, hence PERSON is a Concept and has a Roleset BIRTHDATE.

The best way to illustrate the above principles regarding KL-One is through an example. Assume that one wants to denote that all horses are essentially mammals. This is achieved by stipulating that the Concept denoting mammals subsumes the Concept denoting horses. Hence, a subsumption is represented by a link between Concepts called SuperConcept. KL-One maintains a catalogue (taxonomy) of Concepts with the top of the taxonomy being THING, which is defined to subsume every other Concept. On the other hand, there is no corresponding bottom Concept. Additionally, Concepts inherit the elements from their subsumers, which means that each member of the set represented by a Concept inherits the same properties that are specified by the elements of the Concepts subsumers, including the elements of the Concept itself. Therefore, the HORSE Concept inherits all the elements of MAMMAL. In other words, each horse has all the properties or attributes that are stipulated for mammals and that mammals essentially include horses.

An important feature of this Concept aspect is what is known as Classification. Classification is a process that reveals through logical reasoning that a set signified by some Concept automatically includes the set represented by a second Concept, but where no subsumption relation between the Concepts has been explicitly recorded. Therefore, classification determines the subsumption relations between Concepts and authenticates SuperConcept links between them. Hence, through the classification process, the system automatically categorises a Concept at its proper location in a KL-One taxonomy since it determines the appropriate SuperConcept links between it and other Concepts. To summarise, KL-One consists of five core factors as follows:

*   Concepts: These are abstract objects that represent universal classifications or groups of objects within a domain that can be further specified or subclassed using several taxonomic relationships (e.g., subconcept, superconcept) and inheritance properties (e.g., attributes, roles).
*   Relations: These are binary predicates that describe an activity and depict meaningful links between the different concepts or objects within the domain. These can be used to define various constraints or restrictions on concept attributes and relationships (e.g., role hierarchy properties).
*   Individuals: These are explicit instances of concepts or objects within the domain, which can be categorised or ordered according to their taxonomic relationships and inheritance properties and be designated with various attributes or roles based on their conceptual definitions and constraints.
*   Axioms: These are logical statements or rules that describe the essential and adequate conditions for concepts or individuals within the domain to be categorised according to certain taxonomic relationships or inheritance properties.
*   Inference engine: This has the function for processing and evaluating the different logical statements or rules related to concept definitions, constraints, and relationships within the domain. These are able to be applied for deriving new facts or conclusions based on the given knowledge base.

[Figure 6.6](#ch18.xhtml#f14) provides an example regarding the KL-One frame language concepts. The THINK concept encompasses the taxonomy of the natural world into five kingdoms, namely Animal, Plant, Fungi, Protists, and Monera. The diagram illustrates that within the animal kingdom only four aspects are mentioned, each of which are depictions that may be applied to describe many individual things in the world. As stated previously, several of these Generic Concepts may be formed out of the others (e.g., the Generic Concept HUMAN would have MAMMAL). There are also some structure-forming operations presented for building Concepts, which blend one or more general Concepts, and a set of restrictions on those Concepts.

![Figure 6.6 Example Illustrating the KL-One Frame Language Concepts.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_006.jpg)

**Figure 6.6** Example Illustrating the KL-One Frame Language Concepts.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f14b)

As explained previously, the components of a Concept consist of its subsuming Concepts (i.e., superConcepts) and its local internal structure expressed in Roles. Roles describe possible relationships between occurrences of the Concept and those of other closely associated Concepts (i.e., its properties, elements, etc.), and structural descriptions that articulate the interrelations among the Roles. Additionally, a well-formed KL-One Concept should have more than one superConcept (if there are no local restrictions), must differ from its superConcept in at least one restriction, or be a primitive type. A Concept with no local restrictions is defined as the conjunction of its superConcepts. Hence, once a Concept like HUMAN is specified in terms of one like MAMMAL, one is indirectly identifying that the “more general” subsumes the “more specific.” This means that if Concept X subsumes Concept Y, then every individual that can be described by Y can also be described by X. Hence, when representing the Concept HUMAN so that the Concept MAMMAL subsumes it, the attributes of being a human includes the characteristics of being a mammal and therefore denoting that any human must be a mammal.

It should be noted that KL-One taxonomies will always have one root Concept, typically identified as THING. A root Concept subsumes all other Concepts and has no superConcepts. Primitive Concepts (denoted with an \* in [Figure 6.6](#ch18.xhtml#f14)) are not fully defined, however Concepts not denoted by an “\*” are fully defined by their components. Furthermore, [Figure 6.6](#ch18.xhtml#f14) illustrates that a Generic Concept can have various superConcepts and subConcepts. For instance, the Concept MAN has both MAN-ANIMAL and HUMAN as its superConcepts. Hence, both MAN-ANIMAL and HUMAN subsume MAN. In this example, the Concept MAN is defined to be simply the combination of the two. Moreover, [Figure 6.6](#ch18.xhtml#f14) shows that a Concept such as MAMMAL does not receive any of its properties from the Concept HUMAN. In other words, a Concept’s representation is precisely determined by its subsuming Concepts together with the information related explicitly with the Concept. These principles suggest that KL-One provides several benefits regarding AI, including:

*    Articulateness. KL-One is a highly expressive language that can denote a wide diversity of knowledge, including factual and procedural intelligence. This feature enables it to portray complex ideas and relationships, making it a very powerful instrument for AI applications.
*   Legibility: Representation of knowledge in KL-One is both human-readable and machine-readable, thus facilitating the understanding and manipulation of knowledge by humans and AI systems.
*   Declarative Language: KL-One is a declarative language, which means that knowledge is denoted independently of any specific reasoning or inference algorithm. This facilitates the development of new reasoning algorithms, and to port existing algorithms to new domains.
*   Rational Classifier: KL-One applies a deductive classifier. Classifiers are commonly used in supervised learning systems where the correct class for each input example is known during training. The purpose of a classifier is to learn from the training data to enable it to make accurate predictions on unseen data. Hence, a deductive classifier acts as an automated reasoning engine that validates a frame ontology and deduce new information to allow the system to infer new knowledge based on the existing knowledge base, augmenting its problem-solving capabilities.
*   Effective Toolkit: KL-One comes with a well-developed collection of tools that includes editors, compilers, and inference engines. This toolkit facilitates the development process of applications, mitigating the time and effort needed to develop applications.
*   Extensibility: KL-One is designed to be extended effortlessly. Hence, it has the inherent ability to extend a system and reduce the level of effort required to implement the extension. This principle allows improvements without impairing existing system functions. Hence, new representations and reasoning tools can be added to the language as required, which enables KL-One to adapt to a wide range of AI applications, boosting its versatility and utility.
*   Broad Applicability: KL-One has been applied in several AI applications, including natural language processing, expert systems, and machine learning, illustrating its effectiveness and adaptability in different AI environments.

There are several main features of KL-One in AI that makes it a rich and powerful knowledge representation language for use in AI. These include the following:

*   KL-One acts as a knowledge representation system in AI and the benefits outlined previously enable it to represent a broad scope of knowledge, depicting complex ideas and relationships.
*   KL-One has a unique naming structure called “unification” for easy identification of objects and relations. This feature helps in amalgamating new knowledge into the representation.
*    KL-One is based on well-defined semantics that permits for vibrant and consistent reasoning, using inference rules to draw new conclusions from the knowledge being represented.
*   KL-One’s deductive classifier with its automated reasoning engine validates a frame ontology and determines new information, enhancing its problem-solving abilities.
*   KL-One’s comprehensive toolkit facilitates, including its extensibility and flexibility features facilitate the AI development process.

These key features allow KL-One to be applied in many industrial fields. For instance, it can be applied to depict a medical knowledge base, where the patients are shown as frames, and their symptoms and treatments are denoted as predicates (i.e., describing the activity not the patient). This permits for useful probing and reasoning about patient data and facilitates the development of intelligent systems for diagnosis and treatment planning. KL-One’s knowledge representation features make it ideal for applications regarding medical information processing; expert systems; natural language processing; computer vision for identifying and understand objects and people in images and videos; and predictive modelling.

KL-One is ideal for AI applications development because it allows researchers and developers to definite complex domain-specific knowledge within formalised ontologies or conceptual models, especially for representing taxonomic relationships and concept hierarchies. Additionally, it provides several key concepts and mechanisms for describing, categorising, and deduction about diverse concepts or objects within an application domain, including taxonomy and inheritance attributes; controls and restrictions on concept features; and logical rules and inference abilities. One should note that KL-One is based on the notion of frame-based systems that partition knowledge into small, self-contained units called frames, with each frame containing information about a specific aspect of the world, and the frames are interconnected to form a network of knowledge.

### **6.2.5** Official Production System (OPS5)

OPS5 is a fifth-generation programming language that has the objective of solving problems using constraints provided to a program, rather than using an algorithm written by a programmer. It belongs to a family of rule-based computer programming languages. This feature distinguishes it from fourth-generation programming languages. The primary difference between fourth generation and fifth generation programming languages is that the former are designed to create specific computer programs while fifth-generation computer languages are designed to make the computer solve the problem for the user.

This means that the programmer, instead of writing and implementing an algorithm to solve a problem, must only concern itself about what problem needs to be solved and what conditions need to be met to solve the problem. OPS5 and other fifth-generation computer languages are used mainly in AI research. OPS5 being a rule-based programming language is suitable for designing for implementing efficient expert systems in disciplines such as AI, medical diagnosis, and decision support systems.

Scientists Herbert Simon and Allen Newell from Carnegie-Mellon University who for many decades were studying human problem-solving processes, came up with the notion of the production system. In their view, a production system denoted knowledge as a set of condition-action rules (also referred to as “if-then rules”). Hence, if the conditions for a rule are fulfilled, the specified action stipulated by the rule is carried out. Simon and Newell’s idea was taken up by Charles Forgy in the late 1970s who developed the OPS5 programming language specifically to cater for the rule-based problem-solving idea. [Forgy (1981)](#ch18.xhtml#r057) claims that OPS5 is an interpretive computer programming language implemented in LISP and BLISS that is mainly used for applications in areas of AI, cognitive psychology, and expert systems.

[Figure 6.7](#ch18.xhtml#f15) illustrates that basically OPS5 stores data in working memory, and the “if-then rules” (Rules) are stored in production memory. The Rules in OPS5 are completely independent of one another and can be placed in production memory in any sequential order. OPS5 works by matching the data in working memory with the rules (and their associated conditions) in the production memory. If there is a match between the data and a specific rule (i.e., its conditions) in production memory, the actions associated with the specific matching rule are executed. Possible actions may include altering the contents of working memory that might then match the conditions of another rule; reading data from a file; displaying data on the monitor; and calling external algorithms (programs). There are versions of OPS5 that permit an action of a Rule to create a new rule, which permits systems to learn.

![Figure 6.7 OPS5 Language Processing Concept with Self-Learning Ability.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_007.jpg)

**Figure 6.7** OPS5 Language Processing Concept with Self-Learning Ability.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f15b)

[Figure 6.7](#ch18.xhtml#f15) implies that OPS5 has an integrated deduction procedure and a forward chaining process, which is a form of reasoning for an AI expert system that starts with simple facts and applies inference rules to extract more data until an objective is achieved (i.e., ability to change rules, and modify and add data). OPS5 begins from a set of data in working memory and initiates a sequence of rules to be applied until a goal (conditions) is satisfied. Although backward chaining is not directly available in OPS5, this feature can be implemented with greater effort. Backward chaining is a situation in which a particular goal to be accomplished triggers subgoals to be fulfilled until a specific problem solution is attained.

Allen Newell’s research group in artificial intelligence had been working on production systems for some time, but Forgy’s implementation, based on his Rete algorithm, was especially efficient so that it was possible to scale up to larger problems involving hundreds or thousands of rules. OPS5 adopts the blend of basic principles of the execution engine for a Petri Net extended with inhibitor arcs and the Rete algorithm. Petri Nets were originated by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 with the underlying concepts being broadened and enhanced for application in a variety of fields, including programming languages.

[Figure 6.8](#ch18.xhtml#f16) provides a simple example of a Petri Net illustrating the basic concepts. A Petri Net should be visualised as a collection of directed Arcs (symbolised by an arow) that link Places (symbolised by a circle) and Transitions (symbolised by rectangle). However, Places may hold Tokens (symbolised by a black spot), and the status of a net is determined by its assignment of Tokens to Places. Furthermore, Arcs have capacity 1 by default; if the capacity is not a 1, the capacity is denoted on the arc. In the example at [Figure 6.8](#ch18.xhtml#f16) the capacity is 1 by default. Additionally, Places have an infinite capacity by default, and transitions have no capacity at all, and cannot store tokens. Moreover, Arcs can only link Places to Transitions and vice versa.

![Figure 6.8 Example of Petri Net Illustrating Basic Concepts.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_008.jpg)

**Figure 6.8** Example of Petri Net Illustrating Basic Concepts.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f16b)

[Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) depicts a series of Petri Nets that show how the status of a Petri Net changes depending on the assignment of Tokens to Places through the Transition condition. A Transition is enabled when the number of tokens in each of its input places is at least equal to the Arc capacity (weight) going from the place to the Transition. [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (A) illustrates that in this case, the number of Tokens in each of its input Places is 1 and the Arc weight has a default capacity of 1, which satisfies the condition for the Transition to be enabled. Moreover, an enabled Transition may fire at any time. [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (B) shows the changed status of the Petri Net when the Transition is fired, with the Tokens in the input Places being transferred to the output Places, corresponding to the Arc weights and Place capacities.

![Figure 6.9 Example of Petri Net Illustrating Various Additional Basic Concepts.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_009.jpg)

**Figure 6.9** Example of Petri Net Illustrating Various Additional Basic Concepts.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f17b)

[Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (C) illustrates what happens when Places and Arcs have different token capacity and its status is ready to fire, while [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (D) shows the outcome when fired. Notice that in [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (C), Place P1 (with 2 Tokens) has an Arc capacity of 2, while P2 (with 1 Token) has the default Arc capacity of 1. However, the Arc capacity after Transition is 1 for P3 (with 1 Token), 2 for P4 (with 2 Tokens), 1 for P5 (with 1 Token), and 3 for P6 (with 3 Tokens). Hence, the outcome shown at [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (D) corresponds to these Arc capacities when fired.

In other words, when a Transition fires, it receives the Tokens that enabled it from the input Places and disseminates Tokens to output Places matching the Arc capacity weighting. If the Arc weights are all identical, it gives the impression that the Tokens are transferred through the transition. However, if Arc weights differ, it gives the impression that Tokens may vanish or be generated. In fact, in [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (C) the number of Tokens is 3 (P1, 2 and P2, 1) but after firing at [Figure 6.9](#ch18.xhtml#f17) (D), the number of Tokens is 7 (P3, 1; P4, 2; P5, 1; and P6, 3). Hence, four additional Tokens have been generated (producing output Tokens according to Arc weight). There is also an exceptional type of Arc known as an inhibitor Arc, which is applied to reverse the logic of an input Place. [Figure 6.10](#ch18.xhtml#f18) shows the application of an inhibitor Arc, which is symbolised by having a small box at the end of the arrowhead. [Figure 6.10](#ch18.xhtml#f18) illustrates that the Transition cannot fire since the Token in P2, which has an inhibitor Arc, prevents it from doing so. The above provided a concise description of the Petri Net concepts.

![Figure 6.10 Example of Petri Net Illustrating Inhibitor Arc Concept.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_010.jpg)

**Figure 6.10** Example of Petri Net Illustrating Inhibitor Arc Concept.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f18b)

As stated previously, OPS5 adopts a blend of Petri Net principles and the Rete algorithm. The Rete algorithm is named after the Latin word “net.” It was designed by Charles Forgy in a working paper submitted in 1974. This algorithm is typically a pattern matching algorithm for implementing rule-based systems to apply many rules or patterns to many objects, or facts, in a knowledge base efficiently. The Rete algorithm has the objective of ascertaining which of the system’s rules should fire based on the stored factual data.

The Rete algorithm structures its data as a tree-like formation (similar to the Petri Net). Each node in the tree represents a test that is executed when matched with the data being added or removed from memory. Every node will have one or two inputs but possibly many outputs. As an additional item of data enters the tree, it is filtered through the tree until it reaches a terminal node. If the data item reaches a terminal node, this signifies that a new activation record is created with all the data points that triggered the rule to be true. Rules in Rete systems must be as explicit as possible to achieve better performance. This is achieved by composing rules that search for very detailed items in a given piece of data. This produces a path in the Rete tree to be navigated in a rather determinant approach, which reveals the efficiencies that are fundamental to the Rete algorithm.

Like other methods, the Rete approach has a set of conventions or terminology for explaining its application. A ruleset is a knowledge base consisting of one or more business rules. Each rule in the ruleset denotes some kind of knowledge. Rules are normally defined as an if-then or condition-action rule. The if-then rules are called Rete Rules. An example of a Rete Rule is: *If age > 49 then assign screening-status = 1.*

Note that the words “if,” “then,” and “assign” are keywords. The “If” part signifies a condition and the “then” part represents action. It is possible to have more than one condition, which need to be logical operators. The “then” part denotes one or more actions. Therefore, in the above example, Rule means that if a person’s age is more than 49 then that person is to be screened (0 = not to be screened; 1 = to be screened). Therefore, if the person’s status as to be screened (or not) needs to be verified, then data (called fact) is required about the person’s age. Hence, as the number of distinctive variables or definitions increases, the number of facts also increase. For example: *If age > 49 and gender = “female” then assign screening-status = 1*

To execute (perform) the above rule, two data items or facts are required, namely the “age” and the “gender.” If the status of two or more persons is being verified then there must be a data set for each person. This particular example is a simple event but in real life circumstances there may be hundreds and even thousands of facts where the rule should be applied. Furthermore, there may be a voluminous number (thousands) of different rules as well.

A Rete algorithm requires that a complete ruleset must be given to the rule engine to broaden processing. Typically, the rule engine matches each rule (i.e., condition) in the ruleset with specified facts to determine whether to fire (i.e., execute) the rule (or not). This procedure is referred to as the pattern matching process, which is conducted repeatedly. Additionally, the list of facts can be altered for each cycle. In other words, the list of facts is continually being updated by the inclusion of new facts or/and deletion of old facts from the list of facts.

Therefore, these modifications may trigger (cause) previously unsatisfied (unfulfilled) patterns to be fulfilled (satisfied). Additionally, during each cycle, the set of rules fulfilled must be updated and retained (stored). Often, the actions of the rules change just a few facts in the list of updated facts. This process is known as temporal redundancy. The algorithm is highly efficient because the rule engine does not verify each rule by directing the search for all the facts since most of them are not modified and doing so would delay the process. This is achieved because the algorithm is designed to remember (recall) what had already been matched from cycle to cycle and only process the necessary changes for the newly added or removed facts.

The Rete algorithm structure consists of a network of nodes. As described previously, it is designed to achieve high processing speed by storing in memory the state of each matching process from cycle to cycle and only computing those with modified facts. Therefore, the status of the matching process is only updated when facts are added or/and removed. Hence, a lower number of modifications result in a faster matching process.

[Figure 6.11](#ch18.xhtml#f19) illustrates that each rule has a corresponding inference (deduction) cycle that consists of three stages, namely the match, select, and execute phases. Each stage has a distinct function. For instance, in the match phase, the conditions of the rules are compared to the facts to ascertain which rules are to be executed (fired). Therefore, the rules whose conditions have been satisfied (fulfilled) are stored in a list called agenda-ready for executing (firing). Finally, one of the rules from the list of rules is selected to execute (fire). The selection(s) strategy is contingent on several factors, namely the priority, recentness of usage, rule specifications, or on other specified conditions. The rule selected from the list is executed (fired) by conducting (performing) the actions associated with the rule. The action may consist of several events, such as verification (confirmation); performing a user defined or built-in function; or implementing a decision table through a decision table engine, or otherwise.

![Figure 6.11 Illustration of a Rule Engine Inference Cycle.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_011.jpg)

**Figure 6.11** Illustration of a Rule Engine Inference Cycle.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f19b)

The construction of a Rete network requires the adherence to certain conventions. A Rete network is a direct acyclic graph that consists of nodes representing patterns in the conditions of the rules and is bipartite with no graph cycles. Moreover, its nodes are directionally related to each other and do not form a directional closed loop. The nodes act as filters to test (check) the incoming tokens, and firing (sending) only those tokens that qualify (i.e., pass the test). The Rete network consists of two segments, namely the alpha network and beta network. The alpha network comprises of nodes known as alpha nodes, with each node having one input that defines intra-elements. The beta network comprises of beta nodes with each node having two inputs to define inter-element conditions.

A Rete network begins with the Root node known as the Rete Node. Following the Root node are Kind nodes, with a Kind node for each fact type. Alpha nodes are connected to the corresponding Kind node and are created for each pattern. If a condition has two patterns, then two alpha nodes are created, with each alpha node being associated with a memory known as alpha memory. The alpha memory is used to recall the matching facts. The alpha nodes are linked to beta nodes. Beta node can only receive two inputs. Therefore, if there are three alpha nodes then the first two nodes will be linked to one beta node. Subsequently, the output of this beta node and the third alpha node will be liked by another beta node. Hence, the beta nodes may support partial matching, with each beta node having a memory to store joined patterns.

In the beginning, the tokens move into the root node. Later, the affirmation of each fact generates a token. The network then divides a branch for each token type, with each Kind node receiving a copy of the token and executing the SELECT operation to select tokens of its kind. The kind node sends a copy of the token node it receives to the alpha nodes. On receiving the token, the alpha nodes perform a PROJECT operation and take out elements from the token that match with the variables of the pattern. Basically, the alpha node assesses the conditions, and the beta node then ascertains the feasible cross product for a rule. When this is achieved, the actions in the rule will be performed.

The construction of a Rete Network is best illustrated through an example. Assume that the local health authority has a breast cancer screening scheme for females between the 50 and 70 years of age. The age facts are java type, while the gender facts are xml. The rule for this would be as follows:

> *If age>49 or age<71 or gender = “female” then screen-status = 1*

This rule would be depicted by the Rete Network shown at [Figure 6.12](#ch18.xhtml#f20). The example at [Figure 6.12](#ch18.xhtml#f20) has two kinds of nodes with two types of facts, namely: Kind 1 (java) and Kind 2 (xml). There are three patterns, namely: age>49, age<71 and gender=female and therefore three alpha nodes will be generated. The example shows that Alpha 1 and Alpha 2 denote the first two patterns and are linked to Kind 1, while Alpha 3 denotes the third pattern and is linked to Kind 2. Alpha 1 and Alpha 2 are linked to Beta 1, while Alpha 3 is linked to Beta 2.

![Figure 6.12 Example of Constructing a Rete Network.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_012.jpg)

**Figure 6.12** Example of Constructing a Rete Network.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f20b)

A token is generated as a value for age enters the root. Additionally, this token will be copied and disseminated to kind nodes. Hence, Kind 1 will accept the token because the fact type is java and forwarded to Alpha 1 and Alpha 2. If the value fulfils (satisfies) the constraint, then the token will be forwarded to Beta 1 and then to Beta 2. In this intervening time the value of gender enters the root, which is received by Kind 2 (since it is xml type). Alpha 3 obtains it and verifies if the value fulfils (satisfies) the constraint, gender=female. If this is the case (i.e., yes) then it permits the token to be forwarded to Beta 2. Moreover, if the values (facts) match with the condition in the Beta 2 then the rule will be added to a list for firing (execution). Therefore, if a particular case has age between 50 and 70, and the screen-status is 1, a letter will be sent to invite the individual for a breast screening test.

The Rete algorithm is very efficient in terms of speed. However, it needs a lot of memory because of its feature of saving the state of the system using pattern matches and partial matches. Hence, the main aspects of the Rete algorithm are its ability to retain partial matches between consecutive updates because of the new factual data, and it endeavours to reuse overlapping rules in the matching process. The demand for memory computed by the number of rules (R) multiplied by the number of declared facts (F) multiplied by the average number of patterns per rule (P). Therefore, if R = 100, F = 10,000, and P = 10, the storge needed is 10mb. Research has shown that the Rete algorithm can be successfully applied with Petri nets and that Petri nets can be applied as an underlying mechanism in rule-based systems ([Burdescu and Brezovan, 2001a](#ch18.xhtml#r054), 2001[b](#ch18.xhtml#r055); [Hura, 1993](#ch18.xhtml#r058); [Murata and Yim, 1995](#ch18.xhtml#r060)). Additionally, [Dohlbom (2011)](#ch18.xhtml#r056) illustrated that Petri nets can be applied as efficiently as a rule-based technique created by the Rete algorithm with temporal extensions.

### **6.2.6** Mercury and Prolog

Both Mercury and Prolog are declarative computer programming languages (or logic programming). Prolog has been in use since 1972 and was specifically designed for developing logic-based AI applications. With Prolog, developers can set rules and facts around a problem, and then Prolog’s interpreter will use that information to automatically infer solutions. Mercury was released around 1995 and is a souped-up version of Prolog that has enhanced features to provide better performance.

Declarative programming is a high-level programming concept that basically means that one would state the outcome of a task, and the complier determines the steps that need to be executed to achieve the outcome. Hence, a programmer would write code that describes what is to be done and what outcomes (results) is to be achieved, rather than how they will achieve the results. This is opposite to imperative programming where functions are completely coded for each step required to achieve the desired outcome. In declarative programming it is the compiler that works out the steps required to achieve a task. In other words, declarative programmes depend on preconfigured facilities in the language without specific case-by-case instructions on what steps need to be executed to complete a particular task.

Declarative programmes are context (circumstance) independent because a programmer only needs to declare the eventual goal (the what) and not the logical steps involved to attain the goal (the how). This implies that the same programme expressions have the same meaning in different circumstances and consequently can be applied in different contexts. Therefore, declarative programs such a Mercury and Prolog are much simpler to work with because they formulate computation logic without complicating the programming code with control flows. These types of programmes are easier to understand because they have less ambiguous processes, implied dependencies and changeable states that simplifies programming code and readability.

Mercury being a more recent development has more advanced stable analysis and error detection features. It is also supported by a highly optimised execution algorithm that is far more efficient than other logic programming systems and achieves similar performance to conventional programming systems without complex control flows. Mercury is considered as a pure logic programming language that is designed to generate sizeable, speedy, reliable programs. The coding syntax of Mercury is based on Prolog, but the way it relates to the different meanings of words or signs or symbols (semantically) make the two languages somewhat different because of Mercury’s clarity, style, approach, conditions (determinism) and module systems. Although Mercury and Prolog are both logic programming languages there are several differences between them:

*    Syntax. Mercury’s syntax is similar to modern imperative languages. Prolog uses symbolic syntax, which is a more conventional approach.
*   Type system. Mercury has a robust type of system that permits for more stable type verification making programmes more efficient than Prolog.
*   Mode and determinism. Mercury permits additional control over the computation process since it supports both declarative and imperative semantics, thus permitting the use of non-deterministic predicates. Prolog only supports declarative semantics to express logical relationships, but it does not have the ability to specify how those relationships are to be computed.
*   Performance. Prolog is not as efficient as Mercury. Mercury focuses on static type checking to verify the type of safety of a program based on analysis of a program’s text (source code), mode-directed compilation, and automatically creating specified code.
*   Concurrency: Mercury supports concurrent and parallel execution of predicates that permit the efficient use of multi-core processors, whereas Prolog does not have this feature.
*   Applications: Prolog was designed for AI applications and is used for knowledge representation and natural language processing. Whereas Mercury is used mainly for coding large, complex, and performance-critical systems.

Since, the syntax code for Mercury is based on Prolog, it is appropriate to use Prolog syntax to illustrate certain basic aspects of these programming languages. It should be noted that Prolog is a robust and flexible computer programming language, which is very suitable for creating logic-based AI applications. In fact, it was specifically designed with AI development as a primary objective. Like Mercury, Prolog permits the programmer to specify the rules and facts about a problem domain. Once this is done, the Prolog interpreter will use the given rules and facts to automatically suggest solutions to problems. An important aspect of Prolog is its facility to handle uncertain or incomplete information. Hence, a programmer can define a set of rules and facts that are accepted as being true, but they can also define rules and facts that may possibly be true or false. The Prolog interpreter will use the defined rules and facts and automatically deduce (reason) about the problem domain and discover solutions that are probably correct, given the available information.

Prolog programs consist of two key components, namely facts and rules. Facts are declarations that are accepted as being true, such as “Peter is a man” or “the capital of Germany is Berlin.” Rules are logical declarations that designate the relationships between different facts, such as “If Peter is a man and Rebecca is a woman, then Peter is not Mary.” The syntax for Prolog programs is like natural language. For instance, the above case might be expressed in four lines of code as shown in [Table 6.1](#ch18.xhtml#t10). In this case, the first three rows are facts, while the fourth row is a rule. Observe that the rule uses the ***not/2*** predicate to declare that if ***X*** is a man and ***Y*** is a woman, then ***X*** *is not* ***Y***.

**Table 6.1** Examples of Prolog Syntax Statements[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#t10b)

 
| **Row** || **Syntax** || **Type** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || man(peter). || Fact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 || woman(rebecca). || Fact |
| 3 || capital\_of(germany, berlin). || Fact |
| 4 || not(X1,Y1):- man(X1), woman(Y1). || Rule |

Prolog permits a wide-ranging variety of different programming styles and approaches. This means that there is no specific single “syntax” for Prolog. However, there are several common conventions that are frequently used as described below:

*   Facts are declarations that are presumed to be true; hence, they are written using a predicate name succeeded by a list of arguments enclosed in parentheses (e.g., woman(rebecca) also see [Table 6.1](#ch18.xhtml#t10), rows 1 to 3).
*   Rules are logical statements that specify relationships between facts. Rules are expressed using the predicate name succeeded by a list of arguments enclosed in parentheses, followed by a colon and a hyphen (:-) and the rule (e.g., not(X1,Y1):- man(X1), woman(Y1) also see [Table 6.1](#ch18.xhtml#t10), row 4).
*   Variables denote values that may change or be determined. Variables are normally written using a name that begins with an uppercase letter (e.g., X1).
*   Queries are utilised to find solutions to problems based on the defined rules and facts in the program (e.g., not(peter, rebecca)?).

As mentioned previously, facts are statements that are accepted as being true and provide Prolog with information about the problem domain, which will be used to automatically deduce answers to problems. Facts are expressed by using a predicate name followed by a list of arguments enclosed in parentheses. For example, at [Table 6.1](#ch18.xhtml#t10), row 1 declares that peter is a man; row 2 declares that rebecca is a woman, and row 3 declares that berlin is the capital of Germany. [Table 6.2](#ch18.xhtml#t11) shows a simple computer program that illustrates some basic Prolog principles. The program at [Table 6.2](#ch18.xhtml#t11) identifies several facts and rules about a problem domain. It applies these facts and rules to provide answers to two queries.

**Table 6.2** Example of Simple Prolog Program[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#t11b)

 
| **Row** || **Syntax** || **Type** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || **% Facts** ||  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 || man(peter). || Fact |
| 3 || woman(rebecca). || Fact |
| 4 || boy(jake). || Fact |
| 5 || girl(sue). || Fact |
| 6 || river\_of(germany, danube). || Fact |
| 7 || capital\_of(germany, berlin). || Fact |
| 8 || **% Rule** ||  |
| 9 || not(x1,y1):- man(x1), woman(y1). || Rule |
| 10 || not(x2,y2):- boy(x2), girl(y2). || Rule |
| 11 || **% Query 1** ||  |
| 12 || not(peter, rebecca)? || Query |
| 13 || **% Query 2** ||  |
| 14 || river\_of(germany, X)? || Query |
| 15 || **% Query 3** ||  |
| 16 || capital\_of(germany, Y)? || Query |

The program defines six facts at rows 2 to 7, namely, man(peter), woman(rebecca), boy(jake), girl(sue), river\_of(Germany, Danube), and capital\_of(germany, berlin). These facts basically declare that Peter is a man; Rebecca is a woman; Jake is a boy; Sue is a girl; Danube is a river in Germany; and Berlin is the capital of Germany. Note that row 1 (% Facts) declares that the rows following it are facts. At row 8 (% Rule), the program signifies that the rows following it are rules. The rules are defined at row 9 and row 10. The program declares that the rules are using the not/2 predicate, declaring that if X1 is a man and Y1 is a woman, then X1 is not Y1; and that if X2 is a boy and Y2 is a girl, then X2 is not Y2. The final segment of the program describes the queries. These queries are declared at rows 11 to 16. Note that each query is numbered and headed by the statement %Query 1 at row 11, %Query 2 at row 13, and %Query 3 at row 15 before the actual query statements made are at row 12, 14, and 16.

The query at row 12, not(peter, rebecca)?, requests the interpreter to ascertain whether Peter is not Rebecca, based on the not/2 rule and the man and woman facts. The program will apply these rules and facts to determine that Peter is not Rebecca, and it will respond with true as the solution to the query. The next query at row 14, river\_of(germany, X)?, solicits the interpreter to establish the main river of Germany. The program will apply the river\_of/2 fact to ascertain that the main river of Germany is Danube, and it will respond with the answer Danube for the variable X as the result. The final query, capital\_of(germany, Y)?, seeks the interpreter to disclose the capital of Germany. The program will apply the capital\_of/2 fact to reveal that the capital of Germany is Berlin, and it will respond with the answer of Berlin for the variable Y as the result.

The Prolog program at [Table 6.2](#ch18.xhtml#t11) shows how to define and express rules and facts about a problem domain, and how the rules and facts are applied to automatically deduce solutions to problems. The next example of a Prolog program is shown at [Table 6.3](#ch18.xhtml#t12), which illustrates a simple AI application. This computer program demonstrates a basic diagnostic mechanism to check for three medical conditions, namely Covid-19, Flu, and Cold. The program consists of three main segments. The first segment defines the facts for each specific medical condition (rows 1 to 23). The facts describe the particular symptoms for the three medical conditions, some of which may overlap. The second segment defines the rules, which in this case has only one rule. It declares the rule by applying the illness\_condition/2 predicate, which declares that if a patient has a particular symptom, then they might have the medical condition that is linked with that symptom.

| 24 || **% Rule** ||  |
