| 31 || illness\_condition(headache, Y)? || Query |
| 32 || **% Query 4** ||  |
| 33 || illness\_condition(chills, Y)? || Query |
| 34 || **% Query 5** ||  |
| 35 || illness\_condition(difficulty\_ breathing, Y)? || Query |

The third and final segment(s) of the Prolog program declare the queries to determine the underlying medical condition, whether it is covid-19, flu, or the common cold. A specific query requests the interpreter to ascertain the possible medical condition that a patient might have based on their symptoms. In this example there are five specific queries since the medical conditions may have some common symptoms. The first two queries are meant to determine whether the symptom being experienced by the patient indicate a common cold. The next two queries have the purpose of indicating whether the symptoms indicate flu or Covid-19 since these have common symptoms. The final query will determine whether the patient is experiencing flu or Covid-19, since there is a high probability that the difficulty breathing symptom is applicable to Covid-19. Each individual query is requesting the interpreter to determine which medical condition the patient is likely to be experiencing. As stated previously, the program will apply the illness\_condition/2 rule and the illness\_indicator/2 facts to establish that the patient has either the covid-19, flu, or the common cold, and it will respond with the appropriate solution to each query.

The above example illustrates how a Prolog program can be applied for an AI application. As one may appreciate, in a practical scenario the program is likely to be more sophisticated by accessing a database of symptoms and have more complex rules for diagnosing a medical condition. It should be noted that Prolog has been used instead of Mercury because Prolog is a sub-set of the Mercury computer language. This section has demonstrated that both Mercury and Prolog are powerful and flexible languages for developing AI applications, with Mercury being more recently developed having many added features.

### **6.2.7** IBM Qiskit Software Development Kit (SDK)

IBM have adopted Qiskit, which is an open-source, python-based quantum SDK. The Qiskit SDK is designed specifically to work on the IBM Quantum Platform or on simulators on a local computer at the level of circuits and algorithms. Qiskit has been developed by IBM Research with contributions from academic organisations to facilitate software development for IBM’s cloud quantum computing service. Apart from the Python version, Qiskit versions were considered for Swift and JavaScript, but these initiatives were not pursued. Qiskit also supports Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI), which is a contemporary interdisciplinary research field that combines quantum computing with AI that aims to use the unique properties of quantum computers to enhance the capabilities of AI systems.

Qiskit is composed of several integrated components that enable quantum computing with the primary objective of creating a software package that facilitates users to exploit quantum computers, irrespective of their level of skill or sphere of interest. Hence, Qiskit provides a computing platform for users to create test prototypes and applications to execute on quantum computers and/or conventional simulators. This is achieved by generating quantum software both at the machine code level of OpenQASM, and at abstract levels that are appropriate for end-users without quantum computing expertise.

The functionality for Qiskit is supported by several components which provide some very powerful features. For instance, the Qiskit Terra component is the basis for the other Qiskit modules and provides the necessary tools to generate quantum circuits at or close to the level of quantum machine code. This permits the generated processes that execute on quantum hardware, which are specifically created in terms of quantum gates. These provide the means for the quantum circuits to be optimised for a specific device, apart from managing batches of jobs and executing them on remote-access quantum devices and simulators.

An important component is Qiskit Machine Learning. This component provides the basic computational modules, such as Quantum Kernels and Quantum Neural Networks that are applied in several applications including classification and regression. Qiskit Machine Learning is user friendly, allowing initial prototypes to be created rapidly without having comprehensive quantum computing knowledge. Additionally, it is very flexible and can be broadened to support innovative quantum machine learning research. Qiskit Machine Learning modules, such as FidelityQuantumKernel that applies the BaseStateFidelity algorithm can be utilised to directly compute kernel matrices for given datasets or can be forwarded to a Quantum Support Vector Classifier (QSVC) or Quantum Support Vector Regressor (QSVR) to solve classification or regression problems.

Qiskit Machine Learning has a generic interface for neural networks that is executed by various quantum neural networks that permits users to link parametrised quantum circuits with quantum mechanical observables that may apply Qiskit’s circuit library. Furthermore, Qiskit Machine Learning has a range of learning algorithms such as the NeuralNetworkClassifier and NeuralNetworkRegressor for addressing classification or regression problems. Additionally, it supports the TorchConnector module for integrating all of IBM’s quantum neural networks directly into the PyTorch open-source machine learning library.

Machine learning has become an exceptional tool in contemporary decision making and supported by further developments in quantum computing it is expected to drive this capability to new heights. The integration of quantum principles in neural networks provides the potential for considerable computational advantages, specifically in the sphere of AI and deep learning. In fact, a detailed recognition and understanding of this integration is likely to provide added capability in how complex computations are undertaken.

By combining the Qiskit environment with PyTorch, a framework is created that facilitates efficient prototyping and testing of variational quantum algorithms, which leverage both classical and quantum computing resources to find approximate solutions to problems. Furthermore, performance is significantly enhanced by providing a quicker and more scalable approach to quantum computations. These benefits are achieved through the availability of advanced tools that facilitate simple integration approaches for existing projects. This allows researchers to explore quantum neural networks without significant overhead that spans the gap between quantum computing and traditional neural network methodologies. Hence, quantum neural networks are viewed as having great potential for augmenting the computational abilities of AI systems, fostering further innovations in the field.

### **6.2.8** Other Programming Languages for Specific Hardware Associated with AI

This section provides a brief description of key programming languages for specific hardware associated with AI that have the objective of controlling digital circuits to perform a particular function. The hardware itself was covered in a previous chapter. This chapter provides additional information regarding the programming languages that drive this specific hardware. Generally, hardware refers to the external and internal devices and equipment that enable users to perform major functions such as input, output, storage, communication, processing, and amongst other functions. Hence, hardware refers to the physical parts. However, for these physical parts to function they must receive and execute instructions.

Inherently, hardware has digital circuits as a primary component, that chiefly consist of interconnected transistors. In fact, a central processing unit (CPU) consists of a massive conglomeration of transistors. More specifically, a transistor can function as a switch or gate for electronic signals, opening and closing an electronic gate numerous times per second. Hence, a transistor ensures that the circuit is switched on if the current is flowing and switched off if it is not flowing.

As such, a digital circuit may be depicted by having interconnected diagrams that are referred to as a schematic diagram, which could be quite complex to visualise. In fact, as the complexity increases it becomes impractical to describe the interconnected digital circuit diagrams in a visual style. However, an easier and more practical approach to describing digital circuits is to use a textual language that is specifically aimed to clearly and concisely describe the defining features of digital design. Such, textual languages are termed hardware description languages (HDLs).

In the chapter addressing hardware, it was mentioned that the common hardware description languages are Verilog and VHDL (Very-High-Speed Integrated Circuit Hardware Description Language). These are commonly applied in combination with Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) that are digital devices that are specifically designed to aid and therefore expediate the creation of customised digital circuits. FPGAs are integrated circuits that are often sold off-the-shelf and are known as “field programmable” because they give developers the capability to reconfigure (modify) the hardware to meet their specific use case requirements after the manufacturing process. In other words, HDLs allow developers to define a circuit using words and symbols to create software that can convert the word-based-symbolic description into configuration (design) data that is loaded into the FPGA to execute the required functionality. [Figure 6.13](#ch18.xhtml#f21) provides a simple example of singular circuit schematic diagram and the corresponding HDL code.

![Figure 6.13 Example of Singular Circuit Schematic Diagram and Its HDL code.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_013.jpg)

**Figure 6.13** Example of Singular Circuit Schematic Diagram and Its HDL code.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f21b)

One may ask whether there is a difference between computer programming languages and HDLs (hardware description languages)? HDLs are very similar to high-level programming languages such as Python or C, however there is an important difference. HDL statements represented by HDL code entail having parallel operations, whereas programming languages embody sequential operations. In other words, with a computer program or firmware module the processor executes the program statements (code) one at a time, with a top-to-bottom chain of command like an individual reading text on a page. HDL programming code describes digital hardware, and therefore discrete segments of this hardware can operate concurrently even though the matching lines of code are written using a top-to-bottom approach.

As stated previously VHDL and Verilog are commonly used hardware description languages. The example at [Figure 6.13](#ch18.xhtml#f21) represents a simple HDL for a basic digital circuit using VHDL. VHDL was instigated by the US Department of Defence around 1981 in conjunction with private sector companies like IBM and Texas Instruments that piloted the launching of its first version in 1985. This development was actively supported by the first FPGA that was released in 1984; consequentially contributing to its advancement as an established language in digital circuit design, simulation, and synthesis. The VHDL lines of code are relatively easy to understand. For instance, taking the example at [Figure 6.13](#ch18.xhtml#f21), the following explanation will clarify what each line of code is achieving:

*   Line 1: Adds the library “ieee.” This library contains key definitions regarding data types and operators and may consist of several packages that are applicable to the circuit design.
*   Line 2: Specifies that package “std\_logic\_1164” from the “ieee” library is required. This signifies the data type being used. A “std\_logic” data type can denote a one-bit signal, whilst the “bit” data type can accept a logic one or zero. However, the “std\_logic” option is more powerful since it is not limited to just logic high and low but can have a tri-state inverter condition. This means the circuit outputs a voltage signifying the opposite logic-level to its input, thus inverting the input signal applied, such that when an applied input is low then the output becomes high and vice versa. Hence, the “std\_logic” data type supports the “don’t care” state, which enables better hardware optimisation for look-up tables.
*   Line 3: This specifies an arbitrary name for the circuit being described. The word “circuit\_X” is placed between the keywords “entity” and “is,” thus naming this module.
*   Line 4 to 6: These define the input and output ports of the circuit. Matching these lines to the circuit diagram, it is noted that the ports of the circuit together with their features are listed after the keyword “port.” For example, line 4 denotes an input port called “a” as indicated by the keyword “in” after the colon with a std\_logic data type to describe a one-bit digital signal.
*   Line 7: This line establishes the end of the “entity” statement.

Therefore, the first seven lines of code describe the library to be applied, and the programme entity, consisting of the circuit name being described; and the circuit ports and their attributes, such as input/output and the data type to be passed on by these ports. This basically, describes the interface of a module with its surrounding environment. The next lines of code (lines 8 to 11) describe the operation of the circuit. The operation of the circuit is described by the “architecture” section that specifically relates to circuit\_X, which was defined by the entity statement in Line 3.

*   Line 8: This line establishes the “Behavioural” segment for the architecture to be described by the next lines and is placed between the keywords, “architecture” and “of”. It relates and describes “circuit\_X.”
*   Line 9: This specifies the start of the architecture description.
*   Line 10: This line describes the circuit’s operation. The AND of the two inputs a and b is placed within the parentheses, and the outcome is designated to the output port using the assignment operator “<=.”
*   Line 11: This line specifies the end of the architecture description.

The above lines of code describe the circuit’s internal operation that depict a simple AND gate as shown in [Figure 6.13](#ch18.xhtml#f21) using VHDL. For further information regarding VHDL refer to Arar (2017). The other hardware descriptive language that has already been mentioned is Verilog. Verilog is an alternative to VHDL, and both are viewed as powerful tools for designing a complex digital circuit. Verilog stems from the combination of “verification” and “logic” because the language was initially envisaged as a simulation and verification tool.

Verilog has taken longer to emerge as a popular HDL option. It was initially designed in early 1984 by Gateway Design Automation a few years after VHDL was released by the US Department of Defence. However, with the support from Department of Defence, VHDL was adopted in 1987 as an IEEE standard with Verilog lagging. Verilog HDL was conceived by Phil Moorby and Prabhu Goel around 1984 and was initially a proprietary hardware modelling language owned by Gateway Design Automation. Verilog was continuously upgraded with revisions being released between 1984 to 1990. The breakthrough for Verilog materialised in 1990 when it was acquired by Cadence Design System, which was an important supplier of electronic design technologies and engineering services in the electronic design automation (EDA) industry.

Cadence realised that Verilog could not progress as a proprietary product since it would lack standardisation status. Hence, in 1991 Cadence released Open Verilog International (OVI) and transferred it to the public domain. This was followed by a submission to IEEE to attain standard status, which was achieved in 1995 and became IEEE standard 1364-1995 (Verilog-95). Verilog has been continually revamped with important added features, attaining IEEE standard 1364-2001 (Verilog-2001) and IEEE Standard 1364-2005 (Verilog-2005). In 2005 System Verilog was issued, which was a superset of Verilog-2005, with many new features and functionalities to aid design verification. Additionally, in 2009, SystemVerilog and Verilog language standards were amalgamated into SystemVerilog 2009 (IEEE Standard 1800-2009), which is currently one of the most popular languages for IC design and verification.

The syntax for Verilog can be illustrated by using the circuit example shown previously when explaining VHDL. [Figure 6.14](#ch18.xhtml#f22) shows the circuit design (same as shown in [Figure 6.13](#ch18.xhtml#f21)) and the corresponding Verilog lines of code. Recall that the circuit design has two inputs and one output with the ports being all one bit wide.

![Figure 6.14 Example of Circuit Design and Corresponding Verilog Code.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_014.jpg)

**Figure 6.14** Example of Circuit Design and Corresponding Verilog Code.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f22b)

The circuit has an AND gate with two inputs and passing the result to the out1 port. The Verilog lines of code are as follows:

*   Line 1: This line uses the keyword “module” to specify that the line will start to describe a circuit named “Circuit\_X”. This is an arbitrary name for referencing the circuit.
*   Line 2: This specifies the start of the interface of “Circuit\_X” with its surrounding environment.
*   Line 3: This specifies the input port described with using the keyword “input”. This keyword is followed by another keyword “wire” and then the name of the port in this case “a.” “Wire” is a Verilog data type that represents a physical wire in the design.
*   Line 4: This is like Line 3, but it specifies the input port “b”.
*   Line 5: This specifies the output port using the keyword “output”. Once again, this keyword is followed by the keyword “wire,” and then the name of the port (out1).
*    Line 6: This specifies the end of the module interface of “Circuit\_X”.
*   Line 7: This line applies the bitwise AND operator using the “&” symbol to describe the functionality of the circuit. The keyword “assign” puts a&b on the output port out1. This type of assignment is known as a continuous assignment because it is always active whenever an operand on the right-hand side changes, a&b is evaluated and assigned to out1. A continuous assignment is viewed as a combinational circuit whose output is continuously updated depending on its inputs, which in this case is a simple AND gate.
*   Line 8: This line applies the keyword “endmodule” to specify that end of the description of the circuit named “Circuit\_1”.

[Figure 6.14](#ch18.xhtml#f22) shows the programme coding for both Verilog and VHDL for the same circuit description. Verilog is more concise and does not make use of predefined library routines as VHDL. As you may recall the libraries in VHDL provide the definition for the data types and operators, which for std\_logic data type can have one of nine different values. However, the most used options for std\_logic data type are 0, 1, Z, and ‘-’ (‘-’ denotes a don’t care). On the other hand, Verilog has four basic data types that are often applied. Hence, the wires defined in the example may have one of the following: 0 for a logic low or a false condition; 1 for a logic high or true condition; z for the high-impedance state, which can be used to describe the output of a tri-state buffer; and x for a don’t-care or unknown value, when an input is not initialized or two or more conflicting outputs are connected together.

It should be noted that currently, VHDL and Verilog are the prevalent HDLs that are viewed as industry standard with FPGA design tools ordinarily supporting both languages.

## **6.3** AI Software Algorithms

This section will address AI software algorithms, which is a category of computer software that enables the implementation of AI to process substantial volumes of data for performing tasks that would otherwise require human intelligence. These tasks include speech and voice recognition, text recognition, image recognition, video analytics, generative Al, and natural language processing (NLP).

In recent years, the strategic importance of Al technology has been acknowledged, and its application has increased exponentially across all types of industries. Many private and public sector organisations are studying and investing in Al solutions to strengthen their competitive position in a continually turbulent global market and to improve their organisational processes. It is a well-known experience in technological development that late movers will likely be at risk of being outdated in terms of innovation and will critically lag their competitors in terms of servicing their customers.

### **6.3.1** Voice and Speech Recognition (Conversational AI)

The thrust for Conversational AI is currently from the smart home market. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and others are sustaining their investment in this technology to develop smart assistants as an integral part of people’s lifestyle through smartphones and personal computers. This investment is not aimed at incremental change but to revolutionise the way tasks are executed at home and in the longer term in organisations. Although more needs to be done before this technology is widely accepted, substantial improvement is being made in terms of enhancing the complex mathematical models that drive and control voice and speech recognition technology. However, for these types of mathematical models to be fully complete they must be able to harness vast volumes of data that organisations have accumulated over the years to be able to learn and recognise diverse speech patterns.

It must be recognised that these models are very complex because they must have the capacity to decipher not only vocabulary, regional pronunciations, and colloquialisms but also the context of the conversations. They emphatically need to speedily analyse all recorded conversations of call centre agents with customers and the voluminous daily interactions with a digital assistant. This is highly dependent on having a permanent and fast internet link to provide the necessary processing integration and reliable high-velocity connectivity.

Currently, applicable voice technologies are available from well-known providers, such as Google Assistant, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Cortana, amongst others. However, the current technology is still limited in what it can do. For instance, most chatbots and virtual agents are typically inclined towards having action links (i.e., keys/buttons) that are applied for moving the conversation forward or having external links to divert the customer from a conversation entirely. This is likely to create a problem for voice-only exchanges. Another issue with AI voice recognition technology is that it is still not as robust as the chat-based equivalent and has difficulty in interpreting elusive linguistic distinctions that are commonly used in speech.

It must also be realised that voice and speech recognition are two different functions. Voice recognition is based on technology that recognises the voice of the speaker. On the other hand, speech recognition is the technology that recognises the actual words. This difference in definition illustrates that both functions have a different task. For example, voice recognition includes security features such as voice biometrics, whereas speech recognition is a device that generates automatic transcripts and accurate instructions. Basically, AI voice recognition recognises and decodes human speech patterns and permits a smartphone, computer, or virtual assistant to know what one is saying and respond to this. In contrast, speech recognition technology transforms speech into text by identifying words, and in advanced AI applications may interpret differences based on context. For example, automatic speech recognition (ASR) applies this technology to transcribe voicemails and has an accessibility tool that permits persons unable to type to talk to their computer to compose emails, perform searches, and many other functions.

Furthermore, voice recognition and ASR have distinct roles and process and respond to audio in a different way. Voice recognition is a device like the digital assistants, Amazon Alexa or Google Dot, which execute certain tasks by listening to a person’s voice in real-time and responding to it. For example, Alexa resides in the cloud and is, therefore, accessible from anywhere at any time, responding to requests or answering questions like reading the latest news headlines, playing a specific song, and dimming lights in a particular room, amongst many others. Basically, voice recognition identifies who said what, while ASR captures what people say. Hence, ASR does not identify voices but recognises speech by applying natural language processing (NLP) to produce a transcript of the audio and generating real-time captioning. ASR is not perfect in its interpretation, but it is quick and is a cheap method for converting speech to text.

The benefits of exploiting voice recognition at an individual or organisational level include its effectiveness as a user verification tool, convenience, and better performance. For instance, banks have implemented voice biometrics as a security measure on certain accounts that have resulted in substantial savings from their fraud prevention endeavours. Additionally, voice-based technology mitigates the requirement for error scans by having more accurate communication facilities permitting faster, and better task management. Furthermore, speech recognition AI is being applied to provide business solutions ranging from voice-activated audio content assistants to ATMs by facilitating the interaction of people with technology providing better data transcription accuracy.

Speech recognition is being used at call centres by allowing organisations to listen to what customers have to say and then applying the gained information via cloud models to provide a quick and proper response. It is also being applied for voice or audio biometrics (voice patterns) to identity and authorise users to access systems without the need for passwords, fingerprints, or eye scans. Fintech companies are using speech recognition to help customers resolve basic business queries. Additionally, clients can interact with organisations in real-time 24/7 from anywhere using voice transcription solutions or text messaging applications to resolve their concerns.

### **6.3.2** Text Recognition

AI is also being used for text recognition. Text recognition software does not only decipher typed text through optical character recognition (OCR) but also interprets handwritten documents. OCR basically recognises text within a digital image such as scanned documents and images and convert them into an accessible softcopy version with text. Traditionally, OCR was restricted to printed scanned documents. However, AI handwriting recognition software can be trained to decrypt handwritten documents as well as printed texts, which requires a more complex model. It is being applied for deciphering historical documents that may contain linguistic difference from their modern counterparts.

For instance, Transkribus a company supplying an AI based handwriting recognition software claims that its software can be trained to decipher both handwritten historical documents and printed texts. They maintain that its pre-trained AI model is able to transcribe large number of documents very quickly and make them accessible to be read, searched, and prepared for further applications such as research, data analyses, or publishing. Amazon Textract is another text recognition software for extracting text and structured data (tables and forms) from documents using AI, with no configuration or templates being necessary; and having robust data privacy, encryption, and security controls. This software is being applied by Fintech companies to root out critical information from mortgage applications regarding asset and property valuation, and credit rating or extracting information from insurance forms, claims, and receipts that have varying document layouts and formats.

Text recognition software has been around for some time, but with the support of AI, its transformation and extraction features are improving rapidly, particularly in recognising historical and modern handwritten documents (in various languages). Algorithms to decipher historical and modern handwritten documents are very complex and require extensive machine learning features that can only be resolved by applying AI technology.

### **6.3.3** Image Recognition

AI is being applied to image recognition, sometimes referred to as picture or photo recognition. Image recognition has the specific purpose of identifying and classifying objects of interest within a given image. The human brain is capable of automatically classifying objects that it visually observes, and to link them with individual definitions. While as humans we take this function for granted, it is extremely difficult for machines to achieve this task. However, with the support of AI such a function is being performed but it requires a complex algorithm sustained by considerable processing power.

A primary objective of image recognition is the classification of the discovered (or observed) objects into different categories to assess which group the image is associated with, hence earning the name deep learning object recognition. With the ever-increasing processing power of the computer, machine learning, in particular deep learning technology, has made important and successful advances in computerised vision and image processing. Currently, AI models for image recognition supported by deep learning algorithms are being successfully applied in many private and public industrial sectors. When discussing AI image recognition, it is important to clarify the terminology applicable. For instance, it is necessary to distinguish between image recognition and computer vision; object localisation; and image detection. Although, there are some overlaps in their meaning, there are also some important differences.

Image recognition is the application of computer vision. Image recognition is viewed as a subset of computer vision that focuses on detecting, analysing, and interpreting images for decision-making. It includes tasks like image tagging (identifying and labelling the contents of an image), object detection, and guiding autonomous vehicles using neural networks trained on annotated datasets. Computer vision is a field of AI that applies machine learning and neural networks to train computer systems to obtain meaningful information from digital images, videos, and other visual inputs and to also make suggestions or act when they detect defects or issues. Hence, image recognition performs several functions, such as classification, tagging, detection and segmentation using machine learning.

Object localisation is also a subset of computer vision. It refers to identifying the location of one or more objects in an image and depicting each within a drawn box (demarcation) to show clearly its location, but it does not include the classification of detected objects. On the other hand, image detection is a function that uses an image as input data and searches and discovers various objects within it. For instance, face detection algorithms aim to seek face patterns in images irrespective of whether the detected objects are significant. The reason for this is that the aim of image detection is merely to distinguish one object from another, thus assessing the number of distinct entities that are present within the image. Therefore, boundaries are drawn around each separate detected object. With image recognition, the aim is to pinpoint the objects of interest within an image and identifying with which category they are associated.

The growth and importance of computer vision algorithms has been significant over the years due to its accuracy and speedy processing. The two well developed algorithms are the Mask RCNN (Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network) released around 2017, and YOLO (You Only Look Once) released around 2021. The latest version of the YOLO algorithm is YOLOv9, which was released in early 2024. Mask R-CNN is a deep learning instance segmentation method that executes pixel-level segmentation on detected objects and can accommodate multiple classes and overlapping objects by precisely delineating their boundaries at the pixel level. Mask R-CNN applies Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and the Region of Interest Align (ROIAlign) to attain high accuracy and resilient performance. FPN is a feature extractor that receives a single-scale image of an arbitrary size as input, and produces proportionally sized feature maps at multiple levels, in a fully convolutional fashion as outputs. Hence, it functions as a generic solution for creating feature pyramids inside deep convolutional networks that are applied in executing tasks like object detection.

FPN works in conjunction with RoIAlign, which extracts a small feature map from each RoI (Region of Interest) used in detection and segmentation tasks by removing the harsh quantisation of the RoI Pool and accurately aligning the extracted features with the input. However, Mask R-CNN requires substantial processing power due to its computational complexity and high memory utilisation during training and inference. This may hinder accuracy in segmenting very small objects or handling heavily obscure scenes and may be more resource reliant for training and fine-tuning the model. The YOLO models are a real-time object detection mechanism that identify and classify objects in a single pass of the image. The YOLO model (like Mask R-CNN) uses the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify the objects and regressor networks to accurately predict the bordering (bounding) box coordinates for each detected object. However, YOLO and Mask R-CNN differ in object detection approach, the former uses a single-shot detection (SSD) approach, while the latter applies a two-shot (or multi-shot) method.

An SSD object detection algorithm predicts the bounding box and the class of the object in one single shot through a single forward pass of the network that simultaneously predicts the presence of an object and its respective bounding box. YOLO segments the input image into a grid and predicts a certain number of bounding boxes and class probabilities for each grid cell. On the other hand, Mask R-CNN predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities at multiple scales in different feature maps. Hence, it uses a two-step approach, with the first step suggesting a series of bounding boxes that may possibly contain an object (using a method called region proposal); and the second step entails processing these suggested regions through a CNN to classify the object classes within the box. Hence, an SSD algorithm is very fast and efficient making it very suitable for tasks requiring real-time detection. However, the two-shot detectors are slower but are more accurate because they are more computationally intensive since speed is not their primary objective. Therefore, they can consume added computational resources on each likely object.

YOLOv9 is an improvement on previous versions since it addresses the issue regarding information loss inherent in deep neural networks and ensuring the retention of vital information throughout the detection process, to attain outstanding accuracy and performance. This is achieved by integrating Programmable Gradient Information (PGI) and the versatile Generalized Efficient Layer Aggregation Network (GELAN) architecture. PGI is an innovative concept to mitigate the issue of information bottleneck by safeguarding crucial data across deep network layers and to permit the creation of reliable gradients, expediting accurate model updates, and enhancing the overall detection performance. This concept is combined with GELAN to attain greater parameter application and computational efficiency. The integration of PGI and GELAN permits YOLOv9 to have an adaptable mixture of various computational blocks, allowing it to be used in a wide range of applications without forfeiting speed or accuracy.

The early image processing methods of two decades ago required vast quantities of training data, while the more recent deep learning approaches need much smaller learning samples. Despite this development, deep learning involves manual labelling of data to mark good and bad samples, a process called image annotation. This labelling process to train AI models is known as supervised learning, which entails time-consuming human work. Imagine the amount of human effort that is required to label images and annotate typical traffic conditions for autonomous vehicles.

The early image recognition methods depended on a sequence of image filtering, image segmentation, feature extraction, and rule-based classification (computer vision pipeline). The difficulty at that time was that engineering such pipelines, involved deep expertise in image processing and computer vision, which took a great deal of development time and testing, in addition to manual parameter fine-tuning. This meant that the early computer vision methods supported by pixel-based image recognition systems were not very flexible, hence their reusability in varying scenarios or, and locations was very restrictive.

However, machine learning (with unsupervised learning) resulted in a high level of scalability, since it made use of algorithms to learn hidden knowledge from a dataset of good and bad samples. Additionally, deep learning applies multiple hidden layers of a neural network in its model. Deep learning would not be possible without the support of very powerful AI hardware and graphics processing units (GPUs). These tools provided the much need breakthroughs for the development of robust image recognition technology. AI image recognition technology has many practical uses. In healthcare, image recognition models are applied for identifying diseases or abnormalities in medical images. It has practical uses in security surveillance systems for real-time object detection, tracking, and classification, with face detection being adopted for biometrics, security, and facial recognition systems. In the agricultural industry it is applied to detect and classify crops, pests, and diseases, particularly facilitating precision agriculture techniques and automating farming processes. Although still at the experimental stage, it is used in autonomous vehicles for detecting objects such as other vehicles, pedestrians, traffic signs, and signals in real-time.

The constant challenge with this type of technology is to find an equilibrium between performance and computing efficiency, since an essential prerequisite for deep learning models is the impeccable affiliation of hardware and software to mitigate cost concerns related to computer vision. This impeccable affiliation of deep learning, image classification and deep neural network face recognition algorithms have succeeded in providing extraordinary performance and real-time object detection that exceeds human capabilities.

### **6.3.4** Video Analysis

Video analysis provides a user with the capability of extracting useful information from a video recording, such as counting the number of people or/and identifying specific objects or individuals. Like image recognition, video analytics makes use of computer vision technology that utilises AI for handling the analysis of digital images and videos. Video analysis employs deep learning techniques that use neural networks to learn patterns in data. Deep learning, which is a subset of machine learning, exploits neural networks that consist of multiple layers of interconnected processing nodes. This enables AI video analysis using deep learning algorithms to detect, track objects and recognise specific actions in video footage.

As already explained in the previous section when discussing image recognition, deep learning technology is the basis for this type of analysis using the latest Mask R-CNN and YOLO algorithms to detect objects in video. These algorithms can be custom trained with collected video data or pre-trained on large image datasets such as MS COCO. The MS COCO (Common Objects in Context) dataset is a large-scale object detection, segmentation, and captioning dataset that is designed to encourage research on a wide variety of object categories and is commonly used for benchmarking computer vision models. MS COCO image dataset contains over 320,000 images of everyday objects and humans with annotations that can be utilised to train machine learning models to recognise, label, and describe objects. These deep learning models facilitate the analysis of video by detecting and tracking objects, including object counting and rule-based analysis. For instance, they can be fine-tuned to count people in large crowds.

Another important feature of deep learning models is action recognition, which entails identifying specific actions in a video sequence or real-time video streams. These types of models can be taught to classify actions being executed in different contexts or environments. There are two categories of software systems related to video analysis, namely video management systems (VMS) and computer vision systems. A VMS typically manages camera streams from security cameras by providing a single interface for observing live and recorded video from several cameras, with a search, playback, and export features. Additionally, VMS applications are normally intended to function with a specific type of camera, such as IP cameras or CCTV cameras. These systems precede advances in AI and are considered old-fashioned since many organisations are currently demanding video analytics functionality by including face and person detection and automated tagging or alerts.

On the other hand, computer vision systems focus on video recognition and the usage of complex real-time video analysis. These systems typically apply image processing algorithms using multi-step computer vision pipelines to evaluate images for extracting information from video footage, such as person or object detection, facial recognition, activity recognition, quality inspection, amongst many others. Many organisations opt for a customised computer vision system to satisfy their specific needs regarding system integration, performance, cost effectiveness, scalability, and data privacy.

AI video analytics is being used in private and public industrial sectors, particularly concerning security such as traffic monitoring, incident detection, intrusion management, people counting, augmented reality (AR), and facial recognition. It is also utilised in automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) that uses optical character recognition on images to read vehicle registration plates to create vehicle location data and ego motion that estimates a camera’s motion relative to a rigid scene. Video analytics software can be taught to recognise the subtle differences in motion direction between the regular and irregular behaviour, such as fence claiming and other forms of intrusion by evaluating the difference in direction between horizonal and vertical (claiming) motion. Video analytics software in conjunction with X-ray security screening can be trained to perform object classification on real-time footage of baggage at security check-ins to recognise specific objects of interest, such as weapons and sharp instruments.

AI video analytics can also be applied in healthcare environments such as monitoring elderly patients at their private residence or in care homes for detecting falls, and unusual positions or periods of time in which a person is on the floor or incapacitated. They can also be trained to determine whether an elderly person has taken a given medication when scheduled. Furthermore, facial emotion analysis with AI using video analysis can be taught to identify differences in normal and abnormal facial or physical behaviour and alert designated responsible persons. The above examples illustrate that video analysis is a valuable technology that has a wide range of applications and is somewhat mature in its practical development.

### **6.3.5** Generative Al

Generative AI is a category of AI that can generate new content and ideas, including conversations, stories, images, videos, and music. Generative AI was initiated in the 1960s when the first chatbots were introduced. However, the breakthrough came in June 2014 when Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues at Google Brain developed the concept regarding generative adversarial networks (GANs). GAN is a category of machine learning structure, which has become an important concept in managing generative AI. Generative AI applies a machine learning algorithm that enables it to generate convincing authentic images, videos, and audio of factual people. While Generative AI has provided a powerful tool in the education and movie industry, it has also raised concerns regarding deepfakes. Deepfakes involve digitally fictitious images or videos that may be used to fraudulently launch damaging cybersecurity attacks on an individual and businesses, with the possibility of criminal extortion.

Innovative recent developments such as transformers and large language models (LLMs) have made generative AI an acceptable standard technology. Transformers being a machine learning tool allows technologists to train models that are constantly increasing in size and intensity without the need to initially labelling all the data. Hence, newly initiated models can be trained using an unimaginable volume of pages containing text to provide responses with more depth. This is possible because transformers through the concept of “attention” do not just track the connection of words in individual sentences but allow models to track the linkages between words across an immense volume of text and could track these linkages to examine code, proteins, chemicals, and DNA.

Furthermore, LLMs have billions or even trillions of parameters that strengthen generative AI models to write appealing text, generate impromptu entertaining situation comedy, and may even portray photorealistic images. Therefore, applying the features of transformers and LLMs, generative AI has developed into a very powerful and robust tool that can create content through various types of media, including text, graphics, and video. For example, there are tools like Dall-E (named after the surrealist artist Salvador Dalí) that automatically generate images from a typescript or create text descriptions from images. However, generative AI is still at its early development phase. It requires much enhancement before it may be perfected for generating readable text and photorealistic stylized graphics that is considered highly accurate and unbiased, and free from hallucinations.

[Figure 6.15](#ch18.xhtml#f23) illustrates that generative AI begins with an input prompt, which could be text, a design, an image, musical notes, a video, or any other input that the AI system can process. The input could be from a scanned copy and/or from a repository of stored data. This input is received by the various AI algorithms, which then create new content as a response to the input prompt. The generated content, depending on the input prompt, may take the form of compositions, specific answers to questions or problems, or realistic fakes generated from photographs or images or audio of an individual. Recent versions of generative AI allow users to define their request in plain language rather than using application languages such as Python. This makes them more user friendly, where the user can also modify the initial outcome regarding form, tone, and other specific aspects.

![Figure 6.15 Example of Generative AI Process.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_015.jpg)

**Figure 6.15** Example of Generative AI Process.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f23b)

Typically, generative AI models apply a specific neural network to produce new content in reply to a query or prompt using techniques such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs). These neural networks with a decoder and encoder can create realistic human faces, fake data for AI training or even replicas of individuals.

GANs consist of two neural networks, the generator and the discriminator that are united in a perpetual duel. The generator network has the function of creating data samples by commencing with random noise and endeavours to create data that is as realistic as possible. On the other hand, the discriminator network examines the data with the purpose of distinguishing between real and fake samples. Therefore, the training process is an iterative back-and-forth method with the intention of generating more and more convincing data, while the discriminator refines its abilities in distinguishing between real from fake. Over a span of time, the generator develops into a master counterfeiter, creating data that is almost impossible for the discriminator to distinguish from real examples.

VAEs work differently from GANs. These are probabilistic models that are created on the framework of autoencoders, which are normally applied for dimensionality reduction and feature learning. The autoencoders consist of an encoder and decoder. An encoder network takes the input data and encodes it into a lower-dimensional space by mapping the data into a probabilistic latent space. On the other hand, the decoder considers the points from this latent space and tries to reconstruct the original data. This is achieved by sampling from the latent space’s distribution to statistically generating data, leading to a deeper examination of the data’s generative potential. GANs are inclined to create sharper, higher quality outcomes, but can be somewhat erratic during training, whereas VAEs are more consistent to train but may experience lower quality.

Several tools that apply transformers are now available such as BERT (Google’s Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), OpenAI’s GPT and Google AlphaFold. These neural networks have the capability to encode language, images and generate new content, with ChatGPT, Dall-E and Bard being common generative AI interfaces.

ChatGPT was first released towards the end of 2022 as an interface to OpenAI that provided the ability to interact and fine-tune text responses through a chat interface with interactive feedback. The ChatGPT interface has been improved with refined new versions and has been integrated in Microsoft’s Bing search engine. ChatGPT provides human-like responses creating conversations that are engaging and appear more natural. OpenAI also introduced Dall-E for creating images from textual descriptions. It was trained on a considerable data set of images and their linked text descriptions and is classified as a multimodal AI application that recognises connections across multiple media, such as text, vision, and audio and creates images in multiple forms driven by user prompts.

Google Bard is a multimodal model that exploits the enhanced abilities of the Language Model for Dialogue Applications (LaMDA) to improve conversational AI. Bard is designed to recognise multiple data types, such as text, audio, images, and video that enhances its integrational reasoning abilities. This integration capability permits Bard to execute functions that include summarising text, translation, and code analysis. Google adopted a hurried strategy when initially releasing Bard to catch up with Microsoft. However, this rushed launching resulted in a negative initial acceptance of Bard when it incorrectly stated that the Webb telescope was the first to discover a planet in a foreign solar system. But Microsoft experienced similar outcomes with the ChatGPT implementations when it provided erroneous responses and behaved in an inconsistent manner. In the meantime, both Google and Microsoft have made significant progress in addressing similar unfortunate experiences, but more still needs to be done. The latest version of Bard has some exceptional features that include a multimodal function that is trained on a various data sets enabling Bard to comprehend and generate content over various formats; advanced neural architecture that applies a transformer model with effective attention structures that enable Bard to manage long contexts essential for in depth and complex conversations; and broad safety testing feature to mitigate risks of bias and harmfulness. Bard applications have well developed user interaction capabilities to facilitate the developers’ efforts for generating innovative software.

Generative AI has a lot of potential, but it does have several significant limitations. For instance, generative AI is not always able to identify the content’s source, which could be problematic for evaluating the bias of original sources, particularly for realistic-sounding content that renders it difficult to recognise incorrect information. Therefore, it may present incorrect and misleading information with users being concerned about the reliability of the information provided. Furthermore, when generating content, particularly for academic assignments, it may overlook copyrights and thus inadvertently support plagiarism. Additionally, generative AI facilitates the creation of fake news and may also create an environment where it becomes easier to discredit authentic photographic evidence or imitate individuals as an effective means to achieve social engineering cyber-attacks.
