### **6.3.6** Natural Language Processing (NLP)

NLP is a segment of AI where a computer program is developed to understand human language (natural language) in its spoken and written form. Although there is some overlap with what has been discussed previously, it is appropriate to address it separately due to its importance. The origin of NLP evolved from the field of linguistics, computer science, and computational linguistics. Work with NLP commenced in the 1950s when Alan Turing created the Turing Test to assess whether (or not) a computer is truly intelligent. The Turing test entailed the computerised interpretation and creation of natural language as a critical benchmark of intelligence.

Up to the 1990s, NLP was mostly rules-based, applying human generated rules created by linguists who study every aspect of language, including vocabulary, grammar, and the sound of language to determine how computers would process language. An important milestone occurred on 7 January 1954 with the joint Georgetown University–IBM experiment. This experiment was a significant illustration of machine translation concerning the full automated translation of more than sixty Russian sentences into English. The subsequent several decades witnessed the development of rule-based parsing to identify patterns of text that represent specific concepts; morphology to analyse internal structure of words and the rules governing the formulation of words; and semantics to study meanings of words amongst other forms of natural language understanding.

In the 1990s, computers had higher processing speed that enabled developers to apply a rule-based approach for natural language processing through a statistical approach (i.e., data-driven) without a linguist generating all the rules. Hence, NLP became an engineer-based approach rather than linguist-based that applied a broader application of scientific disciplines. NLP has experienced phenomenal growth for the past few decades. Starting in the early 2000s, developers exploited further enhancements in computer processing power that enabled them to introduce unsupervised and semi-supervised machine learning algorithms. Thus, combining classical linguistics and statistical approaches. The outcome of this development is the initiation of practical applications and improved human interaction through chatbots and virtual assistants. The development cycle of NLP is approaching maturity, but it still has to overcome several concerns related to accuracy, accessibility, and widespread applicability in diverse industrial sectors, such as business intelligence, search engines, linguistics applications, and medical research.

Essentially, an NLP management system consists of two functions, namely the data preprocessing and developing the algorithm to process the data. Data preprocessing is the process of preparing and cleaning the dataset. It involves detecting, correcting, and/or removing corrupt or inaccurate details from a dataset. Hence, it identifies erroneous, incomplete, irrelevant segments of the dataset, and then amends, replaces, or deletes the corrupt or abrasive data content. The objective of data preprocessing is to convert the given dataset into a content and format that enables the computer programme (through an algorithm) to analyse and use it. This is accomplished by several methods that include the following:

*   Tokenisation: This is the process of creating a digital representation by substituting sensitive information with nonsensitive information to protect sensitive data or to efficiently process large amounts of data. For example, it is used in cybersecurity related to payments to disguise the identity of the payment to prevent fraud.
*   Stop word removal: This is the process of removing the words that commonly occur across all the documents permitting only unique words that offer the most information about the text to be retained.
*   Stemming and lemmatisation: Stemming as the process of stripping attachments from words to obtain reduced word strings, and lemmatisation is the process of reducing morphological variants to one dictionary base form. Hence, lemmatisation clusters mutually unique modified versions of the same word. For instance, the word “sleeping” would be reduced to its basic form “sleep.”
*   Part-of-speech (POS) tagging: This involves assigning a grammatical type such as noun, verb, adjective to each word in a sentence. The purpose is to comprehend the syntactical structure of a sentence and identify the grammatical roles of individual words.

When the dataset has been through the preprocessing function, a computer programme (algorithm) is used to process it. The commonly applied natural language processing algorithms fall under two key types, namely rule-based and machine learning based systems. A rule-based system applies meticulously conceived linguistic rules, whilst a machine learning-based system applies statistical methods. Both methods learn to achieve tasks based on training data that are made available and fine-tune their processes as more data is dealt with. Therefore, an NLP algorithm refines its own rules through an iterative process by adopting a combination of approaches such as machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks. NLP as a system is a significant development because enterprises, irrespective of size, require an effective means of processing a considerable volume of unstructured and text-heavy data. There are two chief processing techniques used in NLP, namely syntax and semantic analysis.

Syntax refers to the sentence structure and how words are organised in a sentence according to set rules to make grammatical sense. Hence, NLP applies syntax (sentence structure language rules) to evaluate connotation from a specific language. In NLP, syntax techniques include the following:

*    Parsing: This refers to analysing a sentence by dividing it into grammatical parts and identify the parts and their relations to each other. For instance, when an NLP algorithm is given the sentence, “The cat meowed.” Parsing breaks down the sentence into segments of speech, such that cat = noun, and meowed = verb.
*   Word segmentation: A word is viewed as a linguistic unit made up of one or more morphemes. Hence, word segmentation determines the word boundaries in a sentence or a document deriving word forms. For instance, an algorithm can analyse a handwritten scanned document and recognise that the words are divided by white spaces.
*   Sentence breaking: This is also known as sentence boundary disambiguation (SBD), sentence boundary detection, and sentence segmentation, where NLP decides where sentences begin and end. Hence, the algorithm can analyse text and by using sentence breaking can recognise the full stop (period) that separates the sentences.
*   Morphological segmentation: This is a method for identifying and analysing the structure of words, which is valuable in morphologically-rich languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, where patterns of prefixes, suffixes, and roots form words. It is also helpful in machine translation and speech recognition. For instance, the word unaccountable would be split into \[un\[\[account\]able\]\], where the algorithm identifies “un,” “account,” and “able” as morphemes.
*   Stemming: Stemming is the process of reducing inflected form of a word to one so-called “stem,” or root form, also known as a “lemma” in linguistics. For instance, in the sentence, “The cat meowed” the algorithm recognises that the root of the word “meowed” is “meow.” This is useful when a user is analysing text for all occurrences of the word meow, as well as all the variation of the form of a verb (i.e., its conjugations). The algorithm is able to recognise that they are basically the same word, despite the fact that the letters are different.

The other processing technique is semantic analysis, which essentially entails the use of and meaning behind words. Hence, an NLP algorithm is used to figure out the meaning and structure of sentences. There are basically three main semantic techniques that are applied:

*   Word sense disambiguation: This is the process of determining the intended meaning, or sense, of a word within a specific context. The process is important for machine translation, information retrieval, question answering, and sentiment analysis. For instance, in the sentence, “The horse is in the stable.” The word “stable” has many meanings. Hence, the NLP algorithm will apply this method to understand that the use of the word here refers to a horse barn, and not any other word denoting stability as in steady or constant.
*   Named entity recognition (NER): This technique focuses on identifying and classifying specific data points from textual content. For instance, an algorithm can analyse a document and identify all references to a specific establishment or product. By applying the semantics of the text, it can distinguish between objects that appear to be the same. For instance, in the sentence, “John McPherson the farmer went to purchase a McPherson tractor,” the algorithm can identify that the two occurrences of “McPherson” as two distinct things, one being an individual and the other being a tractor manufacturer.
*   Natural language generation (NLG): This is the process of translating data into text or speech by applying a database to establish the semantics underlying words and create new content. Hence, NLP is the process of accurately translating what is said into machine-readable data, which would enable NLG to apply that data to create a reply.

NLP employs deep learning as a fundamental approach, which is a type of AI that analyses and exploits the patterns in data to improve an algorithm’s interpretation. Deep learning models make use of a massive volume of labelled data, which could be rather challenging in terms of logical and processing power. The pioneering rule-based methods were cumbersome since the algorithms were informed what words, idioms, and phrases they are to search for in the text and provided with specific responses when they found a match. Deep learning models can automatically identify patterns and features in data without being explicitly programmed to do so. These models apply an intuitive (untaught) approach in which the algorithms learn to recognise the writer’s or speakers’ intention from numerous examples that mimics how a child would learn human language. This makes deep learning models immensely powerful and flexible approach. Several opensource tools that are commonly applied for NLP, and which are based on Python, include Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) that has data sets and tutorials; Gensim containing a library for topic modelling and document indexing; and NLP Architect by Intel that uses a library for deep learning topologies and techniques.

The practical applications using NLP include the analysis of social media assessments to be used for customer feedback analysis; speech recognition to recognise what the customer is saying over the phone for directing customer calls to the appropriate location; translating text, audio, and documents into another language; and analysing vast volumes of academic research material based on the metadata for academic research, amongst many others. These and other application areas illustrate that NLP’s key advantage is its ability to enhance the means that humans and computers communicate with each other. However, the main challenge of NLP is to keep pace with the evolution of natural language and its inherent obscurity of meaning in the way words are used and the emotions expressed by the content. This translates to ensuring that an NLP algorithm is accurate and precise in interpreting human speech and text content that may in itself be imprecise and ambiguous; correctly interpreting tone and inflection of content (speech and text); and eliminates bias. NLP systems are not perfect and requires more effort to addressing the above issues.

### **6.3.7** Expert Systems

An expert system is a knowledge-based computer system that has the primary objective of addressing complex problems by extracting knowledge from its knowledge base applying reasoning and inference rules according to user queries, thus providing a decision-making capability like a human expert. However, it is critical to understand that an expert system is not intended to replace human experts but is used as an aid to humans in making a complex decision. Hence, expert systems do not mimic human thinking abilities but merely operate because of the knowledge base of the particular domain for which they are designed.

Expert systems are not a new phenomenon and were first developed over half a century ago by Edward Feigenbaum, a computer science professor at Stanford University and founder of Stanford’s Knowledge Systems Laboratory. These systems are viewed as the first successful use of AI that initially originated in the medical domain. Over the years the knowledge base of a particular domain naturally increases with a resultant significant improvement in performance. Today, expert systems apply machine learning and AI to replicate the behaviour or wisdom of domain experts, and their performance continuously intensifies as they attain more knowledge and experience. Hence, expert systems continuously accumulate knowledge and experience to convert these into wisdom by integrating them with an inference engine to respond to queries.

An inference engine basically interprets and assesses the facts in the knowledge base to provide an answer to a user designed query (refer to [Figure 6.16](#ch18.xhtml#f24)). The basic function of an inference engine is to enable the expert system to derive deductions from the rules in the knowledge base. The inference engine typically applies two approaches for extracting information from the knowledge base, namely forward and backward chaining. The function of forward chaining is to read and process a set of facts to reach a logical extrapolation about a future occurrence, such as predicting the price of commodities (e.g., gain, steel, fuel). On the other hand, backward chaining has the function of reading and processing a set of facts to arrive at a logical conclusion about the reason something had occurred, such as assessing apparent symptoms to reach a medical opinion.

![Figure 6.16 Expert System: Illustration of Inference Engine.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C006_016.jpg)

**Figure 6.16** Expert System: Illustration of Inference Engine.[⏎](#ch18.xhtml#f24b)

Both approaches are dependent on having a significant and accurate knowledge base. In a practical sense, human experts continually add information to the knowledge base with the aim of having perfect information, where nonexperts can utilise the system to solve complex problems that would usually require a human expert. Obviously, attaining perfect information is difficult to achieve in many domains because knowledge continually grows. The holistic expert system process is generally referred to as knowledge engineering. Knowledge engineering refers to the integrated process of creating and maintaining an expert system with essential information to solve a problem using knowledge representation methodologies, such as symbolic patterns where rules and axioms are applied to make inferences and deductions. Hence, an expert system’s competences can be enriched by intensifying the knowledge base or/and generating additional sets of rules.

## **6.4** Neuromorphic Computing

In a previous section of this chapter the topic of neuromorphic hardware was discussed in detail. This section discusses the topic of neuromorphic computing, which goes beyond neuromorphic hardware and includes the software segment within the neuromorphic approach. However, some overlap with neuromorphic hardware is likely to cover the topic completely. Before, specifically discussing neuromorphic computing it is firstly appropriate to discuss neural networks, since they are an important aspect of neuromorphic computing.

### **6.4.1** Neural Networks

Artificial neural networks are algorithms (or software programs) that refer to a network of artificial neurons or nodes, which are inspired by the biological neural networks that form the human brain. Neural networks operate differently from conventional computers in that they could do many things concurrently known as parallel processing. The Von Neumann architecture, which forms the basis of the traditional computer, process instructions in a sequential manner. The concept used in a multiprogramming operating system (allocating a minute time sequence to each individual software application module) makes it appear that many things are happening simultaneously.

The artificial neural network is an inherently multiprocessor-friendly architecture that is specifically designed for parallel processing, which allows the execution of instructions in less time. However, the processors must be specifically designed for the neural network, which means that they perform a specific predetermined task. Additionally, artificial neural networks function differently from traditional computers because artificial neural networks can function through images, pictures, and concepts. On the other hand, traditional computers function logically according to a programmed set of rules and calculations. Hence, traditional computers learn by rules, while artificial neural networks learn through examples, by performing a function and subsequently learning from it. Therefore, the applications adaptable to traditional and artificial neural networks are fundamentally and exceedingly different.

Furthermore, traditional computers function through programmes written in a higher-level computer language such as C and then transforming these programmes into the machine’s assembly language. However, artificial neural networks are constantly adaptable by modifying their own programming, thus are able to “program themselves.” As mentioned previously, neural networks require the use of multiple chips that are customised for the application, which result is extremely high-speed processing when compared to the traditional Von Neumann processors.

### **6.4.2** Neuromorphic Computing Concepts

Neuromorphic computing is the ability to model a computer processor to represent the human brain and nervous system that includes both hardware and software computing elements. Moreover, it makes use of several fields that include computer science, mathematics, electronics, biology, and physics to generate computer systems and hardware. Neuromorphic architectures are frequently modelled after neurons and synapses that are viewed as the fundamental units of the brain.

The human brain consists of many billions of neurons that communicate to each other using a combination of electrical and chemical signals to send information between different regions of the brain and the rest of the nervous system. The linkage-communication points between neurons are known as synapses. Research has shown that neurons and synapses are extremely flexible and much more energy-efficient information processors than the traditional Von Neumann computer systems. Neuromorphic computing is an emerging field that is currently the domain of research programmes at academic institutions and technology companies in a strategic alliance with national defence establishments.

Neuromorphic processors are viewed by many experts as overcoming the confines of Moore’s Law established in 1965, which state that the number of components on a single chip doubles every two years at minimal cost. The main thrust for neuromorphic research is the creation of artificial general intelligence (AGI), which has practical military and commercial implications. The conceptual basis underlying AGI is the notion of having an AI computer that can mimic the human’s ability to understand and learn, by imitating the biological human brain and nervous system with equivalent cognitive ability. Such a significant development will unlock tremendous potential for next-generation semiconductors; transistors and accelerators; deep learning applications; and autonomous systems regarding AI, robotics, self-driving cars, and drones.

As stated previously, neuromorphic computing applies hardware that is based on the configuration, faculties and processes of neurons and synapses in biological brains by applying a spiking neural network (SNN). This approach means that spiking neurons (nodes) process and store/retain data like biological neurons with artificial synaptic devices being used as the linkage-communication points between the spiking neurons. Hence, these spiking neurons use analogue circuitry to transmit electrical signals that mimic brain signals. Whilst traditional Von Neumann computers convert data through a binary system, neuromorphic computing use spiking neurons to measure and encode the discrete analogue signal changes themselves.

### **6.4.3** Characteristics of Neuromorphic Computers

Neuromorphic computers have several unique characteristics. For instance, neuromorphic chips instead of having separate areas for the process and storage tasks, group these tasks on each individual neuron, known as collocate processing. The outcome of this approach is to resolve the Von Neumann bottleneck (using the same channel to retrieve data and instructions, so that only one task is executed at a time), thus increasing performance and deceasing energy consumption. Some neuromorphic chips (e.g., Intel Loihi 2) may have up to one million neurons that makes them extremely parallel by executing as many functions at one time as there are neurons, thus each neuron performs different tasks concurrently.

An advantage of neuromorphic computers is their scalability because one only needs to increase the number of active neurons to have larger networks. Hence, there is literally no limit to their scalability. In other words, neuromorphic computers have the unique ability to achieve significant performance under an expanding workload. Additionally, neuromorphic computers thrive on event-driven computation that focuses on processing events as they occur since the individual neurons and associated synapses process in response to spikes from other neurons. In other words, only those neurons that are processing spikes consume energy, while the remainder are inactive, which results in exceptionally efficient use of energy.

Neuromorphic computers are highly flexible because they are designed to respond to external everchanging stimuli through their spiking neural network (SNN) where each synapse is allotted a voltage output, and adapts this output based on its specific task. Hence, SNNs provide neuromorphic computers with the potential to rapidly adjust to new and changing environments by constantly learning and resolving innovative problems. Furthermore, due to the numerous neurons that process independently and concurrently, neuromorphic computers become extremely fault tolerant, where the failure of one component does not prevent the computer from functioning, since information is stored at various points. It should be noted that neuromorphic computers are mainly utilised in spiking neural network–based machine learning applications that are Turing-complete. This means that theoretically they can perform all general-purpose computation. Whilst neuromorphic computing has the potential to transform the applicable capacity of AI, it needs to overcome many technical difficulties. Neuromorphic computing is currently at its early stage of development and requires significant investment for it to be truly a viable computing platform.

Neuromorphic computers are chiefly available to experts. This is not surprising, and one could say that history is repeating itself. Up to and most of the 1970s traditional computers were accessible to technical experts only, behind closed doors. The computer room was like a holy sanctum for the computer initiated elite. In the 1980s with the growth of personal computers and later the introduction of the internet, this exclusive barrier was being demolished. Neuromorphic computing is going through a similar phase. Once it becomes accessible to nonexperts and software developers create application programming interfaces, programming models and languages, it will make neuromorphic computers more widely available and acceptable. However, before this can happen, neuromorphic computers need to be more accurate, less technically complex, and cost effective. Once, again this is reminiscent of the past (the 1960s) when the cost of computers and their associated operating systems and technical complexities were only practically affordable for large organisations. Once the cost of computing came down and computers were more technically and user friendly in the 1980s and 1990s, the level of acceptance increased exponentially. This is likely to happen with neuromorphic computers in the not-too-distant future, but much further development is necessary.

Before neuromorphic computers can become widely used and accepted more applications software and algorithms must be released. Once again, this is not new. In the 1960s and 1970s, organisations had no option but to develop their own in-house software applications. Very few commercial packages were available at that time, even for rudimentary applications such as the payroll, stock control, and accounting. This is similar to what is happening with neuromorphic computing because most neuromorphic research is carried out with standard deep learning software and algorithms developed for Von Neumann hardware. There is a need to break away from the Von Neumann approach and come up with novel methods that go beyond the Von Neumann techniques. However, to do this there is a need for neuromorphic computing to have clearly defined performance standards. This would permit current and potential users to assess whether progress is being achieved in this field.

Neuromorphic computing has a lot of potential and has attracted substantial investment and research funding. Because of the smaller size and low power consumption, it is envisaged that neuromorphic computers will be utilised to execute AI algorithms at the edge instead of in the cloud. In other words, the AI algorithms would be implemented directly on local devices at the “edge” of the network, rather than depending on centralised cloud servers. This means that processing of data would be conducted at or near the point where data is collected, eliminating the transmission of data over the network, resulting in faster response times and enhanced data security. Therefore, AI applications executing on neuromorphic computers would be able to adjust to their environment and would memorise what is essential, accessing external sources through the cloud if necessary to seek more information when required. This makes them ideal for Internet of Things (IoT) Devices such as security cameras and other linked devices that process data locally; for wearables, like smartwatches; and localised servers that enable on-site processing capacity for manufacturing plants or retail chains systems.

However, more important potential future applications include robots; drones; driverless cars; smart home appliances; natural language, speech, and image processing; data analytics amongst many others, where edge AI is essential. Neuromorphic computing, which may eventually feature emotional awareness in machines, is generating considerable debate about the ethics and legal issues surrounding the treatment of sentient machine behaviour. There are those who argue that sentient machines should be legally considered as a nonhuman animal. However, others contend that a sentient machine should be legally and morally viewed as a person to be protected by the same laws as human beings. These ethical and legal issues are considered extremely important for the future of AI development and will be addressed in separate chapters in greater detail.

## **6.5** Conclusion

Whereas the previous chapter was dedicated to computer hardware in relation to the advancement of AI, this chapter has focused on the other side of the coin, namely the development of computer software and its impact on the development of AI. Software is what drives hardware, therefore, hardware on its own is of no value unless it is supported by the appropriate software and the reverse is also applicable. Hence, it is essential to recognise that hardware and software complement each other. Whereas, hardware defines the physical features of a computer, software is a broad term that is applied to indicate the applications, scripts and programmes that execute on a hardware device. This means that software is a logical collection of instructions, data or programs that are applied to operate computer hardware and execute specific functions. Software applications vary depending on the computer programme that is uploaded on the hardware, whereas the hardware has a predetermined, non-flexible function. This distinction between hardware and software is important.

This chapter has explored various AI programming languages that execute on the traditional Von Neumann computers and are essential for developing current AI applications. The AI programming languages examined included LISP, Python, Intelligent Computer-Aided Design (ICAD), KL-One, Official Production System (OPS5), Mercury and Prolog. Each language has its distinguishing features that take advantage of the current hardware architecture. Additionally, the chapter considers hardware description languages, namely, Verilog and VHDL that are applicable for specific hardware related to AI, such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays. These computer languages are used to create software algorithms on specialised hardware associated with AI that have the objective of controlling digital circuits to perform a particular function.

Although the traditional Von Neumann computer architecture is still currently the dominate hardware architecture platform for AI, it is slowly but surely giving way to other more sophisticated computer architecture, namely the quantum and neuromorphic computers. These are predicted to revolutionise AI development in the not-too-distant future. In this regard the chapter briefly discussed IBM’s Qiskit software development kit (SDK) that is specifically designed for the IBM Quantum Platform to execute specific AI applications. IBM have adopted Qiskit, which is an open-source, python-based quantum SDK and has been designed for the IBM Quantum Platform or on simulators on a local computer at the level of circuits and algorithms. Qiskit has been created to facilitate software development for IBM’s cloud quantum computing service and supports Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI), which combines quantum computing with AI that aims to use the unique properties of quantum computers to enhance the capabilities of AI systems.

The chapter also discussed in some detail AI algorithms that are viewed as an essential category of software that enables the implementation of AI for performing tasks that would otherwise require human intelligence. Currently, these AI algorithms have mostly been designed to execute on the traditional von Neumann computer architecture. AI algorithms include several tasks such as speech and voice recognition; text recognition; image recognition; video analytics; generative Al; and natural language processing. However, it is predicted that these AI algorithms will also execute on quantum and neuromorphic computers.

Finally, the chapter discusses neuromorphic computing and spiked neural networks that are explicitly designed for parallel processing. The topic of neuromorphic computing goes beyond neuromorphic hardware and includes the software segment within the neuromorphic approach. However, some overlap with neuromorphic hardware was necessary to cover the topic more fully. This section examines the underlying computing concepts and characteristics of neuromorphic computing. AI applications executing on neuromorphic computers can adjust to their environment by memorising what is important and seek information from external sources through the cloud if necessary. This makes them ideal for AI applications that require an on-site processing capacity such as driverless cars; robots; drones; and smart home appliances where edge AI is essential. Neuromorphic computing, which may eventually feature emotional awareness raise ethical and legal concerns regarding sentient machine behaviour. However, ethical, and legal issues will be addressed in separate chapters in greater detail later.

# Chapter 7Artificial Intelligence Security

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-9](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-9)

> *“You have your way. I have my way. As for the right way, the correct way, and the only way, it does not exist.”*
> 
> Friedrich Nietzsche
> 
> *German Philosopher (1844-1900)*

Security of computer systems has always been a challenge and currently this challenge has grown to be vastly bigger and tougher. Cutting-edge cyber attackers have a broad strike field, with an ever-growing assault domain, complex, and expanding infrastructure, and an upsurge of information. AI systems because of their devastating power have an exceedingly higher need to be protected. Furthermore, AI itself can be used as a powerful tool by cyber attackers to penetrate the cyber fortress. This hazardous environment is making it extremely difficult for organisations to safeguard data, manage system access, and promptly detect and respond to security threats. This chapter will examine this turbulent security environment and will specifically address the evolving threat landscape, intrusion prevention systems, crack public key infrastructure (PKI), and the centre for AI Safety.

## **7.1** Introduction

[Allan (2023)](#ch19.xhtml#r062) from *Cyber* magazine noted that in 2023 the cybersecurity landscape witnessed an extraordinary transformation. She observed that the growing demand for effective, worldwide threat intelligence continues to increase as geopolitical and economic developments generate an ever more complicated and uncertain world for both businesses and consumers.

It is a well-known fact that technology can be used for the good or as a destructive instrument. This has always been the case. Unfortunately, the development of new technology and their associated tools are providing malevolent perpetrators with the means to assault the cyber fortress. Hence, organisations need to keep ahead of these malicious perpetrators and continually updating their security strategies and related implementation tactics. [Allan (2023)](#ch19.xhtml#r062) argues that cybersecurity professionals must recognise that no one is absolutely safe from cyber-attacks and the need to monitor these rapidly evolving threats is becoming increasingly critical.

According to [IBM (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r070) an intrusion prevention system (IPS) monitors network traffic for potential threats and automatically blocks them by alerting the security team, terminating dangerous connections, removing malicious content or triggering other security devices. IPS is an advancement from intrusion detection systems (IDSs) that they detect and report threats to the security team. However, an IPS apart from having the threat detection and reporting functions also introduces an automated threat prevention capabilities that are at times known as intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDPS).

Basically, an IPS can promptly impede malicious traffic and therefore facilitate the work of the security teams so that they may divert greater effort on the more complicated threats. An IPS plays a crucial function of the enterprise security system, particularly in a multi-cloud network that has numerous access points and manages high volume of traffic, which renders manual monitoring and response an impractical alternative. Furthermore, enterprise security systems are under constant threats from malicious but expert cyber-attackers that also have access to state-of-the-art tools. Therefore, the automated facilities of an IPS permits the organisation to address threats swiftly without placing undue pressure on the IT administration.

However, IPS is just one segment of a robust security system and needs to coherently integrate with other technology aspects for maximum effectiveness. One should note that an IPS is normally located behind the firewall and works in conjunction with it to give added protection by capturing threats that have escaped the firewall detection mechanism. Therefore, an IPS provides an additional level of security by recognising and filtering out threats that other segments of the security infrastructure have not detected. Public key infrastructure (PKI) complements the security systems and refers to the tools that are applied to generate and manage public keys for encryption. This is viewed as a conventional way of securing data transfers on the internet. In fact, PKI is commonly integrated with all web browsers and provide secure public internet traffic.

Organisations apply PKI to secure the communications they send back and forth internally and to ensure that connected devices can connect securely. PKI’s fundamental concept is related to cryptographic keys that are part and parcel of the encryption process that authenticate the different individuals or devices trying to communicate with the network. PKI is important because the encryption and authentication it scrutinises makes it possible to ensure trustworthy secure communication online. Therefore, an PKI can prevent an intruder acquiring access to the network through a connected device by keeping away a potentially malicious and hazardous threat from the organisation.

The other important topic to be addressed by this chapter is the Center for AI Safety (CAIS), which is a non-profit organisation based in San Francisco. CAIS views AI as having the potential to overwhelmingly benefit the world, contingent on the premise that AI can be developed and applied safely. CAIS recognise that extraordinary progress has been made in AI but there are many basic problems in AI safety that have yet to be addressed. Hence, CAIS’s mission is to mitigate societal-scale risks associated with AI by conducting safety research, building the field of AI safety researchers, and advocating for safety standards.

## **7.2** Evolving Threat Landscape

[*Cyber Security* Magazine (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r065) claim that 2023 witnessed an increasing adoption of AI in both offensive and defensive cybersecurity strategies. It maintains that AI-driven threat actors will become more sophisticated, and organisations will dedicate more resources and AI-driven tactics to stay ahead of the evolving threats. Additionally, it viewed AI as becoming a profound battleground for cybersecurity. This analysis supports Deloitte’s argument that the interplay between attacker and victim has become a cat-and-mouse game in which each side perpetually learns and adapts, leveraging creativity and knowledge of the other’s motives to develop new offensive tactics and defensive postures ([Deloitte, 2014](#ch19.xhtml#r066)).

According to [Deloitte (2014)](#ch19.xhtml#r066), the relatively static compliance or policy-centric approaches to security found in many financial services companies may be long outdated. They claim that the critical issue is whether the industry can generate a forceful, intelligence-driven approach to cyber risk management not only as a preventative measure, but also to detect, respond to, and recover from the potential damage that results from these attacks. Yakir Kadkoda, Lead Security Researcher from Aqua Security, predicts that in 2024 the cybersecurity landscape will experience a substantial change because of the strategic inclusion of AI by cyber attackers. For example, ‘Package Illusion’ strikes will likely be a notorious feature where AI will be applied to manipulate software dependency chains. This will unintentionally expose applications to provide unexpected or factually incorrect responses that do not align with its machine learning training data. This departs and conflicts with the normal and planned behaviour for an AI model, which should impart a reply based on the data it was trained upon.

Hence, Kadkoda argues that this tactic is expected to be part of a broader trend where AI is not just a tool for defence but also a weapon in the attacker’s arsenal. Thus, he asserts that by abusing the trust that software developers place in automated dependency management and suggestion systems, attackers can initiate a new class of supply chain vulnerabilities that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Such AI-driven incidents are anticipated to become a regular occurrence that will constrain the cybersecurity industry to actively transform itself to counter such threatening development. However, the cybersecurity industry cannot afford to be reactive but must take proactive and robust action against AI-powered threats by focusing on the creation of new standards and best practices that are supported by an environment of international alliance across industries.

The above concerns are also supported by [Allan (2023)](#ch19.xhtml#r062). She observes that cyber threats are emerging across the globe because advances in technology have enabled malicious players to exploit innovative methods that such state-of-the-art technology can provide. [Allan (2023)](#ch19.xhtml#r062) claims that ransomware due to its growing scope and complexity, alongside alliances with other threat actors through underground forums, remains a continuing hindrance for organisations worldwide. The growing sophistication and complexity level of these devious tools make it very difficult for current security tools to detect and identify them. [Allan (2023)](#ch19.xhtml#r062) endorses Kadkoda’s view that all industries need to embrace a cyber strategy that is constantly vigilant, actionably comprehensible, and adaptable to new threats.

The most serious threat that is likely to be posed by AI is through the creation of malicious large language models (LLMs). LLMs are a leading-edge natural language processing (NLP) that are designed to understand and generate human language. These advanced AI models are trained in massive amounts of text data, enabling them to recognise linguistic patterns, comprehend context, and produce coherent and contextually-relevant responses. LLMs embody a focused approach that has significantly enhanced the machine’s capability to mimic human-like language understanding and generation. Hence, LLMs can be applied for many beneficial purposes. However, they also have the potential to be exploited for malicious purposes, such as spreading misinformation, creating fake news, and conducting cyberattacks. Furthermore, organisations need to be extremely aware that cybercriminals are continually modifying their methods to exploit new weaknesses and capitalize on their gains. Therefore, organisations need to be responsive and keep abreast of these illicit developments to continuously safeguard their systems and data repository.

It must be recognised that the upsurge of AI has expedited matters for cybercriminals to instigate tactical strikes with less expertise and resources. [BlackBerry (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r064) analysing cybersecurity events from March to May 2023 focusing on critical infrastructure and large organisations found that threat actors deployed approximately 11.5 attacks per minute across all sectors, with the healthcare and financial sectors being the most targeted. It is noted that the healthcare and financial sectors are prime targets because of the critical and sensitive information held by these industries, such as bank account information, social security numbers, and personally identifiable information. Such information is viewed as having money-spinning potential for cybercriminals aimed at blackmail and identity theft. Additionally, threat actors will target healthcare facilities because they are fully aware that hospitals are unable to function offline for lengthy periods and will likely yield to ransom demands hastily to get back online. [BlackBerry (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r064) also found that attacks during the period under consideration were mainly through ransomware attacks that targeted local and state government systems.

[Kellerman (2022)](#ch19.xhtml#r071) itemised five trends regarding cybersecurity in the evolving cyber threat landscape, namely: ransomware is getting worse; AI is enhancing cybersecurity; mobile is the main target; data breaches and network intrusions; and increased social engineering attacks. Furthermore, he argues that cyber threat actors present a financial threat, mainly by stealing intellectual property and proprietary information, including personal information that enables further criminal deeds such as identity theft and financial fraud. [Kellerman (2022)](#ch19.xhtml#r071) maintains that ransomware is getting worse. The process with ransomware is to firstly appropriate the data, encrypt it and then demand a ransom. Moreover, he claims that AI is being implemented in all industries and is being merged with machine learning to bring about transformational changes to the cybersecurity landscape. AI is being used to develop applications to automatically detect threats. However, it is also being utilised to create smart malware and launch strikes to circumvent security protocols that manage data.

Kellerman’s research shows that cybersecurity trends suggest a significant increase in mobile banking malware and attacks. Hence, handheld devices are attracting cyber threat actors, since these devices apart from posing a financial threat through mobile banking applications, also contain personal data such as photos, messages, and transaction histories. This is likely to prompt a demand for anti-virus and malware software for smartphones. Additionally, Kellerman notes that data breaches and network intrusions remain a primary source of apprehension for organisations and individuals given the sensitivity of the data being held. Moreover, there are some cyber-attack practices that disguise intrusions such as multi-routing, covert scripts, protocol impersonation, and traffic flooding that increase the vulnerability of users.

Increased social engineering attacks are also on the increase with more sophisticated cyber-attack techniques being applied providing cybercriminals with further access to sensitive and confidential information. Some of these methods include phishing, spear phishing, fraudulent communications, and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. A DDoS attack is particularly devastating because the attacker literally floods a server with internet traffic to prevent users from accessing connected online services and sites. As for phishing emails, these pretend to be renowned services or organisations such as Amazon or Apple so that threat actors can collect login credentials. [Kellerman (2022)](#ch19.xhtml#r071) suggests that organisations assess whether they are adequately safeguarded against these threats and threat actors and recommends that they reflect on the following questions: Do you know who might be targeting you and why you could become a target? Is there anything specific to your organisation or operations that they may be after? Answering these questions in a formal and organised focus group discussion will likely help organisations to initiate a way forward to tackle this growing cybersecurity concerns.

[*Cyber Security* Magazine (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r065) notes that Aqua Nautilus an organisation focusing on cybersecurity research in the cloud native stack, captures more than 80,000 cloud native attacks every month, specifically those unique to containers and microservices that other platforms cannot see. Cloud-native stack describes the layers of cloud-native technologies that developers use to build, manage, and run cloud-native applications. The infrastructure layer that is managed by third-party cloud providers forms the basis of the cloud-native stack, which consists of the supporting components of cloud-native application development, including operating systems, storage, network and other computing resources. A growing concern is that as the cloud computing landscape continues to expand, the attacks within its perimeters are also being refined.

[Cyber Security Magazine (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r065) reports that there are early indications of state sponsored threat actors who have devised methods to execute code directly in user space memory without triggering a system call (i.e., execve and syscalls) that are usually scrutinised by security systems, consequently evading traditional detection mechanisms. A “syscall” is a programming method in which a computer program requests a service from the operating system on which it is executed, while a “execve” system call is used to execute a new program and transforms the calling process into a new process. Hence, these sophisticated approaches are striking at the heart of the system. [*Cyber Security* Magazine (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r065) predicts a significant shift in tactics from cloud attackers by exploiting userland execution methods that implement code that generally replicate what the execve system call does.

Hence, these new security evasion methods need to be countered by implementing nuanced behavioural security measures that include using AI and machine learning algorithms, which are able of recognise normal user behaviour and detect anomalies, along with improving memory scanning and process monitoring technologies. Such a proactive approach is critical for revealing and mitigate threats that circumvent conventional detection procedures to safeguard the ever-evolving cloud ecosystem. However, AI should also be viewed as a double-edged sword since (as stated previously) AI can be applied for the creation of malicious large language models (LLMs) that poses a complex and serious threat.

Another potential threat target area is the result of the proliferation of eBPF technology, which can execute programs in a privileged context such as the operating system kernel. eBPF is being used in areas related to networking, security, or observability, where conventional tools are unable to execute with adequate efficiency or detect events with sufficient granularity. Hence, this feature permits users to apply eBPF filters to specific sockets beyond just packet filtering. For instance, custom scripts can be called with minimal overhead at various points in the kernel. eBPF programs can be attached to various kernel hooks to gather data about what is taking place. This makes eBPF a very powerful tool that enables a whole new class of observability tools within the operational frameworks. However, eBPF is likely to attract the attention of threat actors as it gains broader acceptance across an assortment of industries and is implemented in a variety of tools. As an outcome of this development, [Cyber Security Magazine (2024)](#ch19.xhtml#r065) foresee a heightened prevalence of eBPF deployment assessments, evasion and disabling tactics. This will compel cyber security developers to take additional rigorous security measures and proactive threat mitigation strategies.

Combating cyber threat actors will continue to be a running battle. In fact, it is a lasting state of war with no clear conditions that would lead to its conclusion. However, the technology industry has a responsibility to their users to ensure that the cyber network and the associated systems and data are safeguarded from all types of potential threats. The industry must keep a step (or more) ahead of the threat actors. This can only be achieved with the collaboration of all stakeholders on an international level, roping in governments, technology providers and a broad range of industry.

## **7.3** Intrusion Prevention Systems (IPS)

An IPS is a security system that continuously monitors network traffic to identify threats and incorporates an intrusion detection prevention system (IDPS). Hence, an IPS system is more inclusive in the way it addresses potential security threats. An IPS is placed inline, in the flow of network traffic between the source and destination and usually sits just behind the firewall. [Figure 7.1](#ch19.xhtml#f25) shows the board design of a robust cyber security system regarding the location of an IPS in relation to the Firewall. [Figure 7.1](#ch19.xhtml#f25) illustrates that the IPS and the Firewall have different functions. The firewall is designed to prevent unauthorized access into or out of a computer network and to make sure internet users without access are not able to interface with private networks, or intranets, connected to the internet. On the other hand, the IPS examines network traffic and specifically spots threats and takes appropriate action to address the incoming threat.

![Figure 7.1 Board Design of a Robust Cyber Security System.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C007_001.jpg)

**Figure 7.1** Board Design of a Robust Cyber Security System.[⏎](#ch19.xhtml#f25b)

Hence, an IDPS monitors a network for threats and then takes the necessary action to stop any threats that are detected. Moreover, an IDPS is similar to an intrusion detection system (IDS) but while both systems detect threats and forward alerts about them, an IDPS also endeavours to provide a solution for those threats. An IDPS is synonymous with an IPS and the terms are frequently used interchangeably. However, when referring to IPS it is normally assumed that one is referring to the threat hunting function of an IDPS. Therefore, an IPS is viewed as a security system that continuously monitors network traffic to identify threats and incorporates an intrusion detection prevention system (IDPS). The functionality of an IDPS depends on the provider, the desired deployment method, and the explicit requirements of the organisation using it. Basically, there are two types of IDPS, namely network-based and host-based.

Network-based IDPS (NIPS) is a type of IDPS that is installed at specific points within a network to monitor all of that network’s traffic and scan for threats by analysing the activity taking place and matching each activity with a database of known attacks that is created manually by a security expert. Therefore, if an activity finds a match with a known threat in the database it is not permitted to carry on through the network. A NIPS is often implemented at the boundaries of networks, such as in routers or modems, behind firewalls, and at network remote access points. Furthermore, there are two categories of NIPS, namely wireless intrusion prevention systems (WIPS) and Network behaviour analysis (NBA).

An WIPS monitors wireless networks for the presence of rouge access points and unrecognized devices by examining the network’s radio frequencies and are implemented in wireless networks and in locations that are vulnerable to unauthorised wireless access. On the other hand, network behaviour analysis (NBA) systems assess network traffic for unusual patterns of activity such as a distributed denial of service attack (DDOS), where thousands of requests are sent to the network to overwhelm it. The individual requests themselves might look valid, but collectively they suggest a problem. NBA systems often support a NIPS of an organisation’s internal network.

A host-based IDPS (HIPS) are implemented on a single host such as a key server with critical data or public servers that are gateways to the organisation’s internal network. They can also be used on mobile devices. These types of systems monitor and analyse traffic flow on its host system to detect host operating system activity and internet protocol suite (TCP/IP) activity. HIPS have the specific objective of detecting and blocking malicious activities.

IDPS applies several approaches to detect threats, namely signature-based, anomaly-based, and protocol-based. Signature-based detection examines network traffic, compares it to known signatures on a database of signatures, and generates an alert when a match is made. This approach is effective for detecting well-known threats, but new or unusual threats are likely to avoid detection. Anomaly-based detection is used to identify both computer and network threats by training the system with a normalised baseline that depicts how the system normally works and should work. This approach is continually being improved by advancements in AI and machine learning algorithms. Basically, the approach compares a random selection of network activity with a baseline standard of network activity. If the random selection varies sufficiently from the baseline, then the threat triggers action. However, while this detection method reveals and apprehends novel threats, it also generates more false positives than signature-based threat detection. The protocol-based (or policy-based) threat detection approach is very similar to the signature-based method in that it uses a database of specific protocols defined manually by a security expert and blocks any activity that violates those protocols. When a perceived threat is detected, the system may take several alternative actions contingent on its set up and the nature of threat detected. The preventative actions include:

*   Alerting administrators when an automatic action might not be suitable, or when the system is uncertain if there is a false positive.
*   Employ banishment vigilance by barring incidents before they occur. This is achieved by blocking traffic or flagging users from a threatening IP address such as blocking an IP address that has failed a password check too many times.
*   Change the security environment. This approach modifies the security setup of the network to prevent the threat from gaining access such as reconfiguring a firewall.
*   Modify the attack content. This method entails automatically altering the content of the attack. For example, if a suspicious email is identified, the system would eliminate any facet that may have malicious content and pose a threat to the network, such as the email attachments.

An IDPS has the primary objective of revealing threats that might slip through by assessing system activity for potential threats and taking action without human intervention for the simpler threats. Complex threats are highlighted for human intercession to enable security teams to rapidly respond to these threats before they can cause harm. Additionally, an IDPS ensures that user and security procedures are continuously enforced and the rule-based feature guarantees that threat detection is applied in a consistent way. Furthermore, the outcome of having far less human intervention is that fewer individuals have an opportunity to interact with private data, which may be a regulatory requirement in various industries.

As stated in the beginning of this section, the IDPS features are a subset of an IPS. It should be noted that an IPS works as part of other security solutions (i.e., the firewall), and is able to identify threats that those other solutions cannot detect. This means that it provides a layer of additional security and offers superior protection due to a high level of application awareness. An IPS is placed directly in the flow of the network traffic between the source and destination (refer to [Figure 7.1](#ch19.xhtml#f25)). This is what differentiates an IPS from the traditional intrusion detection system (IDS). It should be noted that an IPS is proactive, while an IDS is a passive system that scans traffic and reports back on threats. Hence, an IPS usually sits directly behind the firewall and analyses all traffic flows that enter the network, acting automatically, when necessary, which saves a lot of time effort for the IT team. Additionally, an IPS sifts for malicious traffic before it can approach other security devices and controls, hence it mitigates the workload for those controls and permits them to function more efficiently. It is also noted that an IPS can be configured to reflect the organisation’s specific security policies making it a very robust and flexible security tool.

An IPS is critical for having a secure system because a multi-cloud network is a highly linked environment with numerous access points and high traffic volume and has an expanded attack surface making it highly vulnerable and exposed to greater threats. This means that manual monitoring with a quick response in this type of environment becomes impractical and unmanageable. [Table 7.1](#ch19.xhtml#t16) provides details of typical attacks that may be detected and prevented by an IPS. According to [Palo Alto Networks (2023b)](#ch19.xhtml#r073), an IPS must have several vital features that include the following:

*   IPS offers vulnerability protection by analysing and monitoring the attack lifecycle for breaches, infections, and ransomware.
*   Antimalware protection by having a stream-based scanning engine that identifies and detects known malware and its unknown varieties and barring them swiftly.
*   Broad command-and-control protection by blocking and preventing unknown C2 inline. A C2 channel serves as the communication link between the compromised device (bot) and the C2 server. This channel is essential for issuing commands, receiving instructions, and exfiltrating data. Hence, this IPS feature is extremely important because after an initial infection, cyber actors link with the host machine through a covert C2 channel, which is used to pull down additional malware, issue further instructions, and steal data. It is noted that these channels cannot be stopped with traditional signature-based approaches, therefore an IPS having this capability is critical.
*   IPS includes an automatic multi-factor authentication feature that requires additional credentials beyond a simple password before the end user can gain access to an application or system. Security operations teams are able to act swiftly, quarantine, and validate policy to control potential infections.
*   IPS allows incident response teams to immediately determine which systems are under attack and which users are potentially infected so that it is more efficient than guessing based on IP addresses. This greatly simplifies network security policy creation and management.
*   IPS can automatically assess threat intelligence to keep abreast of potential attacks.

**Table 7.1** Details of Attacks Detected and Prevented by IPS[⏎](#ch19.xhtml#t16b)

 
| **AttacksDetected and Prevented** || **Attack Details** |
| --- | --- |
| Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Spoofing || Re-directs traffic from a legitimate system to the attacker. Fake ARP messages sent by an attacker create a link between the attacker’s MAC address and IP address of an attacked system. |
| --- | --- |
| Buffer Overflow || Uses vulnerabilities in the buffer overflow to overwrite memory and corrupt the execution of an application. |
| Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) || Initiates a massive flood of traffic from distributed computers meant to overwhelm a system making it unavailable for legitimate requests. |
| IP Fragmentation || Exploits datagram fragmentation mechanisms confusing the targeted system about how to reassemble TCP/UDP datagrams. |
| Operating System (OS) Fingerprinting || Exploits vulnerabilities in the OS. |
| Ping of Death || Using a ping command, an attacker sends oversized or malformed packets that crash a system. |
| Port Scanning || Scans for an open, unprotected port to exploit. |
| Server Message Block (SMB) Probes || Captures SMB protocol authentication requests to relay them to the attacker’s host. |
| Smurf (a DDoS attack) || Using Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) packets to overwhelm a system. |
| Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Evasion || Exploits SSL and Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption that hides malicious content to avoid detection and get past network security. |
| SYN Flood || Considerable volume of SYN (synchronize) packets are sent as connection requests to overwhelm a server or firewall. |
