# IIIThe Practical Implications of Artificial Intelligence

There is no doubt that AI has the potential to provide great benefits for society in general and to humans in particular. To illustrate the impact of AI, [Part III](#ch20.xhtml#c10) commences with a detailed discussion of the knowledge-based economy. The concept of a knowledge-based economy is not new, but the latest developments in AI have elevated this concept to newer and greater dimensions. The foundation of a knowledge-based economy is information that is utilised for the innovative creation and delivery of services, which are focused on knowledge-intensive activities. These activities consequently have the impact of speeding up the evolution of technological and scientific development. This in turn means that there is a much greater dependence on intellectual capabilities then physical efforts or geographical resources. AI augments the intellectual capabilities of humans by its capacity to monitor and analyse the immense volume of data and information, and to learn from these for the development and benefit of nations, organisations, and humans. Therefore, by supplementing human intelligence, AI can propel the knowledge-based economy to greater and unprecedented levels.

Aligned with the concept of the knowledge-based economy is Enterprise AI that is revolutionising the way private businesses and many public sector entities operate. Enterprise AI involves the amalgamation of AI tools to create a complete tailored solution for the particular requirements of all types of organisations. It gives these organisations specific benefits related to customer relationship management, minimising operational expenditure, maximising revenue, and facilitating the formulation of operational strategies resulting in greater competitive advantage. However, like every other high-technology methodology, Enterprise AI needs to overcome several challenges associated with algorithm bias, better data security, and ensuring data privacy. Additionally, Enterprise AI is resource hungry and is likely to be only affordable and suitable for large organisations.

Whilst Enterprise AI is applicable to organisations that operate on a commercial basis, Public Sector AI is relevant for public administrations, whose priority is to provide their services to citizens, civil society, and the commercial sector. [Part III](#ch20.xhtml#c10) provides a dedicated chapter to explain and demonstrate Public Sector AI use cases that are applicable to diverse governmental backdrops. This chapter applies a particular framework for the implementation of AI systems in public administrations at every government level. Public Sector AI encounters major challenges in its deployment, namely, trustworthiness, transparency, public sector employee skills upscaling, and interoperability. Individual governments in deciding to implement Public Sector AI must assess how AI will impact economic growth, employment displacement, technology transfer, healthcare, education, and ethical behaviour.

The final chapter in [Part III](#ch20.xhtml#c10) is dedicated to ethical, moral, and legal considerations. There is consensus by governments and commercial organisations that AI must be trustworthy and developed and deployed in a safe manner. This implies that there is also a consensus that AI might be harmful. No one has specifically defined or identified the extent and impact of this harm to individuals and for national security. While most governments have endorsed voluntary ethical and moral frameworks, there is a reluctance by most governments to introduce binding legislative measures that specifically address AI. This reluctance appears to be based on the premise that specific laws might hinder AI innovation. Most governments have revised certain provisions in existing legislation to address specific AI legal issues. The EU has emerged as the global leader in AI regulation, while most other countries are adopting a wait-and-see attitude.

World events in Ukraine, Gaza, and particularly Lebanon (regarding the detonation of communication devices) raise concerns as to whether AI can be used as a weapon of mass destruction. Mass destruction not in the sense that AI can be used to physically destroy buildings or infrastructure, but whether it can be applied to obliterate the systems that most critical infrastructure depends on, including the destruction of life support systems that sustain the lives for hundreds of thousands (if not millions) of people. It should be kept in mind that world leaders (national government or corporate) will normally act in the interest of the wellbeing of their own nation or organisation, with ethical behaviour playing a secondary role. Therefore, there is an urgent need for each country to have in place strong and forceful legislation to govern the development and deployment of AI systems and ensure that it is safe and trustworthy. There is an even a greater need for an international binding treaty committing nations, as a unified body, to regulate and govern all types of AI systems on an international level, and to classify them by the magnitude of risk they pose and have a continuous monitoring mechanism for such AI systems.

# Chapter 8Knowledge-Based Economy and Artificial Intelligence

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-11](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-11)

> *“To know what you know and what you do not know, that is true knowledge.”*
> 
> Confucius (Kong Qiu)
> 
> *Chinese philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period (551-479 BCE)*

According to [Nguyen (2024)](#ch21.xhtml#r083), AI has the potential to revolutionise the way people work and live in the coming years. He argues that while AI may disrupt some industries, it also presents opportunities for growth and innovation. Hence, he maintains that as the changes brought about by AI are adopted, it becomes critical for all to continue to upskill and reskill to remain relevant in the knowledge economy. Additionally, those with an open mind for adapting and embracing AI will position themselves better for future success. Nguyen maintains that the question is not whether AI will disrupt the knowledge economy, but rather, whether entities are ready to harness its potential?

In support of this, [CNBC (2022)](#ch21.xhtml#r079) reports that the integration of AI helps firms with competitive data analysis helping them to stay ahead of their competitors. Their view is that from production to customer relationship management, AI plays a vital role in transforming an entity to an effective organisation. However, the question is to what type of transformation are they referring? There are those who maintain that society and industry are witnessing the end of the knowledge economy and are experiencing a shifting towards an automation-based economy.

There is no doubt that current global economies are governed by knowledge-driven roles. Economic sectors, such as healthcare, finance, gaming, law, technology, and many others owe their existence to the knowledge industry and are intensely dependent on proficient information management. It is in the sphere of information management that AI dominates and outrivals any other related technologies. However, there are fears that AI may pose a serious threat to human workers. On the other hand, current signs suggest that AI is a useful partner assisting human workers in performing their tasks more effectively and enhances their productivity and decision-making abilities. Whether these signs will materialise for the benefit of society and industry, only time will tell.

## **8.1** Introduction

The Covid-19 pandemic has illustrated that automation enabled much knowledge-based industries to survive and prosper. In the post Covid-19 era, recovery of economies in various countries was partly due to the knowledge economy. Many view a knowledge-based economy as being sturdier and better prepared to act in response to specific problems and economic challenges. There are indications to suggest that the Covid-19 pandemic hastened the use of automation in the day-to-day lives of both individuals and businesses. This is particularly the case for industries that were able to continue their operations and permitted their employees to work from home in a remote information technology (IT) environment.

Technology is viewed as having grown to the extent that it is difficult to differentiate it from businesses. The two have become synonymous, particularly for those industries that provide or are dependent on state-of-the-art, leading-edge solutions that are intended to fully automate tasks that encounter high cost due to their labour-intensive nature. Where does AI feature in this environment? Currently, AI is not viewed as replacing human reasoning. It is viewed as a tool to support business functions that may not be inclined to human intervention, such as automated cybersecurity where businesses can operate in a secure environment. However, this does not mean that this situation will not change in the future.

It must be recognised that information management has enabled the accumulation of data to be transformed to information, and the accumulation of information to be transformed to knowledge. Hence, the foundation for the emergence of knowledge-based economy. However, there is another transformation phase, namely transforming the accumulation of knowledge to wisdom. In the past and the immediate present this transformation of the accumulation of knowledge to wisdom has been mostly a human characteristic. In fact, in a knowledge-based economy the accumulation of knowledge is viewed as a primary asset for organisations to be used by its employees.

[Figure 8.1](#ch21.xhtml#f29) illustrates the phases in the data-to-wisdom transformation process. [Figure 8.1](#ch21.xhtml#f29) shows that the knowledge-based economy encompasses the data-to-knowledge transformation phase. The quicker that new knowledge is generated in combination with enhanced access to that knowledge, the better the organisation is prepared to combat and keep ahead to its competitors. Hence, knowledge becomes the primary resource leading to greater efficiency and competitiveness. This is the fundamental basis of a knowledge-based economy. [Figure 8.1](#ch21.xhtml#f29) demonstrates that a knowledge-based economy consists of several steps that include data collection; data classification; analysis and data integration to create information; generating a knowledge repository; and decision making.

![Figure 8.1 Phases in the Data-to-Wisdom Transformation Process.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C008_001.jpg)

**Figure 8.1** Phases in the Data-to-Wisdom Transformation Process.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f29b)

It should be noted, that under the traditional model the decision-making aspect is a human task. Additionally, [Figure 8.1](#ch21.xhtml#f29) illustrates that there is one further phase, which is wisdom that consists of two key functions, namely understanding and intelligence. However, humans are being overwhelmed with data and information through offline and online sources, and the rapid transformation of the information to knowledge is making it even more difficult for humans to make significant sense of all this input to make the appropriate decisions. Wisdom is normally associated with elder men and women who have accumulated much knowledge over many years to become wise and make better decisions. However, the modern world is generating so much knowledge from the accumulated information that the human brain cannot possibly cope and requires technological tools to do this. As AI’s sophistication develops and flourishes the transformation of the accumulation of knowledge to wisdom will likely be automated using AI supporting tools. Hence, it is foreseen that the outcome of this will be a shift from a knowledge-based economy to an automation-based economy soon, with AI having a critical role in this transformation.

An automation-based economy will utilise AI as a sophisticated tool to assist humans in the understanding of the vast amount of generated knowledge and transform it to wisdom, which is beyond human capacity. This integration of the knowledge base with AI capabilities will likely provide the means for organisations to keep ahead of their competitors. However, it should also be recognised that a technological advantage is short-lived because the competitive arena is not static, and technology is easily attained and implemented. The competitive race is a continuous one and a leader today can be a follower tomorrow (and vice-versa).

## **8.2** Knowledge-Based Economy

The knowledge-based economy, which is often referred to as knowledge economy is not a new concept. In fact, in 1967, Peter Drucker made first reference to the knowledge economy in his book “The Effective Executive” and later in 1969 had a chapter dedicated to knowledge economy in the book *The Age of Discontinuity* ([Drucker, 1967](#ch21.xhtml#r080); [Drucker, 1969](#ch21.xhtml#r081) [Chapter 12](#ch26.xhtml#c16), p247). Drucker in his publications emphasised knowledge, data analysis and measurable performance, and strategic management by objectives (MBO), which appear to have been too advanced to be truly appreciated during the time he proposed them.

[Powell and Kaisa (2004)](#ch21.xhtml#r085) define knowledge economy as the production and the provision of services based on knowledge-intensive activities that contribute to an accelerated pace of technological and scientific advance, as well as its equally rapid obsolescence. They contend that the key components of a knowledge economy include a greater reliance on intellectual capabilities rather than on physical inputs or natural resources, combined with efforts to integrate improvements in every stage of the production process, from the R&D laboratory to the factory floor, to the interface with customers.

[Figure 8.2](#ch21.xhtml#f30) shows the main attributes of a knowledge economy. It illustrates that generally there is a global diffusion of knowledge but there must be the appropriate institutional structures to provide the incentives for entrepreneurship and the application of knowledge, which encourage the development of industrial clusters in specific geographic regions. A core attribute is having the latest information and communications technology (ICT) infrastructure that encourages the exchange of knowledge between industries and innovation-driven users and producers. This would also promote an active innovation landscape that incorporates a wide range of stakeholders such as industrialists, academic institutions, and civil society. However, this holistic development needs to be supported by a good education system that generates the required skilled labour, which in turn increases the demand for STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) workers and a sharp growth in the quantity of patents.

![Figure 8.2 Main Attributes of a Knowledge-Based Economy.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C008_002.jpg)

**Figure 8.2** Main Attributes of a Knowledge-Based Economy.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f30b)

The knowledge economy places high importance on human capital as being not only critical but essential in the 21st-century economy. The tremendous growth of knowledge, the increasing dependence on information management and big data analytics are transforming the economy of the developed world to one that is more reliant on intellectual capital and skills, and less dependent on the production process. This changing environment views the knowledge economy as an economic approach that depends more profoundly on intellectual capabilities and not so much on physical inputs or natural resources. Hence, this economic method views big data analytics and automation as being a fundamental input to the production process.

The emergence of the knowledge economy has resulted in the growth in the generation of intangible assets such as patents, copyrights, or proprietary software or processes. This is in contrast with previous economic eras. For instance, the agrarian economy had land as the primary asset, and in the industrial economy the key assets were manufacturing plants and equipment. At the core of the current economic growth is the technology industry, particularly in the AI and robotics sectors.

Economic indicators suggest that when compared with other investment types, ICT investment is a major factor in productivity growth but only if it is combined with organisational changes. Reference to these organisational changes should be seen in the light that the knowledge economy is characterised by having a greater percentage of highly skilled employees whose jobs require special knowledge or skills that entail the analysis of data, creating and working with financial models, the ability to innovate and apply rational judgement. This implies that an important organisational change may include increased employee involvement in decision-making.

The main thrust for the knowledge economy is technological progress driven by persistent innovation and research. Hence, those that work within the knowledge economy are well qualified with high computer related competencies and capable at developing business and financial models. All these skills depend on having a reliable data repository through a comprehensive data collection and analysis process supported by the development of algorithms and AI applications. This implies that for organisations to survive with the possibility of keeping ahead of their competitors, they must renew themselves by the continual search for doing things differently through innovation and the development of improved business methods. This also implies having an endless collaborative cycle between academic institutions and industry that promotes research to ensure having a continual flow of discoveries from the innovation pipeline.

This knowledge-based environment, particularly the innovation pipeline has generated a huge demand for STEM jobs. STEM is an approach to learning and development that integrates the areas of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. These types of occupations, which are in high demand, are associated with high compensation packages and a rapid escalation of the organisational hierarchical career ladder. The above illustrates that knowledge is the dominant basis that is driving the high demand for technical expertise, data collection and analysis skills, and innovative management practices that is assisting organisations in the private and public sectors to compete in the contemporary global economy. On a macroeconomic level, those countries that have seriously embraced the knowledge economy have excelled in specific areas, such as computer technology in Silicon Valley in the United States, the electronics industry in South Korea, and the automotive engineering industries in Germany, amongst others.

ICT is focused on integrating communication services and information technology that has the primary aim of increasing the efficient application of information by connecting computer servers and data repositories, with the resultant transmission of information to fixed and mobile devices. This has resulted in the knowledge economy becoming heavily dependent on ICT developments. The knowledge economy has revolutionised several industrial sectors such as the use of robotics and just-in-time inventory management systems in the manufacturing of automobiles. This has made automobiles more affordable to a wider range of consumers and encouraged the current developments in driverless cars. The healthcare industry has benefited from the knowledge economy through more research and the creation of new medicines, a greater use of 3D and robotic surgical aids, and the expansion of telemedicine services.

[Figure 8.3](#ch21.xhtml#f31) shows the 2023 global knowledge economy index by country rankings for 133 countries (UNDP, 2023) compiled by United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The global knowledge economy index assesses whether the environment in a country is conducive to the creation of knowledge. The index ranking is assessed on seven aspects, namely pre-university education, technical and vocational education and training, higher education, research development and innovation, ICT, economy, and enabling environment. It is interesting to note that Malta, which is the smallest European Union member state ranks 18th, with its strength being pre-university education, ICT, and an enabling environment. However, its weaknesses are technical and vocational education and training, higher education, and research development and innovation. These weaknesses are also apparent for Singapore and for the Republic of Korea, who rank 12th and 17th respectively. The two small island states (Singapore and Malta) rank in the first top twenty countries out of 133. It is also important to recognise that with no exception, all countries have scored weakly in research development and innovation.

![Figure 8.3 Global Knowledge Economy Index by Country Rankings.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C008_003.jpg)

**Figure 8.3** Global Knowledge Economy Index by Country Rankings.[⏎](#ch21.xhtml#f31b)

The greatest challenge encountered by the knowledge economy is to continually strive to ensure that those who lack the requisite competencies to function and be optimally productive in a knowledge economy are trained to the appropriate level. This concern requires the collaboration of education institutions and the private sector for the development of suitable courses that address the knowledge economy needs, particularly those related to STEM jobs. Furthermore, the private sector needs to design and implement on-the-job training programmes and support employees in upgrading their skills and education by sponsoring them to attend education institutional courses. National governments can also facilitate matters by subsidizing industry through higher tax concessions to sponsor employees to attend specific formal training courses that address STEM careers.

## **8.3** Data-to-Wisdom Transformation Process

[Marchand, Kettinger and Rollins (2000)](#ch21.xhtml#r082) contend that many organisations are having difficulty understanding how to apply information to improve their performance. They argue that these organisations have placed greater emphasis on developing systems and processes to classify and store information rather than improving the way people apply this information. This situation is applicable to both the private and public sectors, where huge investments on ICT have been made. However, management is finding it extremely difficult to exploit the vast amount of collected and generated information and the associated analytical methods to increase organisational performance and keep ahead of their competitors.

[Charan (2005)](#ch21.xhtml#r078) argues that organisations are experiencing a profound transformation in that never has so much power been computerised and made available so broadly. He maintains that sophisticated software and complex algorithms, combined with new tools capable of collecting and storing vast amounts of data, can predict changing patterns in everything from consumer behaviour to the maintenance needs of machinery, thus becoming a critical source for improving performance and attaining a competitive advantage. [Parker (2016)](#ch21.xhtml#r084) cites an example where a hospital conducted traditional roistering of staff in terms of shift allocations instead of using optimisation analytical modelling techniques to test a wide range of alternatives. Thus, he maintains that this hospital missed an opportunity to make substantial savings through more analytical approaches. Information must be viewed as a corporate asset that needs to be comprehensively used and exploited in the decision-making process by applying various analytical tools that are available. It should be noted that the analytical power as applied to data is only limited by one’s imagination.

In above paragraphs the terms data and information have been loosely used. Hence, the first issue that needs to be addressed is whether there is a difference between data, information, knowledge, and wisdom. [Figure 8.1](#ch21.xhtml#f29) shows the process that takes place as data is transformed to information; information is transformed to knowledge; and knowledge is transformed to wisdom. This transformation process may be viewed as the foundation for AI applications, with the transformation process reaching the pinnacle in terms of wisdom. In other words, it is the accumulation of wisdom that generates intelligence.

### **8.3.1** Raw Data

Data is viewed as the basic raw facts that an organisation gathers in its day-to-day operations. However, an organisation is constantly being besieged with raw facts, which may or may not be relevant to the organisation’s needs. Hence, typically the collected data is sifted for relevancy to be accessed and utilised when needed. Data is the factual material utilised as a basis for discussion about what the facts reveal; deciding about a particular issue; and calculating or measuring a specific thing, such as the cost per litre of fuel.

Data may consist of operational data related to such things as revenue, expenditure, inventory, payroll, and accounting, amongst many others; non-operational data, such as macro-economic data, industry sales, and forecasts; and meta-data that consists of descriptive data about the data itself, such as logical database design or data dictionary definitions. Additionally, data is typically organised in a database and may take the form of numbers; words; observations or descriptions of things; pictures; and video and audio recordings.

Generally, there are two sources of data, namely internal and external. The internal data is generated by the organisation itself through its information systems and reflects its internal environment, such as the accounting transactions. External data is generated from sources outside the organisation and reflects the external environment, such as economic trends; commodity prices; and data provided by the National Statistics Office. External data is generated by the information systems of other organisations.

There are also different categories of data, with the most common type being quantitative, such as values and quantities. This type of data is typically utilised for computational purposes. Another type is classification data, such as passport number or component part number. Classification data is normally used for identification purposes, for instance to check whether a particular item is in stock. An important data type is reference data, such as an order number or cheque number. Reference data are used for control purposes, such as tracking an order or payment. The fourth data category is qualitative data, such as remarks and observations that is normally unformatted textual data used for documenting general remarks. The final two data categories are audio and video data. These are analysed by dedicated statistical and mathematical algorithms, applying AI tools. These AI tools use supervised and unsupervised learning for pattern recognition and image analysis for detecting abnormalities, such as terrorist exposure scenarios.

There are several ways that data may be collected that in some cases can be effortless, while in others it can be demanding. For example, data may be collected automatically by using meters or counters, such as palm readers for recording employee attendance or electricity meters for determining energy consumption or production counters for measuring output of manufactured components. Another method may be through direct data entry on a display screen when serving a client, such as entering the client details at a hospital registration desk. Another common method is direct observation by viewing certain general attributes of persons entering a particular shop, such as gender, and general age group. A popular approach of collecting data is conducting market surveys from a number of relevant respondents and asking pertinent questions about particular issues.

### **8.3.2** Information

As explained earlier, data are facts, numbers, text, pictures, video, and audio recordings that are stored in a digital format to allow them to be processed by a computing device, traditionally known as data processing. Information systems process the raw data to generate information. Basically, raw data is transformed into information, which is meaningful, significant and may have implications for the organisation. For example, consider a digital file of customers that may contain their purchasing habits and some personal details. This digital file may contain thousands of entries. However, by itself this data has no value. On the other hand, data may be transformed into information by analysing it by a specific geographic region or locality, typical types of purchases, gender, marital status, age groups, and so forth. This analysis (or transformation) may be needed to establish the typical profile of the customers in a particular locality and their spending habits. Hence, an entity may obtain a better appreciation of the information that is generated in terms of better decision making, such as product or service promotions.

Furthermore, for data and information to be of value to an organisation it must meet three basic criteria, namely: accurate, timely, and relevant. Therefore, a key objective of the data-information transformation process is to get the right information to the right person at the right time. Typically, information is data that is processed to be useful and provides answers to who, what, where and when questions. Additionally, information is generated by summarising and analysing the raw data through the examination of patterns and the relationships among data items. For example, an analysis of retail point of sale transactions can yield information on the products that are being sold, when they are being sold, and who is buying them (particularly if a loyalty card system is in place).

### **8.3.3** Knowledge

The next level of the data-information transformational process is knowledge. Knowledge is the conversion of information into historical patterns and future trends. To convert information to knowledge there is a need to synthesise (integrate) the data and information gathered from the various sources and decide how this knowledge is to be applied. For example, a national tax authority may compare the financial ratios of several companies within a specific industry over number of years to examine financial and income trends.

Knowledge may be viewed as comprising of two aspects, namely the explicit details and the comprehension of these explicit details. The explicit details are obtained from the application of the data and information to address “how” questions to provide an insight about the magnitude and attributes of some object. On the other hand, the comprehension of the explicit details is obtained through the analysis (i.e., why are we analysing these explicit details). For example, a manager of a public health facility may want to know which services are to be encouraged and supported by his/her facility. Hence, data and information regarding the use of the services offered are analysed to obtain the knowledge regarding the beneficiaries of the services being provided. In other words, the service recipient behaviour (how). This in turn will allow the manager to decide which health services should be supported and enhanced. Furthermore, this will assist the health facilities manager to select those services that are most responsive to any promotional effort that may be undertaken (objective or why). The above example illustrates that knowledge is the extensive exploitation of data and information, in combination with the ability, competencies, ideas, intuitions, commitments, and motivations of the manager involved. Hence, the transformation of data and information into knowledge is the outcome of the synergy that combines human aptitudes and the application of the available data and information.

There are various types of knowledge but the most common are tacit and explicit knowledge. Tacit or implicit knowledge is not easy to document since it is more idiosyncratic, it cannot be codified, it is applicable to a particular circumstance, and it is difficult to describe or explain to others. For example, learning a musical instrument takes talent and a lot of practice. Explicit knowledge can be learnt from the application of precise rules and can be codified. For example, take an activity like baking a cake. If a person precisely follows the recipe and baking instructions, the outcome should always be consistent. Therefore, gaining and documenting explicit knowledge is not a concern. The concern is the gaining and transferring of tacit knowledge (as distinct from explicit knowledge), which is a complex matter and can be gained through extensive experience, socialisation, mentorships, and face-to-face communication. It is in this sphere that AI tools can be made useful. However, there is a long road ahead for all issues to be resolved.

### **8.3.4** Wisdom

The accumulation of a great amount of knowledge is wisdom. Through knowledge, an entity learns how to act in its own best interests. Wisdom takes a step further, it reenforces and reveals the principles and standards that an entity applies to its knowledge. Wisdom is the ability to make the right judgments and decisions, and hence transforms data, information, and knowledge into intelligence. Wisdom is gained through extensive experience and when documented forms the basis for supervised learning in AI applications. Therefore, as more experience is attained and documented, the higher level of intelligence that is created. This is not easy to achieve or sustain because to be wise implies a great deal of knowledge and experience that must continually be updated, maintained, and sustained.

With wisdom it is not a matter of grasping the past and present but to be able to define the future. However, it must be recognised that wisdom is the apex, thus it is not easy to achieve since one needs to move successively through the other transformation phases before it may be finally gained. In addition, once wisdom is gained it must be sustained with further knowledge; hence it takes an on-going demanding effort. It is precisely in this area that AI through unsupervised learning may facilitate the information-wisdom transformation process.

## **8.4** The Evolving Knowledge-Based Economy Landscape

According to [Brown (2023)](#ch21.xhtml#r076), the knowledge economy is a concept where the knowledge contained within an entity or an individual drives it, rather than its actual physical output. He argues that this concept differs from the agrarian, manufacturing, and service economies in that knowledge-intensive products become the output, not a physical provision. Typically, knowledge economies have highly skilled and specialised workforces and large institutions in the form of enterprises and centres of learning that capitalise on the generated knowledge. Researchers and other experts are questioning whether AI is threatening this environment. The evolution of the various economic models over the decades is viewed as part of contemporary economic development. The issue is: What is the next economic evolutionary stage considering the tremendous advancements of AI?

Often, knowledge is viewed as something that is normally possessed by humans. One is paid to write a drama for a TV series with creative ideas to keep viewers entertained. Others may prepare marketing campaigns with enticing advertisements that are highly creative to convince a consumer to purchase a product or service. Additionally, most of an entity’s systems are administered under human control. Hence, most of an organisation’s processes are based upon human knowhow with the aid of computer systems as a highly sophisticated tool. It is also a fact that computer systems transform data into knowledge after appropriate analysis, particularly displaying trends. However, the knowledge created by computer systems is deciphered and retained in the human brain, where it is recalled when making decisions or explaining and illustrating matters to others. Moreover, a human accumulates knowledge and becomes wise by using this knowledge, experience, and cognitive intuition.

However, people’s knowledge is stored within an individual who may share his/her knowledge with others. The human absorption of knowledge becomes wisdom; however, humans are limited by how much knowledge an individual can absorb. An individual can become an expert on a particular subject, but it is impossible for an individual to be an expert in all subjects. Furthermore, due to the internet and the exponential rate of discoveries (human or otherwise), everyone is being inundated with more information than any other period in human history and this trend will continue.

The evolving knowledge-based economy landscape must be seen from this context. Will AI replace the human component? The answer is likely to be “no.” However, in life there is no such thing as a definitive “yes” or “no.” One must realise that there are shades of grey. Therefore, the question should be: To what extent will AI replace the human component? Currently, AI has its limitations. Humans can analyse information heuristically. In other words, a heuristic approach of learning entails discovery and problem-solving, using reasoning and experience. This is basically the meaning of wisdom, which is the ability to use knowledge and experience to make good decisions and judgments. Hence, wisdom is the combination of experience, knowledge, and careful judgment.

On the other hand, a heuristic computer program uses rules based on previous experience to solve a problem, rather than using a mathematical procedure. Currently (and the emphasis is on currently), AI has not reached this level of advancement for humans to fully trust its decisions. This is not to say that there are no AI applications that can do this but not in a general context. However, AI is making rapid advancement with deep learning algorithms that aim to resolve complex tasks for use in a variety of fields, including manufacturing, health care, aerospace engineering, technology, and automotive design. Whether AI will reach a level that can be trusted with all different type of circumstances, only time will tell, but the trend is in that direction.

According to [Brown (2023)](#ch21.xhtml#r076), Amazon discontinued using its AI recruitment tool when it became apparent that the original data it used in its AI-machine learning model was defective from the outset. Brown explains that the reason for this defect was because the model had identified male dominance as being preferred (since this was how Amazon had recruited in the past), and it therefore downgraded certain phrases with the word “women” even though the model had been instructed not to focus on gender. However, this does not mean that such issues will not be resolved in the future where great advancements are being made in supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms.

Having said this, the problem with AI becomes precarious if humans place their full faith in the AI systems and blindly let the AI systems take the decisions for them automatically. It becomes even more dangerous if there is a loss of control of the AI applications by their human creators. [Brown (2023)](#ch21.xhtml#r076) argues that even in the military, where split-second decision-making is required, commanders are hesitant to use automation to make decisions even faster. He maintains that the reports of humans being removed from the decision-making process, pushed the UN to propose a ban on AI-led decision-making in battle. However, he claims that this proposal failed due to pressure from several superpower countries. Furthermore, on 21 March 2024, the United Nations General Assembly unanimously adopted the first global resolution on AI that encourages countries to safeguard human rights, protect personal data, and monitor AI for risks.

[Brown (2023)](#ch21.xhtml#r076) argues that currently, AI can only churn out existing ideas that it finds and consequently, does not create new content, such as quotes or new theories and ideas. He also contends that AI, which works more autonomously, such as AutoGPT, can handle less structured questions to deliver results but at times the source of its information is not evident or how it arrived at its conclusions. He argues that this can create difficulties for those who require accountability in their fields such as financial investment decisions or healthcare decisions, particularly when things go wrong. There have been many failures in the use of AI and there are many concerns, but this does not mean that an investigation into the root cause of the various problems will not shed light on how these failures and similar ones may be prevented and resolved.

The core issue is what the impact on the knowledge economy concept will be when (not if) the various AI difficulties are resolved over the coming years. In other words, is the economic world on the verge of the next evolutionary step and if in the affirmative what will the next evolutionary economic concept be? [Brown (2023)](#ch21.xhtml#r076) suggests that we may be on the verge of witnessing the destruction of the knowledge economy because there is the threat that as AI becomes more entrenched in our daily lives, there will be a focus not on people’s knowledge but on the capabilities and utilisation of AI tools.

The knowledge economy will likely be gradually dismantled as knowledge bases (simple and complex) are replaced by safe and sophisticated algorithms that are able to learn, retain and recall knowledge on various matters, and in time will also make decisions and judgements. For example, generative AI (when safe and all issues resolved) will replace the human writer to produce material to one’s specific theme and requirements, with human creativity taking a back seat and gradually fizzle out over time. We already have robots that serve at restaurants, admittedly not very advanced yet but they are bound to improve. In time, General-AI (or Strong-AI) that is designed to perform intellectual tasks that a human can perform by learning, reasoning, and understanding complex concepts will likely take over various human tasks that depend on human knowledge and wisdom. AI will continue to evolve to Super-AI that will have the ability of exceeding human intelligence in all areas. When available, Super-AI would be able to solve complex problems that are beyond human abilities and would be able to learn and adapt at a rate that far exceeds human intelligence.

The most popular type of AIs is Reactive Machines, which are the simplest form of AI systems that perform basic operations by reacting to some input with some output, without any learning occurring. Another type of AIs that are currently available is Limited Theory machines that are able to store historical data and/or predictions for making better predictions. This type of machine learning architecture is more complex. Experimentation is currently being actively conducted with Theory of Mind machines that are designed to interact with the thoughts and emotions of humans. Self-driving cars are the simpler form of Theory of Mind machines, but they still have many issues to overcome before they can be generally used safely. However, the long-term objective in the AI evolution cycle are Self-awareness machines that are aimed towards achieving enlightenment and becoming self-aware, which has independent intelligence, and will not be under the control of the people that created it. This would likely be the final death nail for the knowledge economy concept as we know it today.

A knowledge economy is an economy in which the production of goods and services is based primarily upon knowledge-intensive activities that trigger a large portion of economic growth and employment. In other words, a knowledge economy is where knowledge and expertise are the key drivers for generating economic activity and wealth where the emphasis is on education, creativity, and finding ways of how to use knowledge for economic advancement. Nevertheless, the extensive application of AI systems is likely to generate a new economic concept where economic growth and employment would be the outcome of intense automation. However, this is only likely to happen if much more powerful and speedier computer processors are developed such as quantum and/or neuromorphic technology. Therefore, for the immediate present the knowledge economy concept appears to be safe, but the writing may be on the wall.

## **8.5** The Decline or Resurgence of the Knowledge Economy

It must be recognised that the huge growth is AI is impacting the knowledge economy, and a significant transition process is currently underway. It must also be recognised that the information technology (IT) transition process has been continuous for at least seven decades, moving from data processing to assisting in decision-making, and now to AI. Each stage in the transition process has resulted in the automation of many operations that formerly required human knowledge. This also resulted in the loss of thousands of jobs being taken over by computer systems. However, this IT transition process over the years has also created thousands of jobs that gave birth to the knowledge economy. The question that must be asked is whether the growth of AI will continue to support the knowledge economy or will it contribute to its death and the birth of a new economic order.

The IT developments over the years have been revolutionary but these developments have also been entirely dependent on human thinking and knowledge, which is after all the basis of the knowledge economy. However, the development of AI is turning towards imitating humans that include being creative, having emotional intelligence, and trained in relationship-building. Furthermore, this development is only the commencement of a new generation of AI developments. On the other hand, some practitioners argue that AI is immediately accessible to the knowledge economy since very little technical acumen is needed and the user does not have to build anything. They maintain that an individual can start using AI tools without detailed training with the barriers to entry being very low and the speed of adoption being very high. However, as mentioned previously, General-AI and Super-AI that are designed to perform intellectual tasks that humans can perform and have the ability of exceeding human intelligence in all areas may mean the near total replacement for the need of human knowledge in performing tasks.

Nevertheless, the evolutionary changes in the IT industry have progressively resulted in opportunities and the creation of high-quality jobs. Generally, these opportunities have far exceeded the adverse impact of IT developments in terms of job losses. The developments in AI will likely have the same positive effects with new opportunities being created. This does not mean that individuals will not be adversely impacted, particularly the older persons who are caught unprepared and may find it difficult to adjust. This has always been the case with any economic development. There is no doubt that it will be very challenging (and even painful) for certain groups and class of individuals and organisations to adjust to the evolving labour and consumer markets, where different skills and techniques will be needed. However, these challenges may be mitigated by government economic and fiscal policies and by educational institutions keeping a step ahead of the required industrial trends.

Whether AI or just general computerisation, it is a fact that computers can do things faster and more efficiently than humans. However, currently, it is only humans that have the unique capacity for wisdom and emotional intelligence, which make humans so important and unique. Whether these human qualities will remain unique to humans is a concern. This is why the legal and ethical implications of AI are such important issues, which will be addressed in a separate chapter at a later stage. There are those that are predicting a shift from knowledge-based to a wisdom-based economy, while others are visualising a shift towards autonomy-based economy. Whatever the trend, for individuals to remain relevant in the era of AI they must develop an assortment of skills and behaviours through a dynamic self-improvement programme.

Consequently, there is the positive scenario that AI will actually boost the knowledge economy and not its demise. AI is viewed as providing the potential for profoundly transforming the knowledge economy, which is generally characterised by the creation and exploitation of knowledge for economic and social development. AI has the capacity to analyse huge volume of data and attain significant insights, thus transforming different characteristics of the knowledge economy related to business, innovation, research, and education.

Enterprise AI is changing how entities operate and compete using AI driven analytical tools that can assess consumer trends (at organisational and individual level), customer behaviour, and competitor strategies. This facilitates management to make robust and informed decisions to keep ahead of their competition. Enterprise AI will also strengthen the general computerisation effort by further automating routine tasks that release valuable human resources that can focus on more important activities. AI also assists in the innovation process and is having a considerable impact in the knowledge economy by identifying new marketing opportunities, forecasting consumer trends, and helping in the development of new products and services. This is helping certain enterprises to combat competition. AI is also aiding the research process by having algorithms that can analyse patents and research papers through the identification of information patterns and trends, and providing meaningful insights that are not easily visualised by human researchers. This is helping researchers to reveal new detections and breakthroughs.

AI tools are assisting students having personalised learning experiences through intelligent tutoring that give immediate feedback and support that significantly improve the learning process. Consequently, AI is enhancing current non-AI tools and strengthening the knowledge economy. It is argued that as AI continues to grow and evolve, its impact on the knowledge economy is also predicted to escalate, revealing new opportunities for economic and social development.

The above examples support the contention that AI is likely to rejuvenate the knowledge economy by its ability to help organisations speed up their current strategy formulation process. There is no doubt that AI can analyse huge quantities of historical data from internal and external sources to speedily identify trends and patterns that human analysts might overlook. Hence, AI is a great improvement on the traditional computer systems that are more dependent on human interventions in terms of assessment. The emphasis is on the fact that under traditional computer systems human analysts are likely to overlook certain aspects that AI systems can identify. It is by this process that AI based systems facilitate enterprises to make better informed decisions based on instantaneous data to provide them with a significant advantage over competitors who may still depend on traditional computer systems.

However, one needs to recognise that such advantage is short-term because the competition is likely to adopt the same tools at some time. Hence, one cannot be complacent but always persist in striving to keep ahead by implementing the latest available AI tools. Obviously, this depends on whether an enterprise adopts a strategy where they see themselves as leaders rather than followers. However, there are enterprises that are content on being followers and adopt a wait and see strategy, but these enterprises will likely lose out in the long-term and risk their capacity to survive. Therefore, AI through its ability of analysing the competitors’ strategies and tactics, as well as evaluating the workings of the business environment, can assist management to identify potential threats and opportunities, and turn their own weaknesses to strengths, thus helping them to modify their strategies accordingly.

## **8.6** AI in the Knowledge Economy Industry

The previous sections have shown how AI is impacting the knowledge industry, with future developments determining whether the knowledge economy will decline or flourish further. AI has been shown to automate everyday tasks and enhance the decision-making processes with an improved overall effectiveness. AI has been shown to be extremely useful in environments where strategic decisions are required, irrespective of the industry type such as financial services and manufacturing in both the private and public sectors. AI supports knowledge workers by enabling them to focus on the more intellectually challenging and creative tasks that add value to the organisations.

The learning capabilities of AI results in the continuous enhancement of workflows and processes, by forecasting outcomes that make use of vast volumes of historical data. Furthermore, the organisation’s ability to comprehend information through AI applications enable them to predict market and consumer trends. Chatbots and virtual assistants that are driven by sophisticated AI tools resolve customer concerns quickly by providing personalised recommendations that enhance customer experiences without any human intervention. In the immediate future, AI will become an important and essential factor for the knowledge industry. Whereas, traditional computer systems are important for streamlining the organisation’s processes, AI goes beyond this role by creating new opportunities for innovation and efficiency. AI is ensuring that managers can be more proactive and effective in their decision making.

The concern with AI is likely to be a long-term scenario when AI is expected to become more intelligent than humans and act in its own accord independently from those that created it. The word long-term in this context is, shall we say, 50 years down the human timeline. However, many see AI as a current threat despite the clear benefits it has provided in the past decade. The main concerns are related to employment and ethical issues. However, these types of concerns were also expressed with the traditional computer systems of the early 1960s.

It is argued that AI would displace human workers, particularly those jobs that involve data processing and routine administrative tasks. One needs to recognise that routine administrative tasks were the first to be adversely affected in the 1960s when banks, insurance, and other financial institutions began to computerise their operations. The situation became worst with the onset of personal computers and multi-user systems that became affordable for the smaller organisations and replaced many clerical workers. Robots were also first applied commercially on assembly lines in the early 1960s that were primarily used for heavy lifting. Around the same time, the General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey implemented robots in 1961 for spot welding.

The same may be said for the data processing industry. At first, there were the punch card processing systems that consisted of a punch, sorter, tabulator and other additional machines such as reproducing punches, collators, and sequence calculators, which were used by governmental and non-governmental organisations such as insurance companies and large businesses. The focus was no longer on statistical surveys but on account transactions, payroll accounting, inventory management, and billing. From the 1950s, punched card systems also found their way into medium-sized enterprises. These replaced many clerical workers but also created higher skilled jobs in mechanical and electrical engineering, for technicians, operators, and key punch operators. The same was repeated when personal computers with word processors came on the scene replacing the typing and data entry pools.

I remember the time when a car driver would drive into a service station for petrol, and while the fuel tank is being filled an attendant would clean the windscreen, check the oil, battery, and air pressure in the tyres. In time, these were replaced by self-service petrol stations where you filled the fuel tank, the computer kept a record of the amount and value taken and the driver went to pay the cashier. Later still, the cashier was replaced, and all transactions were paid by electronically. As society advances the means to service the society also changes and advances using automated systems. Old jobs are lost and new jobs that require a higher level of skill are created. This story has been repeated over and over as economic progress is being made, hence, the creation of the knowledge economy. It is a fact that economic progress has generated many more jobs than the number of jobs that were lost through technological progress. Consequently, the arguments against technological progress including AI systems are not new.

There is genuine concern about the decision-making power being possibly delegated to algorithms. There are reservations that algorithms might not fully understand or respect the nuanced ethical and social implications of their outputs. However, one needs to remember that jet liners have been outfitted with an autopilot mechanism that enable a plane fly and land without the assistance of the human pilot. This feature has been available for several decades without much concern. Currently, drones can fly pilotless. Therefore, there is a need to distinguish between applications and closely examine the issues to decide whether there is a real cause for concern. There are those that argue that these fears are not unfounded. Currently, AI is primarily used to complement human capabilities, not replace them. It must be realised that AI tools currently analyse data and identify trends, but human experts are still required to interpret these findings within the context of existing political and social landscapes. Note that the word “currently” is important in the sentences above. This is the reason why I had stated that the concern with AI is likely to be a long-term scenario (50 years down the human timeline) when AI is expected to become more intelligent than humans and act in its own accord independently from those that created it.

Moreover, it must also be recognised that society’s behavioural habits are also changing. People want more leisure time to spend and enjoy their families and participate in more recreational activities. This implies shorter working hours or fewer working days per week. This can only be achieved by having greater automation, even to the extent of trusting certain algorithms to take decisions on behalf of humans. However, there is a need for the integration of AI into the workplace that include checks and balances to ensure safe and ethical AI usage, such as transparent methodologies; accountability for decisions made by AIs or with its assistance; and constant monitoring to ensure equitable and unbiased outcomes. AI and non-AI applications need to be extensively tested. For instance, the CrowdStrike security update failure of 19th July 2024 for Windows based PCs, caused a massive global IT outage that immobilised airlines, hospitals, media, and banks around the globe. Security precautions must be taken on a continuous basis not just for cyberattacks but also for the safe installation of legitimate software activities and updates.

Furthermore, there is an urgent need for comprehensive policies and guidelines to regulate the use of AI applications to ensure that it supports employees and not destabilises them. The previous chapter illustrated that some work has already been done on this issue but more needs to be achieved with international collaboration of all stakeholders. Additionally, it is essential that action is taken to mitigate the perceived fears of AI development by educating and making employees aware of the potential AI’s role in improving the economic activity; promoting a culture of collaboration between human intelligence and AI; and highlighting the social benefits of AI regarding the potential increase in leisure time to increase the quality of one’s life.

AI has transformed the content creation field with generative AI tools that automatically generate reports, presentations, and other materials. Although there are still some issues to be resolved, AI makes it easier to emphasise potential policy impacts and critical points of interest for the relevant stakeholders. AI has been successfully applied in several knowledge management areas. For instance, AI using natural language processing (NLP) tools can quickly and efficiently process and analyse considerable amounts of information containing text data. This has proved to be useful in public policy and government relations field for analysing legislative documents, public feedback, and policy guidelines to assist relevant stakeholders to remain informed about legislative changes and public opinions. AI has also facilitated the complex issue of knowledge management by simplifying the data integration and retrieval processes because it can organise, tag, and classify considerable amounts of data, facilitating information accessibility to team members throughout the organisation. This centralised approach mitigates the risk of creating data silos, thus reducing information retrieval time and more efficient search facilities.

## **8.7** Conclusion

This chapter examined the knowledge economy and its relationship with AI. The chapter illustrated that the knowledge economy is based on a concept where knowledge rather than physical output is the determining factor. Hence, knowledge-intensive products become the output, not a physical provision. The concern expressed by several researchers is whether AI is threatening the knowledge economy environment.

The argument of whether technology will result in the replacement of humans has been ongoing for many years before the AI came on the scene. The spread of computerisation in the 1960s was seen as a threat to people’s jobs. Admittedly, many manual clerical jobs were lost but many more jobs that required higher skills and better pay were generated. This era was the birth of the knowledge economy. The chapter illustrates that AI will likely have the same impact. Certain functions that require human intervention will be replaced by AI technology, but many more jobs are likely to be created that require a higher skill set and probably better renumeration. However, such developments require comprehensive government economic and fiscal policies that support the shift to AI and the updating of the educational programmes by institutions of learning to ensure that the younger generation are equipped to face the technology challenges of the future. Concurrently, organisations have the obligation to launch their own training programmes to upgrade the skills of their current workforce.

AI is viewed as boosting the knowledge economy and not destroy it because AI has the capacity to analyse huge volume of data and attain significant insights, thus transforming different characteristics of the knowledge economy related to business, innovation, research, and education. Several examples were provided illustrating how AI complemented the knowledge economy. Hence, it is likely that AI will revitalise the knowledge economy by its ability to assist management to speed up their current strategy formulation process. Additionally, AI because of its ability to analyse the competitors’ strategies and tactics can help management to identify potential threats and opportunities thus helping them to modify their strategies accordingly. One must also recognise that society is changing, where people want more leisure time to spend with their families and enjoy longer recreational activities implying shorter working hours. This can only be possible by having greater automation that include checks and balances to ensure safe and ethical AI usage.
