# Chapter 9Enterprise AI

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-12](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-12)

> *“The man with a new idea is a crank until the idea succeeds.”*
> 
> Mark Twain
> 
> *Author (1835-1910)*

AI is a field of computer science that looks at ways of training machines to learn, reason, and make decisions. In previous chapters it has been shown that AI has been around for many decades, going through various development cycles that at times have not been very successful. There were times when AI was abandoned by the industry as investment was withdrawn due to very disappointing results. However, research centres at various universities kept up the development momentum despite the lack of adequate finding. The outcome of this perseverance is the success that industry is currently witnessing.

AI and Enterprise AI are associated concepts but differ in their scope and function. AI is more concerned with the use of algorithms and computer programs to conduct tasks that characteristically require human intelligence. On the other hand, Enterprise AI refers to the concept of using AI in an organisational setting and encompasses many different technologies, including rules engines and machine learning, amongst others. Enterprise AI is the application of AI technologies to specifically address business problems and enhance business processes. It achieves this by integrating AI into enterprise systems and workflows using AI tools to automate and augment business processes, enhance customer experiences, and act as the key thrust for business outcomes.

This chapter will illustrate how Enterprise AI facilitates businesses to transform their operations by streamlining workflows and decision-making. This is achieved by automating everyday tasks and providing personalised customer services to bring together significant data insights. The role of AI is to dramatically increase the capabilities and effectiveness of enterprise software.

## **9.1** Introduction

Generally, Enterprise AI refers to the application of AI technologies in business applications to improve organisational processes and decision-making. In other words, Enterprise AI exploits advanced AI systems that include machine learning as the main approach for digital transformation. A key difference between Enterprise AI and AI is their particular focus. Enterprise AI focuses on resolving extensive high-value application situations by utilising and integrating AI tools into the organisation’s business processes to generate significant value.

Organisations that implement Enterprise AI have the potential of achieving step function improvements in business processes all the way through their value chain, resulting in enhanced business flexibility, higher efficiency, greater profitability, and lessened environmental impact. Achieving step function improvements speeds up the intended business direction by reconfiguring workflow, changing some parts and/or implementing new abilities.

The development of enterprise AI applications is due to recent advanced innovations in AI, in particular machine learning, together with the facilities provided by elastic cloud computing, big data, and the internet of things. Of significance is elastic cloud computing since it provides the ability to quickly enlarge or reduce computer processing, memory, and storage resources to meet changing demands without having to be concerned about capacity for peak usage.

Large organisations are likely to develop and implement many Enterprise AI applications to resolve a variety of concerns across their business. However, developing and implementing Enterprise AI applications at scale necessitates considerably greater challenges than earlier generations of enterprise software, requiring a new technology stack. Technology stack refers to a combination of programming languages, frameworks, libraries, tools, and technologies that are utilised to create and implement software applications. [Figure 9.1](#ch22.xhtml#f32) illustrates a typical technology stack for AI applications, which shows the various combination of technologies that are utilised in developing Enterprise AI. The technology stack generally involves front-end technologies that control the user interface with the system and the back-end technologies that consist of a suite of tools, languages, and frameworks, which are necessary for building the server side of the application.

![Figure 9.1 Typical Technology Stack for AI Applications.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C009_001.jpg)

**Figure 9.1** Typical Technology Stack for AI Applications.[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#f32b)

Enterprise AI leverages the general AI features, machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), and predictive analytics as the major thrust to achieve business goals and decisions in industries such as manufacturing, finance, marketing, ICT, and the public sector. The application of AI related to the public sector will be treated in a separate chapter. Our focus in this chapter is the private sector. Furthermore, the following sections will provide a more detailed description of Enterprise AI and how it may be implemented to benefit organisations.

## **9.2** AI in Business Enterprise

There is no doubt that the application of AI in the enterprise sphere is fundamentally changing the way a business functions. Businesses are integrating AI technologies into their business operations with the objective of increasing efficiency and reducing costs, creating new markets, and generating insights regarding industry market trends. The implementation of Enterprise AI applications has resulted in enhanced customer experience, optimised supply chains, improved sales, improved existing products and services, helped to create new products and services, and refined cybersecurity. It has also released employees from performing routine non-value-added tasks. This is not to say that the entities implementing these Enterprise AI applications have not encountered significant challenges.

AI is a dynamic field that is constantly changing due to greater AI research taking place on a global level, which is being supported by governments, large corporations, and education research institutions. Furthermore, AI is being applied to resolve a variety of problems that are being encountered by entities. For instance, AI-enabled hardware and software robotics are predicted to grow as business entities endeavour to become more flexible to meet the global economic challenges. Hence, business leaders need to appreciate how AI works and where AI technologies can be feasibly and reliably applied in their respective business segments.

It is a known fact that many tasks conducted within an enterprise require a specific measure of intelligence that require human intervention, hence they are not automatic. However, intelligence is viewed as the ability to acquire knowledge and applying it to achieve an outcome related to specific circumstances. Hence, AI entails programming a machine to function in this manner and is capable of rationally solving complex problems. Essentially, AI programming focuses on three cognitive skills, namely:

*   Learning: This aspect aims at attaining data and generating rules regarding the conversion of data into actionable information. The rules define the processing instructions required to complete a specific task.
*   Reasoning: This concerns the AI’s capability of selecting the most suitable rule (algorithm), from among a set of rules, to apply in a specific circumstance.
*   Self-correction: This aspect focuses on the AI’s capacity to increasingly fine-tune and enhance a result until it attains the desired goal.

On the other hand, Enterprise AI is somewhat different from merely AI. Enterprise AI focuses on the integration of advanced AI-enabled technologies and techniques within large organisations to improve business functions. Moreover, it incorporates routine tasks such as data collection and analysis that involve more complex operations such as automation, customer service, and risk management. Hence, the essence of Enterprise AI is characterised by AI software tools that leverage leading-edge systems, including machine learning, NLP, and computer vision. These AI tools enable entities to attain process automation in diverse tasks, streamline complex business functions, automate repetitive tasks, and exploit the accumulated data and information. Additionally, entities can acquire significant insights about key performance indicators (KPIs) and improve their business strategies by applying AI to analyse the accumulated data set. However, to attain such benefits, organisations need to make significant investment in the technology infrastructure and skilled employees.

This illustrates that Enterprise AI applies AI tools to deal with business challenges within the internal environment of an organisation. The AI tools range from the use of machine learning, deep learning, NLP, and other available AI methods to automate processes, enhance decision-making capabilities, and conceive new products and services. The integration and application of these various AI tools goes beyond merely automation because their goal is to solve complex business concerns that entail human-like intelligence. These AI tools are utilised to provide insights about customer behaviour, detecting fraud, and improving logistics, amongst many others. Enterprise AI harnesses the organisation’s data repository by applying advanced algorithms that optimise its operations, can discern market insights, and push innovation across the organisation crossing divisional boundaries and departmental functionalities.

## **9.3** The Importance of Enterprise AI

Enterprise AI is well known for its capacity to undertake and unravel complex organisational problems that traditional computer system could not undertake. Even though mathematical models existed under the traditional methods, however these models were not very effective in their ability to accurately forecast and deal with the complexities of global supply chains. Through the integration of various AI tools, Enterprise AI can exploit these mathematical and statistical models to predict with high accuracy future market trends, optimise logistics and inventory levels, and forecast disruptions. Enterprise AI is currently being successfully used for innovative applications regarding financial fraud, healthcare, and making the most effective use of energy resources, amongst many others across various industries.

Later in this chapter there will be a more detailed discussion on the uses of Enterprise AI. However, the objective at this stage is to illustrate the importance of Enterprise AI in enhancing organisational effectiveness. The volume of data generated worldwide is expected to continually increase at a rapid rate. Hence, entities that are committed to a data-driven decision-making strategy will view this expansion as a definite advantage. This increase of data provides far-reaching business intelligence that will act as the main thrust for enhancements in business operations and generating new products and services. Furthermore, AI will help entities to exploit this rapid expansion of data through deep learning to reveal the elusive patterns and hidden relationships that may provide entities a competitive edge. Additionally, AI has the capacity to make meaningful forecasts that may not be noticeable to humans by meticulously exploring the vast repository of data. Hence, Enterprise AI applications are able to provide answers to concerns that were not likely to be resolved by humans or traditional systems.

Organisations in every industry are discovering new ways of utilising Enterprise AI applications to tackle a wide spectrum of use cases, including customer retention; inventory optimisation; fraud detection; and anti-money laundering amongst many others. Enterprise AI applications are also being applied in specialised areas such as predictive maintenance for a variety of industrial assets, including oil and gas production apparatus; energy production and distribution equipment; and vehicle and general transportation production equipment. The list of potential applications is impressive. Enterprise AI applications are only limited by one’s imagination. Enterprise AI has quickly become a key digital transformation enabler and is stimulating customer expectations, which necessitates organisations to be more responsive and embrace new technologies to stay competitive and ultimately survive.

It is a recognisable fact that the sharp increase in the volume and complexity of data generated by businesses is making it extremely difficult for traditional systems and humans to analyse and interpret data effectively. On the other hand, Enterprise AI systems are providing the means and opportunity to unearth meaningful insights from this vast repository of data, information, and knowledge to disclose concealed patterns and trends that traditional approaches are not capable of doing. Additionally, Enterprise AI systems can automate complex decision-making practices that enable organisations to be responsive to market trends and thus gain a competitive edge.

## **9.4** Advantages and Challenges of Enterprise AI

Enterprise AI has been shown to transform business operations by automating everyday tasks and streamlining business processes resulting in improved efficiency and reduced operational costs. The outcome of this transformation is the positive impact on employees and customers, since AI frees employees from routine tasks, giving them the opportunity to provide customers better personalised experiences and to engage in additional strategic activity to combat competition. This has resulted in enhanced customer support through chatbots and virtual assistants to provide a 24/7 service from anywhere providing revenue earning opportunities through better customer support interactions.

Additionally, AI has the necessary tools that exceed traditional data processing methods, to conduct in-depth analysis of huge volumes of data resulting in better informed decisions. Moreover, AI algorithms have also enhanced cybersecurity by detecting and responding to threats effectively through powerful intrusion prevention systems. Research literature has revealed that Enterprise AI offers the following benefits, some of which have been mentioned above:

*    Increased efficiency and productivity: Enterprise AI assists in the automation of recurring and tedious tasks, streamline workflows, and optimise resource allocation, resulting in significant improvements in efficiency and productivity.
*   Cost mitigation: This is achieved through AI’s ability to streamline operations and optimise processes, identify inefficiencies, and mitigating errors, all of which contribute to significant cost reductions.
*   Improved customer service: AI can provide a faster and more personalised customer service. Advances in speech recognition and other NLP tools give chatbots the ability to provide personalised service to customers. These personalised customer interactions, impart tailored recommendations through chatbots and virtual assistants on 24/7 basis from anywhere, resulting in stronger relationships that promote customer loyalty.
*   Enhanced monitoring: AI can process data in real time providing entities with immediate monitoring. For instance, factory shopfloor production is able to apply image recognition and machine learning models in their quality control practices to scrutinise production and identify problems.
*   Higher quality: AI tools can mitigate errors and increasing the likelihood of complying with compliance standards better than manual or traditional automated approaches.
*   Quicker product development: AI can better predict market consumer trends to facilitate shorter service and product development cycles.
*   Enhanced HR management. Entities are utilising Enterprise AI to rationalise the employee engagement process and eliminate bias in business communications. Furthermore, by releasing employees from routine tasks, AI helps to empower employees to focus on higher-value activities that involve creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills.
*   Improved business modelling. The ability for AI to perform in-depth analysis of huge quantities of data rapidly to detect patterns and trends help entities to define better business models when compared with traditional approaches.
*   Better competitive advantage: AI tools provide insights into market trends that allow management to make faster strategic decisions and help management to generate innovative products and services to gain a significant competitive advantage.

Despite the above advantages, Enterprise AI has its potential risks and challenges such as algorithmic bias and possible data security issues. Hence, it is important that organisations define clear ethical guidelines that facilitate robust design, data privacy standards, continuous monitoring, and suitable security systems. Such measures are important to ensure that Enterprise AI systems comply with appropriate standards and maintain users’ trust. Another concern is the impact of AI on employment and the general workforce. This topic was extensively addressed when discussing the knowledge economy. It was concluded that businesses like past technological break throughs need to retrain and reskill their employees to mitigate employee mistrust and anxiety, and that these employees remain an integral part of the evolving work environment.

There is no doubt that technology in general can erode basic skills that can impact one’s performance when technology inadvertently fails. This problem is not restricted to AI but to technology in general, particularly when organisations and individuals are continuously reliant on it. For example, before the invention of the calculator, employees in banks had very high abilities for manually counting lengthy columns of figures and calculating monthly interest on deposits. As the calculators came on the scene and later when computer systems took over, these skills greatly eroded. Obviously, one cannot stop progress and significant cost savings, and much better customer service resulted from these inventions. However, this type of problem becomes very serious in certain circumstances. Research has shown that aircraft accidents are increasingly due to the erosion of basic pilot skills. More specifically, the two plane crashes involving Boeing 737 Max jets, gave rise to concerns that pilots were losing their ability to apply basic flying skills as the aircraft depended increasing on AI in the cockpit.

AI errors are still a great concern. It is a fact that AI can remove human error, but it can also introduce new types of errors due to questionable data, deficient training data or faults in the algorithms. Additionally, these errors can be critically intensified because of the great quantity of transactions that AI systems typically process. However, the greatest concern is regarding unethical and unintentional routines. For example, entities need to be aware and watch for gender or racial or religious bias in reports produced by AI applications.

It is important to recognise that AI is being used in a wide variety of applications that may impact individuals differently depending on their social and income status. Hence, entities need to be watchful for unintended consequences when applying AI for certain business strategic decisions that could have implications on certain sectors of society. For instance, a supermarket chain might apply AI to decide their pricing strategy based on the rivalry from other similar establishments. However, in low-income areas where there may be little or no rivalry, the logical advice from the AI system may infer to have higher food prices, which would go against the social status of the people living in that particular area.

## **9.5** Enterprise AI Scale Concept

The concept regarding Enterprise AI scale concerns the ability of the AI systems and their related technologies to operate successfully within the complex environment of a large organisation. To function in this type of environment, Enterprise AI systems must adhere to several critical prerequisites to be classified as “Enterprise-Scale.” [Figure 9.2](#ch22.xhtml#f33) illustrates that the Enterprise AI scale environment is based on nine essential criteria.

![Figure 9.2 Prerequisites for Enterprise AI Scale Environment.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C009_002.jpg)

**Figure 9.2** Prerequisites for Enterprise AI Scale Environment.[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#f33b)

Whilst all the criteria are equally important, the most prominent factor is high security. The sensitivity of business data demands that Enterprise AI systems must include robust security procedures to protect data integrity and privacy, ensuring safe user access and combat cyber threats. Enterprise AI systems must be scalable so that as the business grows and more complex circumstances and transactions are being conducted, these systems must be able to process and adapt to this growing business environment. An advantage of AI systems is that they do not need major redesign with greater complexity and bigger volume of data but can learn and modify themselves as the business environment changes.

Reliability of systems, data, results, and predictions is vital in any automated system. In the recent past user trust has been an issue with AI applications. Reliability in Enterprise AI entails consistent system behaviour with minimal downtime. These AI applications must perform as intended under fluctuating conditions. They must have robust error handling processes to ensure continuous system accuracy and accessibility. The definition of Enterprise AI emphasised the integration of various AI tools and other business systems. This integration must be seamless to users so that there is an effortless and automatic flow of data and interoperability within the organisation’s ICT infrastructure allowing for an efficient exchange and utilisation of information.

AI systems need a strong regulatory regime based on clearly defined policies, practices and responsibility roles that include: (a) compliance with legal and ethical standards; and (b) data and model management. This will ensure accountability in AI decision-making. A basic objective of automated systems is to contribute towards the achievement of the organisation’s strategic and operational goals that may include increased efficiency, reduced cost, enhanced customer experiences, and the development of new product lines to boost revenue streams. The previous section described various benefits that Enterprise AI is able to provide.

The success of computer systems is not only measured by the results they provide but by their penetration rate within the organisation. Hence, the easier the Enterprise AI system is to use, the greater the probability that it will actually be utilised. There is no point in having a highly sophisticated Enterprise AI system if no one or few utilise it. Therefore, user-friendliness becomes a critical aspect for its successful deployment with AI tools and interfaces being manageable and clear to technical and non-technical organisational users.

An important critical prerequisite is flexibility, which means that the Enterprise AI system must be able to adjust to the changing business requirements and goals. This prerequisite complements the scalability factor by sustaining the organisation’s business strategy and functions, and/or the emergence of new market trends. The final prerequisite is sustainability, which entails the long-term system support, including its environmental impact and the system’s capacity to accommodate business strategic changes and technological advancements.

## **9.6** Implementing Enterprise AI

Generally, when implementing Enterprise AI, it is important to firstly identify the problem by ascertaining the areas where the processes are inefficient so that one may assess how AI can possibly address these weaknesses. Once the problem is defined and assessed, it is essential to evaluate the organisation’s data and document the various processes so that an effective machine learning model may be developed. The machine learning model will use as its input the organisation’s data and the documentation of the processes as its training basis.

Several issues need to be considered in the Enterprise AI deployment process, such as model bias, data privacy and security, and supporting AI technical employees. Bias in AI algorithms is a constant concern since AI is trained to recognise patterns. However, by recognising this bias, the model can be retrained to be more balanced by reframing outcomes around key markers. Data privacy and security must be taken seriously to avoid threat actors from attaining access to the system. Intrusion prevention systems (IPS), and an effective firewall will resolve this issue effectively.

Like every other computer system, an Enterprise AI application requires competent and dedicated AI professionals that focus on ensuring that the deployed AI system achieves the defined business goals considering the ethical and security aspects. It is important to recognise that implementing Enterprise AI requires a strategic approach and careful planning. [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) provides a suggested framework for deploying an Enterprise AI system.

![Figure 9.3 Framework for Deploying an Enterprise AI System.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C009_003.jpg)

**Figure 9.3** Framework for Deploying an Enterprise AI System.[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#f34b)

A fundamental step is to define the organisational goals and objectives. This entails clearly identifying the business problems that need to be addressed and/or the opportunities and outcomes that are anticipated to be gained by the eventual Enterprise AI application. Therefore, one needs to outline what the organisation aims to achieve with AI. This will assist the organisation to focus its efforts and choose the most significant Enterprise AI solutions. Typical goals may include operational efficiency, better customer experience, and the identification of new revenue streams. Hence, knowing these objectives helps the AI team to determine the direction of the AI strategy and to align it with the overall business objectives.

The evaluation of internal capabilities is very important since management must establish whether the organisation has adequate competencies or if these competencies need to be attained. Moreover, the method of attaining the required competencies must also be decided, in terms of whether to recruit professional staff or outsource the requirement. This evaluation provides adequate information to determine the training and development programme for existing technical and non-technical employees.

It is important that a management executive is chosen to act as the authoritative sponsor and champion for each AI initiative with an adequate budget. To deploy Enterprise AI successfully, an organisation requires a competent cross-functional team. This executive would need to identify skill shortages so that an appropriate team is created, which has a combination of technical skills and business knowhow. In other words, this team requires technical and business professionals. Creating a cross-functional team ensures that a holistic approach to implementing the project is taken, where different views and knowledge are merged to tackle the various aspects of the Enterprise AI project. The team’s composition and size must align with the scope of the project and reviewed as various AI sub-systems materialise.

Identifying high-impact use cases to ascertain the areas of opportunity is essential. This step requires management to explore relevant AI use cases and identify the business processes where AI can add value and support the business goals. This step allows management to establish a case list to prioritise the possible business functions that provide the highest possible returns. Factors that should be considered are data availability, deployment feasibility, and return on investment. This will ensure that cases which offer the greatest potential impact are selected.

The next step is to build data fluency within the organisational culture so that employees are able to familiarise themselves with data and its possible interpretation, and to have the capacity to create and communicate information from the data. This will encourage employees not only to understand the data but to also exploit it to convey complex ideas, engage in discussions, and absorb information from others effortlessly. This will enable individuals across various roles to connect through a shared understanding of data, transforming raw data into actionable insights.

Concurrently with building data fluency, the organisation’s data preparedness is assessed so that data strategy is adequately prepared. Management needs to assess the quality, quantity, and accessibility of the organisation’s data. One must recognise that AI algorithms require huge volumes of data to train and operate effectively. This stage entails identifying the data sources, ensuring data quality, and establishing data governance and compliance processes. Therefore, this step ensures that the organisation has access to adequate and relevant data supported by an effective data strategy and robust data management practices.

Management is also required to define a detailed but flexible development plan with the aid of competent internal or external professionals that can select potential AI projects that are likely to give value. These professionals should also be able to commit to deliver a viable project beyond the pilot stage and refine each project as it moves into the deployment phase. The plan should also define the technical and business phases of the Enterprise AI implementation that includes an indication of the AI technologies and tools, defining the scope of the AI projects, establishing timelines, and necessary resources.

An important step is the identification of the primary business drivers for Enterprise AI. Some of the key business drivers include enhanced efficiency and productivity; data-driven decision-making; improved customer experience; streamlined operations and supply chain management; and enhanced cybersecurity. This step will enable the AI implementation team to establish performance parameters; use these key performance indicators to monitor the progress of the AI plans; and help them prepare a risk management strategy to define contingencies in case of difficulties. To assess the defined plans, it is suggested that a pilot project is initiated to ensure that the plans for full scale deployment of Enterprise AI are viable, realistic, and anticipate potential issues that may adversely impact the Enterprise AI project.

The Enterprise AI project plan will initially indicate the type of technology required. However, once the plan is being refined and implemented, it is important that suitable AI technologies and tools that best fit the specific selected use cases and data requirements are acquired. Important factors to be considered when determining which tools and software are to be used include sustainability and long-term support; scalability; performance; and the integration capabilities with the existing systems. Once the AI technologies and tools have been selected and acquired, these need to be integrated into the existing systems and workflows to provide a holistic solution. This step requires meticulous planning to ensure the highest level of compatibility, a minimal level of disruption to current operations, and a high penetration rate at the user level.

Developing and implementing the selected Enterprise AI solutions requires a systematic process, exhaustive testing, and validation. This will ensure that the systems are operationally reliable with a minimised user dissatisfaction level. The success of the Enterprise AI system is determined by its usability and user trust and acceptance. It is also essential that the AI implementation team habitually monitor performance, fine-tune the system parameters as necessary, and continuously train the system by iterating to improve accuracy and effectiveness.

The next phase is to bring overall AI capabilities to maturity by further testing and fine-tuning of system parameters ensuring that all modules are fully integrated to provide an effective holistic system. It is important to ensure that there is adequate abundance of reliable and trustworthy data from internal and external sources, which is supported by a suitable infrastructure to collect, filter, store, and deliver the necessary data. The final step is to continuously improve the AI models and the supporting processes. Significant attention should be given to security, privacy, and ethical AI issues by factoring activities for complying with government regulations and having courses that support best practice.

The AI team must also establish whether the Enterprise AI deployed applications are realistically supporting the business goals. This may be achieved by comparing the consequent system outcomes with the baseline metrics, particularly the established performance KPIs. Finally, support the health of the technology by having regular post-implementation reviews with ongoing maintenance, including recurrent updates, monitoring AI performance, and fine-tuning the system. This will ensure that the AI investment is safeguarded by having the AI systems remaining effective, secure, and aligned with the evolving business needs.

The framework depicted at [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) ensures that the deployed Enterprise AI systems are trustworthy and provide an explanation of how a decision was attained. Moreover, organisations that deploy Enterprise AI normally require 24/7 service from anywhere. Hence, defining the specific requirements will ensure that this criterion is achieved. Research has also indicated that natural language processing (NLP) is the most common tool that is adopted for Enterprise AI systems, particularly for customer service functions. Additionally, the framework provided aims to mitigate the main barriers that are normally encountered by organisations, namely scarce AI expertise, escalating data complexity and data silos, and the lack of tools for developing AI models.

One must recognise that AI is supported by several tools, namely machine learning, deep learning, predictive analytics, NLP, computer vision and automation. However, to gain value from these AI tools, entities must address key issues related to people, processes, and technology, all supported by enormous and timely volumes of high-quality data in a robust and secure environment. This requires substantial processing power with supercomputing platforms. Currently, Enterprise AI is viable for large organisations that can afford to have their own infrastructure or to partner with high-technology companies that can provide the necessary computing power over a leading-edge cloud environment.

Furthermore, the framework provided at [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) ensures that Enterprise AI, which is a multifaceted process, is implemented as a strategic methodology, ranging from identifying unambiguous objectives to conducting technology post-deployment reviews. Only through such a strategic approach can an organisation achieve the required return of investment from its Enterprise AI applications.

## **9.7** Enterprise AI Use Cases

Enterprise AI is being deployed across a broad spectrum of industries related to various business functions. The objective in most cases is to leverage the data these organisations possess and utilise it to attain tangible business value from the Enterprise AI applications. Enterprise AI facilitates management’s ability to make better informed data-driven decision-making, increases operational efficiency, enhances workflows, and improves customer experience. This in turn is assisting organisations to make significant advances in their business processes and attain better operational robustness and profitability.

Enterprise AI is transforming the way entities are managing their internal processes and engaging with their customers. The ensuing Enterprise AI models can address high-scale complicated problems regarding the automation of workloads, promoting products and services, providing personalised user experiences, assisting customers to make decisions, and tackling difficult business concerns. [Table 9.1](#ch22.xhtml#t19) provides typical examples of Enterprise AI use cases. AI has transformed industries due to its strategic impact on organisations through its ability to further automate the tasks that are normally performed by humans. Moreover, labour gains using AI are envisaged to grow at a faster rate than the job losses that result from using current workplace automation tools.

**Table 9.1** Examples of Enterprise AI Use Cases[⏎](#ch22.xhtml#t19b)

 
| **Industry** || **Use Case** |
| --- | --- |
| Agriculture || To yield healthier crops, reduce workloads and organise data. |
| --- | --- |
| Customer Relations: Enhanced customer service || Chatbots and virtual assistants provide 24/7 customer service from anywhere to answer inquiries and resolving issues. They learn from customer interactions to improve their ability to assist customers. |
| Customer Relations: Personalised marketing || Analyse customer data to generate personalised marketing campaigns by understanding customer preferences and behaviours, leading to increased engagement and sales. |
| Education || Automating the process of grading exams by assessing students and adapting curricula to their needs. |
| Energy || Optimise power grids and improve the integration of renewable resources. |
| Financial services: Fraud Detection || Detect fraudulent activities by analysing transaction patterns and flag unusual activities to significantly reducing the risk of financial fraud. |
| Financial services: General || To improve back-office banking systems and automate customer service to create new opportunities. |
| Healthcare || Assists to diagnosing diseases, analysing medical images, and predicting patient outcomes enhancing the accuracy of the findings. |
| HR management || Assist in resume screening and candidate matching to identify the most suitable applicants. To analyse employee data and advise on training, development, and retention strategy decisions. |
| IT service management || Use NLP to automate user requests for IT services. Apply machine learning to IT service management (ITSM) data to gain a better knowledge of the infrastructure and processes. |
| Law || Use machine learning to mine data and predict outcomes. Appling computer vision to classify and extract information from documents, and NLP to interpret requests for information. |
| Manufacturing: Robotics || Use of collaborative robots on assembly lines and in warehouses to assist humans. |
| Manufacturing: Predictive maintenance || Use predictive maintenance for machinery. Use machine learning algorithms to identify buying habits to predict product demand for production planning. |
| Marketing || To analyse historical sales data, market trends, and other relevant variables to accurately predict sales to enable businesses to optimise inventory, enhance resource allocation process, and make better informed decisions about pricing policies and marketing strategies. |
| Security: Cybersecurity threat detection || To identify and mitigate cybersecurity threats by analysing network traffic and identifying unusual patterns to detect potential security breaches before they cause significant harm. |
| Other: Predictive maintenance || Analysing sensor data and identifying patterns to indicate likely equipment failures to predictive maintenance needs to mitigate downtime, optimise maintenance schedules, and extend the lifespan of assets. |
| Other: Supply chain optimisation || Forecast product demand, optimise inventory levels, and identify potential disruptions in the supply chain ecosystem to assist in having smoother operations, reduced costs and improve responsiveness to market changes. |

The strength of AI is its analytical ability. This means that AI is not simply automating processes but is able to initiate the most efficient way to perform a task and fine-tune workflows immediately as circumstances change. As [Table 9.1](#ch22.xhtml#t19) illustrates, AI is already complementing human work in many fields, from agriculture to help yield healthier crops; assisting medical staff to diagnose a patient’s condition; and helping to optimise the organisation’s supply chain by forecasting product demand, improve inventory levels and identify potential disruptions in the supply chain ecosystem to achieve smoother operations, mitigate costs, and enhance awareness of market changes.

AI algorithms have been deployed as an additional security layer by automatically detecting and responding to cybersecurity threats. Moreover, natural language generation tools are also being adopted to enhance customer service, while facial recognition tools are used by law enforcement agencies. Deep learning platforms are also currently being applied for experimenting with automated driving. However, safety aspects need further development before automated driving can be adopted in a practical environment. The financial sector, particularly banks are using AI to hasten and support loan processing, while maintaining regulatory compliance.

## **9.8** Enterprise AI Potential

Enterprise AI is expected to be greatly impacted by the advances of generative AI technology due to its capacity to use large language models (LLMs) for creating new content and providing solutions that go beyond traditional predictive models. Generative AI is not only capable of managing vast volumes of data but has the capacity to make sense of this data and is able to replicate patterns within data to provide innovative solutions. Hence, the abilities of generative AI will be a further instrument that will be integrated into the Enterprise AI toolbox.

An important objective is the seamless integration of Enterprise AI with an ever-ending range of AI tools that are currently available or will be available in the time ahead. Enterprise AI will be able to use real-time data from Internet-of-things (IoT) devices to enhance predictive maintenance and provide better customer service. Furthermore, edge computing will enable faster localised AI processing that is very critical for time-sensitive applications. Hence, the integration of technology is not restricted to AI software but also to leading-edge hardware. A basic strength of AI is its capacity to manage large volumes of data. Therefore, in the big data context it will provide greater processing power for analysing and unearthing significant insights about a host of scenarios, including marketing trends. Enterprise AI’s integration with blockchain technology will enhance transaction security and transparency, which are essential for the financial and supply chain management sectors. A separate chapter regarding predicted future AI developments will be provided in [Part IV](#ch25.xhtml#c15) of this book.

It is important that ethical factors are addressed in a serious and responsible manner. Organisations applying AI need to adopt a strategy that promotes trust by ensuring equitable and transparent decision-making processes. AI should be viewed as complementing human talent not replacing it. A detailed chapter dedicated to ethical and legal considerations will be provided as the final chapter for [Part III](#ch20.xhtml#c10) of this book.

## **9.9** Practical Enterprise AI Applications

AI is no longer a distant fantasy from science fiction. Everyday new applications are being released that have a profound impact on how organisations conduct their businesses and provide their products and services to their customers. This section presents some practical AI applications that are having a great beneficial impact on all types of customers, irrespective of whether they are organisations or individuals.

### **9.9.1** Case Study 1: eCommerce Operational Efficiency and Customer Satisfaction

[Tang (2025a)](#ch22.xhtml#r089) illustrates how an enterprise was able to profitably employ AI-driven solutions and mobile app development to enhance its operational efficiency by reducing its order processing time by 30%, increase user engagement by 25% and enhance its mobile sales by 15%.

This AI initiative took place at a time when the company was encountering significant concerns regarding the need to improve employee skills and enhance the supply chain effectiveness to eliminate a persistent 20% stockout rate. These concerns were further intensified by regulatory privacy requirements that entailed sound risk management strategies to avoid harsh legal penalties for non-compliance. This case study illustrates that AI solutions are typically implemented in combination with other strategic initiatives, such as employee development programmes, integration of technology and process improvement frameworks. Therefore, it is not just a question of implementing an AI solution in isolation.

The first step taken by the company was an assessment of its internal and external environments using well established methodologies. For the internal environment assessment, the ADDIE (Analyse, Design, Develop, Implement, and Evaluate) model was utilised for employee upskilling. This model depends on each stage being done in the given order but with a focus on reflection and iteration. The Lean Six Sigma was applied for process improvements (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), pp. 380–401). These tools permitted the company to identify key areas that required attention, which resulted in defining measurable improvements in productivity and operational efficiency, and generating a more responsive and capable workforce.

The assessment of the company’s external environment mainly encompassed techniques, such as Value Chain Analysis and the Kano Model (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), pp. 386–388). These models focus on enhancing activities that add value and prioritizing app features based on customer satisfaction. Competitive benchmarks (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), p. 369) were ascertained to evaluate performance against industry standards, specifically in order processing and mobile user engagement. According to [Tang (2025a)](#ch22.xhtml#r089), this strategic analysis improved the company’s market position and greatly increased its responsiveness to customer requirements and market trends. This positively impacted overall business growth and customer loyalty.

The internal and external environment assessment enabled management to identify several strategic initiatives that included:

*   AI-Driven Order Processing Automation. Lean Six Sigma and the Value Chain Analysis were used to implement this initiative. These tools enabled the implementation team to streamline the order processing process and mitigate any identified inefficiencies by adhering to a precise procedure, namely: 
    *   Specify the scope of the order processing automation project and define the key performance indicators (KPIs).
    *   Measure current order processing time statistics and identify the bottlenecks by mapping the process, including the data collection practice.
    *   Examine the data to determine root causes for the inefficiencies using root cause analysis, such as the 5-Whys (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), p. 76).
    *   Enhance the process by implementing AI-driven automation solutions to target the identified inefficiencies.
    *   Collect critical information and accurately monitor the new process, including the KPIs to ensure continuous progress (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), pp. 307–313).
    *    Utilise Value Chain Analysis to determine and fine-tune the activities that add value to the order processing function. This sheds light on how each task in the order processing process impacts the overall value creation (refer to [Camilleri, 2019](#ch22.xhtml#r087), pp. 217-223). [<?tab?> Tang (2025a)](#ch22.xhtml#r089) reports that this approach resulted in a 30% decrease in the order processing times and a significant improvement in operational efficiency and accuracy that lead to a 20% increase in customer satisfaction.
*   Mobile App Development. This phase applied several analytical tools such as the Agile Methodology and the Kano Model. The Agile methodology is a project management and software development approach that emphasises flexibility, collaboration, and customer-centricity. Major companies like Facebook, Google, and Amazon use this approach because of its adaptability, customer-focused style, and its capability for developing a user-friendly mobile app quickly and efficiently. <?tab?>The Kano Model was used to prioritise the features that were to be adopted based on the extent to which they were likely to satisfy customers. This approach allowed the product team to evaluate whether the inclusion of a high-satisfaction feature against its implementation cost was a strategically sound decision. Hence, the model was very useful for pinpointing which app features would delight users and which were essential for basic functionality. <?tab?>The Kano Model is unique from other prioritisation frameworks because it has a rigorous focus on how customers respond to each feature. Hence, its key analysis for any new feature is to what degree it will satisfy users. The above approach ensured the successful implementation of a user-friendly mobile app that heightened the overall user experience, positively impacting customer satisfaction and loyalty. User-feedback allowed the mobile app to be fine-tuned resulting in a 25% increase in user engagement and a 15% growth in mobile sales. The app’s prioritised features enhanced the overall user experience, contributing to higher customer satisfaction and loyalty.
*   Data Privacy Compliance. The project team examined GDPR compliance requirements and identified and evaluated probable risks to data privacy, such as data breaches and unauthorised access. The primary objective was to foster customer trust and mitigate as much as possible the identified risks and avoid legal penalties. This resulted in the mitigation of risks associated with data breaches and unauthorised access, thus boosting customer trust and brand reputation minimising legal infringements.
*   Customer Experience Improvement. The frameworks applied for this activity were mainly Customer Journey Mapping and the Net Promoter Score (NPS). Customer journey mapping provided a visual depiction of the customer’s experience during their ordering journey. It provided a deeper understanding of customers’ emotions and actions highlighting pain points, unmet needs, and opportunities for improvement. NPS is often viewed as the gold standard customer experience metric. It measures customer loyalty and satisfaction by considering the customer’s probability of recommending a given service or product over time. Typically, the NPS score is measured by a single-question survey and reported with a number ranging from -100 to +100, where a higher score is desirable. Using NPS, the project team developed and implemented strategies to convert passives and detractors into promoters. The NPS trends were monitored over a significant duration to measure the effectiveness of customer experience initiatives. This resulted in the identification and subsequent resolution of key pain points, leading to a 20% improvement in customer satisfaction, with a 10-point improvement in NPS. Hence, this resulted in higher customer loyalty and repeat business, pushing long-term growth.
*   Employee Upskilling Program. This phase utilised the ADDIE and Kirkpatrick models. The Addie model is an instructional design methodology that is used to facilitate the streamlining and composition of the course content. In contrast, the Kirkpatrick Model appraises the outcome of training and learning programs. This model evaluates both formal and informal training approaches, assessing them against four levels of criteria: reaction, learning, behaviour, and results. The project team applied the ADDIE model to analyse the competencies gap of employees and to develop the training modules according to the organisational business needs. The effectiveness of the training programme using the Kirkpatrick Model was evaluated by assessments and feedback. This model measured the impact of the upskilling program on employee performance and business outcomes. The adoption of these models ensured a significant improvement in employee competencies resulting in a 25% increase in employee performance and a 15% growth in overall productivity. The process mitigated the resistance to change and encouraged a culture of continuous learning and innovation.
*   Supply Chain Optimisation. The project team applied the Supply Chain Operations Reference (SCOR) Model to map the supply chain process and the Demand Forecasting (DF) model to predict future demand based on historical data and market trends. The SCOR model was used to evaluate an organisation’s supply chain for effectiveness and efficiency of sales and operational planning by optimising key processes with the aim of mitigating stockouts and overstock situations. The DF model helped to optimise inventory levels and safeguard timely product availability. The use of these models reduced stockouts by 20% and overstock situations by 15%, providing greater profitability and customer satisfaction. The AI-driven solutions emanating from the use of these models improved the organisation’s capacity to respond to market conditions and demand fluctuations, leading to better overall business responsiveness and resilience.

The above support the contention that implementing an AI solution is a lengthy and meticulous process requiring the use of various management models, each focused on a specific operational aspect. Furthermore, the Critical Success Factor approach can also be applied to manage the implementation of the defined strategic initiatives (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), pp. 299–326) thus ensuring that the defined strategic objectives are achieved. The AI solution enabled the order processing operations to be streamlined by replacing the traditional methods that were time consuming and inclined towards human error. The implemented solution enabled the AI system to process tasks such as sorting, prioritising, and handling orders automatically to expedite the entire operation and mitigate the risk of mistakes.

A significant benefit of the AI orders processing system was its capability to enhance accuracy and efficiency. AI solutions are able to identify and correct errors in orders, making sure that the correct information is entered into the system. This mitigates the requirement for manual control and verification, thus streamlining the process, which lowers the likelihood of errors and delays. The resultant AI system also improved customer experience because the time needed to process orders was reduced, resulting in faster delivery times. Additionally, the AI system continuously kept customers informed throughout the process, reducing anxiety, and strengthening their satisfaction, which in turn may have positively impacted their loyalty, retention, and upbeat reviews.

Typically, AI solutions work on 24/7 basis, thus reducing the need for human intervention, which releases employees to focus on higher-value tasks. Costs associated with manual processing are definitely reduced to a minimum with overall productivity increasing. Furthermore, AI solutions also have the potential to reduce the need for office space and other resources, resulting in more cost savings. The AI system features significant insights and analytics regarding the order processing method, permitting the organisation to determine patterns, trends, and areas for improvement. With such information organisations are able to optimise their processes, mitigate bottlenecks, and enhance overall efficiency that can result in greater profits, lesser costs, and improved customer satisfaction.

An important feature of an AI solution is that it can be customised to meet the needs of individual businesses, which may be focused for the specific requirements of the organisation, leading to even higher efficiency and accuracy. The provided AI solution make use of several AI algorithms that support the automation process and optimise operations. These AI algorithms have a different and specific objective that build a robust AI system for an order processing system. As one may appreciate, there is continuous progress being made in machine learning and data science. Thus, algorithms continue to evolve, making AI systems more effective. This example has illustrated that AI has a multifaceted role in revolutionising order processing by removing inefficiencies, delivering actionable insights through data analytics, enhancing customer and supplier relationships, and keeps the organisation competitive, while ensuring regulatory compliance and security.

### **9.9.2** Case Study 2: AI-Driven Inventory Management

[Tang (2025b)](#ch22.xhtml#r090) describes how a mid-sized company specialising in consumer electronics with a global customer base, encountered serious concerns regarding its inventory management. These concerns were mostly related to inappropriate demand forecasting, resulting in significant stockouts and overstocking across multiple product categories that negatively impacted sales and costs. He reports that by incorporating advanced AI demand forecasting models, the company was able to realise a 25% decrease in inventory related concerns and an 18% reduction in holding costs, underlining the effectiveness of a systematic approach to AI in Operational Excellence. It has transpired that the company’s existing AI system is lacking features for predicting demand patterns, which is viewed as the reason for the significant loss in sales and an increase in holding costs.

Root cause analysis was conducted using several methods, such as 5-Whys, process mapping and Ishikawa diagrams amongst others (refer to [Camilleri, 2024](#ch22.xhtml#r088), pp. 78–99). The 5-Whys approach is a simple way to identify the root cause of a problem. Basically, when a problem has been defined, ask: “Why did this happen?” Then, without stopping at the answer to this first question, ask: “Why?” again and again until the root cause is attained. The Ishikawa diagram (or fishbone diagram), which is also known as a cause-and-effect diagram, helps management identify the many possible causes for a problem by sorting ideas into useful categories and is especially useful in structuring brainstorming sessions. The outcome of this analysis suggested that the problems originated from an absence of accurate demand forecasting, poor inventory allocation, and unsatisfactory integration of AI with the existing supply chain management systems. These problem areas were the likely contributors to inventory mismanagement that may have also undermined the company’s operational efficiency and profitability.

Management adopted a 5-phase consulting process to acquire a systematic and data-driven methodology for improving the AI facilities for inventory management. This ensured a complete analysis, design, and implementation of an upgraded system that included greater forecasting accuracy, improved inventory levels, and lower costs. The consulting process consisted of the following five phases:

*   Diagnostic Evaluation: Assessing the current inventory systems, data quality, and AI technologies to ascertain the existing capabilities and the evident data gaps. This included data collection, stakeholder interviews, and process mapping to identify areas for AI integration.
*   AI Capability Building: Increasing AI competencies based on the diagnostic evaluation by identifying the AI tools and technologies that best fit the company’s needs and taking advantage of data analytics for better forecasting. This phase involved choosing appropriate AI solutions and devising pilot projects.
*   Developing a Demand Forecasting Model: This task involved developing a cutting-edge AI model to predict sales trends. This phase incorporated determining how to utilise historical sales data to forecast demand and deciding on the external factors to be included in the model. The aim was to develop and test predictive algorithms.
*   Inventory Optimisation: This involved integrating the upgraded AI models with the inventory management systems. The main issues included ascertaining how AI-driven insights could lead to optimal stock levels and identifying the reordering strategies to be adopted. This mainly involved the creation of dashboards and decision-support tools for inventory planning.
*    Implementation and Continuous Improvement: This entailed the implementation of the AI-enhanced inventory system across the company. This included securing agreement on the implementation strategy and KPIs to be adopted for the individual departments for ensuring success. This phase embraced training, monitoring, and iterative fine-tuning of the AI applications.

Several implementation challenges were encountered by the company that required careful consideration. For instance, compatibility of new AI technologies with the company’s existing IT infrastructure; seamless integration to avoid disruptions in supply chain operations; having an inclusive change management strategy to ensure that stakeholders understood and accepted the new AI-driven processes; and sustainable investment for continuing AI training and development to maintain the system’s effectiveness and adaptability to changing market dynamics.

[Tang (2025b)](#ch22.xhtml#r090) claims that the company anticipated a 20-30% reduction in stockouts and overstock situations, a more responsive reaction to market demands, and an overall increase in customer satisfaction due to better product availability once the new AI systems were in place. Additionally, the company envisaged a decrease in holding costs by at least 15%, contributing directly to the bottom line. The main implementation challenges encountered were data privacy concerns since AI systems required access to vast amounts of consumer and transactional data; and data accuracy and consistency across global operations to ensure successful AI-driven forecasting.

KPIs were a critical aspect because they provided measurable spot checks to verify the alignment of operational activities with the defined strategic goals. This guaranteed that deployment is not just activity-driven, but results-oriented. KPIs act as an early warning system since they indicate progress or deviation from established targets, enabling responsive decision-making and course correction if necessary. Important KPIs included: (a) demand forecast accuracy that measured the percentage of accuracy between forecasted and actual sales, signifying the effectiveness of the AI models; (b) inventory turnover ratio, which evaluated how often inventory is traded and replaced over a period, reflecting the optimisation of stock levels; and (c) stockout and overstock rate that tracks the incidence of these events, with improvements signifying better demand prediction and inventory management.

As explained in the previous case study, AI is a tool that requires a strategic approach applying several other management tools in the system development life cycle. [Tang (2025b)](#ch22.xhtml#r090) argues that it is vital for management to promote data-driven decision-making and a continuous learning culture to exploit AI’s capabilities. Additionally, the old aphorism in data processing: garbage-in, garbage-out is imperative. In other words, the AI systems are only as good as the data they process, ensuring data quality and integrity is paramount for reliable outcomes ([Tang, 2025b](#ch22.xhtml#r090)). Furthermore, AI technology is continuously evolving, what is current today is quickly outdated. Therefore, keeping up-to-date with the latest developments and be willing to experiment with new approaches is important for gaining a competitive edge in a turbulent economic environment. Furthermore, a company having gained a competitive edge is a short-lived reality because other competitors are also striving to gain a competitive edge. One must recognise that gaining a competition edge is a continuous struggle for business survival.

[Tang (2025b)](#ch22.xhtml#r090) identifies the following key results: (a) 25% lower stockouts and overstock situations through the integration of advanced AI-driven demand forecasting models; (b) 18% reduced stock holding costs that directly improved in the company’s bottom line; (c) 35% increase in the accuracy of forecasting demand, leading to more efficient inventory management; (d) 20% improvement in the inventory turnover ratio, signifying a more effective and responsive approach to market demands; and (e) 40% increase in staff proficiency with the new system by the deployment of a comprehensive AI training program.

It must also be recognised that several AI algorithms are employed that support the inventory automation process and optimise operations. For instance, supervised learning algorithms, such as linear regression are often applied for forecasting to assist in predicting demand based on one or more predictor variables. Decision trees are beneficial for classifying tasks that identify the categories of products, which are most likely to be purchased by specific customer segments. Additionally, unsupervised learning algorithms like principal component analysis (PCA) is frequently applied for dimensionality reduction when dealing with large sets of correlated variables, such as product features. The above are only a few AI algorithms that may be exploited when considering AI solutions.

## **9.10** Conclusion

This chapter provided a detailed description regarding Enterprise AI. It illustrated that Enterprise AI is a subset of AI that is specifically focused on driving business value in a large-scale organisation. It also supported the contention that businesses that harness the advantages emanating from the power of Enterprise AI applications will most likely experience significant advances in their value chain operations. Before specifically focusing on Enterprise AI, this chapter examined how AI is generally transforming business enterprises and how the concept of Enterprise AI came into fruition by integrating the various available AI tools into a seamless system to exploit the vast volumes of data that organisations generate during their operations.

In recent years, Enterprise AI has been shown to be important in maintaining a competitive advantage. In fact, organisations in a broad range of industries are uncovering new ways of applying Enterprise AI applications, including enhancing customer loyalty; providing greater individualised customer experience; inventory optimisation; fraud detection; and anti-money laundering amongst many others. Enterprise AI is also being used in specific industry segments such as predictive maintenance regarding oil and gas production equipment, and energy production and distribution systems. These are just a few worthwhile examples.

The chapter has illustrated the tremendous advantages of applying Enterprise AI ranging from cost mitigation, proving better business models, and particularly keeping ahead of competition. It was illustrated that Enterprise AI is a significant tool for ensuring the business survival of an organisation. However, despite the many advantages, Enterprise AI has its potential risks such as algorithmic bias, possible data security issues, and eroding basic human skills. Hence, the importance for organisations to compile clear ethical guidelines about developing human talent, designing reliable AI systems, having data privacy standards, continuous monitoring, and having suitable security systems. Two important issues that require special attention are to maintain the users’ trust in the AI application systems and mitigating the impact of AI on the workforce by introducing reskilling programmes so that employees remain an integral part of the evolving work environment.

The Chapter also provided a suitable framework for the successful deployment of Enterprise AI. Each step in this implementation framework was described in detail to provide the reader with a viable and practical deployment approach that may be adapted and customised to their individual organisation. Finally, the chapter itemised and explained several use cases to give the reader an idea how Enterprise AI can benefit their organisation. Additionally, a brief explanation was provided regarding the potential of Enterprise AI, which will be further described in more detail later in a separate chapter.
