# Chapter 10Public Sector AI

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-13](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-13)

> *“When it is obvious that the goals cannot be reached, don’t adjust the goals; adjust the action steps.”*
> 
> Confucius (Kong Qiu)
> 
> *Chinese philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period (551-479 BCE)*

According to World Bank ([2021](#ch23.xhtml#h1-070)), disruptive technologies like AI have the potential to transform governments because AI can deliver a personalised service delivery experience, enhance efficiency of back-end processes, strengthen policy compliance and facilitate fraud identification within government disbursements. If used appropriately and exploited together with human management and decision-making, governments can also use AI to address development challenges ([World Bank, 2021](#ch23.xhtml#r098)). Similar to Enterprise AI, Public Sector AI is viewed as helping organisations to perform certain tasks that have in the past typically required human intelligence and tasks that involved human vision, speech, language, knowledge, and exploration of data.

As governments continually confront the economic challenges arising from a turbulent global economy, and recently the challenges arising from worldwide pandemics such as Covid-19, governments are under tremendous fiscal stress exacerbated by mobility limitations on citizens and civil servants when epidemics arise. This environment is acting as the main thrust for governments to discover better technologically enabled solutions to enable them to continue and enhance their services at a reduced cost and mitigate corruption. The World Bank contends that a common pattern of government’s AI use cases is focusing on citizen engagement; compliance and risk management; fraud and anti-corruption; business process automation; service delivery; asset management and analytics for decision-making; and policy design.

Furthermore, the World Bank argues that with careful deployment, Public Sector AI applications can help governments to deliver their services faster and more personalised to the needs of beneficiaries and citizens, and the public administration charged with delivering them. However, care is also required to mitigate the risks, such as managing inherent biases in data and algorithms that aggravate or create problems. Generally, governments view AI as an essential factor in the expansion of the knowledge economy and regard it as a major strategic resource to enhance their country’s competitiveness and to further increase economic growth. A 2023 report by McKinsey & Company predicted that AI is likely to contribute to $17.7 trillion annually in economic value. Unfortunately, the growth in the application of AI is mostly in developed countries with some important inroads being made in developing counties. There is a concern that a slower adoption of AI in various countries may lead to inequality between the rich and the poor nations.

## **10.1** Introduction

It must be recognised that the Public Sector in most countries is the biggest employer of human resources, and its services extends across the whole spectrum of society, including the business sector. It is also the principal user of non-human resources and provider of a wide-ranging number of services. Therefore, Public Sector AI has the possibility to greatly enhance government operations and aid in providing the extensive needs of citizens by applying cutting-edge technology, ranging from traffic management to healthcare delivery to processing revenue and value added tax returns.

However, there are still many public entities that have not embraced this powerful technology. Some public sector officials are fully aware of the transformational impact of AI applications by exploiting their entity’s data. Although public entities have an enormous wealth of data, in most cases this data is held in separate data silos that make it difficult to apply AI solutions. Hence, a primary challenge for public sector entities is having an effective data management process that generates a comprehensive central data repository, which supports a data sharing and data discovery mentality.

Moreover, public sector officials may not have suitable knowledge and expertise to make strategic decisions for acquiring the necessary AI tools. However, this challenge may be overcome by engaging private sector expertise through a lawful outsourcing process. One needs to recognise that public sector management officials have less freedom than their private counterparts because they are under constant public scrutiny and restrictive procurement regulations (including lengthy appeal procedures), apart from restricted fiscal allocation processes. Additionally, the risk and possible public condemnation through the media about ethical considerations increases further layers of complexity in initiating AI projects, particularly in developing countries. The outcome of this uncertain environment is that public sector management will be inclined to procrastinate procurement decisions and thus continually postpone the apparent risk. However, there is no doubt that AI has great possibilities to facilitate the government’s effort to deliver services that are more responsive, efficient, and personalised.

## **10.2** AI and the Public Sector

[Berryhill et al. (2019)](#ch23.xhtml#r092) contend that despite the lack of research, AI is a significant and growing issue in governments. They imply that AI can facilitate the governments’ effort to achieve its purpose, namely, to elaborate and improve laws and policies, provide public goods and services to citizens and residents, and to deliver and maintain the tools, resources, and structures needed for civil servants to perform their respective functions. They also identify several roles that governments have regarding AI. They view these roles as a way of transforming public sector processes, practices, policies, and services, rather than how they affect the broader economy. [Berryhill et al. (2019)](#ch23.xhtml#r092) refer to the following functions that governments can perform regarding AI, with these functions in most cases being conducted concurrently:

1.  Government as a financier or direct investor to sustain financial support for the development and deployment of emerging technologies.
2.  Government as a smart buyer and co-developer through innovative procurement practices, or as a co-developer through public-private partnerships (PPP) and other forms of collaboration to build new or tailored solutions.
3.  Government as a regulator or rules maker can accelerate the innovation cycles of emerging digital technologies by having creative types of policy and regulatory instruments that also evaluate compliance and taking appropriate action for nonconformity.
4.  Government as a convener and standards-setter by bringing together stakeholders, such as citizens, residents, businesses, organisations, and academics to facilitate the achievement of their objectives and to understand multiple aspects of relevant issues.
5.  Government as a data steward by having a vast data repository to drive AI-based technologies.
6.  Government as a user and service provider by applying AI technologies, both for the public and for back-office functions.

The application of AI in the Public Sector differs from Enterprise AI, nevertheless there are some commonalities. For instance, both Public Sector AI and Enterprise AI seek to provide a better customer service experience at a lower cost on a 24/7 basis from anywhere. However, Public Sector AI is more focused on improving laws, and social and economic policies, including the development and implementation of national strategies in various disciplines, such as education, health, law enforcement, and transportation. [Berryhill et al. (2019)](#ch23.xhtml#r092) present several recommendations that are being promoted by OECD for policy makers concerning national policies and international co-operation for trustworthy AI. Admittedly, these proposals go beyond public sector innovation and transformation, but they are still relevant to assist government policy makers to explore possible opportunities for deploying AI in the public sector. These recommendations include:

*   Investing in AI research and development to support the use of AI in the public sector with a view to transforming and innovating the way they design and implement policies and services.
*   Better data management to mitigate the data silos syndrome that is so common in government and serve as a driver for AI deployment.
*    Promoting a digital ecosystem for AI by building connection points, knowledge-sharing mechanisms and ecosystems within the public sector and other stakeholders to sustain AI experimentation in government.
*   Shaping an enabling policy environment for AI by documenting how AI is used to develop AI strategies and the extent to which these strategies specifically provide for public sector transformation.
*   Building human capacity and preparing for a labour market transformation to build AI capacity among civil servants.
*   Establishing international co-operation for trustworthy AI by exploiting continuous international collaboration opportunities.

These recommendations will facilitate the transformation of public administrations by the application of AI trustworthy solutions.

## **10.3** Recognising Different AI Approaches and Importance of Data Management

AI consists of several techniques, such as Machine Learning, Neural Networks, and Deep Learning, with each technique being applied to address specific issues. Hence, the application of AI takes different approaches. The introductory chapters of this book provided clear definitions and objectives for the different aspects of AI. However, it is important to note that particularly in the Public Sector, there is a general lack of awareness about how AI works and its inherent capabilities and risks.

All too often AI is viewed as a “black box” with data going in at one end and a solution being provided at the other. Most public service officers are simply not aware of what takes place within the box and most of those who are aware have only rudimentary knowledge. One must start by recognising that AI is a disruptive field, which impacts society as a whole and drives innovation across sectors and industries. One must also recognise that the public sector provides products and services to a much wider spectrum of clients than the private sector. For instance, the private sector is segmented into marketing spheres, with each sphere being further segmented by having different companies and entities competing. The point is that no specific private enterprise or organisation caters for the whole spectrum of possible users or customers.

On the other hand, government (public sector) caters for everyone, from citizens, civil society and businesses. Therefore, for governmental policy makers and public servants in general, this poses several challenges about how to regulate, support, use, and maximise possible value from AI while mitigating its possible negative risks. This suggests that decision makers in all sectors, particularly the public sector, are required to recognise the benefits and drawbacks of AI, and to acknowledge that easier solutions may exist, which deal with a specific concern. Hence, AI should be applied when it has a distinct advantage over other possible solutions. It is therefore important that public sector decision-makers are knowledgeable about AI because its wide potential applicability across different cultures and environments will likely impact how it is implemented and applied. Thus, having basic technical knowledge about AI can assist public servants to generally determine possible AI tools to apply for a specific concern and help them negotiate better terms with suppliers.

The basis for all AI applications is the quality of the data. The chapter addressing the knowledge economy provided detailed information regarding the transformation of data to information and from information to knowledge. It was also illustrated that this transformation process contributed to the success of AI projects. The public sector has a tremendous amount of data. However, most of the governmental data is stored in data silos and not shared across departments within a ministry, let alone shared across ministries. Hence, data quality in the public sector is a major concern that needs to be addressed before undertaking major AI projects. This is not to say that AI applications cannot be implemented. However, the deployment of AI will likely be restricted to the most basic uses and certainly not for helping with building major strategies or for defining wide-ranging policies. This is likely to lead to deploying AI in a fragmented approach that may not maximise its potential. This also means that better data management systems are required to widen the range of AI applications that may be suitably deployed.

Therefore, before an AI application can be successfully deployed on a large scale, government users must ensure that a robust data management system is in place to ensure that a data repository is generated which is accurate, reliable, and relevant. This is especially the case for applications that use machine learning, where an algorithm continuously learns from the available data. Hence, most governments do not lack data and information, what is normally lacking are adequate data management systems that provide a comprehensive data repository.

## **10.4** Major Challenges Confronting Public Sector AI

Research by the World Bank (related to its clients) highlights that the main challenges confronting the public sector regarding the deployment of AI are lack of AI awareness by public sector management; inadequate policies, legislation and incentives for AI; insufficient digital data and other digital infrastructure; and lack of digital talent and skill ([World Bank, 2021](#ch23.xhtml#r098)). This supports the contention in the previous section that public sector management need to be knowledgeable about the potential of AI, have a basic understanding of digital technologies, and recognise the importance of the availability and quality of data. Furthermore, low access to digital skills was also revealed as being a major barrier to the deployment of AI in the public sector.

As at mid-2024, several nations have adopted some basic AI policies and legislation, namely USA, European Union, China, Canada and Australia. However, the USA has no comprehensive AI federal regulation framework specifically but has established several sector-specific AI-related agencies and organisations that address some of the challenges arising from the evolution of AI. Furthermore, OECD and the UN are actively involved in setting and outlining global guidelines on AI regulation. This illustrates that most countries do not have a legal framework that is so critical for deploying trustworthy AI applications safely. Moreover, these counties also lack digital processes, data collection abilities, technical skills and supporting digital infrastructure to currently benefit from the application of AI. Hence, as a priority they must focus on adopting an appropriate policy and legal framework before considering AI as a possible solution. Notwithstanding this lack of policy and legal framework, and the apparent digital divide across various countries, the World Bank have noted several AI use cases materialising or are at the piloting AI stage at their client countries. Several use cases will be discussed later in a separate section.

Like Enterprise AI, Public Sector AI is likely to impact the demand for workers in terms of an increased demand for higher skilled workers and a decreasing need for the lower skilled workers in the medium to long term. Hence, governments are likely to encounter a rising risk in job losses in both the private and public sectors, which would need to be adequately managed by the introduction of labour reskilling programmes and continuously upgrading the post-secondary school educational curriculum to reflect the changing technological environment. Additionally, the impact on developing and underdeveloped nations will likely be higher depending on their individual development status.

Several countries have modified and strengthened their legislative framework for data protection and privacy to complement and encompass AI related activities. These changes are viewed as permitting the interoperability and accessibility of government-held data and its governance, particularly for data use and reuse utilising machine learning and AI specifically to mitigate bias and inequity. Since, the legislative framework for data protection and privacy have been commonly legislated across many counties, it provides a robust basis aimed at catering for the AI ecosystem, particularly in developing countries.

As highlighted in the previous section, the lack of adequate data quality is a serious barrier for implementing AI applications successfully within the public sector. Furthermore, unnecessary government control, poor cybersecurity, and inadequate personal privacy may also pose a critical challenge. Resolving the data quality and unnecessary government control issues are difficult to resolve since they require extensive effort to ensure timely, accurate and complete data, and necessitate major reviews of internal processes. Poor cybersecurity and inadequate personal privacy are not as difficult to address since exceptional cybersecurity applications are widely available (at a cost) and personal privacy can be strengthened through legislative acts of government.

The [World Bank (2021)](#ch23.xhtml#r098) maintains that governments should allocate more investment funding in digital skills so that they may formulate suitable policies and risk management strategies for their specific circumstances. It must be recognised that escalating the digital skills of a workforce on a national basis requires long-term commitment on the part of governments, both in terms of human and financial resources. The World Bank are also of the opinion that having a policy for the ethical application of AI as being of paramount importance to manage the adverse consequences of using AI in the public sector. In fact, the next chapter will address in detail the legal and ethical aspects of AI use. Having said this, it is important to emphasise that there is an urgent need for governments to define and implement policies for addressing the issues of governance and oversight in the use of AI solutions.

Each country has its individual priorities and available resources regarding the deployment of AI and other technologies. Considering this, the World Bank suggests that countries adopt a holistic methodology for the deployment of AI rather than having a fragmented approach. This necessitates a holistic national strategy to build and maintain the crucial infrastructure, and the standardisation of systems, data, and governance frameworks to coordinate its implementation and continuous monitoring. As stated earlier in this section, a serious concern for governments in tackling AI applications is the data quality, including having an environment that supports data silos. Systems that are based on a data-silo approach can never achieve interoperability to truly provide effective technological solutions that are so necessary for increasing the living standards of citizens of the respective countries.

## **10.5** Emerging Global Public Sector AI Landscape

The previous sections have demonstrated that AI is quickly changing many facets of people’s everyday lives. The public sector is contributing to this change by having governments recognising the benefits of AI and upgrading AI as a national priority. This is reflected by increased AI investments and compiling regulatory regimens to cater for the constant growth of AI in the wider social and business community.

A government is the biggest entity in any nation and is therefore able to leverage the tremendous potential of AI to transform the public sector into an effective organisation. This may be achieved by reviewing and changing the processes for defining and implementing policies for delivering services to its constituents, civil society, and commercial enterprises. It is this context that one needs to understand the emerging global public sector AI landscape. The innovative application of AI and its transformational impact on the public sector is critical for governments to confront the continuous growth of the demands and expectations from their constituents, civil society, and commercial enterprises. Moreover, as nations climb the development scale, these demands and expectations are constantly escalating in complexity.

In this scenario, interoperability of public services becomes essential, where standards, protocols, technologies, and mechanisms that allow data to flow between diverse systems require very minimal human intervention. This allows diverse systems to talk to each other and share information in real time. As highlighted in the previous section, this also depends on having highly integrated holistic systems that are supported by high quality data (i.e., timely, accurate, reliable, consistent, and relevant for its intended use) across government. This permits AI to be integrated into the complete policymaking and service design cycle. Hence, as AI tools such as machine learning and deep learning develop, more administrative and process-driven processes will be automated, enhancing greatly public sector efficiency and releasing public service employees to focus on other essential tasks.

Additionally, such developments will allow senior government officials to enhance their understanding of the various circumstances and help them to make better decisions by knowing and predicting the demands of their diverse customers (i.e., constituents, civil society and commercial enterprises). This will facilitate government to make more precise and equitable decisions. Many national governments are in the process or have defined their AI strategies with the focus on instigating economic development through research and R&D funding. However, the most essential and fundamental principle that underline these governmental AI strategies is the successful development of trustworthy AI.

OECD have proposed that international collaboration as a key principle for the successful development of trustworthy AI ([Berryhill et al., 2019](#ch23.xhtml#r092)). According to [Berryhill et al. (2019)](#ch23.xhtml#r092), a commitment to such collaboration is reflected in several declarations, namely:

*   G20 AI Principles that were based directly from the OECD Recommendation (G20 Ministerial Statement on Trade and Digital Economy: [www.mofa.go.jp/files/000486596.pdf](http://www.mofa.go.jp/files/000486596.pdf)).
*   In 2018, all EU member countries signed the Declaration of Cooperation on AI committing cooperation to boost European AI capacity and adoption, address socio-economic challenges and ethics, and ensure an adequate legal and ethical framework ([Berryhill et al., 2019](#ch23.xhtml#r092)).
*   The EU member states also committed to making AI available and beneficial to public administrations, to sharing best practices in procuring and using AI in government, to implementing open data practices, and to maximise the impact of investments at EU and national levels, encourage synergies and cooperation across the EU ([Berryhill et al., 2019](#ch23.xhtml#r092)).
*   Ten governments from the Nordic-Baltic Region signed the Declaration on AI pledging to improve skills development and access to data, and to develop ethical guidelines ([Berryhill et al., 2019](#ch23.xhtml#r092)).

The above demonstrates that most national government AI strategies contain obligations for ensuring secure designed and implemented AI systems that are ethical and trustworthy. Additionally, [Berryhill et al. (2019)](#ch23.xhtml#r092) note that most strategies also promote the strengthening of the national AI talent through educational programmes and training and for applying AI to innovate and transform the public sector.

Research suggests that many public sector administrations already apply AI in a range of fields, such as smart recognition, supporting various assessment processes, environmental protection, law enforcement, and healthcare. However, most AI projects appear to be based on the initiative of individuals (not necessarily from a senior management level) who have an adequate degree of AI awareness to pursue such projects.

This type of environment does not support the interoperability of systems, processes, services and organisations, despite the fact interoperability may be recognised as a critical factor by the individuals concerned. This is viewed as a serious weakness by public administrations, and most have taken appropriate action to remedy the situation by consolidating the AI strategic process, emphasising the importance of the interoperability aspect for supporting sustainable AI-based. The main features emerging from the global public sector AI Landscape include the following applications (Tangi et. al., 2023):

*    Experimentation with AI in government by identifying certain AI projects to discover the benefits and potential to be exploited from AI. As highlighted above AI cannot depend on individual initiatives but must be an organisational objective by increasing the general awareness of AI throughout public administration.
*   Collaboration across sectors. AI can be applied as a tool to improve interoperability between public organisations and private entities through public-private partnerships and facilitated through innovation hubs and labs.
*   Promoting cross-government focus groups, networks and communities to support suitable systems methodologies. Applying AI-based applications that support interoperability poses significant challenges for the public sector that include scarcity of skills and expertise, cross-organisational interoperability, complexity, system integration concerns, compliance with regulatory regimes, financial constraints, and data quality.
*   Promoting robust data management process. AI solutions are dependent on the availability and quality of data, but they can also contribute to increase data quality. However, as an initial step, public administrations must implement a comprehensive data management process to have a quality data baseline.
*   Legal, regulatory and ethical compliance. This is a critical factor that requires a collaborative approach between public sector organisations, legal experts, technology providers and other relevant stakeholders to assist organisations navigate the legal landscape associated with implementing AI.
*   Automation of everyday government processes to improve efficiency. Public sector employees conduct many different tasks often of a routine nature leaving them insufficient time to focus on finding ways to improve public services. AI provides an opportunity to conduct these routine tasks and release public sector employees to perform more worthwhile functions.
*   Applying AI to assist in governmental decision-making. AI is being used by several governments to help public administrators to evaluate various policies by predicting their potential impact on target users. AI is also being used in designing and implementing preventative measures such as flood barriers and early warning systems. AI-driven solutions have been found to be critical for predicting possible disasters and enabling authorities to take timely action that can significantly mitigate the impact of such events.
*   Strategic management, harnessing government data for designing public and private services. Public administers are applying AI to help them define their operational strategies by harnessing their data to design customised services and predicting the demand for new possible services through services trend analysis. Furthermore, non-sensitive personal data is being made available to the private sector as a key input to Enterprise AI.
*   Provision of guidance on the transparent and ethical use of public sector AI. Having legal consistency among various national and international systems creates difficulties to develop common protocols for data exchange. Often legal concerns occur when public administrations are required to interchange data between them.
*   Enhancement of public service capacity through training, recruitment, tools and funding. A critical challenge for public sector AI is the need to acquire the essential skills and capabilities to develop, implement and maintain AI-based solutions. However, governments recognise that upskilling civil servants is vital for ensuring that government entities operate effectively. It is also widely accepted that training and various types of development programs help public servants acquire exposure to new techniques and technologies, build their leadership skills, and remain current on evolving policies and regulations.

Being aware of the emerging global Public Sector AI landscape will help individual public service administrations to improve their level of readiness for the initiation of AI applications or to fine tune their defined AI strategies.

## **10.6** Implementing Public Sector AI

There is no doubt that Public Sector AI has significant potential in all types of public sector fields. It is also evident that implementing Public Sector AI will encounter many challenges and will have considerable implications that government leaders and public servants need to consider when determining whether AI can contribute to the achievement of their missions and specifically assist them in addressing the various problems that frequently confront them.

[Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) of the previous chapter provided an effective and comprehensive user-friendly approach for implementing Enterprise AI. This framework is also applicable to the deployment of Public Sector AI at every government level (i.e., national, state, or municipal). Therefore, the focus of this section will be on the challenges and practical aspects that are related to the public sector. An important phase in Public Sector AI is building support and having management champions that enthusiastically carry the torch for the deployment of AI. However, building support for AI within the public sector is contingent on identifying a clear vision and defining the practical implications for use of AI in the public sector to better serve citizens, civil society and businesses.

Governments need to encourage its senior management in the public service to be receptive to AI by providing the necessary freedom for flexibility and experimentation to expedite speedy learning. Once this foundation is established, public service management will be required to formulate a policy for determining whether AI is the best solution for a specific problem and provide the necessary instruments for identifying and devoting awareness to such problems. This may possibly be achieved by understanding the needs of their diverse customers and identifying high impact use cases to determine areas of opportunity.

However, it is important that such policies are implemented after building and setting up of cross-functional team(s). Several cross-functional teams may be required to cater for each specific government ministry, since it would not be practical to have one national cross-functional team. Each cross-functional team will consist of multi-disciplinary and diverse members to assist in identifying AI opportunities and to promote the development and deployment of AI assignments that are ethical and effective. The cross-functional team must ensure that AI is developed (i.e., designed and deployed) according to a trustworthy, fair, and accountable methodology that recognises trade-offs, mitigates risk and bias, and guarantees an appropriate role for humans. Hence, during the AI development life cycle a persistent effort must be made to focus on users and individuals who may be impacted by the AI applications.

[Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) highlights that building data fluency is a key implementation task, since it makes AI-driven innovation possible. Data is the fundamental basis for AI. Therefore, there is the need to assess the data preparedness status and develop a data strategy that allows governments to access robust, timely, accurate and complete data. This must be achieved through an approach that safeguards privacy and adheres to societal and ethical standards.

Implementing AI on a governmental scale requires a high degree of knowhow and expertise, which will likely consist of a consortium of public and private sector talent, and needed products, services, and infrastructure. This consortium will probably be initially inclined towards having a greater participation from the private sector, but as the internal capabilities within a public administration are developed there will be a greater reliance on the internal public service structure. However, such decisions are country and context-specific and are contingent on the explicit vision of the senior public servants at the time, including the budgeted allocations to ICT, specifically AI projects.

Being fully dependent on the private sector, particularly for AI projects, would be a strategic oversight. It is critical that governments through their public servants have a structure that supports at a minimum, a baseline level of data fluency and knowledge of data science, including related AI tools to avoid governing complications by having a situation where suppliers have complete power over the government. Therefore, the public service should define a human resource development plan to give public service employees the opportunity to develop relevant capabilities to support the AI initiatives and to ascertain the required future competencies that are likely from future public servants. This would form a robust and healthy basis for having a collaborate Public Sector AI deployment approach between the public and private sectors.

Governments should be aware that there will likely be various shifts regarding AI in the future. Hence, the public service must continuously improve their AI models and processes. They need to research and explore the changing AI landscape environment and take a proactive stand by predicting possibilities and take immediate preparatory action to keep a step ahead of developments (or at least not falling behind). This will ensure that government exploits and leverages its AI investment to maximise the inherent benefits of AI and mitigate its potential risks.

### **10.6.1** Practical Implications for Implementation Public Sector AI Strategies

Research has revealed that the application of AI by public administrations is growing, with several organisations using AI in their daily operations. Chatbots are being successfully used to assist citizens with typical income taxation and social services enquiries and are helping companies with income tax and value added tax management. This has resulted in a significant reduction in telephone and email exchanges. AI is also being used as a legal dictation system, which allows an automatic transcription of voice notes of legal text. This application is capable of transcribing correct legal terminology at a rate of over 150 words per minute. This application reduces the tedious effort for public service employees and allows them to focus on more challenging tasks.

As stated previously, the literature review revealed that AI poses several challenges. These challenges include trustworthiness, cooperation, procurement, data quality, skills, and human resources. Most of these challenges correspond with Enterprise AI, except for procurement. Procurement appears to be a customary concern for the public sector and not just restricted to AI related acquisitions.

However, ensuring a trustworthy use of AI is viewed as a critical challenge for the public sector, driven by the natural concern about the impact of AI systems regarding the lack of accuracy and bias, and inadequate supervision that may impact the citizens’ health, safety or their fundamental rights. Hence, an AI application needs to be vigorously and extensively tested to ensure that it performs as intended and does not risk harming citizens. Moreover, every effort must be made to mitigate the perception of untrustworthiness because resistance to using AI is very likely if untrustworthiness becomes an issue. Having adequate mechanisms available to public administrations ensuring the ethical use of AI would be helpful in this regard.

There is a vital need for a suitable collaboration agreement in developing and using AI between public administrations and with the private sector. As stated previously, competencies and resources involved for successfully developing and deploying AI systems require the collaboration of the public service, universities, and research institutions, and private sector entities, particularly with start-ups who may present fresh ideas. Cooperation may also involve employing a centralised approach for the provision of AI services and products with different authorities using them at their own rate depending on their individual level of preparedness.

Procurement has always been a concern for public administrations, but it becomes a lot worse for AI applications namely due to a lack of AI knowledgeable and competent resources, and its inherent technical complexity. The difficulty is not the public sector procurement procedures but detailing the technical specifications and describing the requirements in terms of the quality and accuracy level of the output, the explainability and transparency of the algorithm, and the algorithm’s non-discriminatory quality. Outsourcing AI technical specifications and related needs is not desirable due to the possibility of conflict of interest. Additionally, public administrations need innovative scalable solutions, prevent supplier lock-in and acquiring non-explainable solutions, and inhibit fraudulent behaviours by the supplier. These concerns confirm the argument that public sector employees need to attain expertise is AI technology through exposure to AI techniques, be well-informed in relevant AI regulatory regimes (if any), and initiating formal development programmes.

Another practical implication for implementing public sector AI strategies is the collection of huge volumes of high-quality data that are utilised to train the AI systems. The higher the data quality the less likelihood of having biased AI systems. [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34) illustrates that assessing the data preparedness of the organisation and defining the data strategy precedes the definition of the AI development strategy. However, it comes after building and establishing the cross-functional team, since human resources are required to generate the data repository for training the AI models and algorithms. Other human resources with the appropriate skills are also required from the various business units to train and test the AI algorithms.

The above issues have focused on a technical and resource centricity of implementing public sector AI strategies. However, a most essential objective is citizen centricity, where AI is brought closer to the citizens, civil society, and businesses by encouraging smart communities or cities. All too often public sector AI systems are conveyed for negative or restrictive applications, such as fraud detection, surveillance and law enforcement. It is important that the public sector conveys positive implications, such as better customer experiences in relationship management and for the provision of services on 24/7 basis from everywhere.

Bringing AI closer to the citizen and businesses has its unique complexities, not in terms of the applications themselves (and the technical support) but also ensuring a sufficient penetration rate by public sector customers (i.e., citizens, civil society and commercial entities). There is no point in having a very beneficial citizen centric AI application, but no one uses it. The main concern is related to digital literacy that enables public sector customers to access data and related AI applications, and to understand the outcomes presented by the AI application. This concern is somewhat greater for the older generation (e.g., pre-1970s).

It is important that public administrations actively engage with the public conveying an assurance of having trustworthy AI applications based on a robust governance framework. Public administration customers must be viewed as having a central role in the development of AI-based public services and applications from beginning to end, and not just as users. However, this requires robust and resilient partnerships and collaboration with different relevant stakeholders ranging from having reliable and user-friendly AI solutions supported by a comprehensive communication strategy to involve public sector customers in the development process and educating them on the use of the deployed AI applications. The development of reliable and user-friendly AI solutions can be based on a rapid application development (RAD) methodology by having a “toolbox” with solutions that can be replicated and supported by standard processes to ensure compliance with established regulations. This avoids a situation of reinventing the wheel syndrome.

## **10.7** Public Sector AI Use Cases

Many governments have recognised the tremendous potential that AI provides for a more effective public administration across the public sector. Furthermore, this recognition has been translated by governments through their definition of comprehensive long-term AI strategies to enhance how governments engage with and serve their constituents. However, research has shown that AI is not just at the strategic planning phase for many governments but has moved rapidly to the practical deployment phase with the collaboration of educational institutions of higher learning (Universities and Technology Institutes) and private sector AI providers.

For instance, the Biden-Harris Administration, was dedicated to ensuring that the United States of America (USA) took a lead in safe, secure, and trustworthy AI innovation to harness the opportunities of AI while mitigating its risks, itemise over 700 applications that were deployed across federal government ([https://ai.gov/ai-use-cases/](https://ai.gov)). According to the Biden-Harris Administration, the USA federal government was leveraging AI to better serve the public across a wide array of use cases, such as healthcare, transportation, the environment, and benefits delivery, and establishing strong guardrails to ensure its use of AI keeps people safe and does not violate their rights.

[Table 10.1](#ch23.xhtml#t20) provides an indication of several AI use cases that have been implemented in numerous countries. There is no doubt that AI usage provides important benefits related to back-office automation since it is viewed as being an indispensable enabling technology for government entities encountering continuous pressure to provide higher levels of service to a growing population with fewer human capital resources. A particular AI application uses historical data from application forms completed by millions of previous applicants to generate predictive scores to expedite social security benefits claims. While other public administration AI applications optimise customer service approvals and improve engagement, increasing the speed and quality of service delivery, transforming employee work experiences, and decreasing workloads. In various use cases, Chatbots are automating interactions by providing a detailed knowledge base for citizens with multilingual support and collect citizen feedback on a large scale for use in better public policy making.

| --- | --- |
| Administration || Digitising paper documents and speed up claims processing and back-office automation. |
| --- | --- |
| Benefits Administration || Optimise service approvals and improve customer engagement, increasing the speed and quality of service delivery, and transforming employee work experiences and decreasing workloads. |
| Benefits Administration || Using historical data from application forms completed by millions of previous applicants to generate predictive scores to expedite social security disability benefits claims. |
| Customer Relations || Chatbots automate interactions by providing a detailed knowledge base for citizens with multilingual support and collect citizen feedback on a large scale. |
| Enforcement || Enforcement of policies that result in better large-scale infrastructure monitoring to fight tax evasion and unlawful property changes. |
| Environment || Optimise street lights; reduce traffic congestion; automatically alert authorities in case of any incident; and optimise energy consumption. |
| Environment || AI-enabled remote sensors monitor water usage and detect leaks in the water supply network to conserve water and reduce waste. |
| Healthcare || Early disease detection and prevention, and clinical decision support. |
| Healthcare || Analyse vast volume of biomedical data including genomic, imaging, and clinical data to fast-track discovery of new ways to prevent, diagnose and treat diseases. |
| Healthcare || Identify patterns, effects, and mitigation options for issues related to public health and climate change. |
| Healthcare || Optimising medical records management by analysing historical records and performing robot-assisted surgery. |
| Healthcare || Interpret the images to detect counterfeit pharmaceuticals. |
| Policy Making || Analytics on public data to identify emerging issues related to their regions and constituents. |
| Policy Making || Enhance public policy to improve citizens’ quality of life by predicting insecurity risk for housing, food, addictions, and mental health. |
