AI is making headways in the enforcement of policies that result in better large-scale infrastructure monitoring to fight tax evasion and unlawful property changes. In human resources utilisation, AI is being deployed to gain a deeper insight into how employees engage with benefits programs, enhancing the employers’ ability to make more informed benefit investment decisions that optimise employee satisfaction and total benefits spend efficiency. Intelligent personalised recommendation engines are also being applied to bridge the gap between optimised offerings and broad employee awareness and education, leading to higher program engagement from employees.

AI is also being used by several governments to define environmental policies, such as gaining a deeper understanding of climate change causes and impacts. Predictive analytics, computer vision, machine learning, and simulation models are assisting in monitoring and predicting the impact of climate change on weather patterns, environmental health, and human emissions. This is enabling governments to define their respective policy positions regarding their global efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change, and to create more resilient health systems. Other AI applications to enhance environmental conditions include the optimisation of streetlights; reducing traffic congestion; automatically alerting authorities of any traffic related incidents; and optimising energy consumption. Moreover, AI-enabled remote sensors are being used to monitor water consumption and detect leaks in the water supply network to safeguard water resources and reduce waste.

Healthcare has always been a priority area for AI applications. AI is being used to enhance the knowledge of the key health contributing factors using trend analysis of population risk factors combined with local policies and programs to give an insight of the social and environmental factors that most impact people’s health. Additionally, AI is being applied to better predict the impact of proposed health policies by using machine learning to leverage health data and the known local risk factors to predict the impact of proposed policies and inform targeted legislation to achieve specific population health goals. The analysis of vast volumes of biomedical data including genomic, imaging, and clinical data is being utilised to fast-track discovery of new ways to prevent, diagnose and treat diseases. Moreover, natural language processing is making complex biomedical data more available to medical professionals to enable greater use of the ongoing research and data being collected. Machine learning algorithms are also providing insights from immense data sets to uncover new disease trends and drugs to improve diagnostic and treatment capabilities.

On an individual level, AI applications are being used to track a patients’ health in real-time by monitoring weight, height, blood glucose, stress levels, heart rate, and other indicators and feeding this information to AI healthcare systems, which can inform doctors of likely risks. Other applications include, optimising medical records management by analysing historical records, performing robot-assisted surgery, and interpreting medicinal label images to detect counterfeit pharmaceuticals.

AI is playing an important role in the governments’ policy making process by identify emerging issues related to their districts and constituents. Speedier detection of changing societal trends allows governments to alter policies accordingly. This enhanced policy planning efficiency and effectiveness is making it easier for public administrations to understand expectations and target major problems. The improvement in policy making decisions is positively impacting the constituents’ quality of life by predicting insecurity risk for housing, food, addictions, and mental health.

AI is also being used to strengthen cyber-security by monitoring abnormal network activity and entry points; identifying likely data vulnerabilities and boost access restrictions; enhancing accuracy of intrusion detection systems; simulating cyber-attacks in controlled conditions to identify system vulnerabilities; and automate system patching and security updates. Cyber AI solutions are assisting governments and enterprises to manage cutting-edge cyber workflows by incorporating network behavioural modelling, malware detection, and credential misuse detection. A powerful feature of these security solutions is detecting domain-generated algorithms (DGA). A DGA algorithm generates large numbers of new domain names that cybercriminals and botnet operators use to change the target domain for launching malware attacks. Therefore, this feature determines whether a domain is likely to have been generated by an algorithm, rather than a person, by reverse-engineering and analysing other frequently used techniques found in DGAs.

Some countries have implemented AI to ascertain possible export markets by analysing current trade patterns. By specifying a particular class of products they produce and the markets they currently export to, this application applies a machine learning algorithm to analyse product-specific trade and tariff data, economy-level macroeconomic and governance data to detect and compare markets the user should consider. AI is being successfully used by governments to considerably mitigate road safety issues. Currently, 1.19 million people annually are killed on roadways around the world, with road traffic crashes being the leading cause of death for individuals aged 5 and 29. The AI application using computer vision, object detection, drone tracking, and camera-based traffic systems, identifies areas susceptible to accidents and recommend additional road safety measures to prevent future mishaps. Additionally, data-driven analyses using machine learning algorithms assist traffic flow, preventing accidents and congestion, monitoring logistics, and increasing road safety.

AI applications are being used to assist town planners recognise and respond to emerging trends in demographic data, such as population growth in particular districts and demographic shifts (such as age or income) that are likely to impact demand for government services. Urban planning and development are being enhanced through AI applications by analysing environmental factors, demographic data, traffic patterns, and other data to make more informed decisions about infrastructure projects and zoning regulations.

As illustrated above, AI complements human expertise by vastly improving the way that public administrators conduct their tasks. There is no doubt that AI applications aid governments to move from low-value to high-value efforts and focus more on their core responsibilities. This is achieved by mitigating or removing tedious tasks and uncovering new insights from the collected data. Information overload is a concern for public servants; however, AI is helping them to make sense of the vast and increasing amount of available data giving them new insights and generating forecasts to help them make better policy decisions.

## **10.8** Public Sector AI Implications

This chapter has illustrated that Public Sector AI will likely have several implications regarding how public administrations will be managed. It must be recognised that the development and deployment of AI in the public sector involves different stakeholders. However, a fundamental issue insisted by all stakeholders is having trustworthy AI. This implies that trustworthy AI applications for government entails the involvement of multiple collaborators within and outside public administrations. From an internal aspect, the participation of policy specialists, legal and technical units, and competent decision-makers are essential. On the other hand, from an external aspect, the contribution of private sector organisations, AI specialists, and civil society are needed to offer a multidisciplinary input for defining trustworthy AI-powered innovative public services.

One cannot be complacent about having trustworthiness as a primary objective of AI use cases since there are Public Sector AI applications that might be classified as high-risk. Government entities cannot risk allowing the implementation of non-transparent and biased AI applications, which might result in inequitable decisions, since government’s own legitimacy can be at risk. Therefore, it is important that governments implement AI applications according to robust and secure ethical frameworks, which are founded on suitable legislative and governance regimes.

Public Sector AI specialists suggest that public administrators should first conduct pilot AI projects and increasing scale at a later stage. However, public administrators should always deploy AI (even at the experimental stage) according to a strategic AI roadmap. Reference is made once again to the framework for deploying an Enterprise AI system at [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34). It must be acknowledged that AI projects in both the public and private sectors need some flexibility for experimentation. This will enable the respective practitioners to learn from their mistakes and successes to increase the likelihood of overall success at the scale-up stage. Nevertheless, any AI development activity should always be within a robust governance and ethical framework, having reusable modules, and driven by the appropriate data quality to suit the specific AI purpose.

Concurrently, with the AI pilot phase, public administrations should define and implement an upskilling training programme for public sector employees. The intensity of the training programme for these employees is contingent on the anticipated role they will play in the AI process. In other words, some will need to have a high level of AI technical skills, while many others might only need a sound knowledge of AI awareness. The AI revolution is here to stay and therefore public administrations need to be well prepared. This preparedness status is like other transformational developments that public administrations have confronted in the past, whether through traditional computerisation or administrative approaches, such as the implementation of accrual accounting processes from the traditional cash accounting systems. Every major public administration reform in the past required trustworthy solutions and the general upskilling of the public servant employees; AI is no different. However, AI is more sensitive to ethical issues due to its extraordinary self-learning capabilities through machine or deep learning methods. Therefore, public servants need to be well prepared to ensure the correct interpretation and oversight of the AI application output that drive future public services.

Interoperability has always been an issue for ICT development. ICT made it possible to link organisations and achieve cross-organisational collaboration through efficient data access routines and responsive data transmission on a 24/7 basis from anywhere. Additionally, the Year-2000 millennium bug had highlighted that those organisations had to concern themselves not only with their own critical supply chain but the critical supply chains of their suppliers. Interoperability refers to the degree to which a software system, devices and applications can connect and communicate with other entities in a coordinated manner without effort from the end user.

While the concept of interoperability has been widely accepted by the private sector, it has proven to be a serious challenge and concern for governments. However, the growth of public services digitalisation, the increased awareness of big data, and the realisation of new technologies have created a suitable environment for governments to seek and achieve interoperability. This does not mean that the challenges have suddenly disappeared. What it means is the realisation by public administrations of the tremendous potential that interoperability may bring to effective governmental operations. Governments are realising that the envisaged challenges are now mitigated and manageable by adopting AI-based solutions to support the interoperability concept.

Interoperability has made it possible to implement AI applications based on smart recognition or to support assessment processes in many public administration areas, such as public services, health and environmental protection, amongst others. Public Sector AI is flourishing in many jurisdictions and will continue to thrive as long as public administrations support several key principles in deploying their AI applications. These key principles are interoperability, trustworthiness, transparency, upgrading skills of public servants and maintaining high data quality.

## **10.9** Public Sector AI’s Impact on Society

As has been illustrated throughout this chapter, AI has promptly become an integral part of people’s lives that has transformed several aspects of society providing far-reaching opportunities. However, this potential brings with it great challenges and apprehensions about AI’s impact on society, particularly the economy, employment, healthcare, education, and ethics. [Behailu (2023)](#ch23.xhtml#r091) argues that the development and implementation of AI has raised important ethical, social, and economic issues that need attention.

Some researchers view AI as part of the second machine age in which machines are replacing human brain power, and contrast this with a first period of industrialisation in which machines replaced human and animal muscle-power ([Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014](#ch23.xhtml#r093)). While others have expressed their concern about the susceptibility of jobs to digitalisation resulting in massive job losses ([Frey and Osborne, 2017](#ch23.xhtml#r096)). The future of employment and job growth is anticipated to be more focused in high-skill STEM jobs, while middle- and low-skill jobs (such as food service, production work, and office support tasks) will likely decline considerably. Hence, there will likely be a shift in the labour market where certain job categories might experience more growth than others. These paradigms provide a general view of the economic implications of AI.

AI is also likely to cause intense social transformations in healthcare and education. Use cases cited previously illustrate that AI applications are likely to improve healthcare outcomes through predictive analytics and personalised treatments. Additionally, AI applications in the education field is rapidly advancing through AI-Driven learning experiences by adjusting to the needs of the individual student. A concern regarding these advances is whether the AI applications related to healthcare and education would be available to all, or whether they will be available only to those who can afford them. One should be aware that some countries provide free healthcare and education to all. However, there are many countries where healthcare and education are only within reach for the affluent members of society.

There is no doubt that AI has become increasingly integrated into society, but ethical concerns need to be addressed. The ethical and legal issues will be discussed in detail in the next chapter. However, it is essential to stress that AI developments and deployment must adhere to strict ethical standards, particularly in relation to data privacy and security, bias, fairness, and transparency. Each national government will need to assess its existing status regarding the deployment of AI applications and define the necessary policies to suit its specific needs and that of its constituents. Furthermore, governments must also endeavour to collaborate with each other to ensure that AI’s potential is exploited for the benefit of all and any challenges encountered are resolved and concerns mitigated, and if possible, eliminated.

## **10.10** Practical Public Sector AI Applications

Public Sector AI applications are gaining extensive attention because they impact a wide spectrum of a nation’s population. Public Sector AI systems have an enormous effect on how public sector organisations conduct their operations and provide their services to a wide range of individuals, businesses, and society in general. This section provides some useful public sector AI applications that are having a significant favourable impact on the way governmental organisations operate and how they provide the respective services to their clients.

### **10.10.1** Case Study 1: Healthcare Effectiveness and Customer Satisfaction at a Public Hospital

The management of a large public hospital conducted an operations review with the objective of modernising the way the hospital provides its services to the public using technology, in particular AI. The hospital was confronted with several challenges that included staff shortages mainly due to high turnover as a result of work pressure and burnout; unacceptable waiting periods for elective (non-urgent) treatment such as cataract surgery or a knee replacement; shortage of medical supplies, including medicines; and general customer dissatisfaction, amongst other grievances.

To address these challenges and increase it healthcare effectiveness to its customers, the hospital management established a taskforce to implement the various recommendations of the operations review. A key recommendation was a substantial investment in modern technology, including AI. This investment was viewed as an effective way of addressing the various identified difficulties. The taskforce consisted of a full-time chairperson (supported by administrative and technical staff) and five senior medical professionals on a part time basis. The task force also had the authority to establish full-time dedicated technical teams (internally or outsourced) as required to implement the strategic measures approved by the taskforce.

The identified concerns were examined in detail by applying root-cause analysis and Ishikawa diagrams amongst other methods. Root-cause analysis is closely linked to service and product quality. It reveals in a very explicit way the source of a problem, in terms of when, where, and why the problem has occurred. Thus, pointing towards an appropriate approach to resolving the concern. [Figure 10.1](#ch23.xhtml#f35) illustrates a simple and effective method for identifying the root cause to a problem. It should be noted that before a problem can be addressed, it must be explicitly identified. A more detailed approach to identifying complex problems is the Ishikawa diagram (refer to [Figure 10.2](#ch23.xhtml#f36)). The Ishikawa diagram or the fishbone diagram is often used in the analysis of processes as a causal analysis tool to identify the many possible causes for a problem or situation.

![Figure 10.1 Root Cause Analysis: Five-Whys Approach.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C010_001.jpg)

**Figure 10.1** Root Cause Analysis: Five-Whys Approach.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f35b)

![Figure 10.2 Constructing an Ishikawa Diagram.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C010_002.jpg)

**Figure 10.2** Constructing an Ishikawa Diagram.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f36b)

The Ishikawa diagram was applied to structure brainstorming sessions to identify possible causes. This method was able to generate added examples of root causes and enabled the team to swiftly detect if the root cause is found multiple times in the same or different causal tree. It also permitted them to view all causes concurrently and provided helpful visualisation for displaying concerns. Furthermore, this approach provided a highly structured method and an excellent way for conducting the brainstorming sessions to detect the possible causes of a problem and sorting thoughts about the causes into suitable categories. The Ishikawa diagram is often used in conjunction with the Five-Whys tool (illustrated at [Figure 10.1](#ch23.xhtml#f35)).

The identification of the root cause to the problems and respective solutions provided a sound basis for defining a strategy that did not exceed five years. To implement the defined strategy, the task force applied a meticulous methodology illustrated by [Figure 10.3](#ch23.xhtml#f37). It shows that there were two concurrent processes, both starting with the definition of the defined strategy and ending with the outcome of the strategy. Each process branch had a distinct focus, one related to strategy implementation (action execution) and the other focusing on the performance (critical success factors and KPIs). Furthermore, the focus of performance monitoring is through the KPIs. For example, from a critical success factor (CSF) and KPI perspective, the CSFs focus on specific aspects, while the KPIs related to each specific aspect establish the target performance level.

![Figure 10.3 Relationship between Strategic Planning, CSFs and KPIs.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C010_003.jpg)

**Figure 10.3** Relationship between Strategic Planning, CSFs and KPIs.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f37b)

The CSF approach was applied for each identified initiative related to the various problem areas. The CSF methodology is based on the concept that a critical success factor is a high-level objective feature that is vital for an initiative (project) to achieve its mission. Therefore, the defined CSFs signified those areas that had to receive special and continual attention to bring about high performance and included those concerns that were most important to the organisation’s operating activities and to its future success. CSFs were expressed as action aphorisms that defined the method, desired outcome, and the action to be taken (e.g., waiting for elective treatment, such as cataract surgery or a knee replacement no longer than 12 weeks from referral to their first treatment). [Figure 10.4](#ch23.xhtml#f38) illustrates the CSF framework that was used, which consisted of five critical processes, each one being related to the other:

![Figure 10.4 Critical Success Factors Methodology Framework.⏎](html/images/9781041102168_C010_004.jpg)

**Figure 10.4** Critical Success Factors Methodology Framework.[⏎](#ch23.xhtml#f38b)

1.  Objectives: Where do we want our organisation to go? This is the overall target of what the organisation is trying to achieve.
2.  Strategy: How are we going to get there? These are measures that will be taken by the organisation to achieve the overall target.
3.  Identify the CSFs: What must be done absolutely right? These are the tasks that support the attainment of the measures being taken by the organisation to achieve the overall target.
4.   Define the KPIs: How do we measure if we are getting there? These are the measures that are established to evaluate whether the tasks are being achieved.
5.  Determine the critical information set: What information should be collected to track progress of each individual CSF. Thus, the information collected should be sufficient to verify whether the KPIs are being achieved.

The above methodology enabled the taskforce to implement various identified AI initiatives that were highlighted by the root cause analysis and defined in the strategy. Various AI tools and applications were evaluated and selected for implementation in critical healthcare areas as follows:

1.  Medical Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations. IBM Watson was able to assist healthcare professionals in making accurate diagnoses and treatment recommendations. Its capabilities enabled it to analyse patient data, including medical records, laboratory results, and various research papers, to generate insights and suggest personalised treatment plans. Watson for Oncology assisted oncologists by postulating evidence-based treatment options personalised to individual patient profiles, leading to more effective and targeted cancer care.
2.  Patient Engagement and Support. IBM Watson provided AI-driven solutions, such as virtual health assistants that improved patient engagement and support. These virtual assistants were able to interact with patients, answer their healthcare queries, provided medication reminders, and offered personalised health advice based on their medical history and preferences. This personalised care enhanced patient outcomes resulting in higher patient satisfaction and also encouraged proactive healthcare management.
3.  Healthcare Operations Optimisation. IBM Watson enabled the hospital management to analyse operational data, identify inefficiencies, and make data-driven decisions to improve resource allocation, reduce waiting times, and improve overall workflow efficiency. This resulted in a more streamlined healthcare delivery system and substantial cost savings.
4.  Medicinals Inventory Management. This phase consisted of integrating an AI inventory model and upgrading the existing inventory management systems. The key issues to be addressed were related to attaining optimal stock levels and identifying the reordering strategies that were to be implemented. This eliminated stockouts and overstock situations and decreased the holding costs.
5.  Resource Scheduling and Preventative Equipment Maintenance. AI models were implemented for resource scheduling, including a predictive element and assisted in the preventative maintenance of the medical equipment and facilities. This ensured the maximisation of medical equipment and facilities that resulted in a reduction in waiting lists for medical interventions and enhanced patient satisfaction.

Several AI algorithms were applied in the above models, such as Monte Carlo methods to simulate and analyse multiple scenarios, such as the probable outcomes of different inventory strategies and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), which is a recurrent neural network used for sequence prediction problems like stock level forecasting. Other AI predictive models focused on resource scheduling and equipment maintenance, such as Linear Programming, which was useful for resource allocation.

### **10.10.2** Case Study 2: Urban Traffic Management

A metropolitan authority was under pressure by persistent grievances regarding traffic congestion and the need to urgently address the growing problem. Traffic had become insanely unmanageable with the arterial roads being saturated by light and heavy vehicles. Thus, traffic congestion had developed into a pressing issue that was affecting the city in various ways. This metropolitan area witnesses a significant amount of traffic on a daily basis, leading to long delays, frustration, and increased levels of air pollution. While traffic congestion was recognised as a common feature of metropolitan cities, it had become unmanageable, impacting both cargo and passenger transport.

A study commissioned by the competent government transport authority found that the growing problem of traffic congestion was attributed to several factors, including population growth, rapid urbanisation, a need for a more effective public transportation systems, careless driving such as the use of mobiles while driving, and an increase in the number of private vehicles on the roads. The outcome of these factors was frequent gridlocks on major roads, making it difficult for people to commute to work, access services, or deliver goods in a timely manner. In terms of cargo transport, the congestion on the roads was leading to a significant impact on the economy. Delays in the delivery of goods was resulting in increased costs for businesses that would eventually affect the prices of goods and services. This, in turn had the potential to negatively impact consumers and lead to a decrease in overall economic productivity. Furthermore, traffic congestion affected passenger transport, since commuters tended to spend more time on the roads, leading to frustration, stress, and a decrease in the overall quality of life. This concern was worsened by the need for a more reliable and efficient public transportation options, forcing many residents to rely on private vehicles that only compounded the issue of congestion further.

The government transport authority appointed a taskforce to examine the findings of the commissioned study and to develop a strategic transport plan. Additionally, once the strategic transport plan was approved, the taskforce was to be given the remit to implement it. After examining the commissioned study and its conclusions regarding the main causes of the traffic congestion, the taskforce set about finding solutions to mitigate the concerns. The taskforce recognised that the traffic congestion concerns could never be eliminated. The taskforce also commissioned an environmental and social impact assessment. This impact study concluded that constructing new roads or widening existing roads by expropriating private property were not a feasible option from an environmental and social impact viewpoint. However, through a public consultation process and subsequent brainstorming sessions comprising of expert panels representing several key disciplines, several solutions were identified, which were deemed to be acceptable to most stakeholders.

One potential solution was to invest in the improvement and expansion of the public transportation system, including alternative transport methods (e.g., apart from land transport using also sea transport). This was seen as making it more convenient for people to leave their cars at home and rely on public transportation for their daily commutes. Another solution identified was to incentivise the use of alternative modes of transportation, such as walking and cycling. This could be achieved through the development of dedicated bike lanes and pedestrian-friendly infrastructure, as well as initiatives to promote active transportation, such as subsidising the cost of bicycles and manual/motorised scooters.

Additionally, given that more people were shopping online, the taskforce considered the controlled use of drones as means of shipment for small and light objects. Furthermore, the taskforce identified a need to develop and maintain the road infrastructure in a way that supported efficient traffic flow. This involved rejuvenating the existing road network and implementing intelligent traffic management systems to reduce bottlenecks and keep traffic moving smoothly. A key solution was the need to enforce regulations that promote efficient traffic flow, including strict enforcement of traffic laws and regulations, such as speed limits, and the reduction of the number of roadside parking that often contributes to the flow of traffic.

The taskforce concluded that traffic congestion was indeed a pressing issue that required immediate attention. Hence, it concluded that by investing in public transportation, improving road infrastructure, promoting alternative modes of transportation, and enforcing traffic regulations, the city would be able to work towards a more efficient and sustainable transportation system that benefits both cargo and passenger transport. Furthermore, the taskforce recognised that most of the solutions identified could be effectively implemented through the support of technological solutions, particularly those related to intelligent traffic management systems and enforcing regulations.

These conclusions formed the basis of its transport strategic plan. A technical team was established to identify the appropriate technological support solutions, including the use of AI. The technical team evaluated “City Brain” an AI system developed by Alibaba (BABA). This system made extensive use of AI to collect information, such as video from intersection cameras and GPS data on the locations of cars and buses. The information was to be analysed in real time, while the system harmonised numerous traffic road signals with the aim of preventing or easing gridlock. Hence, the first phase was the identification of key road intersections and the installation of video cameras at these locations. Furthermore, all public vehicles were installed with GPS tracking devices. After several months of testing, commuters witnessed a significant improvement. The system also facilitated the work of first responders by enabling civil protection vehicles and ambulances to almost halve the amount of time it took them to the scene of accidents and address emergencies. The rapid clearance of broken-down vehicles due to minor accidents or mechanical faults assisted in keeping traffic flow at its maximum rate. By 2027, it was estimated that these AI systems could decrease commutes by an average of 18% to 25%.

The combined use of cameras and AI, and amendments to legislation enabled a more effective system of enforcing traffic regulations. Major roads were automatically monitored by the AI system using video feeds as input in real time to identify traffic infringements. These traffic infringements were instantly categorised by severity to enable timely interventions by law enforcers for serious offences, whilst other offenders were issued with customary traffic tickets supported by appropriate evidence for the respective traffic violations. Hence, the AI system was viewed as a preventative tool as well as an enforcement instrument. Admittedly, the AI system raised privacy concerns related to vehicle surveillance and possible facial recognition issues. However, the benefits from this type of system far outweighed the concerns because it brought more discipline to the roads and in several cases saved lives.

As mentioned previously, traffic management solutions using big data and AI-based solutions were applied to monitor and control traffic signals and street cameras to optimise driving and walking routes. Additionally, sensors and cameras were able to monitor the condition of roads and prompt warnings for any immediate maintenance work. Moreover, digital signages and augmented reality (AR) based messaging systems replaced conventional road signages.

The problem of urban growth was not viewed as a recent phenomenon. Urban development in some of the older regions going back to possibly centuries was allowed to take place in a haphazard manner. Hence, authorities, architects, town planners, and civil engineers encountered problems that have their roots possibly many decades (if not centuries) in the past. However, technology was seen as having a critical role to the development of sustainable smart cities. For instance, internet of things (IoT) in combination with AI were applied to have an intelligent street lighting system that responded to changes in weather and traffic conditions to conserve energy and reduce light pollution. Autonomous vehicles were still at the acceptance testing stage. However, these were seen as a means of providing office goers with additional time to check their emails and attend any calls while commuting. Furthermore, these driverless autonomous vehicles could communicate automatically with a smart parking solution and even park themselves to the nearest available spot. Hence, they were able to select parking areas that offer charging-facilities to recharge batteries.

The technical team also revealed and reported to the competent authorities that there existed extensive potential from the emerging technologies like machine learning to address other problems encountered by communities, such as:

*   Structural integrity monitoring. IoT based devices integrated with AI would issue warnings for maintenance required in any building, bridge, or historical monument by continuously monitoring vibrations and material conditions.
*   Electrical energy and water supply management. Smart grids would help in the reduction of electrical power and water distribution losses with IoT enabled equipment maintenance improving operational efficiency.
*   Pollution management. A city-wide network of sensors integrated with AI would generate a map showing levels of sound, water, ground, air, and light pollution to assist administrators in taking mitigating and remedial measures.

The technical team believed that all the recommended solutions were technologically feasible. However, they also recognised that several limitations such as logistical, legal, and budgetary considerations constrained their immediate implementation. It was also recognised that such measures would transform their city and greatly increase the quality of life for its citizens.

## **10.11** Conclusion

This chapter has focused on Public Sector AI and illustrated the considerable potential AI applications have on public administrations and the constitutes they serve. The word “constituents” is being applied in a broad sense and includes all citizens irrespective of their demographic status, civil society, and the commercial sector. The chapter has also shown that governments are the largest employer in each respective country and have a wide-ranging customer base that expect to be provided with an ever-increasing number of products and services.

AI has been recognised as a powerful tool to cater to such a broad spectrum of expectations from the different categories of customers. The chapter has demonstrated that Public Sector AI and Enterprise AI share a common aim, that is to provide a better customer service experience at a lower cost on a 24/7 basis from anywhere. However, an important distinction must be made between Enterprise AI and Public Sector AI. Enterprise AI focuses on improving the profitability of a commercial entity by improving efficiency and providing personalised customer experiences. On the other hand, Public Sector AI is focused on improving laws and social and economic policies. These policies include the development and implementation of national strategies in various disciplines, such as education, health, law enforcement, and transportation. But both have a common underlying objective to improve efficiency and provide personalised customer experiences.

Furthermore, governments face greater challenges when contemplating the deployment of AI because they need to consider the holistic national interest, particularly its economic development and the impact of AI on the different segments of society. These concerns are basically related to how AI will impact the economic growth, employment displacement, technology transfer and skills upscaling, healthcare, and education, amongst others. The bottom line is that every government is required to evaluate its status regarding the need to deploy AI applications and define the essential policies to suit its specific needs and that of its constituents. The chapter itemised and explained several use cases to give the reader an idea of how Public Sector AI can benefit their public administration entities and their respective customer base.

Finally, the chapter referred to a suitable framework for the successful deployment of AI, which was fully describe in the previous chapter when discussing Enterprise AI (see [Figure 9.3](#ch22.xhtml#f34)). Each step in this implementation framework was explained in detail to provide the reader with a viable and practical deployment approach that may be adapted and customised to their individual public administration organisations. Furthermore, this framework is suitable for all categories of public sector organisations, irrespective of the nature of the government level, namely national, state or municipal. It is contended that the suggested framework provides an effective and comprehensive user-friendly approach to the deployment of Public Sector AI in public administrations at every government level. However, every government is required to evaluate its current circumstances regarding the deployment of AI applications and identify the required policies to suit its specific requirements and that of its constituents.
