# Chapter 11AI Ethical, Moral, and Legal Considerations

DOI: [10.1201/9781003653950-14](http://doi.org/10.1201/9781003653950-14)

> *“It is not wisdom but Authority that makes a law.”*
> 
> Thomas Hobbes
> 
> *English philosopher (1588-1679)*

Often the use of AI is justified due to its inherent benefits, such as faster data analysis, time savings in performing tedious tasks, increased levels of predictive accuracy, more in-depth insight into business processes, and enhanced customer service experience. It has been established that AI is an emerging technology that has the objective of imitating the cognitive skills and judgment of humans and has the potential of providing a competitive advantage. Industry has recognised these objectives as being feasible and achievable, and as a result, the take up of AI is constantly growing. AI is being applied in innovative ways such as risk assessments, analytics, predictive business modelling, and routine operational tasks.

As the application and benefits of AI continue to materialise within the various industries, there is a steady and persistent realisation that unintended consequences may also arise with its use. There are numerous researchers advocating caution regarding the use of AI. They implore practitioners to not only explore the benefits of AI but to also identify and scrutinise the ethical implications that such powerful technology may bring about. It is important that a collaborative approach is taken amongst stakeholders, such as government, enterprises, civil society, and educational institutions (Universities and Institutes of Technology) to explore this issue.

It is critical that a conceptual evaluation of the practical ethical and social issues encompassing AI is undertaken to ensure trustworthy AI applications that operate in a safe environment. [Fassbender (2014)](#ch24.xhtml#r105) quoted Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla Motors in an interview at the AeroAStro Centennial Symposium as describing AI as the biggest existential threat to humanity and that we should be careful with AI as it might summon “the demon.” This implies that there is a pressing need for having a suitable mechanism for ensuring that AI applications are developed and implemented according to robust ethical and moral guidelines. Furthermore, governments have a civic duty to protect their citizens from any adverse consequences that AI may bring about and ensure that AI is applied in a way that brings economic prosperity to their constituents.

## **11.1** Introduction

In the emerging technology landscape, AI has developed into a world-shattering force that continues to influence numerous aspects of people’s lives. It has revolutionised various industries and has also altered the way individuals interact with machines. The growing movement towards the various ways that AI is being applied is only limited by the innovative imagination of technologists and practitioners. Having said this, the amazing wonders of AI’s capabilities should not distract society to the risks that may emerge from using it. It is becoming increasingly critical for society to contemplate the ethical and moral dilemmas, and societal implications of creating algorithms that endeavour to replicate the intelligence of human beings.

According to [Patowary (2023)](#ch24.xhtml#r116), Mary Shelley’s iconic literary masterpiece, *Frankenstein*, published in 1831 nearly two centuries ago, remains an enduring cautionary story about the hazards of unrestricted determination and the outcomes of playing God. Patowary argues that AI obscures the peripheries between human and machine, with society finding itself treading on the very themes explored by Mary Shelley. Patowary (2023) contends that this story of excessive pride, self-confidence, moral predicaments, and the intricate relationships between creator and creation continues to go beyond time, finding a striking resonance in contemporary discussions on AI and its potential implications.

There is no doubt that AI provides great opportunities to positively transform people’s lives and offers enormous benefits to enable societies to progress in numerous fields, be it healthcare, education, improved quality of life, and many others. AI is also viewed as enabling nations to develop further their economies for the benefit of their constituents. However, the dark echoes of Victor Frankenstein’s missteps serve as a stark reminder of the need for ethical frameworks and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure that AI remains a powerful force for good ([Patowary, 2023](#ch24.xhtml#r116)).

[Wallach and Allen (2009)](#ch24.xhtml#r122) contend that the human-built environment is increasingly being populated by artificial agents which can act autonomously through AI. They argue that the algorithms controlling these AI applications are currently “ethically blind” since their decision-making abilities do not involve any explicit moral reasoning. Wallach and Allen maintain that there is an urgent need for these increasingly autonomous systems (robots and software bots) to factor ethical and moral considerations into their decision-making algorithms.

[Patowary (2023)](#ch24.xhtml#r116) further argues that it is imperative that society learns from the cautionary tale of *Frankenstein* and embrace a multidisciplinary approach, integrating ethics, philosophy, and technology to guide the future of AI in a manner that respects humanity and safeguards society’s collective well-being. This chapter will focus on two distinct aspects, namely: (a) the ethical and moral considerations for the development and deployment of AI applications; and (b) the AI legal considerations by examining the legislative developments in various countries.

## **11.2** AI Ethical and Moral Considerations

After decades of research and several AI winters, AI has become an essential feature across many industries. AI has now been widely accepted, and its use has been fruitful in healthcare, banking, retail, transport, education, and manufacturing. However, like other technologies that have been introduced in the past, little thought has been given to its possible dark side. Pazzanese (2020) argues that AI’s game-changing capacity to do things like increasing efficiency, reducing costs, and fast-track research and development has now been moderated with concerns that these complex, opaque systems may do more societal harm than economic good. Pazzanese contends that up to 2020, with almost no government oversight, private companies in the USA applied AI software to make decisions about health and medicine, employment, creditworthiness, and even criminal justice without having to answer for how they’re ensuring that these programs were not encoded, consciously or unconsciously, with structural biases.

AI is here to stay. This is confirmed by the predicted worldwide spending on AI solutions that will grow to more than $500 billion in 2027, with most organisations experiencing a notable shift in the weight of technology investments toward AI implementation and adoption of AI-enhanced products and services ([IDC, 2023](#ch24.xhtml#r109)). It is now an accepted fact that practically every large company now has multiple AI systems and includes the use of AI as an integral and essential part of their corporate strategy. Initially, AI was viewed as being applied to automate simple tedious and repetitive tasks requiring low-level decision-making, but powerful computers and the accumulation of massive data sets has facilitated AI’s rapid development into a very sophisticated device (Pazzanese, 2020).

The emerging AI application environment, where AI systems are now making certain determinations about individuals is causing serious concerns. These critics worry whether AI will bring about newer, quicker, and unobstructed methods to discriminate and divide at scale. At first glance, algorithmic decision-making appears to provide an objective approach of overcoming human subjectivity, bias, and prejudice. However, experience has shown that these algorithms show bias because they learn from the data set they are provided with. Hence, if the data has an inherent bias the resultant outcome will reflect this bias.

Pazzanese (2020) cites three major areas of ethical concern for society regarding AI, namely, privacy and surveillance, bias and discrimination, and the role of human judgment. Pazzanese cites political philosopher Michael Sandel of Harvard University who when discussing how to overcome bias in algorithmic decision-making in sentencing, parole, and employment practices refers to conscious and unconscious prejudices of program developers and those built into datasets used to train the software. He contemplates that we have not yet wrapped our minds around the hardest question: Can smart machines outthink us, or are certain elements of human judgment indispensable in deciding some of the most important things in life?

There are those who accept that AI does indeed introduce bias in its resultant outputs, but they also believe that it is not worse than all types of biases that humans introduce in their decision-making process. For instance, using resume-screening AI software would mitigate the chance of favouritism when fine-tuned and aligned with the requirements. However, there is disagreement regarding this premise because AI is widely viewed as being reliable due to its scientific basis and considered as an objective assessment, even though in reality it imitates and reflects human preferences. This “bias” tendency of AI software is because machine learning is based on historical data sets that reflects former “good” and “not-so-good” human decisions. Therefore, the data sets will inherently contain a predisposition towards all types of decisions, irrespective of whether they are good, bad, or mediocre. This concern is applicable to all decisions when assessing different types of applications, such as in banking, social security pensions, insurance, credit rating, and social housing, amongst many others.

There is wide consensus in the industry that AI should be regulated. However, there is disagreement regarding how this should be done and who should do it. Developers and private sector AI users prefer self-policing within existing legal regimes. However, civil society look to the government to take the lead in the specific regulation of AI applications. A major difficulty is the fact that regulatory organisations lack the AI expertise necessary to identify and define what needs to be regulated and what practical approach should be adopted to regulate it. Self-policing is appropriate to some extent in terms of having a code of ethics that would serve as a guide to developers, providers and user organisations. However, one needs to remember that this would not exonerate developers, providers, and user organisations from legal action by aggrieved parties. Therefore, legislation is necessary to regulate AI and clearly define the legal obligations of all concerned.

As stated previously, regulatory organisations lack AI expertise to identify and define what needs to be regulated, and what practical approach should be adopted to regulate it. However, this difficulty might be mitigated by having a collaborative approach through a taskforce between government, and representatives from developers, providers, major users and civil society. This combination would mean that government and civil society would contribute towards the legal and social expertise and the other representatives towards the technical aspects. Furthermore, the taskforce may have various panels or sub-committees to tackle specific industries, such as finance, automobile, aviation, healthcare, education, and manufacturing, amongst others. Having said this, each National, State, and municipal jurisdiction would need to consider its circumstances and adapt the appropriate mechanism that suits its environment.

### **11.2.1** The Need for AI Ethics and Moral Guidelines

Generally, AI ethics in technological advancements can facilitate and promote a world with less bias and more fairness. As AI becomes more significant to society, it has become evident that there is a need for ethical boundaries in the development and deployment of AI tools. Acknowledging this need and in the absence of a wide-scale governing body to write and enforce ethical rules, many technology companies have introduced their own version of AI ethics or code of conduct. The urgent need for AI ethics and moral guidance has arisen due to the concerns about the harmful impact that AI applications might have on society in general.

Fundamentally, AI ethics are the moral values that companies employ to guide responsible and fair development and application of AI. In other words, ethics in the context of AI, is a set of moral principles that help one to determine between right and wrong, and how to enhance AI’s beneficial impact while mitigating risks and harmful outcomes. Guidelines are required to assist developers, providers, and users in ensuring that the AI applications are trustworthy, safe, secure, humane, and environmentally friendly. There are numerous AI ethical and moral issues to be considered, namely, privacy and security, fairness, inclusion, data responsibility, transparency, explainability, robustness, environmental sustainability, moral agency, value alignment, accountability, trust, and technology misuse. There are broadly two main approaches to defining codes of ethics, namely by companies and government-led regulatory frameworks. Both methods facilitate the regulation of AI technology.

According to [Leslie (2019)](#ch24.xhtml#r112), the field of AI ethics has largely emerged as a response to the range of individual and societal harms that the misuse, abuse, poor design, or negative unintended consequences of AI systems may cause. This illustrates that AI ethics has been tackled as a reactive approach rather than a proactive measure. Governments and society appear to be repeating past faults when dealing with technological developments in that the response has always been reactive. [Lesile (2019)](#ch24.xhtml#r112) identifies several possible harmful causes of AI applications:

*   Bias and Discrimination: AI algorithms use historical data sets that might contain an inherent human predisposition and preconceptions to certain decisions. Also, the data set used to train and test algorithmic systems may not be adequately representative of the population from which they are drawing inferences and hence might generate biased and discriminatory outcomes.
*   Denial of Individual Autonomy, Recourse, and Rights: There may be difficulty to hold directly accountable the parties responsible for AI outcomes in situations where citizens are subject to decisions, predictions, or classifications from these AI systems, thus harming the autonomy and violate the rights of the affected persons.
*   Non-transparent, Unexplainable, or Unjustifiable Outcomes: There are cases where the rational for the outcomes from machine learning models are not clear and could conceal traces of discrimination, bias, or inequity.
*   Invasions of Privacy: AI applications might use personal data that may have been attained without proper consent or may reveal personal information that may harm a person’s basic right.
*   Isolation and Disintegration of Social Connection: AI systems might reduce the need for human-to-human interaction, while algorithmically enable hyper-personalisation by limiting one’s exposure to worldviews different from one’s own that might polarise social relationships. It is important that these social relations be preserved.
*   Shoddy AI development practices will likely result in unreliable, unsafe, or poor-quality outcomes that damage the wellbeing of individual persons and the public welfare, which contribute to trustworthiness among the user community.

It must be recognised that AI ethics are critically essential because AI technology has the objective to amplify or replace human intelligence. Hence, in a situation where technology is designed to imitate human intelligence then similar concerns that can blur or confuse human judgment can also be replicated by AI.

The need for AI ethics and moral guidelines can be illustrated by examples that have caused concern. According to [Ovide (2022)](#ch24.xhtml#r115), photos and videos posted on Instagram or other similar media may be used to coach AI software without any consent. She reports that Lensa AI was being trained on a massive volume of photographs that are sourced from the internet without consent to generate trendy, cartoon-looking profile photos from people’s regular images. Ovide cites another similar example regarding ChatGPT, which learns to mimic humans by analysing recipes, social media posts, product reviews and other text from everyone on the internet without consent. Beyond those two technologies, birthday party photos on Facebook helped train Clearview AI facial recognition software that police departments use in criminal investigations ([Ovide, 2022](#ch24.xhtml#r115)).

Formulating ethical guidelines that define fundamental principles for responsible AI development and deployment requires industry actors to collaborate as a team. These stakeholders must study how social, economic, and political issues interconnect with AI, and establish how machines and humans may harmoniously coexist. Key stakeholders might include:

*   Academics: These have the essential role of conducting research studies and developing theory-based statistics and concepts that can support governments, corporations, and non-profit organisations.
*   Government: Entities and taskforces within a government can help to expediate the definition of a nation’s AI ethics. This can be achieved through public consultations for identifying appropriate regulations and defining governance, economic and security policies.
*   Intergovernmental Bodies: Institutions like the United Nations, the World Bank and OECD play a vital role for enhancing awareness and drafting agreements for AI ethics globally.
*   Non-Profit Organisations: These organisations assist various groups attain representation within AI technology. For example, the Future of Life Institute who believe that frontier AI is currently being developed in an unsafe and unaccountable manner has compiled twenty-three guidelines that outline specific risks, challenges, outcomes for AI technologies.
*   Private Companies: Technology leaders, such as Google, Meta, and others, as well as leading AI users, such as banks, consultants, healthcare providers, and other industries, establish ethics teams and codes of conduct that are viewed as a standard for a wide range of companies.

All these stakeholders have a vital role for contributing towards ensuring less bias and risk form AI technologies.

### **11.2.2** Establishing Principles for AI Ethics

Researchers from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have suggested that a report released in 1979 on the ethical treatment of human subjects (Belmont Report) could set a precedent for Ethical AI Research ([CDO, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r101)). This is confirmed by [IBM (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r108), which reports that the academic community in USA has leveraged the Belmont Report to guide ethics within experimental research and algorithmic development. The Belmont Report has three key principles ([IBM, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r108)):

*   Respect for Persons: This principle acknowledges the autonomy of individuals and advocates the expectation of researchers to protect individuals with diminished autonomy, which could be due to a variety of circumstances, such as illness, a mental disability, and age restrictions. This principle is viewed as supporting the concept of consent, where individuals should be aware of the possible risks and benefits of any experiment that they participate in and be able to choose to participate or withdraw at any time before and during the experiment.
*   Beneficence: This principle has its basis on healthcare ethics, where doctors undertake to “do no harm.” This concept can be applied to AI where algorithms can intensify biases regarding race, gender, political leanings, and others, irrespective of the intent to do good and enhance a given system.
*   Justice: This principle is based on fairness and equality. The Belmont Report proposes five modes to disseminate burdens and benefits, namely: equal share; individual need; individual effort; societal contribution; and merit. These may be applied for the distribution of the benefits from experimentation and machine learning.

The European Union (EU) Commission in 2019 proposed a guideline for trustworthy AI systems based on seven key requirements as follows:

*   Human Agency and Oversight: AI systems should empower human beings, allowing them to make informed decisions and fostering their fundamental rights. At the same time, proper oversight mechanisms need to be ensured, which can be achieved through human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, and human-in-command approaches
*   Technical Robustness and Safety: AI systems need to be resilient, secure and safe, ensuring that a contingency plan is in place in case something goes wrong. They also need to be accurate, reliable and reproducible. This would ensure that unintentional harm can be mitigated and prevented.
*   Privacy and Data Governance: Apart from ensuring full respect for privacy and data protection, AI systems must have sufficient data governance mechanisms, consider the quality and integrity of the data, and ensuring authorised access to data.
*   Transparency: The data, system and AI business models should be transparent with traceability mechanisms. Additionally, AI systems and their decisions should be explained in a manner adapted to the stakeholder concerned. Humans need to be aware that they are interacting with an AI system and must be informed of the system’s capabilities and limitations.
*   Diversity, Non-Discrimination and Fairness: Unfair bias must be avoided, since it might include multiple negative implications, from the marginalisation of vulnerable groups to the exacerbation of prejudice and discrimination. AI systems should be accessible to all, regardless of any disability, and involve relevant stakeholders throughout their entire life circle.
*   Societal and environmental well-being: AI systems must benefit all human beings, including future generations and ensure that they are sustainable and environmentally friendly. AI systems should take into consideration the environment, including other living beings, and their social and societal impact should be carefully studied.
*   Accountability: Mechanisms must be introduced to ensure responsibility and accountability for AI systems and their outcomes, and that adequate and accessible redress is ensured. Auditability to assess algorithms, data and design processes is required particularly for critical applications.

Developing and deploying more ethical AI involves a careful study of the ethical implications of policy, education, and technology. There is no doubt that regulatory frameworks can guarantee that technologies benefit society and not harm it. Globally, governments are initiating policies for ethical AI, including how entities should deal with legal issues if bias or other harm arises. AI users should be able to appreciate the risks and possible negative impact of unethical or fake AI. The generation and dissemination of accessible resources can help to mitigate these types of risks. On the other hand, one must also appreciate that AI tools can help and may be applied to determine whether video, audio, or text (hate speech on Facebook, for example) is fake by detecting unethical data sources and bias better and more efficiently than humans.

AI algorithms execute according to how they are designed, developed, trained, tuned, and applied, with AI ethics being about creating an ecosystem of ethical standards and guardrails around and throughout all phases of an AI system’s lifecycle ([IBM, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r108)). According to IBM, entities, governments, and researchers have recognised the importance of ethical frameworks and have commenced to compile charters for addressing AI ethical concerns and configure the future of work within the field. The structure of AI ethical guidelines is being constantly enhanced and incorporate governance as a common aspect ([IBM, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r108)).

[IBM (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r108) contend that governance is an organisation’s act of overseeing the AI lifecycle through internal policies and processes, staff, and systems, which help to ensure that the AI systems are operating as an organisation’s principles and values intend, as stakeholders expect, and as required by relevant regulation. Moreover, IBM view a successful governance program as one that: (a) defines the roles and responsibilities of people working with AI; (b) educates all people involved in the AI lifecycle about building AI in a responsible way; (c) establishes processes for building, managing, monitoring, and communicating about AI and AI risks; and (d) leverages tools to improve AI’s performance and trustworthiness throughout the AI lifecycle. IBM recommends the establishment of an AI Ethics Board to manage the governance mechanism that would comprise of diverse leaders from across the business. The objective of this ethics board is to provide a centralised governance, review, and decision-making process for the ethics policies and practices.

According to the [World Bank (2021)](#ch24.xhtml#r126), many advanced digital governments have published governance frameworks, including ethical standards for the use of AI that include the ethical principles, the role of a central agency, and operational framework. The World Bank notes that national governments in addition to international organisations are actively proposing governance models for AI that emphasise several common principles as shown in [Table 11.1](#ch24.xhtml#t21). These national governments include Australia, Canada, China, Japan, Singapore, United Arab Emirates, and the United States and the international organisations consist of the EU Commission, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, International Organization for Standardization, United Nations, and World Economic Forum.

**Table 11.1** Common Ethical Principles Adopted by National Governments[⏎](#ch24.xhtml#t21b)

 
| **Principle** || **Description** |
| --- | --- |
| Privacy & data protection || AI solutions should respect an individual’s right to privacy and civil liberties. Individuals should have control over their data, with their consent required for repurposing, redistributing or erasure. |
| --- | --- |
| Accountability || Mechanisms must ensure accountable behaviour during the life cycle of AI design and implementation. An entity must be liable for monitoring accountability. |
| Safety & security || Cybersecurity is critical. Leaders must ensure the well-being of society at large and private individual humans. |
| Transparency & explainability || The algorithm, business case, data collection, design, and policy information must be transparent to stakeholders and those impacted. Individuals should get notifications when interacting with AI or when AI decides for them. |
| Fairness || AI solutions should minimize bias and identify and manage risk. Inclusiveness should be ensured in design and impact. |
| Human control of technology || The AI should be under human control. People should review automated decisions and have the right to opt-out of automated decisions. |
| Professional responsibility || Multistakeholder collaboration, accuracy, and scientific integrity of the solution should be ensured. |
| Promotion of human values || AI should be human-centric. It should promote human values and benefit society. |

Source: [World Bank (2021)](#ch24.xhtml#r126). *Artificial Intelligence in the Public Sector*. World Bank Group.

The World Bank maintains that some governance models and guidelines highlight common program and project management practices that include a cost-benefit analysis, legal and regulatory compliance, risk management, flexibility, and the application of a responsive methodology.

### **11.2.3** Building-Blocks of a Responsible AI Project Delivery Ecosystem

According to [Leslie (2019)](#ch24.xhtml#r112), setting up an ethical platform for responsible AI project delivery involves more than building from the cultural ground up. He maintains that it also involves providing the project team with the means to achieve the goals of establishing ethical acceptability, impartiality, trustworthiness, and project justification. Additionally, [Leslie (2019)](#ch24.xhtml#r112) argues that an ethical platform for responsible AI project delivery should be based on three building-blocks, namely:

1.  Basic Level: This obliges one to attain a working knowledge of a framework of ethical values that supports, guarantees, and inspires a responsible data design and use ecosystem. These values consist of four key notions: Respect, Connect, Care, and Protect. The objectives are to provide an accessible framework to start thinking about the moral scope of the societal and ethical impacts of the project; and to establish clearly defined criteria to evaluate its ethical permissibility.
2.  Second Tier Tangible Level: This entails a set of actionable principles that assist in achieving an orientation to the responsible design and use of AI systems. These embrace four key concepts: Fairness, Accountability, Sustainability, and Transparency. The objectives of these principles are to provide the moral and practical tools to ensure that the project is bias-mitigating, non-discriminatory, and fair; and to safeguard public trust in the project’s capacity to deliver safe and reliable AI innovation.
3.  Third Tier Definite Level: This necessitates a process-based governance framework that operationalises the basic level values and the second-tier tangible principles across the entire AI project delivery workflow. The objective is to establish transparent processes of design and implementation that safeguard and enable the justifiability of both the AI project and its product.

The building-blocks for a responsible AI project delivery ecosystem are intended to provide a robust, processed-based foundation of values, principles, and protocols that enable an AI project team to improve the design and implement AI systems ethically, equitably, and safely. Additionally, it is intended to help an entity create a culture of responsible AI innovation based on an ethical platform that ensures a united collective spirit is fostered within the AI project team to enable the development of AI technologies for the public good.

## **11.3** AI Legislative Global Landscape

The above sections focused on ethical and moral behaviour regarding AI. This section will focus on the legislative aspect related to AI around the world. It is important to understand that typically, ethics and law are the different systems of rules by which humans are expected to behave themselves in the society. However, ethics represents the internal system of controls, and Law refers to an external mechanism of control. Both these systems of controls are essential for optimal behaviour, which includes pursuing and imparting treatment.

The sections below will provide a detailed outline of AI regulations of several regions around the globe and will discuss how various nations are governing AI. Furthermore, the key considerations for developing AI regulations will be explained. Although ethics and law are different, it is important that the legal frameworks governing AI are understood because a legal code needs to be applied in an ethical manner by various entities. The ethical application of the law regarding AI is to ensure that societal benefits are attained as technological advances shape humanity’s future. The emerging global landscape of AI regulations might differ since countries will possibly adopt dissimilar approaches. Having said this, it is also likely that there may be some similarities regarding the fundamental factors that underline the creation of AI legislation.

There is no doubt that governments are belatedly recognising that AI developments are impacting people’s lives quicker than expected and has become a disrupting mechanism. This is impacting how businesses operate, which in turn affects their respective employees and the recipients of products and services. Additionally, this scenario is provoking moral, legal, and social concerns, which is forcing governments to adopt appropriate legislation for regulating the design, development and application of AI based systems. This section will consider the following regional areas that are viewed as providing a suitable global AI legislative outlook:

*   Europe: EU and UK.
*   North American: USA and Canada.
*   Africa: Mauritius, Kenya, Egypt, and South Africa.
*   South America: Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, and Peru.
*   Australasia: Australia and New Zealand.
*   Asia: China, India, Japan, and Singapore.

### **11.3.1** Europe

The European legislative segment will focus on the European Union and the United Kingdom.

#### **11.3.1.1** European Union (EU)

According to [European Parliament (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r104), the application of AI in the EU is regulated by the AI Act, which is the world’s first comprehensive AI law. The priority of this Act is to ensure that AI systems used in the EU are safe, transparent, traceable, non-discriminatory, and environmentally friendly. Additionally, the EU maintains that AI systems must be administered by people, rather than by automation, to prevent harmful outcomes. Moreover, an important aim is to have a technology-neutral uniform definition for AI that might be applied to future AI systems.

A critical aspect of the Act is to establish different rules for various risk levels and defining obligations for providers and users depending on the level of risk from AI. All AI systems require assessment irrespective of whether they pose minimal risk. According to [European Parliament (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r104), AI systems that are considered a threat to people are viewed as having unacceptable risk and will be banned. AI systems that are classified as having unacceptable risk by the EU include:

*    Cognitive behavioural manipulation of people or specific vulnerable groups, such as voice-activated toys that incite dangerous behaviour in children.
*   Social scoring that classifies people based on behaviour, socio-economic status or personal characteristics.
*   Biometric identification and categorisation of people.
*   Real-time and remote biometric identification systems, such as facial recognition.

However, the EU identifies some exceptions that may be permitted for law enforcement purposes. For example, “Real-time” remote biometric identification systems are permitted in some serious cases, while “post” remote biometric identification systems, where identification occurs after a significant delay, will be permitted to prosecute serious crimes and only after court approval ([European Parliament, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r104)).

AI systems may also be classified as high risk if they negatively affect safety or fundamental rights. All high-risk AI systems will require assessment prior to being released on the market and throughout their lifecycle. Additionally, individuals will have the right to file complaints about AI systems to designated national authorities. High risk systems are divided into two categories, namely:

*   AI systems that are applied in products that are within the EU’s product safety legislation, such as toys, aviation, cars, medical devices, and lifts.
*   AI systems applied in specialised areas that need to be registered in an EU database, such as management and operation of critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, worker management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and assistance in legal interpretation and application of the law.

According to [European Parliament (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r104), Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) will not be classified as high-risk, but will need to comply with transparency requirements and EU copyright law, namely disclosing that the content was generated by AI; designing the model to prevent it from generating illegal content; and publishing summaries of copyrighted data used for training. High-impact general-purpose AI models that may perhaps present systemic risk, such as the more advanced AI model GPT-4, would need to go through a detailed assessment and any serious incidents would need to be reported to the European Commission. Furthermore, content that is either generated or modified with the support of AI algorithms, such as images, audio or video files (for example deepfakes) are required to be clearly identified as being AI generated to ensure that users are conscious of them when they encounter such content.

The AI Act supports innovation by obliging national authorities to provide companies with a testing environment that simulates conditions close to the real world. This gives start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises the opportunity to develop and train AI models before being released to the public. According to [European Parliament (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r104), the AI Act was adopted in March 2024 and the EU Council followed with its approval in May 2024 with the Act being fully applicable 24 months after coming into effect. However, some articles of the Act will be adopted sooner. For instance, the ban of AI systems posing unacceptable risks; the codes of practice; and the rules on general-purpose AI systems that need to comply with transparency requirements will come into effect after six, nine and 12 months respectively. On the other hand, the obligations concerning high-risk systems will come into effect after thirty-six months, thus giving them more compliance time.

According to [Symbio6 (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r119), the main criticism regarding the AI Act is its complexity and lack of clarity. The definition of an AI system in the AI Act (Article 3.1) means a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. They contend that this definition is largely vague, leading to uncertainties about its scope and application, which could hinder effective implementation and compliance.

Furthermore, [Symbio6 (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r119) claim that even though the AI Act makes sixteen references to human vulnerability, the concept of human vulnerability is still difficult to understand because the words like “vulnerability” are not precisely defined. It is also argued that the Act might lead to overregulation for the business community, which might hinder technological innovation and establish a globally limiting standard. There is also some concern regarding the EU’s decision not to completely ban public mass surveillance. However, this decision is viewed as being based on the individual security needs of member states. Additionally, [Symbio6 (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r119) contend that while the AI Act has the objective of safeguarding fundamental rights and ensure transparency, human rights organisations argue that the act should more robustly tackle the potential harms of AI, including invasive surveillance and social scoring systems, which could undermine personal freedoms and privacy.

#### **11.3.1.2** United Kingdom (UK)

According to [Tobin (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r121), the AI (Regulation) Bill was proposed as a private member’s bill by Lord Holmes with the chief objective of establishing a new body, namely the AI Authority. This authority would have various functions intended to facilitate AI regulation in the UK. The AI Authority is to ensure that relevant existing regulators take into consideration AI developments to guarantee an alignment approach is applied between these regulators and to undertake a gap analysis of regulatory responsibilities regarding AI. Other functions proposed for the AI authority include monitoring economic risks arising from AI; conducting horizon-scanning of developing technologies; facilitating sandbox initiatives to allow the testing of new AI models; and accrediting AI auditors.

The proposed Act would also institute several regulatory principles to govern the development and application of AI. The bill to establish an AI Authority is not an Act to regulate AI because regulating AI in the present technological environment is viewed as premature and may be counterproductive. Hence, it is argued that existing sectoral regulators are in a better position to regulate AI with the backing of a central function currently in development within the Department of Science, Innovation and Technology ([Tobin, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r121)).

According to [Gallo and Nair (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r106), the UK Government has opted for a cross-sector and outcome-based framework for regulating AI, which is supported by five fundamental principles. The fundamental principles are safety; security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; and contestability and redress. These five cross-sectoral principles are intended for the existing regulators to interpret and use within their individual area of interest as a guide to ensure responsible AI design, development, and application. [Gallo and Nair (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r106) contend that the UK Government’s strategy for implementing these principles is based on three core pillars, namely:

*   Leveraging existing regulatory authorities and frameworks. The UK Government does not intend to establish a new AI regulator to oversee the implementation of the framework but is mandating existing regulators to put into action the five principles to regulate and supervise AI within their respective domains. Regulators, such as Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), Office of Communications (Ofcom), or the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) are required to apply a harmonious context-based approach, making use of the existing laws and regulations. Hence, these regulators are not legally obliged to implement the principles or to work together. However, government will likely introduce a legislation in the future, but this will depend on the regulators’ strategic AI plans and the outcome of a review to be carried out by the Central Function regarding likely regulatory powers and remits.
*   Establishing a central function to facilitate effective risk monitoring and regulatory coordination. The government recognises that due to the extensive impact of AI, individual regulators will not be able to effectively deal with the opportunities and risks posed by AI technologies in isolation. Therefore, a Central Function will be established within Department of Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) to administer and assess AI risks, promote coherence and address regulatory gaps.
*   Supporting innovation by piloting a multi-agency advisory service, specifically the AI and Digital Hub. The UK Government will establish a pilot multi-regulator advisory service known as the AI and Digital Hub. This service has the aim of assisting innovators to navigate multiple legal and regulatory obligations before launching a product. This Digital Hub has the remit to facilitate compliance and encourage greater collaboration between regulators and help companies meeting the eligibility criteria.

Regulators will be required to implement the framework in their respective domains by applying existing laws and issuing additional regulatory guidance for organisations to follow. The framework and endeavours of the individual regulators will be enhanced by the voluntary safety and transparency measures that are aimed for developers of highly capable AI models and systems. The Government does not intend to codify the framework into law for the present. However, it plans to make legislative interventions in the future, especially regarding the risks presented by complex General Purpose AI and the leaders involved in its development.

While this approach has some support from the industry, there are others that have expressed concerns regarding the reliance on voluntary commitments from major AI developers instead of having obligatory legal requirements. However, the current arrangement is viewed as an initial step. [Gallo and Nair (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r106) argue that the challenge is to ensure its effective implementation across various regulatory domains, including data protection, competition, communications, and financial services. They contend that given the variety of regulatory bodies involved, effective governance of the framework is essential. They view the newly established Central Function as having a key role in guaranteeing effective collaboration between regulators and easing possible negative impact of conflicting interpretations. They further contend that the Central Function will be vital for supporting organisations with the obligatory regulatory transparency to adopt and scale their investment in AI, thus strengthening UK’s competitive edge.

The UK approach is in direct contrast with the EU’s method that is based on wide-ranging legislation to regulate the development and application of AI across all member states. However, the UK approach has some similarity to the USA’s federal system where no AI legislation is currently proposed. Having said this, some USA States have currently initiated legislation aimed at the regulation of AI specifically related to privacy and accountability. The USA AI legal scenario will be discussed separately at a later stage.

Unlike the EU approach, the UK framework does not provide a formal definition of AI. However, the outcomes-based approach that focuses on two defining characteristics, namely adaptivity and autonomy are aimed at guiding sectoral interpretations. For example, UK regulators, like the ICO, Ofcom or FCA, can interpret adaptivity and autonomy to create domain-specific definitions, if beneficial ([Gallo and Nair, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r106)). [Gallo and Nair (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r106) contend that this increases the risk of diverse interpretations by regulators that might create regulatory uncertainty for organisations operating across sectors. To mitigate this risk, the Government intends to institute a Central Function as a coordinating body between regulators. It is noted that the conventional definition of AI is maintained, with the framework classifying AI into three types, namely highly capable general-purpose AI; highly capable narrow AI; and AI agents. The framework also provides a definition of each type.

### **11.3.2** North America

The section on North American will focus on the United States of America and Canada.

#### **11.3.2.1** United States of America (USA)

Generally, USA applies a decentralised model of AI regulation as its overall approach to governance. Most of its regulatory practices and policies are focused on sectoral levels that reflects very closely the AI segmentation. Moreover, USA has no specific wide-ranging federal regulation framework regarding AI. Having said this, USA has launched several sector-specific AI-related agencies and institutions that deal with some of the complications resulting from the fruition of AI. For example, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) specifically focuses on the issue of consumer protection and attempts to apply fair and transparent business practices in the field. Similarly, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) regulates the safety aspects of AI-powered technologies, particularly their application in autonomous cars.

Although the USA AI legislation lacks centralisation, the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 established an American AI Initiative and guidance on AI research, development, and evaluation activities at federal science agencies. Further acts have required specific agencies to guide AI programmes and policies throughout the federal government (e.g., AI in Government Act of 2020 and Advancing American AI Act of 2021).

The number of bills passed by Congress since 2015 were nine, with 33 legislations still pending up to November 2023. According to [Szczepański (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r120), during 2021, Congress introduced at least 75 bills that focused on either AI and machine learning or related provisions but only six of these were enacted. He further maintains that between January and June 2023, Congress had introduced at least 40 AI-relevant bills, none of which has been enacted. This seems to suggest that at a federal level, the US Government is reluctant to introduce comprehensive AI regulatory measures.

[Szczepański (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r120) notes that in January 2023 the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy published its proposal for an AI Bill of Rights and the National Institute of Standards and Technology released an AI Risk Management Framework. In mid-2023 two broad policy frameworks were announced to guide the Congress in developing future AI legislation. These included the SAFE Innovation Framework for AI Policy (Security, Accountability, protecting Foundations, Explainability) and Blumental & Hawley Comprehensive AI Framework (known as the Bipartisan Framework for US AI Act). Additionally, in April 2023 four federal agencies jointly emphasised that their enforcement powers incorporated AI, and that advanced technology should not be a pretext for breaking the law.

On 30 October 2023, US President Joe Biden issued an executive order regarding the safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of AI. This expands on earlier work, such as the executive order that directed agencies to combat algorithmic discrimination and the securing of voluntary commitments from major US companies (such as Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI) to drive safe, secure, and trustworthy AI development. The executive order of 2023 embraces several policy areas, namely:

*   To establish new standards for AI safety and security. Developers of the most powerful AI systems are required to share their safety test results and other critical information with the US government. Additionally, government agencies have the responsibility to develop standards, tools and tests to help ensure AI systems are safe, secure, and trustworthy. These new standards aim to protect against the risks of applying AI to engineer dangerous biological materials and protect US citizens from AI-enabled fraud and deception.
*   To establish an advanced cybersecurity programme to create AI tools that uncover and resolve weaknesses in critical software. The National Security Council and White House Chief of Staff are responsible with the development of a national security memorandum to direct further action on AI and security.
*   To protect citizens’ privacy from AI-related risks. Federal support is to give priority to hasten the expansion and application of privacy-preserving techniques. This is aimed at strengthening applicable research and technologies; emphasises the need for the evaluation of how agencies collect and apply commercially available data; and makes it necessary to develop guidelines for federal agencies to assess the effectiveness of privacy-preserving techniques.
*   To advance equity and civil rights. The executive order demands clear guidance for property-owners, federal benefits programmes and federal contractors, and processes to address logarithmic discrimination and fairness certainty throughout the criminal justice system by developing best practice on AI use.
*   To protect consumers, patients and students. The executive order demands that measures are in place to advance the responsible application of AI in healthcare and shape its potential to transform education.
*   To support workers. This solicits the development of principles and best practice to minimise harm from AI and maximise its benefits. It also calls for a report on the possible impact of AI on the labour-market and on approaches to ease this impact through stronger federal support.
*   To promote innovation and competition. This strives to stimulate research across the US and requests new measures to support fair, open, and competitive AI ecosystems. It also calls for efforts to attract highly skilled immigrants and non-immigrants with expertise in critical areas to study, stay and work in the US. To progress US leadership abroad, it also calls for the expansion of bilateral and multilateral AI engagements, accelerated development and implementation of vital AI standards, and promotion of the safe, responsible, and rights-affirming development and deployment of AI abroad to address global challenges.
*   To ensure responsible and effective government use of AI. The executive order pursues new support for agencies using AI, more proficient and speedy contracting to obtain AI products and services, and government-wide hastening in employing AI experts.

The executive order was supported by a comprehensive implementation guidance from the Office of Management and Budget. The AI industry has generally applauded the executive order, with some reservations regarding its heavy handedness, but various experts view it a good first step that requires major implementation challenges. [Szczepański (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r120) notes that observers have characterised this executive order as “landmark” and “sweeping” with a strong bipartisan support for its main provisions. However, he also remarks that the Centre for Strategic and International Studies opinions that unlike the EU approach, the most likely outcome over the next few years “is a bottom-up patchwork quilt of executive branch actions.”

On the other hand, the Brookings Institution sees the executive order as sending a strong signal to the international community that the US is finally taking a stand on AI, however, data privacy legislation is necessary to create effective and resilient AI ([Szczepański, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r120)). According to [Szczepański (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r120), the Trade and Technology Council (TTC) provides the setting for EU and US cooperation concerning AI and are implementing a joint roadmap on evaluation and measurement tools for trustworthy AI and risk management. He contends that: (i) the TTC expert groups have itemised 65 key AI terms essential to understanding risk-based approaches to AI, accompanied by their EU and US interpretations and shared EU-US definitions; (ii) they have mapped the respective involvement of both the EU and the US in standardisation activities, aiming to identify relevant AI-related standards of mutual interest; and (iii) they are compiling a catalogue of existing and emerging risks, including an understanding of the challenges posed by generative AI. Additionally, in January 2023, the EU and the US signed an administrative arrangement on “AI for the Public Good”, aimed at boosting AI research collaboration ([Szczepański, 2024](#ch24.xhtml#r120)).

At a state level, [NCSL (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r114) reports that in 2023 at least 25 states, Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia introduced AI bills, and 18 states and Puerto Rico adopted resolutions or enacted legislation. [Table 11.2](#ch24.xhtml#t22) provides the legislation proposed by the various US jurisdictions, illustrating that New York state has 24 pending legislations, California having enacted two laws and has ten pending. It is interesting to note that 24 jurisdictions have no legislative action regarding AI. In this regard, the state of Delaware is of particular interest in that it is a leading domicile for the US and international corporations with more than 1,000,000 business entities and over 66% of the Fortune 500, yet it has no apparent plans to initiate AI laws.

#### **11.3.2.2** Canada

According to [White and Case (2024a)](#ch24.xhtml#r123), Canada is to regulate AI at the federal government level, through the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) that was introduced in June 2022 and effectively passed its second reading. Subsequently this Act was referred to the Standing Committee on Industry Science and Technology on April 24, 2023. However, the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry in November 2023 presented the Standing Committee with several amendments since the original version had limited substantive content that left most key elements of the legal regime to be set out later in regulations. These proposed amendments have not been adopted, and it is unlikely that the Act will be passed before October 2025.

The proposed Act will also include the Consumer Privacy Protection Act, which is a revision of the current federal privacy law and the Personal Information and Data Protection Tribunal Act. However, unlike the USA situation, no laws have been proposed to directly regulate AI at the provincial level. On the other hand, the Innovation Council of Quebec, which has the remit from the government of Quebec, has recommended specific regulation of AI through a provincial legislature of a law. Additionally, [White and Case (2024a)](#ch24.xhtml#r123) contend that there are several other laws that may impact the development and/or application of AI in Canada, whether federal, provincial or territorial, these include:

*   At federal level: Privacy Act and the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA).
*   At a provincial level: Personal Information Protection Act (in Alberta); the Personal Information Protection Act (in British Columbia); and the Act Representing the Protection of Personal Information in the Private Sector (in Quebec). The revisions of September 2023 to the Quebec Act regulate automated decision-making based on the processing of personal information and require disclosure of the occurrence of processing and the provision of information about the reasons and factors that have led to a decision.
*   Intellectual property laws may impact aspects of AI development and application.
*   Competition law might impact the structure of the AI market in Canada.
*   The Innovation Council of Quebec has also proposed amending the Quebec labour law to address the impacts of AI.
*    Existing human rights and anti-discrimination laws (including the Canadian Human Rights Act) regulate discriminatory outcomes and practices, such as those that may result from biased outputs and decisions from AI systems.

Generally, AIDA has the objective to standardise cross-border trade in AI systems by instituting common obligations applicable across Canada, for the design, development, and application of those systems; and to forbid any AI systems behaviour that may cause serious harm to individuals or harm to their interests, particularly biased outputs. AIDA has wide territorial domain and is applicable regarding: (a) AI systems or machine learning models made available during international or interprovincial trade and commerce (cross-border trade); and (b) the management of the operations of AI systems used during cross-border trade ([White and Case, 2024a](#ch24.xhtml#r123)).

In general, AIDA does not adopt a sector-specific approach but imposes various responsibilities on specific persons contingent on the kind of AI system that they are involved with and their status down the AI value chain. For instance, individuals who manage, or who make available, or make available for the first time during cross-border trade of general-purpose AI systems and high-impact systems have obligations under AIDA. This also applies to those individuals who first make a machine-learning model available, for incorporation into a high-impact system, during cross-border trade.

AIDA embraces several key definitions, namely: (a) an AI system means a system that, using a model, makes inferences in order to generate output, including predictions, recommendations or decisions; (b) a General-purpose system means an AI system that is designed for use, or that is designed to be adapted for use, in many fields and for many purposes and activities, including fields, purposes, and activities not contemplated during the system’s development; and (c) Machine-learning model is a digital representation of patterns identified in data through the automated processing of the data using an algorithm designed to enable the recognition or replication of those patterns ([White and Case, 2024a](#ch24.xhtml#r123)). Moreover, the proposed amendments explain that an AI system may be a general-purpose system and a high-risk system concurrently. AIDA incorporates a risk categorisation concept. Hence, an AI system will be a “high-impact system” if it has the following application:

*   To decide on employment issues such as to ascertain employment levels, recruitment, referral, engagement, remuneration, promotion, training, apprenticeship, transfer or termination.
*   To adopt decisions associated to service access such as to establish whether to supply services to an individual, or the type or cost of services to be given to an individual; or to prioritise services to be made available to individuals.
*   To process biometric information for the identification of individuals, without their consent; or the evaluation an individual’s behaviour or frame of mind.
*    To make decisions concerning content moderation and prioritisation, namely for the moderation of content acquired on an online communications platform, including a search engine or social media facility, or the prioritisation of the presentation of such content.
*   To decide on matters regarding healthcare or emergency services, with certain exceptions, in accordance with the Food and Drugs Act.
*   In determinations by a court or administrative body concerning an individual who is a party to the proceedings.
*   To assist law enforcement officers, as stated in the Criminal Code, in the exercise and performance of their law enforcement powers, duties, and functions.

According [White and Case (2024a)](#ch24.xhtml#r123), AIDA implements a comprehensive method regarding compliance requirements, particularly for those relating to risk management measures, which are specific to certain roles in the AI value chain. They cite two specific examples:

*   Persons who originally make a machine-learning model accessible for incorporation into a high-impact system during cross-border trade (i.e., developers) must define processes that identify, assess, and mitigate against the risks of biased output before the model is made available.
*   Persons who originally make high-impact systems available must make sure that risk mitigation measures are implemented, and that these measures have been tested; and those who manage such systems are responsible for conducting the tests to ascertain the effectiveness of the mitigation measures.

Furthermore, White and Case contend that AIDA obligations are styled according to the different challenges and objectives at each point in the AI value chain. For instance, persons who initially make a machine-learning model accessible for incorporation into a high-impact system in the course of cross-border trade, must guarantee that measures respecting the data used in developing the model have been instituted in accordance with regulations; and that high-impact system operators must institute procedures that permit users to provide feedback on the system’s performance.

An important requirement of AIDA is the creation and maintenance of written accountability frameworks by those individuals who make a general-purpose system or high-impact system available, or who manage the operations of such systems. These frameworks apart from other points, are to include: a description of the roles, responsibilities, and reporting structure for all those who contribute to making the system available or managing its operations; the policies and procedures respecting the management of risks relating to the system and the data used by the system; and any other items required by regulation. It is also noted that the AI and Data Commissioner is appointed by the Minister responsible for the Act and has the remit for enforcing AIDA. AIDA also imposes different penalties for individuals and companies for certain offences that may result in substantial fines or imprisonment.

### **11.3.3** Africa

According to [Sulaiman, Olën and Bezuidenhout (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r118), several African jurisdictions are currently implementing AI strategies with some being in the consultation process with stakeholders, while others have yet to make any pronouncements regarding AI regulation. Furthermore, they also refer to a draft AI policy of the African Union (AU) related to AI regulation that is expected to be officially endorsed by members in 2025. It is noted that the AU currently has 55 members that incorporate most African states. [Sulaiman, Olën and Bezuidenhout (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r118) maintain that the AU Draft Policy incorporates recommendations for industry-specific codes and practices, standards, and certification bodies, which are focused on evaluating and benchmarking AI systems, providing regulatory oversight for the testing of AI, and establishing national AI councils.

Hence, this framework provides the opportunity for those members without AI policies or regulation to catch up with the more advanced members and encourages all members to review and align their existing policies with the AU Draft Policy to ensure a degree of consistency among AU members. Mauritius, Kenya, and Egypt lead as the African AI policymakers, while South Africa and Nigeria, are consulting stakeholders about initiating AI policies

#### **11.3.3.1** Mauritius

The Mauritian Government set up a working group on AI in recognition of the opportunities that AI may provide to help stimulate the country’s economy as well as a means of tackling the financial and social issues being encountered. This work group formulated and published the Mauritian AI Strategy in 2018 after due consultations with stakeholders.

This strategy defined three key requirements, including identifying possible applications and impact of AI; the creation of an ecosystem to encourage AI development; and the formation of a regulatory framework for AI oversight. Additionally, the Mauritian AI Strategy acknowledges the capacity of AI technologies to integrate into the broader nation’s economy and support productivity, economic growth, and quality of life. The Mauritian AI Strategy is intended to be upgraded and augmented in the medium and long term to emerge as a key pillar for sustainable growth and economic development in Mauritius. The strategy is focused on:

*   Concentrating on specific sectors and identifying national projects.
*   Developing capacity and attracting skills.
*   Having incentives to catalyse implementation.
*   Contemplating ethical concerns of AI.
*   Developing strategic alliances in emerging technologies.
*    Increasing awareness of AI through focused campaigns.
*   Implementing new technologies to enhance public services delivery.

Additionally, several projects are proposed to support the AI Strategy that include making use of blockchain technology for tax payment, land registration and managing health insurance; using AI to enhance the energy sector; using AI to bolster efficiency and competitiveness in the manufacturing sector; using AI for leapfrogging in the healthcare and biotech industry; and employing AI in agro-industry, the ocean economy, and for transport.

The AI Strategy emphasises several issues concerning the legal and regulatory framework, ethics and data protection. Moreover, it recommends government to expedite the Intellectual Property Bill; update outdated regulations to permit the development of AI, such as in Fintech, mobile payment, crowdfunding and crowdlending; guarantee an ethical AI system by instituting a permanent committee on ethics; set up a special working group to make the necessary amendments to data protection legislation; and consider policies on open data access.

#### **11.3.3.2** Kenya

Like Mauritius, the Government of Kenya also acknowledged that AI applications might provide economic opportunities. Hence, in 2018 it formed the Distributed Ledgers Technology and AI Task Force. In 2019, this Task Force released a report that advocated the potential of AI to contribute to the growth of Kenya’s global economic competitiveness. The Task Force report generated the basic ideas to position the country as a regional and international leader in Information and Communications Technology (ICT) by promoting a substantial escalation of investment in infrastructure and skills. It also proposed strategies to harmonise innovation and regulation in the private sector.

A National Digital Master Plan 2022-2032 has been presented by the Minister for ICT that accepts the critical points of the Task Force Report and endorses its support for fostering research and development in the AI industry. Moreover, the master plan defines the Ministry’s ICT strategy to implement AI solutions that are aimed at overcoming the challenges for deploying AI and its regulation and disseminating the AI solutions to other countries. The master plan also stresses the significance of developing international partnerships with leading actors in the AI industry, including those in the emerging technologies space.

Additionally, significant progress was made in 2024 for finalising a national AI strategy for Kenya through the strategic alliance of the Government of Kenya and the German Development Cooperation (GIZ). This alliance resulted in initiating the Forward Artificial Intelligence for All (FAIR) Initiative, which is also supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development and the European Union.

#### **11.3.3.3** Egypt

Like Kenya, Egypt emphasises the need to facilitate technology transfers and attracting foreign investments. The Egyptian National Council for AI (NCAI) formulated the national Egyptian AI Strategy that supports Egypt’s implementation of AI in specific phases. The first phase of the AI strategy has the objective of launching Egypt as a key role player in enabling regional cooperation in AI. Hence, this phase accentuates the growth of cooperative AI capabilities between Egyptian and foreign stakeholders, in preference to its national or internal development.

Exploiting Egypt’s internal AI growth potential will be pursued in later phases of the AI Strategy. Having said this, discussions related to the second phase have already commenced with the Minister of ICT and the NCAI. The second phase will be inclined towards commencing several priority initiatives identified in the first phase that are intended to enhance investment, increase public awareness, and developing greater AI capabilities in Egypt.

There does not appear to be any direct laws in Egypt regarding AI. However, AI is indirectly governed through existing laws, such as the Telecommunication Regulation Law (2003). This law is mainly focused on telecommunication services, but also deals with digital data management, which is viewed as an essential component of AI operations. Additionally, the Egyptian Data Protection Law of 2020 plays a crucial role in regulating AI. This law is modelled on the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which establishes standards for data privacy and security, directly impacting AI systems that process vast amounts of personal data. This law also makes it mandatory to obtain consent for data collection, which is an important factor in AI’s functionality, particularly for consumer-facing applications.

According to [Iskander (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r110), as AI in Egypt continues to evolve, there is a need for ongoing legal and regulatory development. He maintains that this includes updating existing laws and introducing new regulations that address the unique challenges posed by AI technologies. [Iskander (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r110) argues that embracing AI’s potential while mitigating its risks requires a balanced approach, combining legal rigor with ethical considerations and global best practices.

#### **11.3.3.4** South Africa

Generally, South Africa, Nigeria, and Morocco rely on existing legislation for AI regulation like Egypt. According to [White and Case (2024b)](#ch24.xhtml#r124), South Africa has not announced any AI regulation proposals but is in the consultation process for a draft National AI plan. Generally, AI is unregulated in South Africa. However, certain aspects of existing legislation regulate some activities conducted by organisations using AI, including the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA), the Copyright Act, the Patents Act, and the Competition Act.

[White and Case (2024b)](#ch24.xhtml#r124) maintain that South Africa has not released any policy documents or entered bills to parliament for the regulation of AI. However, White and Case identify the following developments that are viewed as significant in considering any expected future regulation:

*   April 2019: The President appointed members to the Presidential Commission on the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR Commission) to identify relevant policies, strategies, and action plans that will position South Africa as a competitive global player.
*   May 2019: OECD and partner countries, including South Africa, formally adopted the first set of nonbinding intergovernmental policy guidelines on AI agreeing to support international standards that aim to ensure AI systems are designed to be robust, safe, fair, and trustworthy.
*   November 2022: The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies launched the AI Institute of South Africa and AI hubs (University of Johannesburg and Tshwane University of Technology).
*   April 2024: The Minister of the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies organised an AI Summit to reveal the contents of a draft National AI Plan discussion document, intended as a pre-policy process to obtain and collate inputs to be incorporated into a draft plan.

Like other African countries, there are several laws that do not directly regulate AI but might impact the development or use of AI in South Africa. [White and Case (2024b)](#ch24.xhtml#r124) provide some key examples as follows:

*   Protection of Personal Information Act that encompasses any automatic processing of personal data.
*   Copyright Act and Patents Act that are applicable to AI generated efforts, one of which has been granted a patent in South Africa.
*   Competition Act that although it does not directly regulate the technology is applicable to digital mergers and digital platforms.
*   A Draft Cyber Security Bill was published in 2024, which includes AI in the definition of a regulated ICT System and ICT Infrastructure and contains provisions that may require AI products to be certified against minimum standards.

Since South Africa does not have any laws to directly regulate AI there is no single legally recognised definition of AI. However, the draft National AI Plan discussion document refers to the European Union Commission definition. Furthermore, the lack of AI legislation means that currently there are no specific or unique obligations imposed on developers, users, operators and/or deployers of AI systems, apart from those that might relate to the automated processing of personal information as provided for in the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). However, Section 71(1) of POPIA governs automated decision-making that protects data subjects from being subjected to decisions based exclusively on automated decision-making, which results in legal consequences for the data subject and the data subject being profiled.

[White and Case (2024b)](#ch24.xhtml#r124) remark that South Africa’s AI Planning Discussion Document notes several regulatory areas that are to be eventually considered:

*   Disinformation and fake news created by Generative AI applications and software.
*   Bias and discrimination that could be demonstrated by AI developers and users.
*   Copyright abuse in alignment with World Intellectual Property Organisation.
*   Privacy to protect personal, private, and public data.

White and Case also remark that the AI Planning Discussion Document lacks a risk-based methodology but instead focuses on considering the optimal form of regulation regarding:

*   Anti-competitive behaviour if provisions of key AI models, or other enablers are focused on a small number of players.
*   Risks in robotic or autonomous devices that apply AI to determine actions, such as AI driven autonomous vehicles.
*   Insistent employment losses that lead to social risks.
*   Criminal behaviour or other highly dangerous outcomes.
*   Experiential risks in situations where AI gets out of control and engages in goals harmful to humanity.
*   Risks that AI intended for military purposes outflows into the wider world and leads to greater criminal conduct or other highly dangerous outcomes.

South Africa is enlarging its AI knowledge centres through the South African Centre for Artificial Intelligence Research (CAIR) that incorporates eight universities conducting AI research in South Africa. The funding for CAIR activities is mainly supported by the South African Department of Science and Innovation and by the AI Institute of South Africa.

The above illustrates that several African countries are active contributors in developing a balance between AI regulation and innovation. There are also several African countries that are defining and implementing AI strategies and policies for public sector reform, education, and research. However, although the African AI innovation ecosystem is active, there is a lack of direct AI laws in most jurisdictions. Having said this, the AU Draft Policy, once agreed by members, may empower AU member states to leapfrog AI regulatory development, including those in the developmental and experimental stages of their AI regulation.

### **11.3.4** South America

The trend in South American countries is to actively develop AI regulations to support ethical AI development, protect human rights, and foster innovation. Generally, many South American countries are proactively seeking legislative action with several bills having been introduced in respective parliaments and legislative bodies. This suggests that there is an increasing awareness and commitment towards instituting a legal framework for effectively regulating AI. Furthermore, these legislative endeavours are focused to address the socioeconomic, educational and political challenges of the region.

[Muñoz (2024)](#ch24.xhtml#r113) contends that the recent elections in Latin America have underscored the dangerous impact of algorithms and AI, particularly generative AI, at the voting booth.
