[Vassev (2021)](#ch27.xhtml#r150) argues that with the continuous increasing pace of technology, it is essential that everyone is made aware of the forthcoming disruptions and not just unquestionably accept the bright side of AI future without also considering the negative aspects. Finally, he contends that computer superintelligence at worst could threaten human’s very existence and at best it offers great challenges that need to be settled if society can sensibly give rise to the Fourth Industrial Revolution. [Freedland (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r143) maintains that there are things governments can do, such as imposing restrictions on how much computing power the tech companies are allowed to use to train AI, and how much data they can feed it with the aim of constraining the bounds of its knowledge. These ethical issues have been considered in detail in a previous chapter, but it is essential that ethical and moral issues are not overlooked.

## **13.3** Human and AI Collaboration

The rapid progress of AI technology these past few years has generated general anxiety regarding the future employment prospects of humans. The concept of having AI to displace humans at work is already a topic of public debate with AI proponents saying that AI will introduce new opportunities, while opponents view AI as an impending disaster for humans.

João da Silva and Natalie Sherman, Business reporters for BBC News cite Tesla boss Elon Musk as saying that the electric car maker will start producing, selling, and using humanoid robots from 2026 ([da Silva and Sherman, 2024](#ch27.xhtml#r141)). It is known that Tesla has experienced weakening demand for its cars, and the use of the humanoids is aimed at cutting costs. Musk states that generally their focus remains on company-wide cost reduction and that the autonomous humanoid robot (Optimus) will be produced to conduct unsafe, repetitive or boring tasks ([da Silva and Sherman, 2024](#ch27.xhtml#r141)). Furthermore, [da Silva and Sherman (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r141) also report that other firms, including Honda and Boston Dynamics, have also been developing their own humanoid robots.

There is no doubt that AI is proving to be beneficial for various industries and that intelligent algorithms have increased operational efficiency and optimised organisational resources. Opponents to AI view this as a reflection of the job losses taking place, while proponents see this as increasing an organisation’s profitability and its capacity to introduce new products and services that still require human intervention.

There is also no doubt that technology has always had the effect of reducing the functions that were normally performed by humans (and animals being replaced by tractors and vehicles), but it is also a reality that technology has generated many new functions and created new fields. For example, in the car industry, robots have replaced human workers in performing repetitive and sometimes hazardous tasks. But the converse is also true in that new fields regarding engineering and computer science have been created, including the many jobs associated with them. Furthermore, the lowering of operational costs has meant lower prices for the goods and services, which has made them more affordable for humans and their usability in most cases brought more leisure time and enjoyment.

In the 1800s, many Americans worked 70 hours or more per week and this continued decreasing to 40 hours per week at around 1940. According to the ILO, in 2024 most workers in developed countries worked less than 40 hours per week. According to the European Commission, the average for the European Union countries was 36.1 hours per week. These figures illustrate that most humans have experienced more leisure time. There is consensus that technology has played a key role in the reduction in the working hours per week. Many believe that further reduction in working hours is likely as technology progresses. The concern is whether this reduction will continue to a state where most humans are no longer required. This brings us back to the “universal basic income, or something like that” concept predicted by Elon Musk as reported on CNBC ([Clifford, 2018](#ch27.xhtml#r139)).

A key issue is whether AI should be embraced as a powerful potential collaborative partner for humans rather than a threat to human workers. Like most social issues, it is not just black or white but there are many shades of grey in between. While it is fact that AI can perform various tasks more quickly and efficiently than humans, there are many characteristics that humans excel at and currently cannot be replaced by AI. A key word in the previous sentence is “currently.” Therefore, when considering such issues it is important to anticipate the future not just the present. It is also a fact that many things that were not possible in the past are achievable today because of technological progress.

Currently, creativity, complex problem solving, and empathy is primarily the domain of humans. However, generative AI is already encroaching on the creativity aspect. The future potential of General AI and Super AI is unfathomable. What may be very difficult for machines to replicate today could be very possible tomorrow. However, if we adopt a collaborative mindset when considering the potential application of AI, our anxiety about its potential may be mitigated. To be successful in the implementation of AI applications, a high level of technical skills, such as programming, software engineering, and data science are critical. These skills are currently all human skills and with the right ethical guidelines supported by legislation we would ensure that they remain so. Additionally, education institutions need to keep ahead of progress and update their curriculum to ensure specialisation in AI-based application system development and related skills. This would allow progress to continue based on human capacity and not create an environment where we become dependent on the capacity of AI to dictate our progress. In other words, we need to avoid a situation where the rate of progress depends on the ingenuity of AI instead of human ingenuity. AI needs to remain under the control of humans and not be allowed to roam free to regenerate itself and generate other AIs.

According to [Wroe (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r151), thinking and learning about AI are the mental equivalent of a fission chain reaction where the questions get really big, really quickly. He further argues that there is the current tendency to concern ourselves with the issues that are of an immediate or short-term nature, such as the opportunities for economic productivity, health care, manufacturing, education, solving global challenges like climate change and, on the reverse side, the risks of mass unemployment, disinformation, killer robots, and concentrations of economic and strategic power. Although in his view these matters are important, there are more profound issues to be considered, such as the human capacity to live meaningful, fulfilling lives in a world in which we no longer have intelligence supremacy. He further argues that as long as humanity has existed, it has had an effective monopoly on intelligence in its sphere of influence.

It has taken modern humans about 200,000 years to evolve from the now extinct Homo erectus, whereas computer technology through human intelligence has taken less than a hundred years to evolve to the state it is now. The rate of such development is without precedent. [Wroe (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r151) argues that humans over the centuries have built a vast intellectual empire made up of science, philosophy, theology, engineering, storytelling, art, technology, and culture. He contends that it is human nature to explore, discover, and expand its intellectual capacity.

Yet having General AI and Super AI as the long-term objective would mean that humans have created intelligence which is superior to their own. Humans would no longer be the smartest entities in our universe. Humans, particularly decision makers, need to see the wood for the trees. Currently, we are getting very involved in the short-term details but are ignoring what is important about the thing as a whole. The whole issue about the impact of future AI is not just based on economics but it becomes an issue involving human development and its social implications. [Wroe (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r151) argues that even if world leaders can solve the economic equality issues by introducing a universal basic income as Elon Musk suggested, and replace notions of “paid work” with “meaningful activity”, how will humans spend their lives in ways that they find meaningful, given that the basis of human evolution is founded on striving, thriving, and competing?

On the other hand, General AI and Super AI can help humans to strive (determination), thrive (flourish), and compete (rivalry) and to achieve things that until now have not been within our knowledge, if this technology is tightly controlled and not allowed to roam freely. [Wroe (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r151) argues that if General AI and Super AI could answer all of our most profound questions and solve all of our problems, how much satisfaction do we get from having the solutions handed to us? However, this argument assumes that knowledge is finite. But indications are that knowledge is infinite and therefore our satisfaction will be attained from gaining more knowledge and understanding, which is not currently known. It is a fact that humans have different talents and a diverse level of creativity.

Not everyone enjoys writing or reading poetry or be a literary genius or be a painter or musician or performer. Those that enjoy such activities will continue to practice them within their own creative talents. Whilst those that do not have such talents can seek collaboration from AI with their own conscious knowledge that the work being produced is not entirely their creation. The medical field is still wide open to new discoveries, whilst exploration of our oceans is only at a basic level. Basically, the issue is about maintaining human control over all the types of AI. [Wroe (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r151) cites AI pioneer Stuart Russell who compared this situation to the King Midas story where, turning everything into gold by touching it sounds fantastic, until you try to eat an apple or hug your kids.

[Anderson and Rainie (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r136) from the Pew Research Centre maintain that experts are divided about how much control people will retain over essential decision-making as digital systems and AI spread. There appears to be consensus that government authorities and large companies are likely to intensify their efforts to deploy AI systems with the objective of improving people’s living standards. However, there are also grave concerns that the outcome of these AI applications will reduce the individual’s capacity to manage their options. This concern is driven by the prediction that smart machines, bots, and systems powered mostly by machine learning and AI will rapidly increase in speed and sophistication between now and 2035 ([Anderson and Rainie, 2023](#ch27.xhtml#r136)).

Their concern is based on the scenario where individuals become more addicted to these technologies in their daily lives, and they are also steadily being lured to relinquish their decision-making and personal autonomy to digital tools. The added concern is that they may be doing this unconsciously or instinctively and thus losing the capacity to exercise judgment and make decisions independent of these systems. Research has already found that many people are being addicted to social media apps like TikTok, Facebook, and Snapchat, mobile sports betting apps, video watching websites like YouTube, and mobile games that are keeping smartphone users hooked to their device more and more. However, AI applications are different and normally delve into the decision-making realm with the consequence that people will be heavily influenced by AI in reaching their decisions.

There is consensus that AI technology will provide great benefits to humans but like everything else it requires careful monitoring to ensure that no intentional or unintentional abuse takes place. Research by Pew Research Centre and Elon University found that 56% of the experts questioned agreed that by 2035 smart machines, bots, and systems will not be designed to allow humans to easily be in control of most tech-aided decision-making ([Anderson and Rainie, 2023](#ch27.xhtml#r136)).

## **13.4** Future Human Development

According to [Jones (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r144), to understand the future evolution of humans, we need to look to our past. Jones poses a very valid question regarding our descendants, namely: Will our descendants be cyborgs with hi-tech machine implants, re-growable limbs and cameras for eyes or might humans morph into a hybrid species of biological and artificial beings? Furthermore, she questions whether humans can become smaller or taller, thinner or fatter, or even with different facial features and skin colour?

Historical evidence reveals that it is only during the last 10,000 years that there have been major changes in which humans had to adapt to. Jones argues that agricultural living and plentiful food have led to human health problems, which have been addressed with the aid of science, such as treating diabetes with insulin. Additionally, humans’ physical features have also changed in that generally humans have become overweight and, in some zones, have developed taller. [Jones (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r144) cites Thomas Mailund, Senior Lecturer in Bioinformatics and Big Data at Anglia Ruskin University, London who suggested that humans may evolve in ways that would help us to adopt to the developing environment and specifically the changes taking place around us. For instance, Mailund suggests that as urban populations increase our daily social interactions would also increase substantially, where humans may develop in ways that facilitate these interactions by for example remembering people’s names, which would be a vital skill in such an environment.

However, technology can help in this human evolving environment. For example, Mailund suggests that an implant in the brain would permit humans to recall people’s names, since scientists already know what genes are involved in building a brain that’s good at remembering people’s names ([Jones, 2024](#ch27.xhtml#r144)). Admittedly, this type of technology is still at the early experimental stage because while the implant may exist, the input/output interface still needs to be resolved. Mailund argues that it is not a biological issue but technological one. For instance, humans are already having implants to repair various biological appendages, such as a pacemaker or hip or knee implant. Mailund maintains that there may be the possibility in the future for implants to be applied to enhance a person’s capability, such as an artificial eye with a camera that can read different frequencies of colour and visuals ([Jones, 2024](#ch27.xhtml#r144)).

[Jones (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r144) cites Dr. Hodgson, Lecturer, Grand Challenges in Ecosystems and the Environment who maintains that using bioinformatics it is possible to accurately predict how genetic variation will change. For instance, he foresees that urban and rural areas will become increasingly genetically diverse due to the migration of people from rural areas into cities, with an increase in genetic diversity in cities and a decrease in rural areas being the outcome. AI algorithms that predict this genetic diversity would provide an extremely accurate depiction of how humans are evolving across countries.

[Pester (2021)](#ch27.xhtml#r148) claims that futurists predict two significant milestones, namely singularity, where AI will progressively become smarter until it is immeasurably superior to our own intelligence; and virtual immortality that will enable the scanning of one’s human brain and transfer its contents to a non-biological medium, like a computer or robot. [Pester (2021)](#ch27.xhtml#r148) argues that once the human mind is deposited in a computer, which in turn can be uploaded to the internet, an individual does not need to be apprehensive about the human body perishing. However, according to [Schneider (2019)](#ch27.xhtml#r149) this does not mean achieving physical immortality. She maintains that a better approach to achieve extreme longevity (i.e., the ability to live a long life beyond the human’s average age at death), while also preserving the person, would be through biological enhancements compatible with the survival of the human brain or through brain chips. [Schneider (2019)](#ch27.xhtml#r149) views this as a future development where a human would gradually have replacement parts using brain chips, which would eventually result in having a human driven by AI. Thus, a human over time would progressively transition into a cyborg and thinking in chips rather than neurons. However, she maintains that if the human brain is intimately connected to you, then replacing it could mean suicide. She also believes that the human body appears to have an expiration date, regardless of how it is upgraded or uploaded.

The technology regarding brain implants has already become a reality but still needs perfection. [Chow (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r138) from NBC News reported that the first brain-computer interface was implanted into a human in the late 1990s, where these devices were able to tap into the brain circuitry that remains intact after injury to perform basic movements and functions. Moreover, [Limehouse (2024)](#ch27.xhtml#r147) for USA Today reported that a Quadriplegic patient with a dislocated spine had a Neuralink implanted that has helped his life, including allowing him to play video games and chess and surf the Internet with ease. Despite some reservations [Schneider (2019)](#ch27.xhtml#r149) views the potential brain and body enhancements of the future as exciting since it allows humans to rid itself of death by old age and permits technology to cure ailments and make humans smarter.

[Diaz (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r142) a journalist with New York Post cited futurist and author Ray Kurzweil as predicting that humans will achieve immortality in just seven years. Kurzweil has previously suggested that humans will have created technology to fend off aging and illness with microscopic robots, sent to repair our bodies on a cellular level ([Diaz, 2023](#ch27.xhtml#r142)). According to [Belachew (2023)](#ch27.xhtml#r137) nanotechnology can repair damaged tissue at the cellular level and is assisting in detecting, diagnosing, and treating severe diseases such as HIV, cancer, and others. However, this technology is still at an embryonic stage. Combined with AI this technology has the potential of making humans immortal.

## **13.5** Conclusion

This chapter has examined three key themes that include AI and the future of humans; human and AI collaboration; and what will humans are likely to look like in the long-term future. The greatest fear is the displacement of humans from the job market for routine and repetitive tasks resulting in massive unemployment and an economic catastrophe. Furthermore, there are also grave fears that certain types of AI could cause the possible extinction of humans altogether.

The research has revealed that AI is likely to result in many jobs being taken over by AI and related technology. On the other hand, there are also predictions that AI will provide great benefits in healthcare, transport, education, manufacturing, amongst many others. Moreover, it is predicted based on past technological evolutionarily experiences that AI and its associated technology will create countless opportunities in all fields. Research has also revealed that a collaborative approach between humans and AI technology will ensure that humans reap the benefits with little adverse consequences. However, this scenario becomes realistic if governments introduce ethical standards supported by legislative measures to protect the human job market. Additionally, research has also revealed that the evolution of technology, including AI has meant an increase in leisure time for humans resulting in a lower number of working hours per week. However, lowering the working hours was not a voluntary act but through labour trade union demands and government intervention.

Research has also shown that General AI and Super AI could be dangerous, particularly if these AI systems are allowed to operate in an uncontrolled environment. Such systems should be prohibited through international treaties to prevent malicious behaviour, such as cyberterrorism and launching weapons, particularly nuclear warheads. The general conclusion is that AI requires constant monitoring both within nations and internationally but this needs to be supported by extensive legislation and sincere international collaboration.

The research has revealed that whilst General AI and Super AI are feared as a contributor to the extinction of humans, yet it has also revealed that AI associated with other technological developments have to the potential to make humans quasi-immortal. Hence, there appears to be a contradiction, on one hand the extinction of humanity and on the other hand its immortality.

I would like to finish this chapter on the same theme that I choose in the first chapter of this book. The Garden of Eden as described in the book of Genesis, depicts an earthly paradise inhabited by the first created man and woman, where humans and animals lived in peace and harmony, living off plant life. God tasked Adam with looking after the garden on the condition that he and Eve were not to eat the fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. It was utopia. The serpent convinced Eve that eating from the forbidden fruit will bring immortality and that similar to God they (Adam and Eve) will know things that only God knows. The outcome was a human calamity, resulting in the creation of pain and hardship. The moral of the story is that we humans should not play God. Who wants to live for ever?

“Who Wants to Live Forever,” the theme song for the Highlander film stresses the importance of living for today. While eternal life might seem appealing, it loses its significance if it not meaningful and fulfilling, and most important devoid of feeling. We should not live under the shadow of technology but as humans we must maintain our intellectual superiority by ensuring that technology remains a tool to be exploited for the good of humanity.
